chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

First impressions last. This rule, however, holds no water in the face of curiosity. Phainon learns this lesson the hard way.

“That’s the thing!” Phainon exclaims, wincing when he feels the left side of his face sting phenomenally that it almost goes numb. “I had no clue this entire time!”

Castorice passes him another roll of bandages, sliding it across the table. Phainon catches it with half of his usual finesse considering that the bones of his left arm are currently working far beyond their limits—feeling broken beyond repair while his right arm is stuck in a cast.

“I’m not well-versed in the traditions of Castrum Kremnos,” Castorice began, shifting uncomfortably, contemplating the right words to say. “But I do believe that your best course of action is to apologize.”

Phainon sighs. Winces again because, right, his ribs are also broken. Why he’s still alive is genuinely a mystery. Or perhaps it’s all thanks to the golden blood running through his veins that makes him capable of surviving death-defying situations.

“I would have done that,” Phainon replies, trying to keep his tone in check. It would do him no good to vent his frustrations out on someone who’s only trying to help. “But the timeframe was a bit tight, you see. Considering that before I could even get the chance to tearfully grovel on my knees and ask for forgiveness, he already had me thrown off the balcony.”

He, as in referring to a certain blonde Kremnoan prince who’s currently posing as a threat to Phainon’s life.

His wounds throb at the thought of what transpired this morning. Even if the healers have done their job and the golden waters from the Heroes’ Baths have miraculous effects, the pain from his injuries are far from just being purely physical.

The door opens and in comes Tribbie carrying a tray bigger than her body, stacked full with vials, bottles, towels, and more rolls of bandages. Phainon watches her struggle to place the tray on top of the table with a heavy sense of guilt in his gut.

Lady Tribios is essential to Okhema, and here is Phainon reducing her forms to be his mere personal nurse. Thankfully, Castorice steps in to assist Tribbie with the tray, careful to maintain a certain distance.

“Thank you, Cas,” Tribbie says with a smile. She pulls out a stool from underneath the table before stepping on it. “How are you feeling, Snowy?”

“Like I just got run over by a bunch of dromases carrying sacks of wheat,” Phainon answers drily. “Other than that, I feel perfectly fine.”

“If you can manage to make jokes, we suppose that the healing bath Agy arranged for you helped tremendously,” Tribbie notes as she pours a slodgy green liquid into a cup. Horrifyingly, she hands it over to Phainon. “Drink up, Snowy. This will help you heal faster.”

Phainon stares at the cup in his hand, filled to the brim with—Oh, Kephale. The liquid is hissing and bubbling. It looks more alive than Phainon is at the moment.

Do I really have to drink this? “It stinks.”

“We fully expected you to ask if you’re supposed to drink that before reasoning your way out,” Tribbie says teasingly, capable of reading Phainon like an open book. “Drink it and your bones will be back to normal by the Curtain-Fall Hour, good as new.”

Phainon sighs, closes his eyes and stops breathing before bringing the rim of the cup to his lips, downing the contents in one painful gulp. Goosebumps erupt all over his skin as he slams the cup onto the table indignantly with his broken left arm.

“Did Phagousa Themself put a curse in that?” he asks, glaring at the cup like it had just offended him thrice more.

The aftertaste in his mouth feels as if something had crawled in it, died, and has now started decomposing.

“Just some herbs and a sprinkle of a dromas’ fecal matter,” Tribbie replies.

Phainon thinks his injuries must have affected his hearing because there’s just no way— “I’m sorry, a sprinkle of a what now?”

Tribbie grins like she’s happy Phainon even asked. “Dromases have a unique digestive system,” she explained matter-of-factly, like a sage who knows too much. “The caretakers mixed some medicinal herbs into their diet. While that’s digesting, the dromas’ gastric juices help with enhancing the herbs’ medicinal properties.”

Phainon feels very faint. More faint than when Mydei threw him off the balcony five storeys off the ground and left him for dead.

“I guess this is the comeuppance Talanton has deemed acceptable for me,” he says, unable to hide the misery in his tone.

Tribbie offers him a sympathetic smile. “We think De is really angry this time, Snowy.”

“Well. He could’ve actually just killed me, but I guess he’s not angry enough to do just that.” Phainon buries his head in his left hand whose fingers appear all crooked and grotesque, the bones within equally as affected by the fatal ordeal as the rest of his body. “Titans, what have I done?”

“Should we go find De so you can talk to him?” Tribbie offers.

Phainon shakes his head. “Thank you, Lady Tribbie. But I’m afraid there’s no need for that,” he says. “I should probably give him some space considering all that’s happened.”

That, and Phainon is more than a hundred percent sure that Mydei would not take kindly to having him within twenty pous distance.

Tribbie looked concerned. “Are you sure, Snowy? It’s no bother at all for us to do it.”

“I’m sure, Lady Tribbie. Not to mention, this is something I believe I must fix on my own.”

Castorice nods, finally joining the discussion after keeping to herself for so long. “I support this decision, Lord Phainon. Lord Mydei is, after all, your husband.”

The words echo like a death knell.

Yes, indeed. Mydeimos, the one and only crown prince of Kremnos and a fellow Chryos Heir, is Phainon’s husband for more than four months already and Phainon didn’t have a single clue. There wasn’t even a wedding ceremony—or, if there was, perhaps Zagreus had robbed Phainon of his wits and vision when it took place.

A moment of silence encompasses the room as Tribbie and Castorice let Phainon wallow in his obvious distress, or maybe it’s their way of paying their respects in advance for his eventual demise at the hands of Mydei. What great friends, Phainon is very thankful.

Castorice clears her throat after a while and Phainon allows himself a little relief for having something else to hear in place of his self-deprecating thoughts yelling at him. As an example, it goes pretty much like this: “YOU’RE AN IDIOT!”

“Forgive me, Lord Phainon, I can’t help but be curious,” Castorice began hesitantly. “How could you possibly not know that Lord Mydei has been your spouse for… four months?”

Phainon slumps in his chair, also at a loss. “To be honest, Miss Castorice, I haven’t the slightest idea,” he says morosely. “I, too, had just found out about it during today’s breakfast and now, Mydei might actually just kill me on sight.”

How much Phainon wished he’s speaking falsehoods at the moment. But alas, his mind really does come up with a blank whenever he runs through all of the established facts that are of no help in answering the essential questions.

How did he come to marry Mydei? How long should he have to wait for Mydei’s temper to cool off enough to guarantee his safety when he’s within Mydei’s impressive range of strangling distance?

Questions, questions. And no answers to the lot of them. Even fulfilling the prophecy single-handedly seemed more feasible at the moment.

Tribbie crosses her arms, an uncharacteristic frown on her face as she regards Phainon. Like this, Phainon would’ve had a hard time distinguishing Tribbie from Trianne.

“That just won’t do, Snowy. You have to think harder!” Tribbie admonishes. “What happened during the Month of Joy that made De think you’re married to him?”

Phainon worries his bottom lip, reopening a cut in the process as a ribbon of golden blood drips steadily from the slit. He licks it absentmindedly.

He married Mydei during the Month of Joy—that’s been established. By a very angry Mydei, no less. Golden eyes were set aflame and the surge of an unforgiving power coursed through the scarlet markings on his exposed skin. The only thing that was left for Mydei to do at that moment was to breathe fire.

Phainon would have loved to see that.

Regardless of the potential for some cheap entertainment, it changes nothing. Phainon still has no clue what caused this turn of events

“I don’t know.”

There were no wedding feasts during the Month of Joy as far as Phainon was concerned. He’d know if there had been one considering that the Chrysos Heirs have always gotten invitations to such occasions. But Phainon’s mailbox was devoid of any such invites.

The only remarkable memory Phainon had during this year’s Month of Joy was when that happened, and he doubts those actions had an ounce of matrimony rites in them.

If he considered the sensuous slide of his body against Mydei's in a heated embrace as they traded gasps against each other's parted lips, their limbs entangled, and sheets reduced to a debauched mess to be a wedding feast, then perhaps Phainon had indeed been married since the Month of Joy.

All things considered, the sight of Mydei laid bare and open before him did look like a feast —

“Might I suggest you start from the beginning, Lord Phainon?” Castorice says, unfortunately interrupting Phainon’s train of thought. “Perhaps it will help if you recall your encounters with Lord Mydei from the first time you met him.”

“Do I have to?” Phainon asks faintly.

Tribbie resolutely nods in agreement, also curious. “Yes, Snowy. We want all the details.”

Phainon knew he had no chance of escaping without giving these two a proper story time that could rival that of a bard’s. Given his current state, he supposes that the presence of song and dance is out of the question, not like Phainon possessed any ounce of lyrical talent anyway.

And since he can barely stand and Mydei wants nothing to do with him, Phainon thinks he has enough time to spare to recount everything.

Starting from the very beginning.

calamity season, month of mourning

10 months before the present time

Phainon pants as he rushes his way towards the Marmoreal Palace, heeding Aglaea's call.

“Make haste to the Vortex of Genesis,” she had said, barely a whisper as a golden thread had fluttered by while Phainon was busy stuffing his mouth full with moussaka at the Marmoreal Diner.

He had then forlornly abandoned his meal in favor of his duties (and out of fear because Aglaea disliked tardiness), muttering apologies to a baffled Kyros as he handed him a pouch filled with colorful stones that he’s sure are of equal worth to the food he ordered, before setting course towards the Marmoreal Palace.

Phainon already had an inkling as to what reasons require such an urgent summon.

War had broken out of Castrum Kremnos, a king was slain, and the Titan of Strife had fallen into a complete madness. The mobile nation had then been subsequently lost into the sea of fog and the continuous invasion of the Black Tide was of no help. Nikador’s Titankin run rampant all across the Abyss and the Chrysos Heirs are in dire need of unity to go against a doomed fate.

Truly, there’s never a dull moment in Amphoreus.

There are a couple of hidden portals scattered all around the Marmoreal Palace which led to the Vortex of Genesis that only the Chrysos Heirs are privy to. Phainon takes the one closest to the entrance, an unsuspecting small fountain that didn’t even spit out a single drop of water. He gently caresses its rounded edges as if coaxing it to come to life. The fountain does so, its spout immediately spurting waters mired in a golden shimmer, flooding the basin in no time at all.

Dipping a hand in, Phainon takes a deep breath before plunging head first into the portal. A second later, the echoing chatter of the Marmoreal Palace was no more, only to be replaced by a profound silence.

The Vortex of Genesis is always a sight to behold and Phainon can never seem to get enough of it ever since he’s been chosen by the prophecy and granted access within the domain.

He spots Aglaea and Tribbie in the distance conversing with… a blonde, half-dressed man in red, streaks of scarlet marring his exposed tanned skin, and glistening muscles out for display for all of Amphoreus to gawk over.

Phainon approaches the three of them hesitantly, careful not to interrupt their hushed conversation. Before he could make an announcement of his presence, however, Aglaea’s clouded gaze had already landed on him.

“Phainon, you’re here.”

Phainon stops just beside Tribbie and the guest. “My apologies for being late.” He turns to the stranger who was also looking at him, eyes of gold sharp and piercing as if sizing him up. Phainon feels a shiver run down his spine. “This is?”

“Snowy, meet De,” Tribbie says. “You know about the Kremnoan detachment that arrived during today’s Entry Hour? De was the one who led them here.”

Phainon does know of the Kremnoan detachment. Their tales of renown across Amphoreus are sung by bards, echoed in halls, and debated upon by historians. Wherever they waged war, victory was sure to follow for they are led by a mighty leader, a king with no crown.

To say that Phainon might be a fan has some semblance of truth in it.

However, despite such a glorious (and bloodstained) track record, the newly arrived tribe are still Kremnoans by blood. And it is of no secret to anyone who is learned that Okhemans and Kremnoans go together like oil and water.

The Kremnoan detachment’s arrival sparked quite the discussion amongst the citizens of Okhema whose prejudice have now come to light. It was all the talk Phainon had heard during his daily trip to the market.

“Welcome to Okhema,” Phainon says, holding his hand out for a friendly handshake. “It’s a pleasure to make your acquaintance, De.”

That came out wrong, he was supposed to introduce himself first. Titans, a mere second beneath the golden gaze of a beautiful man and Phainon is already fumbling his introduction.

Before he could right his mistakes, Phainon is interrupted by a deep voice, each syllable reverberating with a tangible power, vibrations settling into Phainon’s bones and wrapping itself around his very soul like an insistent whisper of fate.

“I am Mydeimos of Castrum Kremnos,” the man says, eyeing Phainon’s hand with an obvious disdain like he’s only seconds away from separating the offending limb from Phainon’s body before throwing it into the endless sea of stars. “I am here to respond to the call of the Chrysos Heirs after the fall of my nation. You will address me as Mydeimos, or Mydei. I would take anything else as an offense to my person, and an invitation to fight.”

Phainon blinks, utterly taken aback. He knew people of Kremnos had a certain… temper to them. But he never expected to be on the receiving end of such temper.

He withdraws his hand awkwardly. It was evident that Mydei wasn’t about to take it anytime soon after his unintended slight. To salvage his dignity, Phainon hides his discomfort with a smile.

“My apologies for offending you, Mydei. Believe me, it was not my intention,” Phainon says, getting an aggrieved scoff in return. “I am Phainon of Aedes Elysiae. You can call me Phainon, or anything really.”

Mydei raises an eyebrow. “I’ve heard of you. You’re that great hero of Okhema who saves everyone from calamity,” he drawls out, eyes glinting with something that Phainon couldn’t quite put a name on. “The Deliverer.”

Phainon laughs sheepishly, very much uncomfortable. “Ah, well—”

“But in all my travels across the land, I have not heard of a place called Aedes Elysiae,” Mydei interrupts. His gaze is searing, as if carefully observing Phainon for any cracks in the facade.

Phainon makes sure there is none. Before he could even reply with an answer, one that he has spoken of countless times before to anyone who had the will to point out his questionable origins, Aglaea decides to put an end to the tense exchange with a slight cough.

“Phainon, now that you and Mydei are acquainted, why don’t you show him around the holy city while I have his lodgings prepared?”

Aglaea might just as well send Phainon to his death.

“I care not for such,” Mydei says, crossing his arms petulantly. “I will stay with my men.”

“Rest assured, your men will be seen to and will be provided places to call their own during their stay here in Okhema,” Aglaea replies smoothly. “As a Chrysos Heir yourself, it would be suitable for you to stay somewhere more appropriate for your standing.”

Mydei frowns at this, looking poised to argue. In the end, he seemed to decide against it and Phainon can’t help but think that perhaps Mydei had already subjected himself to Aglaea’s golden threads and had thus formed an agreement with her prior.

“Fine,” Mydei acquiesces before turning his glare towards Phainon’s direction. “Lead the way, Deliverer.”

Phainon smiles stiffly. He did say that Mydei could call him anything, but he didn’t expect the other to settle for such a nickname.

“This way, then.”

He tours Mydei around the vast city of Okhema, starting from the different sections of the Marmoreal Palace, passing through all the popular landmarks, before finally ending up at the Marmoreal Market.

“You can find basically everything you need in this place,” Phainon says, voice a bit louder to go above the noisy chatter of citizens browsing through shops. “There’s food, clothing, relics, scrolls, and even weapons.”

As he said these, he gestures at their respective stalls. Mydei follows, surprisingly obedient as Phainon leads him to be introduced to the vendors and a couple of patrons lingering in the area.

Their unsettled gazes do not go unnoticed by Phainon, and perhaps Mydei as well, considering that Kremnoans are not exactly a common sight in the holy city.

Even if Mydei did not seem to be bothered by this at all, Phainon takes it up to himself to be uncomfortable in place of the other, leading Mydei somewhere else where the heavy air of prejudice is absent.

“This is Chartonus,” Phainon tells Mydei as they arrive at the smithy. “He is the best blacksmith around these parts. Perhaps even in all of the land, if I do say so myself.”

Mydei looks up and nods lightly at the Mountain Dweller who had stopped in the middle of bevelling the edges of what looks to be the makings of a steel sword.

“Chartonus, this is Mydei,” Phainon introduces. “He is a Chrysos Heir from Kremnos.”

“Of Crown Prince Mydeimos, you speak of, Phainon?” Chartonus asks, his attention darting between Phainon and Mydei.

“In the flesh!” Phainon exclaims, his enthusiasm too pronounced to appear genuine.

He still can’t believe that this ill-tempered man is actually royalty. The princes he’s read about in Cyrene’s storybooks were both chivalrous and kind. At some point, Phainon even dreamed of becoming one.

The person beside him, however—

“A prince without a nation is simply a man,” Mydei says curtly. “There is no need to address me as such.”

Chartonus nods, it is fortunate that Mountain Dwellers are capable of reading the room. The tension Mydei exudes is enough to make even Phainon uneasy.

“Understood,” Chartonus says. “Esteemed Heirs, what do you need?”

“Just here to show Mydei around,” Phainon answers with a strained smile, eager for a change of topic. “Mydei, if you ever find yourself in need of a weapon fixed or forged, Chartonus is your guy.”

Mydei merely hums, eyes fixed absentmindedly on the blade atop the anvil. There’s a certain distant look in his eyes that reflected the flickering flames of the furnace. He looks almost sad, the sight of the blade perhaps invoking a deep sense of melancholy.

Before Phainon could decipher such a strange expression, it’s already disappeared the moment that Mydei turns his attention back to him.

“Any other interesting places I should see, Deliverer?” Mydei inquires with the enthusiasm of a grain of sand.

Phainon grins. “Lots.” He looks over to Chartonus. “We won’t take up too much of your time now, Chartonus. I’ll drop by when I have the chance, yeah?”

Chartonus nods in agreement. “Always welcome, here you are, Phainon. To serve the Chrysos Heirs, it is an honor.”

Phainon then leads Mydei towards the spot where they could get a good view of the World-Bearing Titan. Kephale and Their Dawn Device remains as imposing as the first time Phainon saw it.

“So, there’s truth in the words of an Okheman after all. Kephale does look magnificent up close,” Mydei notes.

To someone with an unobservant ear and a predisposed judgement, the tone in which Mydei conveys the compliment might sound a tad bit sarcastic, enough to warrant the offense of the devout believers that flock around Kephale Plaza. But Phainon thinks Mydei is genuinely impressed despite the lack of effort to show it like a normal person.

“I share your sentiment,” Phainon says with a smile that comes easy for once. “Would you like to take a picture?”

A sharp glare from Mydei is all the answer he needed.

As they spend the day roaming more stalls, it doesn’t take long for Phainon to realize that Mydei is not much of a talker, more of a ‘grunt and glare’ kind of guy paired with ‘crossing my arms so I can appear aloof and intimidating.’ Not to mention, when he speaks, his words lack the sweetness of sugar, coming out bitter and jagged. Tactless and direct.

More often than not, Mydei’s disposition do not adhere to the tastes of the Okheman born and raised citizens, conversations ending up either strained or on the brink of an argument. Phainon diffuses the situation fast enough to the best of his ability—which is just him leading Mydei away to have him face the wall in a secluded spot.

“I don’t know how you lived your life in Kremnos, but the citizens of Okhema have a sensitive nature,” Phainon admonishes. Gently, of course, lest Mydei becomes offended and sees it fit to engage him in a duel in the middle of a busy market. “Please, watch what you say next time.”

Mydei rolls his eyes, still facing the wall with his arms crossed. “I lived most of my life away from Kremnos,” is all he says.

Phainon is at a loss, confused as to what the statement entailed. Nevertheless, there’s an issue here that needs to be addressed. “Even if that’s the case, you can’t just randomly insult a citizen for, what, preferring Okheman baklava over… Kremnoan baklava?”

Now that Phainon says it out loud, it sounds incredibly ridiculous. More ridiculous is the fact that Mydei does seem thoroughly aggrieved over this matter.

“My insults are never random for they are always deliberately given,” Mydei argues with a scoff, nose turned up and everything. Phainon is exhausted. “And what I said to that Okheman was far from an insult, Deliverer. I was merely conveying my opinion. If he finds fault in my words, then that’s his problem.”

Phainon gives up. “Fine, alright. You’re lucky I’m here or else everyone and their mother might just rally together and throw you off a cliff.”

Mydei snorts. “They can try. Death is not a foreign concept.”

There’s something in the nonchalant way Mydei said it that makes Phainon frown, a tinge of curiosity as to why Mydei views death as such. Familiar and within reach.

If Phainon asks, it would be too personal. He and Mydei are the furthest from being friends at the moment. He could even dub them as strangers still, regardless if they’ve already spent the majority of their day together.

Acceptance is best done early on. Phainon had already made peace with the fact that he and Mydei would never get along. They are too different regardless if their paths are made to be intertwined by the prophecy. It would be Phainon’s first failure to make friends, but it certainly won’t be the last.

Mydei turns around, deeming his time-out to have already run its course. Gold eyes scour the market as if looking for something.

“Do you know a place where I could procure some fresh fruits, Deliverer?”

Phainon raises an eyebrow. It was not what he expected to hear. He thought perhaps Mydei would ask him for some dining recommendations, or even inquire if the Kremnoan relics sold in the market are authentic.

Still, Phainon nods. “You can never go wrong with Demetria’s fruit stand,” he says, leading Mydei to the right direction.

After a round of introductions and pleasantries with Demetria, which thankfully did not result in Phainon trying to rein in Mydei’s filterless mouth, Phainon watches as Mydei places a bag filled with gold upon Talanton’s Scale, balancing it out with the worth of a sack of fresh pomegranates, emptying the stock.

“Would you like to sample the other fruits I have for sale, Lord Mydei?” Demetria asks with a smile, no doubt she already developed a soft spot for a new avid patron of her store. “The figs were freshly harvested just this morning, sweet and juicy. I’ll give you three minae's worth of them, free of charge.”

Mydei shakes his head. “Thank you for the offer, but I’m afraid I would have to decline for now. I'm in a hurry to cross off all the items on my list and I don't think I'll have enough time to sample your produce in its peak condition.”

So he can be civil, Phainon thinks amusedly. Maybe the elderly are an exception to Mydei’s callous attitude. Phainon finds this discovery strangely endearing. And then Mydei’s words properly register in his head.

“You have a shopping list?” Phainon asks, unable to hide the surprise in his voice. “Why didn’t you say so earlier?”

Mydei gives him an unimpressed look. “You kept going on and on about this and that, dragging me here and there until my arm was about to fall off. You think I had such a chance to do so?”

“Reducing my shop recommendations into mere ‘this and that’ saddens me deeply,” Phainon chides, feigning offense. “Mydei, were you simply allowing my words to enter in one ear and out the other?”

“Perhaps.”

Phainon couldn't believe this man. He shakes his head in resignation before turning to Demetria. “Ma’am, can I take those fresh figs on his behalf if that’s okay?”

Demetria nods enthusiastically. “But of course!” She then proceeds to get a bag to store the fruits in before handing it to Phainon. “Do let me know what you think!”

“Certainly, ma’am.” He turns his attention back to Mydei whose impatience seeps through every wrinkle of the frown gracing his fine face. “Mydei, your youth would be wasted if you’re so adamant to look twice your age.”

Mydei does not indulge him with a retort. Instead, he says, “Direct me to a place where I would be able to purchase some firewood, barrels of the finest quality to store juice, hay, and incense. And I need a cart to help me carry all those things.”

Phainon raises an eyebrow. “Are you preparing a feast with no food and only drinks?”

“There are no feasts to be held during the Month of Mourning, idiot Deliverer,” Mydei chastises. “Or does the holy city not follow such a tradition?”

To say that Phainon simply forgot about this fact would be akin to admitting defeat. “I was merely assuming that the Kremnoans were the ones who would find time to celebrate during such a month, but it seems that your nation and Okhema can find a common ground when it comes to matters of life and death.”

Mydei huffs. “Kremnos and Okhema can never find a common ground on anything. It would do you well to remember this fact, Deliverer.”

“No need to be so negative.”

“Direct me to a place where I would be able to purchase some firewood, barrels of the finest quality to store juice, hay, and incense,” Mydei says in lieu of a reply, an impatient repetition of his words from earlier. “And I need a cart to—”

“To help you carry all those things,” Phainon finishes for him. “Yes, Your Highness. I heard your directives loud and clear the first time around.”

Mydei rolls his eyes. “I have until the Parting Hour. We’ve dawdled enough already.”

“Well, if you just told me about your list earlier—”

Mydei steps on his foot and Phainon bites back a yelp. His leather boots are of no match against Mydei’s. On Kephale’s mercy, the gold metallic footwear Mydei wears could pass off as weapons on their own, clinking against the ground as Mydei walks off like he knows the place, Phainon trailing miserably behind him.

The rest of the Action Hour passes by without much fanfare. By the final quint, Mydei is able to purchase all the items he needs, dragging a huge cart filled haphazardly to the brim, uncaring of the way the citizens of Okhema point and stare at his questionable buying habits.

“You still haven’t told me what these things are for,” Phainon says as they make their way towards a Dromas Post, a hand supporting a bundle of hay that looked seconds away from toppling over.

“The war in Kremnos waged for weeks. The detachment has lost a lot of people during the carnage,” Mydei replies. “Once the old king was felled, Kremnos was already on the brink of collapse, and Nikador’s Titankin were swarming like locusts. I had to get my people out of there.”

Phainon furrows his eyebrows. “The old king? Don’t you mean—”

“My father, yes.” He doesn’t look at Phainon when he says the next words. “It was my spear that drove straight through his heart that ultimately killed him. It was his death that signified the end of the battle at Kremnos.”

Again, it would be too personal to inquire as to what had led to such a drastic turn of events. Based on Mydei’s rigid countenance and the edge in his voice, Phainon could deduce as much that Mydei would rather not talk about the matter either.

“Due to our hasty retreat, we didn’t have the time to hold a proper Rite of Parting for the deceased,” Mydei continues, an answer to Phainon’s initial question that Phainon forgot he even asked.

Perhaps it would have been better if he kept his mouth shut. “I’m sorry.”

Mydei raises an eyebrow at him. “What for? My soldiers died with honor. They fought for a cause they believed in and their deaths had not been a waste.”

He pauses, as if his thoughts had interrupted him, and Phainon is able to witness that look in his face again—a grief so profound that it makes even Phainon mourn for those people he never even met.

“Everyone lost someone important to them during the war,” Mydei continues resolutely. “It is only right to properly commemorate the souls of the departed, for both the dead and the living to be at ease.”

They arrive at the Dromas Post, thankfully there’s no line of people awaiting their turn for a ride. Phainon rings the bell for Mydei, somehow desperate to make himself useful to wash away the guilt of bringing up such a topic.

“Will you be needing a priest?” Phainon asks. “I just happen to know someone—”

“No,” Mydei answers, effectively cutting him off. “I don’t need Okheman blood soiling the traditions of Kremnos.”

That’s a shame, Phainon thinks, helplessly looking down at the ground as he tries to come up with another way to assist, only for his mind to end up as blank as the day he was born for he doesn’t even have the slightest idea on how Kremnoans conduct funerals.

A heavy sigh interrupts Phainon’s train of thought. He looks up and sees Mydei sporting a conflicted expression.

“You look like a kicked chimera.”

Phainon’s frown deepens. “Why would anyone kick a chimera? They’re adorable.”

“Exactly.”

It would take days to decipher Mydei’s one-liners. Phainon knows how to choose his battles and gives this one up when he sees a dromas approach. It’s time for him to take his leave for the Parting Hour is upon them.

He clasps his hands together, ignoring how sweaty his palms had gotten. “If there’s anything else I can help you with, Mydei, you already have my contact in your teleslate.”

“Spoken like a true Deliverer,” Mydei muses. “While I appreciate your concern for this matter, there truly is nothing else to be done.”

Phainon feels his smile falter for a little bit. It would be pathetic to push his luck a third time considering how adamant Mydei is to make it known that he is not needed.

“Right.” Phainon nods, agreeing to nothing in particular. “I’ll, uh, take my leave now.”

He turns around without waiting for Mydei to bid his goodbye. He doubts Mydei would even do such a thing in the first place given his open hostility towards Phainon. Well, it’s not like Phainon didn’t try his best in befriending the difficult crown prince of Kremnos—

“Deliverer.”

Phainon turns his head back so quickly that he thinks he might've stretched a muscle in the process. “Yes?”

Mydei hesitates, an uncharacteristic look that Phainon didn’t expect he’d be able to witness this early on in their acquaintance.

“If you wish to witness the rites with my tribe, you’re free to do so,” Mydei says. Even if he seemed like he’s at odds with himself for saying such words, he makes no move to take it back. “Consider it as my thanks for helping me out today.”

Phainon would like to reiterate that a show of thanks is unnecessary. Touring Mydei around Okhema is more of an honor than a bother, regardless if Mydei is admittedly not the easiest person to be around and neither is he the most enthusiastic conversation partner Phainon has had the pleasure of talking to.

However, Mydei's invitation somewhat causes Phainon to retract most of his initial thoughts. Perhaps the crown prince isn't so unsociable after all.

He can't believe this, a mere gesture of cordiality from Mydei has him thinking that the world is indeed beautiful despite the impending doom. The rainbows that swirled around Okhema is such a fascinating sight, the roar of the dromases livening up the atmosphere, the chirping of birds, the rustle of leaves, the sway of every blade of grass—

“Yes. I’ll be there.”

Mydei rolls his eyes at the blatant show of enthusiasm. “No need to look so happy. You can come on one condition.”

Phainon is all ears. “Anything.”

“You’re not to bring anybody else.”

The funeral rites are held later that day during the Curtain-Fall Hour in the middle of a secluded clearing in the forest, some ways away from the Marmoreal Palace. The trees are tall and their trunks are thick, the foliage abundant enough to shroud the area in an almost complete darkness despite the presence of Kephale’s Dawn.

Torches lit up the place and the warriors of the Kremnoan detachment all wore their full battle regalia, skin streaked with red and gold paint as they chatted minimally amongst themselves. If Phainon didn’t know any better, he’d think the tribe is planning a full-fledged siege against Okhema.

When the detachment notices Phainon’s presence, they stop and stare. His garb of blue and white does not exactly fit with the theme so perhaps he does stick out like a sore thumb.

To try and dissipate the awkwardness in the air, Phainon waves his hand and smiles at a group of Kremnoan warriors unsubtly eyeing him up and down in the same manner that Aglaea does whenever Phainon decides that he’s in charge of his outfit for the day.

The Kremnoans don’t return his smile, nor do they bother to wave back, simply baffled by Phainon’s attendance. Phainon feels sweat beginning to trickle at the back of his neck. It’s not that he feels unwelcome…

No, he definitely feels unwelcome. Like he’s intruding—

“You’ve come.”

Phainon nearly jumps out of his skin. Turning around, he comes face to face with none other than Mydei. Gold streaks marred his solemn face as he offers Phainon a chalice filled with crimson liquid.

Phainon takes it with a mutter of thanks before throwing a quick glance at the group of warriors, only to find that they’ve engaged themselves in conversation once more.

“Is something wrong, Deliverer?”

Phainon turns his attention back to Mydei, willing out a smile. “Everything’s fine. It’s just…” He inspects the contents of his chalice, gently swirling the liquid within. He recalls a distant legend he’s read in a scroll once and can’t help but ask, “Is it true that Kremnoans sustain their bodies with fresh blood?”

Mydei seemed thoroughly amused by this, golden eyes glinting from the dim lighting of the clearing. “Why don’t you find out for yourself?” he says, nodding at the cup as a way of urging Phainon to take a sip.

The warning bells ring within Phainon’s mind causing him to have a brief moment of regret for even accepting Mydei’s invite. He shakes it off for cowardice is not something befitting of a hero.

Blatantly ignoring Mydei’s goading gaze, Phainon gingerly brings the rim of the chalice to his lips, tipping his head back and bracing himself for the coppery taste of blood.

Only, it doesn’t come.

A sweet, almost syrupy taste floods his tongue. Fruity, a bit of tartness, a creamy texture… Phainon downs the rest of it, pleasantly surprised by this turn of events and at the same time, baffled at the stark contrast of reality from his expectations.

Once the chalice has been emptied of its contents, Phainon is left wanting more. He licks the corners of his lips to savor the remaining taste of heaven, one that’s even akin to ambrosia. He looks up and finds Mydei staring, leaving him to belatedly realize his shamelessness for downing a drink so hurriedly.

Perhaps it’s because of the poor lighting in the clearing that Phainon could see a hint of a smile gracing Mydei’s lips.

“Did the ‘blood’ taste that good for you to finish the whole drink before the ceremony has even begun?” Mydei snickers.

Phainon goes along with the jest, throwing Mydei a smile of his own. “I have to admit that it does.” He inspects his empty cup. “Pomegranate juice and milk?”

Mydei crosses his arms defensively, an eyebrow raised. “Do you have a problem with that? Milk is usually not a part of the recipe. If you prefer its traditional version, you can ask Idaeus over there for a pour.”

Phainon marvels at Mydei’s talent for assuming things. It gives him the urge to learn more about the ways Mydei’s profound mind works and how he manages to come up with conclusions that are not even supposed to be there.

“I quite like this combination, actually,” Phainon admits earnestly despite tasting the drink for the first time in his life. “Do you have any more of where that came from?”

Mydei’s eyes widened for a fraction, it only takes him a split second to school his expression back to normal which seemingly conveys something along the lines of a grumpy ‘you better not be trifling with me’ look.

“Give me a moment,” is his response, leading Phainon to a table where a barrel is placed. Beside it, there’s a pitcher of milk.

Phainon watches quietly as Mydei turns the knob of the spout, dark crimson liquid pouring out until the cup has been filled midway. Mydei then proceeds to add the milk, swirling the liquid gently with a teaspoon as he does so.

The action is mesmerizing. How could such formidable hands enclosed in fearsome golden gauntlets be capable of doing something so reposeful? So much so that Phainon finds himself having trouble looking away.

Mydei hands him his cup. “I do hope you won’t finish it in one sip this time, Deliverer,” he chastises without much heat. More of a tease, if anything. “It is meant to be drunk with the rest of us after dousing an amount on the shields of the deceased.”

The unusualness of such an action does not escape Phainon's confused mind. “Shields?”

“Yes,” Mydei answers with a nod, surprisingly patient to indulge Phainon with his questions that might’ve sounded quite foolish. “In Kremnos, when an army returns with shields bathed in blood, it is seen as a symbol of triumph—the shields have fulfilled their purpose, and so did the warriors. It is the reason why we douse the shields of the deceased with pomegranate juice during the Kremnoan Rite of Parting. A symbol of a triumphant return despite death.”

Phainon looks over at the crowd of Kremnoan warriors, somber as they spoke amongst themselves. The atmosphere is far from being triumphant.

“I see,” he says absentmindedly, eyeing the liquid in his cup.

In the face of death, Phainon can’t help but feel the helpless doubt gnaw at his gut incessantly. Like a knife constantly twisting and stabbing, reopening wounds and making them worse. How could the people of Kremnos view death alongside triumph like the two contrasting concepts were nothing but old friends?

He jolts when a hand suddenly clamps on his shoulder, the action catching Phainon off-guard that he almost spills his drink. He turns to Mydei who seemed amused for some reason.

“No need to think too deeply of it, Deliverer,” Mydei tells him with a light squeeze on Phainon’s shoulder, a grounding gesture. He withdraws his hand afterwards with no intent of lingering. “We Kremnoans handle death differently. If this tradition leaves you unsettled, then feel free to take your leave. I won’t hold it against you.”

Phainon attempts a laugh. “How could pouring pomegranate juice over the shields of deceased warriors leave me unsettled? If anything, I find it quite interesting.”

“Is that so?”

“Well, I admit I do feel somewhat forlorn.” Phainon lightly swirls his cup. “To spill such a delicious drink that tastes much like ambrosia, it makes me think that I’m not cut out to participate in the rites at all.”

Mydei huffs. “I didn’t think you’d be capable of offending three Titans in a single breath, Deliverer. Phagousa, Nikador, and perhaps even Thanatos. Not to mention, my kingdom as well who have observed this tradition since the late days of Era Bellica.”

“If it allows me to express my sincerest compliments to the maker of this drink, then I consider the offense of the Titans as a worthy consequence.”

It was supposed to be in jest and Phainon was just about to apologize for his impropriety. But seeing Mydei’s fair face color in the slightest tinge of pink has caused his tongue to go still, utterly lost for words.

A tense silence befalls them. Phainon wishes he’d simply kept his sentiments to himself. He wonders what Mydei is thinking now who seemed insistent to avoid eye contact.

“The ceremony will commence soon,” Mydei eventually says, clearing his throat. He looked poised to leave. “I shall be on my way.”

Phainon doesn’t bother chasing after Mydei this time, choosing to join a group of warriors who seemed agreeable to have a non-Kremnoan amongst them. Most of them held two to three shields in both arms. Phainon gratefully accepts one from a warrior, allowing himself to listen in to their chatter as he awaits the ceremony to start.

The rites consisted of a huge burning stake, with warriors tossing a variety of items into the flames—a broken sword, a cloak, a satchel, a quill, a teleslate, and many more. There seems to be no pattern to it. Phainon can deduce as much that these items must’ve belonged to their dead comrades, all of whom the tribe wishes to commemorate.

Once all the items were burned to ash, Mydei makes his way in the middle. Even without uttering a single word, Mydei commands the undivided attention of everyone as easy as it is to breathe. Even Phainon seems to be caught in a trance himself.

Perhaps it is Mydei’s status as royalty that makes him appear regal without so much as an effort. Or the way he conducts himself with pride that amplifies his worth. Even now, the way he spoke lacked tawdry pleasantries that run shallow, only choosing to convey words that hold weight.

“There is no grief for parting in Kremnos, only the promise of glory,” Mydei begins, his own chalice in hand as his deep voice echoes throughout the clearing.

Everyone maintains the silence, listening with rapt attention. Phainon awaits the next words with bated breath.

Mydei continues, “As the spirits of our fellows traverse the River of Souls, their names shall forever be etched in the annals of history. Their victory will undoubtedly be spoken of, transcending generations—never forgotten.” He raises his chalice up high. “My fellows, our time of glory has yet to come. But for now, we shall spill this blood and drink to those who have already achieved it.”

The Kremnoan warriors erupt into cries and roars, raising their chalices in a show of esprit de corps, no room for melancholy and regrets for death is seen as an honor.

The splash of crimson liquid against the surface of battered shields follow suit, mimicking the sight of shields bathed in blood as Mydei had explained beforehand. Phainon douses a relative amount of his drink onto the scratched surface, his reflection a blurry sight.

Before he could take a sip from his cup, his eyes meet that of Mydei’s from afar. Mydei gives him a slight nod of acknowledgement before partaking in his own drink, gaze akin to that of molten gold. Sharp like a lion’s, searing its way into Phainon’s mind until it’s forever etched into his memory.

Mydei shines like a flaming beacon for his people, even brighter than the burning stake behind him. His kin gazes at their prince with hope for the future, entrusting their lives to him, willing to lay them down when necessary.

It hasn’t even been a day since Phainon had met the crown prince of Castrum Kremnos. And yet, there’s a strong pull, an unavoidable urge to get closer.

Even if he’d end up likened to a moth lured by the ever so tempting flame.

Only a true Kremnoan is worthy of bearing witness and participating in said rite; one must embody the virtues of the Titan of Strife in order to bid farewell to the glorious souls of one's kin.

Exceptions include...

...a spouse or a significant other that is of non-Kremnoan descent may participate in the ritual provided that they already exemplify the appropriate virtues to be chosen by a true Kremnoan... apart from this, it is absolute to decline the presence of outsiders...

chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Phainon is no stranger to establishing connections with others. Nevertheless, it still takes him by surprise when he successfully manages to form one with the unlikeliest of fellows.

calamity season, month of fortune

9 months before the present time

· · ─ ·𖥸· ─ · ·

The Kremnos Festival was my chance to prove my worth. His Majesty, King Eurypon is as mighty as the tales depict him to be. I believe I have met my true match. He asked me to be his queen after our duel, one that he insisted concluded in a draw.

My whole life, I saw him as a figure to be conquered. I never thought Mnestia’s influence would come to play. To find one’s equal—there’s something inherently romantic to it even if there is no place for Romance in a kingdom who glorifies Strife.

— an entry from Her Majesty, the late Queen Gorgo’s diary, dated ███

· · ─ · ─ · ·

Cards fly into the air as Mydei stands up from his seat and flips the table with fiery contempt. It all happened in a mere blink of an eye, barely a second after Phainon proclaimed his victory in their game of koum-kan.

Phainon watches as Mydei finishes the job—slamming a foot down on the side of the toppled table, splitting it in half. It’s a clean cut, more impressive to witness than the performance of a random busker on the streets of Okhema.

“Mydei, this table is not ours to play havoc with,” Phainon says lightly, making no move to leave his chair. “We’re going to have to pay for this—”

Mydei lunges towards him, aiming for a quick jab to Phainon’s face before swiftly following it up with a low kick aimed at his foot. Phainon dodges on instinct, rolling out of his seat and causing both of Mydei’s hits to miss him by a fraction.

Phainon’s chair did not survive the ordeal, three of its legs broken and the backrest cleanly separated, skidding some ways away from the seat itself.

Panicked yells erupt from the market at the sudden display of violence. Some citizens chose to flee and board up their stalls while others stayed to watch.

“Dear Mydeimos, I doubt such a reaction is needed for a mere silly little game of cards,” Phainon says, attempting to pat away the dust in his clothes.

Mydei’s scowl darkens, eyes narrowed into slits that spell danger. “You cheated.”

“It’s called strategy,” Phainon retorts.

It was the wrong thing to say. Mydei lunges a second time, tackling Phainon by the neck as they tumbled onto the ground. Phainon attempts to gain the upper hand only for Mydei to land a knee into his chest, knocking the air out of his lungs.

Mydei settles on top of him, bearing down on Phainon with gritted teeth. “You chose not to discard the ace. Why?”

Phainon smiles despite the situation, finding it very hard to breathe. The reason for it is surprisingly not because Mydei is currently restricting his airflow.

“If I did such a thing, it would have been your victory,” Phainon replies, voice strained as he tries not to get lost into the molten gold of Mydei’s eyes, sharper than before in his rage.

Mydei tightens his grip on Phainon’s neck. “You had no need for it. You chose not to meld by discarding that queen instead of the ace.”

Phainon relishes the cool metal of Mydei’s gauntlets beneath his palm, holding onto Mydei’s wrist to ground himself. “In the end, it worked in my favor, didn’t it?”

As Mydei registers his words, Phainon chooses this moment to flip them over, pinning Mydei to the ground, Phainon’s chest pressed on his back.

Mydei thrashes in his hold with a growl, hands akin to deadly talons as it tries to swipe at anything of Phainon he could reach behind him. Phainon takes hold of both his wrists, locking them in place upon Mydei’s back.

“You play with cheap tricks,” Mydei says coolly, his attempts to escape have stopped. Or perhaps it’s to subject Phainon to a false sense of security.

Phainon aims to relish this brief show of pliantness, leaning close, allowing his breath to ghost over the shell of Mydei’s ear. “I fail to see how my tactfulness could be considered as cheap tricks.”

He gets a sharp glare in return, Mydei eyeing him vindictively from the side. If Phainon lets his hold on the other falter, he might not survive the retaliation Mydei would unleash upon him.

“Now that I think about it,” Phainon continues, doubling down and playing with risks out of curiosity. He wonders how the honorable Mydeimos would react when his patience is being pushed to the brink. “Your play mostly consisted of you melding your cards on the table, purely offensive in nature with no room for contingencies.”

“You meld when you have the hand for it,” Mydei snaps back. “Isn’t that part of the rules you spoke of when you challenged me to partake in your game?”

“Melding is optional, Mydei,” Phainon corrects, biting back a laugh when he sees something snap within Mydei—his patience or sanity, Phainon wonders which one. “Now that you know, you can use that to your advantage in our next round.”

Mydei’s eyes flash, muscles tensed beneath Phainon’s hold. “You withheld this information from me.”

“Not deliberately,” Phainon simpers. “I simply must have forgotten.”

At a blatant show of strength, Mydei contorts his body in an attempt to slip free, successfully managing to loosen Phainon’s hold on his arms. The brief moment allows for just enough window of time for Mydei to wrench himself away, hands finding purchase on the ground, the sharp fingertips of his gauntlets drawing angry lines. With a sudden twist, he elbows Phainon right on the sternum before rolling away to regain his footing.

As Phainon scrambles, Mydei takes this chance to land a kick squarely at the side of the his face, hard enough for him to see stars. But before anything could fully register, Mydei was on top of him again.

And Phainon finds it hard to breathe. Again.

Kephale’s Dawn shines magnificently behind Mydei, painting him in an almost haloed light, holy despite the presence of brute strength. It’s hard to decide which of those two things Phainon prefers to see more of.

He tastes copper in his tongue and spits to the side, eyes never leaving Mydei’s as he does so. He grins, gold staining his teeth. The man above him truly doesn’t know what it means to hold back.

“My apologies for winning?”

Mydei roughly grabs his chin, pinning Phainon’s head further into the ground. “A foul opponent who still indulges in his spoils,” he snarls. “How low can you go?”

“It’s just a game, Mydei,” Phainon offers, an attempt to diffuse the situation.

“My issue lies with you not playing fair,” Mydei tells him, his grip on Phainon’s chin tightening. Phainon feels the sharp fingertips of the gauntlet starting to dig into his skin. “You should have informed me of all the rules beforehand.”

Phainon sighs. This is what his curiosity has led him to. Rest assured, it will be the last time he’ll provoke the crown prince of Kremnos. No promises, however.

“Alright. I sincerely apologize,” Phainon says, attempting to sound sincere, yielding out of necessity. “Now, enough of this. People are staring.”

In his periphery, he could already see a crowd of people watching the exchange within a safe distance with their teleslates out, capturing the scene in real time. There’s no doubt that this event would be talked about for a week.

He can already predict the articles that would circulate around the holy city: Two Chrysos Heirs unable to get along. Will this spell disaster for Okhema?

A bit exaggerated, but knowing the Verax Leos’ creativity, his exaggeration might pale in comparison to the actual thing.

Thankfully, Mydei does peel himself away. Phainon only manages to sit up followed by a single deep inhale to regain his bearings before the sharp end of a red crystal is directed at his throat. He looks up at Mydei questioningly.

“I challenge you to a fight to settle our differences,” Mydei declares.

Phainon winces, leaning away from the range of the crystal’s sharp tip just in case Mydei does stab him accidentally. “I’m not fond of destroying public property,” he reasons to someone he is well aware isn’t capable of being reasoned with at the moment. “Accepting would mean that such an occurrence is unavoidable.”

Mydei seems to consider his words, lowering the red crystal. Phainon thinks that perhaps he had thought wrong of Mydei’s capabilities for a civil discussion in the presence of certain grievances.

Just as Phainon concludes he’s managed to quell what was about to become a city-wide disaster, the red crystal in Mydei’s hand grows thrice in size, almost as tall as his height. Before Phainon could ask, Mydei directs his attention towards one of the city’s stone walls, leaning back and raising the red crystal with an intent to throw—

In a split second, a resounding boom echoes throughout the market. What had been a flawless ivory brick wall has now been impaled by Mydei’s red crystal, cracks continuing to form from where the crystal was lodged so deeply that Phainon wonders just how much force Mydei used during the throw.

The wall crumbles and the crowd starts to panic after being stunned into silence. This time, even the gossip mongers knew that staying for the show was not worth it if they wanted to preserve their lives.

Phainon stares at the wall in shock. He turns to Mydei who looks rather pleased with himself despite the strife he had just caused.

“There,” Mydei muses, eyeing his work one last time before meeting Phainon’s gaze. “Now the inevitable you’re worried about is done.”

Phainon huffs in disbelief. It seems that someone is in dire need to be put in their place.

Extending his hand to the side, Phainon summons his greatsword. It is a welcome weight in his hand and it’s been a while since he last had it drawn while within the safety of Okhema’s borders for the threat was always coming from the outside.

Right now, there might be some semblance of truth to that.

“Destruction of public property warrants an arrest,” Phainon proclaims, readjusting his grip on his weapon before flinging it to the air, the tip of the blade just shy away from Mydei’s bare chest. “I’m going to have to bring you to justice, Your Highness.”

Mydei smirks. “I’m not opposed to that.”

How a mere tussle ends up being a full-blown fight, Phainon has no idea. As the citizens flee for cover, Phainon and Mydei utilize the Marmoreal Market as their arena, trading blows with a complete disregard to the surrounding structures.

“Someone stop them!”

“Send for Lady Aglaea!”

“My stall is ruined!”

Despite the panicked yells, the urge to stop never crosses Phainon’s mind as he drags the tip of his greatsword to the ground before launching it towards Mydei’s direction, clicking his tongue when he misses by a mere hairbreadth’s distance.

Mydei lets his amusement be known, leaping over a canopy before launching another attack —deadly sharp red crystals soaring the air, trailing after Phainon’s hasty steps with the fervent intent of subduing him.

“Tired, Deliverer?”

Phainon swipes at the red crystals with his greatsword, shielding his face from the broken shards. He turns to Mydei with a smirk of his own. “I’m just getting started.”

Mydei smiles, and Phainon is… caught off-guard.

Wow.

Kephale’s Dawn Device may shine light in all of Okhema. But right now, it is Mydei’s eyes of molten gold and a smile so brilliant that Phainon is able to exist in a world with two suns.

A red crystal soars towards him and Phainon barely manages to dodge, the whistle of air sharp and shrill against his ear as he still wraps his head around what he had just seen and what he had just thought. His heart is pounding and he hopes that it is due to the exertion and not something else that’s currently beyond reason.

The only way to get a hold of his senses is to wrap this fight up. They’ve already caused quite the mess around the market, more than Phainon could deem acceptable.

He leaps onto the canopy where Mydei is perched, the latter’s eyes glinting with a certain liveliness. Phainon comes to realize that Mydei is enjoying this. Even if the same could be said for him, he had already allowed Mydei get away with a lot.

“Enough, Mydei.”

Mydei’s smile fades, almost carrying along with it Phainon’s resolve to put an end to their ‘conflict.’ Phainon dismisses his greatsword, slivers of gold flickering as it disappears into thin air.

“You yield?” Mydei asks, arms crossed. The perplexity in his voice does not go unnoticed.

Phainon sighs. “Not necessarily.”

“Then take out your weapon and we shall conclude this dispute once and for all.”

A Kremnoan’s bull-headedness would be one of the things that would truly drive Phainon mad one day. “The market is already a mess. We’ve inconvenienced the citizens far more than what is considered as justifiable.”

“Caring about such trivialities,” Mydei scoffs with a roll of his eyes. “Truly a Deliverer in every aspect.”

Phainon frowns, taking a step forward. The canopy dips beneath his and Mydei’s combined weight. “The comfort of the citizens is not a triviality. In Okhema, we—”

A sequence of snaps was heard as the ropes that tied the canopy to its poles finally gave in, unable to hold on any longer. The canopy falls through, enclosing both Phainon and Mydei into its heavy fabric like a cocoon as they fall to the ground in a lumpy pile of white cloth.

The squabble resumes, both Phainon and Mydei clawing at each other despite the current circumstance limiting their range of motions. Phainon feels something sharp graze his cheek as the sole of his boot makes contact with something hard and solid.

Their frantic movements caused the fabric to entangle even more upon them, until it encompasses them within a tight roll with only their heads out for display, bodies glued together from chest to foot.

Their faces are merely a breadth of a finger apart as they both regain their bearings after being under the heavy fabric for so long. The lack of oxygen must have affected their minds because how in Amphoreus do you even end up in a situation such as this?

Phainon’s mind has a set of answers prepared, all of which evaporates into thin air the moment that Mydei moves against him in a futile struggle. Even if the rub of their bodies against each other is purely incidental, Phainon is grasping at loose straws just to stop himself from relishing in the sensation.

He is simply a man.

Mydei mutters a curse under his breath in a language that sounded foreign. Phainon wishes that the other would just stop moving, internally reciting prayers and hymns for strength and restraint to all the Titans—corrupted or dead, it matters not. As long as They’ll listen.

“Deliverer, are you—?”

Phainon closes his eyes. “Please. Stop moving—”

“I’m trying to get us out of here,” Mydei snaps, evidently affronted by the request.

“You’re doing a great job,” Phainon replies sarcastically, voice strained beyond belief. “Now, I’d like you to stay still.”

Mydei scoffs, puffs of air blowing against the sweaty skin of Phainon’s neck as he continues to squirm most likely out of spite. “If you didn’t come up on the canopy with me, this wouldn’t have happened.”

“Yes, yes. My fault and all.”

A brush of a hand against his thigh, dangerously close to the current wellspring of his unbearable shame causes Phainon to inhale sharply. If Mydei’s hand had been a tad bit higher, Phainon’s humiliation would be set in stone.

“Mydeimos—”

Both of them tense when they hear the slow clack of heels against the ground. The Titans must have heard Phainon’s prayers.

It is but a brief moment of reprieve. Phainon may be spared from enduring a lifetime of embarrassment due to his flawed nature of being born as a human male, the punishment for the destruction he'd caused today still remains to be a part of his fate.

In a flash, the Marmoreal Market becomes overtaken by threads of gold, making it seem as if both Phainon and Mydei are ensnared in a spider’s web, helpless prey to a predator who now casts shadows as she looms upon them.

The two Chrysos Heirs look up slowly, hesitantly, and finds Aglaea gazing down at them. Even if her face rarely shows any distinct emotions, her displeasure is made known clearly with the downturn of her lips, a frown that conveys nothing but clear disappointment.

“Heroes,” she says, voice silky smooth. Her calmness belies her displeasure. Something about the way she addressed them as such holds a certain weight, like a reminder of what he and Mydei’s purpose are. “May I inquire as to what had transpired here?”

Knowing Aglaea, she probably already knew but simply wished to hear the answers from the people involved herself. Phainon shares a look with Mydei, a mix of terror and uncertainty.

They’re so close that the scent of something inherently sweet invades Phainon’s nostrils. Despite the sweat and the dust, Mydei smells like warm pastries and the sharpness of freshly harvested pomegranates. It’s a stark contrast, one that Phainon realizes he can’t seem to get enough of.

I’m screwed.

The situation is most unfortunate. Phainon thinks he’s at a disadvantage here, especially when his mind makes the decision against his will of wanting to shoulder all the blame in favor of letting Mydei walk free from Aglaea’s wrath.

Why? Because the man is a delight to his depraved nostrils, apparently. Phainon thinks a rigorous soul-searching is overdue.

Only, before he could even open his mouth to speak, Mydei had already beaten him to it.

“It was me,” Mydei says. “I started it.”

Phainon blanches. “I— What? No! I provoked you!”

Mydei narrows his eyes at him, wordlessly telling him to go along. “Aglaea and I had an agreement that I am not to cause trouble during my stay in Okhema.”

The statement does sound believable enough. However—

“It is due to my shortcomings that I failed to apprehend you,” Phainon shoots back, adamant to take the fall. “If I was a tad bit more competent, the mess would’ve no doubt been minimal.”

Mydei doesn’t give up. As expected of a Kremnoan. “I openly disregarded the law. You don’t blame an authority for the crimes committed by a malefactor.”

“You’re not from Okhema—”

“I’ve been staying here for more than a month now.”

Phainon exhales sharply. “It took me two years to memorize all the rules and regulations of this city. A month is barely enough time.”

There’s an unreadable expression on Mydei’s face as he struggles to come up with something to snap back. Phainon thinks that he’s won, only to realize that such things matter not when Aglaea clears her throat, reminding them of her presence.

“Heroes, there is no need to argue on who is to take the blame for all this,” she says. “For it shall be the both of you who will be detained for three days in the dungeons.”

Phainon and Mydei give each other a look. They expected their punishment to come in the form of something much more gruelling.

Aglaea makes a nondescript gesture with her hand and two Garmentmakers step forward. “Help them up.”

The Garmentmakers unroll the fabric of the canopy, freeing Phainon and Mydei from its bind. Phainon helps Mydei up before turning to Aglaea.

“You’ll only subject us to confinement?” he asks.

“Of course not,” Aglaea replies. “You will have no meals while you’re detained. Once you’re released, you are to clear the borders of Okhema of any roaming Titankin. This will last for another three days and you will only be provided a mere jug of water as sustenance. After that, you will spend the seventh day in your quarters to recuperate and hopefully, reflect on the troubles you’ve caused to the citizens.”

Mydei says nothing. Phainon feels guilt gnaw at him as he looks around the state of the Marmoreal Market. He wonders if people got hurt during the tussle.

“There are no casualties, Phainon,” Aglaea says, able to read his mind. “Despite your delay in awareness, you can rest assured.”

Phainon nods gingerly.

Aglaea continues, “If there are no objections, please follow me to your confinement cells.”

No conversations were made as Aglaea escorted them to the basement of the Marmoreal Palace where the dungeons are located, rows and rows of Garmentmakers trailing behind them like a makeshift army.

If Phainon and Mydei were to resist arrest, their odds of winning would be miniscule regardless of their combined strength. Not like they plan to anger Aglaea even more than they already have.

Two Garmentmakers open the cells facing each other. Aglaea gestures for Phainon and Mydei to get in, both of them choosing a cell of their own.

“Someone will come fetch you in three days’ time,” Aglaea tells them as the Garmentmakers ensure the locks on the cells are secure. “Now then, heroes, I shall take my leave.”

Phainon waves at her retreating figure while Mydei simply crosses his arms and manages a grunt.

Finding a comfortable spot in the cramped and uncomfortable cell, Phainon settles for resting his back against the wall where he could get a good look at his trouble-making companion. He makes sure that Aglaea and her terrifying minions have completely left the dungeons before attempting conversation.

“Are you good at chess?”

Mydei furrows his eyebrows, also leaning against the wall. It’s a shame that the iron bars enclosing their cells are significantly thick enough to relatively hinder Phainon’s vision of the prince.

“Has it not occurred to you that we are being punished?” Mydei asks, deep voice reverberating all throughout the stone walls and floors.

Phainon shoots him a smile. He’s not sure if Mydei can see him any better than he does Mydei. “It has, and there’s nothing I can do about it. So, chess?”

Mydei shakes his head in disbelief. Nevertheless, he still indulges Phainon in his whims. “A close friend of mine liked to play. Some nights by the campfire in between campaigns, he would call upon me to have a match with him so he could practice the techniques he’s read about in his books.”

Phainon can’t help but notice that the other’s tone has significantly mellowed down compared to how he usually speaks. It must have been a really close friend of Mydei’s to warrant such a tone that thinly belies a hint of fondness.

“I know of the rules enough that you won’t be able to deceive me like you did so earlier,” Mydei finishes.

Now that he’s addressing Phainon, the sharp edges have returned and the walls are put up, traces of vulnerability hidden and out of sight.

“To be fair, I really did forget about melding being optional,” Phainon explains earnestly. Despite his teasing, he really did intend to play fair. “When I saw you in the market, my eagerness to have you partake in a game of koum-kan with me must have overtaken my senses.”

“You don’t say,” Mydei drawls, sarcasm coating his words thickly.

Phainon presses on. “Let’s have a game of chess once we get out of here— I mean, when our punishment has run its course. I’m pretty good! I was once known as the chess grandmaster back in my hometown.”

Mydei doesn’t respond to his offer right away and Phainon feels the unwelcome sensation of uncertainty beginning to crawl upon his skin.

Phainon, you are an embarrassment.

In the hopes of trying to convince Mydei, he successfully managed to make himself appear ostentatious. If he assumed that Mydei had harbored a poor opinion of him before, then it’s most likely the definitive truth now. From poor to abysmal, no doubt.

A sigh can be heard from Mydei’s cell. “I dislike foul tactics,” Mydei says to a Phainon that’s been tense from head to toe, barely breathing. “I will partake in trivial games with you as long as you keep your honor and play fair.”

Phainon cannot believe his ears. “Of course! Allow me to take this moment to apologize for not admitting to my mistake earlier.”

“It’s fine. In turn, I’d like to apologize for creating a… mess.” Phainon sees Mydei shift uncomfortably in his cell, the crimson fabric of his garb a stark contrast against the gray of stone. “You seemed really distressed when Aglaea was scolding us.”

“It’s the lack of scolding that makes me uneasy,” Phainon points out. “And I seemed to find you enjoying yourself when creating such messes.”

Mydei’s smile that was as radiant as Kephale’s Dawn would forever live in Phainon’s memory. When he finds himself obscured in darkness, no fear would ensnare him for he’ll be carrying a piece of light with him until the end of the times.

“I’ve never had an equal in battle,” Mydei tells him. “Even if what we did was far from being an all-out fight, you held your own splendidly well against me.”

“Is that a compliment, Your Highness?” Phainon teases, unable to stop himself. No one must know how the feeling of warmth seeps into him like a gentle caress. “To be considered as your equal is nothing but an honor. Especially when it’s coming from the crown prince of Kremnos himself.”

Mydei scoffs. “Don’t let it get to your head, Deliverer.”

“It’s already embedded in the deepest crevices of my mind,” Phainon says, smiling so hard his cheeks are beginning to hurt. He can’t seem to remember a time since arriving in Okhema where he was this giddy.

“Think however you want of it,” Mydei says, an obvious dismissal. He clears his throat. “If you’re amenable, I’d like to engage you in a spar from time to time.”

Phainon pretends to think about it. He fails spectacularly. “Absolutely. Let me know when it suits you. I’ll make sure to free up my schedule then.”

“Setting aside your Deliverer duties in favor of heeding my call?” Mydei muses. “There is no need to go leaps and bounds for me, Deliverer. I can take a no for an answer in the event that you’re unavailable.”

Most people would think Phainon to be somewhat thick-faced. Phainon thinks so, too. He wonders when the exact moment it was that shame has departed his body without so much as looking back. Mydei must think him pathetic for implying that he’s willing to drop anything for him.

“I apologize,” Phainon says in an attempt to salvage his pride. “It’s simply because I, too, have found myself unsuccessful when it comes to finding a suitable sparring partner. I admit, it has hindered my progress on improving my abilities in battle. You’ll have to forgive me for appearing so eager.”

It’s quiet in Mydei’s cell after that. Phainon assumes that he must have offended the other in some way once again seeing as how it comes so naturally for him to do so. Pondering his words, he wonders when exactly had Mydei seen him as an equal despite their clear differences in almost everything. Perhaps the only thing they have in common is combat prowess.

“There is no need for apologies,” comes Mydei’s voice after quite some time that Phainon almost forgot their conversation had halted prematurely. “In fact, I should thank you for being so willing. As a Kremnoan, my honor shall see to it that your efforts to accommodate me are repaid.”

Phainon blinks, perplexed, catching a glimpse of a searing golden gaze behind the iron bars ahead of him. “I— Really, Mydei. You said it yourself that we’re equals. I would assume that formalities are not necessary. No need for all that ‘repayment’ fuss.”

A deliberately audible sigh. “If that is your preference, Deliverer.”

“It is,” Phainon confirms.

“Okay.”

“Great.”

“I’d like some peace and quiet now,” Mydei says, an implication for Phainon to keep his mouth shut most likely.

Phainon does so out of gratitude for Mydei’s surprisingly generous indulgence of his whims. Mydei’s peace and quiet, however, does not last for as long as Phainon had predicted it.

“Do you know of a game we can play during our stay here?” Mydei asks after what had seemed to be half a quint. “I’m beginning to feel rather dull.”

Phainon allows himself to smile, wondering if Mydei could see his glee from within his own cell. “I thought you’d never ask.”
