chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Sail the Sea of Souls with no way of turning back, for Death is a destination where the prospect of return is out of the question. This applies to every living being. All, except one.

Chapter Notes

⚠️ click for chapter warnings (contains spoilers)

fate season, month of gate

8 months before the present time

· · ─ ·𖥸· ─ · ·

…the Sea of Souls have rejected me. My father has succumbed to his own selfishness, and our Titan is now on the brink of madness…

…I have met with exiles from my land of birth. They speak of my mother with profound admiration. As of this moment, she is nothing more than a stranger to me…

…they said she wept for my fate, pleaded for my life until her dying breaths at the hands of her husband whom she considered her equal. My father’s betrayal led to her demise…

…the tears from my mother’s love fuels me, I shall make everything right once more.

— words etched in scraps of paper with dates of entry spanning years, written by unknown;

the author depicts a lack of mastery in using the Kremnoan alphabet

· · ─ · ─ · ·

“The ritual is going to be performed in three different locations, each commemorating the Titans of Fate,” Tribbie says, her small finger pointing at three spots in the map consecutively. “We’re going to have to split up to be able to find all the disciples quickly.”

Phainon nods absentmindedly. “I see.”

The map of the Abyss of Fate may appear simple, significantly reduced in size from its former glory after the invasion of the Black Tide. But that doesn’t mean the puzzles scattered around the ruins are sparse in nature.  Beside Phainon, Mydei sports the same pinched expression as he frowns at the map. There’s no doubt that he also harbors the same sentiments.

Tribbie seems to see through both of them, able to read their perturbation. She smiles. “Don’t worry, the puzzles you two will come across aren’t that complicated to solve. At least, you wouldn’t need our help to get past them.”

Both Phainon and Mydei let out sighs of relief. Neither of them are really that gifted to wield the power of Oronyx’s Miracle.

“Just to be clear, our tasks are to reach the site of the ritual assigned to each of us, get the disciples, and rendezvous back here,” Mydei clarifies.

Tribbie nods. “Yup.”

“Is the ritual going to be a problem?” Phainon asks. “I have no intentions of indirectly offending the Fate Titans.”

At the statement, Mydei snorts pointedly. If he speaks of Phainon’s recurring habit of committing blasphemy against the Titans in front of Tribbie, Phainon is going to have to throw him off a cliff in order to keep his misdeeds a secret from the Holy Maiden.

Thankfully, Mydei merely throws a smirk at Phainon’s direction and nothing else. Phainon ignores him.

“Not necessarily,” Tribbie answers, a finger on her chin. “The disciples are simply discarding items and keepsakes in accordance with the Month of Gate’s tradition.”

“Except, they chose a perilous location,” Mydei adds with a huff, pouring scorn over the disciples’ evident lack of good judgement.

Tribbie musters a wry smile. “We can’t fault them for it, De. Followers of Janus used to do these rituals here before the Black Tide’s invasion, back when this place was still called the Janusopolis.”

Mydei seems conflicted by this, as if he regrets speaking so callously over the matter. He doesn’t make a move to argue this time.

“I suppose we should get going,” Phainon says in an attempt to get rid of the awkwardness. “Better for us to find those disciples first before they fall prey to the roaming Titankin.”

“We agree,” Tribbie says. The look of concern on her face makes both Phainon and Mydei equally unsettled. “If one of us is not here by two quints, the ones who managed to return here shall saddle the disciples to the dromases and send them back to Okhema first before proceeding to look for one another.”

Phainon and Mydei nod. “Understood.”

Tribbie seems satisfied with this response. “We’ll get going now. The site we need to reach is the furthest from here.”

And one with the most puzzles, no doubt. Phainon and Mydei got away with the easy ones, headed east and west respectively with far lesser obstacles, as well as a straight-cut route with barely any twists and turns.

“Take care, Lady Tribbie,” Phainon says, trying hard not to let his worries and guilt show.

Tribbie smiles at him reassuringly. “We’ll be fine. We know this place like the back of our hands. If anything, we’re more worried about how you and De will fare on your own.”

“I’ll be alright.” Mydei throws Phainon a look. “Can’t say the same for this Deliverer, though.”

Phainon scoffs. “Oh, really now—”

“Please don’t fight,” Tribbie says, standing in the middle of the other two with her small arms outstretched. “We don’t have time for this.”

Both Phainon and Mydei immediately throw away the urge for a brawl. It’s a wonder how Lady Tribbie can appear intimidating despite her small stature.

“We really have to go now,” Tribbie tells the other two, poised to begin her journey into the Abyss of Fate, taking the route headed north. “Be careful out there, De, Snowy.”

“I will, Lady Tribbie.”

“Yes, Lady Tribios.”

Tribbie nods and smiles. She then makes her way into the ruins without looking back, leaving Phainon and Mydei to stare at her retreating figure until she’s out of sight.

Phainon turns to Mydei. “Fancy a tally? Loser treats the winner to a meal.”

Mydei chuckles darkly. “A bold challenge from someone who lost his money pouch only a day prior.”

Oh, right.

Phainon had completely forgotten about that entire ordeal. Ten thousand balance coins may be of no consequence for a Chrysos Heir like him, but it’s still ten thousand balance coins. That amount just doesn’t simply fall from the sky out of nowhere.

“Dear Mydeimos, I think you’ve forgotten one crucial detail,” Phainon starts. “From what I can remember, it was you who lost my money pouch. Are you finally able to remember the thief’s face now that you’re sober?”

Even if Phainon generally doesn’t mind considering that he still has some spare money stored somewhere else, the circumstance does give him a valid reason to tease Mydei, risking it all at the rare chance that Mydei might’ve felt guilty about the whole thing and chooses to indulge Phainon’s antics as a way to compensate for failing to apprehend the thief.

Mydei simply turns away at the question that was evidently meant to throw him off. Even if Mydei still retained most of his composure despite the jab, Phainon is more than willing to count this as a small win.

“I’ll see you later with trophies a far greater number than yours,” is Mydei’s response, amusingly elusive.

Whether or not Mydei is embarrassed to discuss his inebriation, or the fact that he still cannot remember the thief’s face, Phainon is merciful enough to let this slide. He’ll take a flustered Mydei over an angry Mydei any day.

“We shall see, then,” Phainon says.

Mydei merely responds with a noncommittal hum before turning around, his back on Phainon as he heads west. Phainon takes the route to the east, following the directions as Tribbie’s map had illustrated.

As Phainon navigated the desolate halls of the Abyss of Fate, he noticed with dismay that there’s a significant lack of Titankin in the area. The trophies on his person still remained less than ten, a far from ideal amount if he were to go against Mydei who most likely had about twenty by now.

At the end of the day, it all comes down to luck.

From memory alone, the location of the ritual should not be too far from where he is. A couple paces forward and Phainon finds himself in front of a closed double door, tall and looming over him.

The initial grandeur of it might have been lost to time, but Phainon can still marvel at its magnificence. He fiddles with the lock, muttering prayers to Janus until a click resounds. He then pushes the heavy double door open with a bit of effort, making his way inside.

The room within was vast, dimly lit by candles that did no better in dissipating the shadows from the corners. In the middle was a pile of tomes and treasures arranged haphazardly over a faintly drawn inscription on the floor.

The disciples of Janus were surrounding the said inscription, hooded faces turning their attention towards Phainon with their hands still clasped together in prayer.

Phainon waves at them, feeling awkward for the interruption. “Um, greetings.”

The disciples turn their attention amongst themselves before unanimously returning their gaze back at Phainon.

“Is Lord Phainon here to join us in this ritual?” one of them asks.

Phainon can’t tell which of the disciples had spoken due to the hoods they all fashioned. “I’m sorry to disappoint you, but I’m afraid the ritual has to be postponed for the time being.”

The disciples let out sounds of disgruntlement, murmuring amongst themselves.

“How so?” one of them demands, the medallion hanging from his neck signifies his leadership of the group.

“Lady Aglaea has tasked me to return you all back to Okhema,” Phainon answers amicably despite the growing agitation of the disciples. “This place is not safe.”

A scoff resounds before another one speaks, “But the ritual must see completion!”

“Indeed,” says the leader with a firm nod. “We will return once it’s done.”

“You will only serve to endanger your fellows, good sir,” Phainon says. “Whatever it is you plan to do here, it can be done just the same in Okhema. Not to mention, it will be safer.”

The room erupts into an uproar as the disciples leave their prayer positions, crowding around Phainon oppressively and using their numbers to their advantage to make him bend to their will.

Phainon sighs. Convincing others to understand his intentions might be his strong suit (most of the time), but it never comes easy.

It takes a while to calm down the agitated disciples, and it also takes another while longer of negotiations to convince them that leaving the place is the better option. It was ever a surprise that no roaming Titankin have found them by now because of the raucousness in the room.

After some more reassurances that involved Phainon mentioning Aglaea’s willingness to accommodate the disciples’ rather absurd demands for the ritual, as well as the Holy Maidens’ well-sought participation, Phainon had finally managed to convince the disciples of Janus to leave.

Even if the clauses he mentioned were made up on the spot and there’s absolutely no way that Aglaea would agree to them, it was better than having to tie them all together with a rope and drag them out forcefully.

As they make their way back to the agreed location, few Titankin block their way but it was never really much of a hindrance. Phainon is more than happy to take them down considering that it adds more trophies to his rather pitiful count.

When Phainon reaches the entrance to the Abyss of Fate, only Tribbie had made it back safely with her share of disciples.

“Lady Tribbie, your expertise never fails to amaze me,” he says as he helps Tribbie settle the newly arrived disciples with the others. “Even if the location you chose was the furthest, not to mention, barred by a significant amount of puzzles, you still managed to return the quickest.”

Tribbie grins toothily at the praise. “It wasn’t that long since we returned, Snowy. Seeing that you were able to make it out safely without mishaps is already impressive enough, too.”

Aside from the grueling task of convincing the disciples, Phainon could say that his trip to the ruins went pretty smoothly. So smoothly that it’s almost unsettling.

“Mydei’s not here yet, huh.”

Tribbie nods, looking over to the direction where Mydei went. “Not yet. But there’s no doubt he’ll be here soon. Let’s just wait a bit.”

“He’s probably hunting down all the Titankin in the area to inflate his trophy count,” Phainon says lightly, unable to hide a smile.

“You two and your silly little games,” Tribbie admonishes without much heat, shaking her head like she's a tired mother of two unruly kids despite her child-like appearance.

While Tribbie ensures that none of the disciples are injured, Phainon keeps watch from on top of a dilapidated pillar, making sure that he’s able to see any Titankin’s approach from afar (as well as Mydei’s).

A quint passes and there’s still no crimson silhouette coming from the west. Phainon feels the nerves start to kick in as he fiddles with a fragment of debris in between his fingers. Mydei was supposed to be here by now.

Two quints was the agreed upon time, but the silence of the ruins was loud enough to render Phainon ill at ease. Mydei is not someone who usually takes too long when it comes to things like these. Titankin shouldn’t even be a problem. Needless to say, Phainon barely saw any Titankin roaming around the area so what was taking Mydei so long?

The disciples couldn’t be giving him a hard time…

Phainon jumps down from the pillar and finds Tribbie waiting for him there. The disciples of Janus are all taking a rest by the dromases, quietly murmuring amongst themselves.

“Lady Tribbie—”

“You’re worried about De, aren’t you?” Tribbie asks before Phainon could get a word out.

There’s no use denying it. Phainon replies, “It’s not something I can help with.”

Tribbie smiles. As always, she is able to understand. “You can go ahead and find De,” she tells Phainon. “We’ll stay here with the disciples. But don’t take too long, okay?”

Phainon had no intention of keeping Tribbie waiting on her own anyway. “You have my word, Lady Tribbie.”

He wastes no time and heads west. It was fortunate that, very much like his trip to the east of the ruins, there’s not much of Nikador’s Titankin roaming around. Or perhaps Mydei had already made quick work of them.

But there’s no Titankin remains anywhere.

As Phainon makes his way further into the building in search of Mydei, the desolation of the place only serves to fuel his dread even more. Since the fall of Castrum Kremnos, the ruins of the Abyss of Fate has always been teeming with Titankin. The significant lack of them makes one assume that something has gone terribly wrong.

Dread creeps in like a slow, invisible tide. Its presence barely perceptible at first, but gradually worsens with each step that Phainon takes as he navigates the maze of empty hallways, the sound of his own labored breathing deafening amidst the silence.

The air thickens, unnerving. Mydei shouldn’t be too far from him now. And then he hears it, feels it upon the ground, vibrations reverberating across stone walls—

The building rumbles, a loud roar resounds followed by an ear-piercing crash. Phainon feels his pulse quicken as he makes haste towards the source of the commotion. The huge door at the end of the hall was slightly agape. The sounds grow louder, the stench of rust ever so pronounced.

Phainon hears screams.

He bursts into the room, greatsword at hand and ready to strike. The sight that greets him makes him feel faint.

Titankin are amass, a mix of white and gold, barely distinguishable like a swarm of insects, a relentless sea of hostile intent.

In the middle of the room was a flurry of blood red crystals taking down every Titankin that comes close with deadly precision. But no matter how vicious of a defense is put up, the sheer number of enemies are just seemingly endless.

A hundred against one. Phainon chokes on air.

“Mydei!”

Phainon rushes over to the center, his own greatsword slaying every Titankin he comes across —as many as possible, enough to at least make a difference.

He steps over the remains of the felled enemies that bled golden ichor on the floor, paying no mind to the mess soiling the soles of his boots or the fear of tripping for his eyes are glued ahead.

To that mesmerizing whirling movement, the dance of crimson fabric and a glint of gold, the sight of tanned skin marred with cuts. The vision of Mydei grows clearer, mighty and magnificent despite the odds stacked against him.

His gaze meets that of Phainon’s briefly, a fervid and brilliant gold. Phainon swings his greatsword in a sweeping motion, taking down the remaining Titankin that hinders his path towards Mydei.

At last.

“Are you alright?” Phainon yells at Mydei, hoping his voice was loud enough to be heard above the carnage.

The response he gets is a rough shove on his shoulder as Mydei pushes him away without so much as meeting his eyes. Phainon feels his shoulder ache, a distinct sting he tries not to dwell on too much, whispering the bitter implication of rejection.

“Take the disciples by the fallen pillar and go!” Mydei yells back, the red crystal in his hand impaling a Titankin straight through, golden ichor splattering over his face as he throws the Titankin towards the hoard, knocking down several in the process.

Phainon refocuses his attention back to the battle. “You didn’t answer my question!”

The ground beneath them rumbles as Mydei’s red crystals emerge from the stone floor, fatally injuring some of the Titankin. He turns to Phainon with a hint of irritation.

“Just go!”

“Not without you!”

Phainon narrowly dodges an arrow aimed at his head, the sharp tip almost grazing his cheek. He feels Mydei’s back against his own as they’re further cornered at the center of the room, the swarm of Titankin upon them seemingly endless.

Trying to spot an opening, Phainon instead catches sight of the fallen pillar Mydei had mentioned earlier. There’s a large red crystal making sure that it won’t crumble any further in a manner that would harm the disciples huddled beneath.

They’re hidden enough that the Titankin don’t seem to pay them any mind, their attention solely focused on taking down the two people in the middle of the room.

Phainon hears Mydei curse. The word is familiar, undeniably Kremnoan.

“What happened here?” Phainon asks, keeping his guard high and his blade raised. “Why are there so many of them?”

“Those disciples of Janus activated a mechanism that lured all the Titankin in the area,” Mydei explains, back heaving against Phainon as he tries to catch his breath.

That explains the lack of Titankin, Phainon thinks. No wonder the ruins of the Abyss of Fate was almost devoid of them for they all came running into this one single room for Mydei to fend off.

Alone.

Phainon feels his throat begin to tighten up. He wonders how Mydei was able to hold up for so long, thankful that all this time, all the injuries Mydei was able to sustain were a few cuts —quite telling of the battle prowess Mydei possesses.

While the Titankin had let up on their attacks temporarily in favor of ominously approaching Phainon and Mydei—almost as if there is no need to rush for the defeat of the two men is imminent—Phainon uses this as his chance to communicate without the hindrance of loud noises and blatant attempts on his life.

“Mydei, we need to leave now,” Phainon says, pointing his blade threateningly at a Titankin who got too close for comfort. “You’ve found the disciples. No use in lingering here.”

Mydei scoffs behind him, the essence of his power palpable enough to make even Phainon shiver. “These Titankin will follow us to the trail if they’re not taken care of at this instant. Go ahead and leave with the others. I’ll handle this.”

Phainon grits his teeth. Kremnoans and their bull-headednes.

“Now’s not the time for arrogance,” Phainon argues, his grip on the hilt of his blade tightening. The Titankin are bound to resume their attack soon, perhaps only a few paces in and they will strike. “Mydei, you can’t possibly fend them all on your own—”

You’ll die.

The Titankin charges, arrows fly with a woosh, Phainon’s greatsword crosses with another, and Mydei leaps off, grabbing three enemies by the scruff before crushing them with a flurry of red crystals into the wall.

He watches through the reflection in his blade how Mydei swiftly dodges the lunge of a Titankin’s spear, watches as Mydei leans back to avoid an arrow aimed at his heart, watches as Mydei stops the sword of a Titankin with one hand, the sharp tip barely a hairbreadth away from Mydei’s eye.

Phainon hears the sharp sound of another arrow being released, distinct amidst the chaos. It brushes past him, it’s aim soaring straight and true towards a target behind him—

Towards Mydei.

Phainon pushes the Titankin off of him with the edge of his greatsword, feels his muscles ache at the exertion so extreme that he almost could’ve broken his wrist. The Titankin is thankfully knocked back, and Phainon swiftly turns behind him, a hand outstretched as he tries to reach Mydei, an attempt to stop the arrow from reaching its destination.

Mydei meets Phainon’s gaze, an instance so brief and yet Phainon could’ve sworn that it had lasted much longer. Time slows down, everything else fades into vision. Any moment now, the arrow that flies midair would find itself a new terminus.

It would no longer be Mydei’s heart, for how could it be so in the first place? How could Phainon allow another to die before his very eyes?

The belligerent tip of an enemy’s arrow could pierce any part of Phainon’s body. Though his skin is littered with cuts of varying depth, Mydei’s flesh shall never be acquainted with the sensation of cold metal that swoops like an eagle that spotted its prey.

Phainon sees Mydei’s eyes widen a fraction, the product of realization perhaps. For Mydei to be the last person he sees is more than what Phainon could ever deserve. He just hopes his death would be able to serve some semblance of purpose.

It all happens in a blink of an eye. One moment Mydei was surrounded by Titankin, outnumbered to almost an extreme that he fails to notice the arrow nocked specifically aiming at his direction. In the next, blood red crystals dominates Phainon’s vision, followed by a flurry of red fabric and exposed tanned skin.

Phainon feels the world spin, Mydei’s scent permeating his senses. A grunt follows, Mydei’s ankle twisting awkwardly as he maneuvers Phainon out of the way and onto the ground, covering Phainon’s body with his own like a forbidden shield.

The glint of a spearhead’s tip is caught from Phainon’s periphery, and then there’s the soft thwack as the dreaded arrow finally meets flesh. The blade of the spear follows, piercing mercilessly through muscle and bone.

Golden ichor spills and lands on Phainon’s face in rivulets from where he’s laid on the ground. There’s nothing else he could do but stare ahead, look up to the source of the golden waterfall, harrowing despite the mesmerizing shimmer.

Mydei’s eyes are unfocused, muted gold as he meets Phainon’s gaze. Although, it feels as if he’s barely even there anymore.

Phainon chokes out a gasp when Mydei collapses on top of him. He catches him with ease as he sits up, ears ringing when he pulls out the spear that impaled Mydei’s side without much thought, absent minded as if his body is being controlled by another being.

A hateful, vengeful being.

Mydei’s soft groan echoes in Phainon’s ears like a devastating plea. Hands stained in golden ichor finds the wounded skin of Mydei’s back, pulling Mydei closer towards a body whose blood had run cold despite the thrum of life and anguish.

Without letting his hold upon Mydei falter, Phainon throws the spear with deadly precision towards the closest Titankin with so much force that it pierces five others, pushing them further away until the spearhead meets the hard surface of the cracked stone wall, stopping its momentum entirely.

Phainon’s other hand shakily snakes up towards the wound on Mydei’s throat where the arrow is lodged so deeply that the tip protrudes from the other side of Mydei’s neck. Phainon stares at nothing in particular as he pulls the arrow out, jaw clenched tight when he feels the warm gush of blood flow, further staining his hand in glistening gold.

The arrow flies without the need of a bowstring, its tip trailing the blood of someone precious as it soars, striking the Titankin archer situated far away who had so graciously bestowed such a gift, the fated arrow it chose from its quiver carved in marble.

The Titankin archer falls. The rest of the damned retreats, a hoard without a leader. A little too late, Phainon is finally able to know silence.

Mydei’s body lay limp against him, head resting heavy on Phainon’s shoulder, golden ichor pooling onto the ground around them like a gruesome puddle, wetting fabrics both red and blue. Phainon blinks the haze away, a stained hand making its way onto Mydei’s hair, blonde strands dipped in crimson soft to the touch.

“Mydei,” Phainon calls out quietly.

There’s no hint of a breath ghosting Phainon’s neck where Mydei’s face is buried. No thump of a beating heart within Mydei’s chest. Mydei does not indulge Phainon with a reply like he usually does, always responding to each one of Phainon’s calls of his name without fail.

Right now, Mydei has gone quiet.

With a gentle push, Phainon repositions Mydei to lay on his lap. Mydei’s eyes remain open, half-lidded, dull and unblinking. Gone is the fervid flame in those eyes that Phainon admires so much. He fears that he may never see them again, dreads a life without it.

Phainon cups Mydei’s face with shaky hands, sticky and wet with warm liquid gold. “Mydei…”

Mydei remains still. Thanatos is ever so unforgiving. Phainon makes a tally of his possessions that he could give up when he eventually sets sail to the Sea of Souls, a barter ready for the Hand of Shadow—all his treasures and all that he is, all for the life of a man who is far more precious than anything Phainon could possibly offer.

A most dearest, most cherished equal who saved his life without hesitation.

“Mydeimos.”

Surely, Mydei’s soul still lingers within the room. Perhaps Mydei could hear Phainon, feel pity on him, enough to convince the dead to return to his mortal body.

But Mydei doesn’t budge, and golden blood continues to flow ceaselessly until fair skin turns pale, the once pink and full lips fading into lifelessness.

Phainon has seen countless corpses before. He’s seen people equally as significant die before him, souls reaped as he dwells in his suffering. He vowed that he would never witness such a thing again. As long as he lived, no harm would befall the people he considers as friends, as family.

That was supposed to be the last time, scenes of a harrowing past coming to haunt Phainon once more. And yet, before Phainon’s very eyes was the proof of his failure.

Not again.

“Mydei, wake up.”

Not again.

“Mydeimos.”

NOT AGAIN. NOT AGAIN. NOT AGAIN!

“Myd—”

Phainon chokes on his words, a stinging behind his eyes as he wallows in his delusions that Mydei might just survive this ordeal even if his heart had stopped beating long ago.

You didn’t even say goodbye.

He hears a soft murmur of voices from the distance followed by the scuffling of sandals against stone and the rustle of fabric. Phainon watches dazedly as the disciples of Janus make their way out from beneath the fallen pillar. He completely forgot that they were even there in the first place, forgot the reason why he even went here.

Phainon felt his throat tighten when he couldn’t spot the once present cluster of red crystals supporting the pillar. The red crystals that used to scatter around the room during the battle had also disappeared, as if erasing the memory of Mydei’s power from existence.

The disciples looked terrified out of their minds. Phainon couldn’t even bring himself to care at the moment. There’s a chance that the group must have some knowledge of healing. They are no followers of Aquila from the Twilight Courtyard with miraculous healing abilities, but Phainon can’t afford to be picky right now.

“I need a healer!” he yells at the huddled group of pale-faced disciples.

The disciples visibly jolt at the sudden harsh address, murmuring amongst themselves, gazes darting at each other. Their shoulders shake, most of them starts fiddling with their fingers, but they make no move to step forward and help.

Phainon’s patience runs out.

“Quickly!”

A young man is pushed forward by his fellows. He looked like he would rather be anywhere than here. Seeing Phainon’s piercing gaze at him, weighed with profound expectation, the young man gingerly makes his way to the center of the vast room, crouching beside Phainon and the bleeding man he held in his arms.

Phainon watches with rapt attention as the young man removes Mydei’s gauntlets, muttering prayers as he takes both Mydei’s bare hands in his before ripping a piece of fabric from his clothes to cover the wounds and stop the bleeding. Once done, he checks Mydei’s pulse— both on his wrist and neck. He inspects Mydei’s half-lidded eyes closely, monitoring for any pupil dilation before bringing his ear close to Mydei’s chest.

The disciple had a grim look after his inspection. “My lord, I’m afraid that he’s already—”

“You must be mistaken,” Phainon says, the sound of his own voice foreign to him. “Check again. Heal him.”

“But—”

Before Phainon was about to unleash disaster that could even rival the Black Tide upon the poor disciple of Janus, the sound of the double doors being pried open catches his attention.

The disciple of Janus uses Phainon’s distraction to bolt away back towards the huddled group in the corner lest Phainon remembers his grievances and punish him for being unable to do the impossible.

Tribbie rushes in, the little wings on her back fluttering ever so slightly. She had a worried look on her face. “Snowy! And—”

Her gaze drops to Mydei, nothing but a lifeless corpse on Phainon’s lap. She gasps, faltering in her approach.

Phainon’s lip quivers, his grip on Mydei’s stiff body growing tighter. “Lady Tribbie, Mydei is…

Not dead. Anything but dead.

He feels something warm and wet trickle down his cheek. His vision of Tribbie blurs as he tastes blood in his mouth, belatedly realizing that he’d bit his tongue hard enough to warrant a bleeding.

The sting is dull compared to the terrible ache of sorrow that wedges itself deeper into the crevices of his heart, enough so that it would be nigh impossible to flush it out.

Upon seeing Phainon’s tears, Tribbie sports an equally tearful expression, empathizing with Phainon’s pain. She opens her mouth to say something, perhaps to offer consolation.

But it would be futile. Phainon couldn’t be consoled at all. It took him years to mourn the death of a close friend from the past. Who’s to say that it wouldn’t take decades for him to mourn the loss of Mydei? Someone who’s not just a close friend, but also—

A cold finger pokes the tip of Phainon’s nose.

Phainon startles, looking down in an instant with no preparation whatsoever to what sight was about to greet him.

Mydei blinks up at him. Once, then twice. The light in his eyes of gold have returned, the fairness of his skin restored, the bleeding on his throat and on the side of his torso have stopped, the cuts that once littered his skin gone.

No wounds, no scars. Nothing.

Phainon furrows his eyebrows. He must have truly lost his mind. Mydei, on the other hand, seemed far from being amused as he withdrew his hand.

“I knew you were dramatic. But not this dramatic,” Mydei admonishes without much heat.

It’s Mydei’s voice. No other voices could hold such power over Phainon in the same way Mydei’s does. He would be able to single it out in a noisy room full of people, would be able to listen for its echoes even if he and Mydei are valleys apart.

As of this moment, however, even if he knew that it is Mydei who spoke, Phainon finds it difficult distinguishing reality from illusion. No matter how much he’s able to recognize Mydei’s voice in any shape or form, it would only be in vain if such a sound merely stemmed from his imaginations rather than the truth of the circumstance.

A teardrop falls from Phainon’s chin, landing squarely on Mydei’s cheek. Mydei sighs as if the unintended act has aggrieved him thoroughly.

“Tears,” Mydei notes, disbelief etched in his tone as he brings a hand towards his face. The tip of his finger lightly touches the spot where Phainon’s tear had fallen, pulling his hand away to examine the wetness. “For me?”

This allows Phainon a moment of sobriety from the haze of pure bafflement, hastily wiping his face with the back of his hands, further smearing golden ichor onto his skin—proof that death had indeed occurred in his presence.

The sight of Mydei alive and conversing with him might simply be just a product of some deceptive illusion that’s spurred on by the profound grief that Phainon is able to see the dead coming back to life.

Mydei sighs, puffs of air blown lightly against Phainon’s face as he awaits for Phainon to snap out of his self-induced haze. Phainon thankfully does so some moments later.

“You!”

Mydei raises an eyebrow. “Me?”

“You died! You were…” Phainon tries to at least make himself sound coherent. “Your heart stopped beating!”

Mydei had the audacity to roll his eyes, as if all this was something merely trivial to him. He sits up like nothing had happened, ignoring Phainon’s jumbled mess of accusations altogether.

“I’m still talking to you!”

Phainon watches with a disbelieving scowl as Mydei hoists himself off the floor as if he had not been skewered and pierced by an arrow and a spear moments prior. He offers a hand to Phainon in an attempt to help the latter up.

Indignantly, Phainon slaps Mydei’s hand away, azure eyes glaring daggers at the man before him.

Mydei hums lightly, rubbing the back of his hand. The skin is starting to turn red from where Phainon had hit it. Phainon feels guilt swirl in his gut, an apology on the tip of his tongue.

“Suit yourself,” is all Mydei says.

Phainon notices the tinge of pink coloring Mydei’s face as well as the tips of his ears, a stark contrast to the paleness from earlier. Even if relief awashes Phainon’s body anew, the thumping of his heart within his chest has yet to be calmed.

There’s just so many questions—

Is this real?

Mydei, are you really alive?

Are you okay?

How did you defy death?

Why did you save me?

None of those words are able to escape Phainon’s frozen lips as he watches Mydei inspect his garb of red and black fabric, frowning at the stain of golden ichor that had seeped through. It was his very own blood that had ruined his garments, the dreadful puddle something that Phainon is still settled upon.

Perhaps it would be better to challenge Mydei in a duel after all, for Phainon to be able to let off all the surging emotions that have rendered him almost a stranger to his own body. He wants to do so much, say so much more—

There’s a small hand on his shoulder, grounding him. Phainon turns to his side and sees Tribbie. There’s no smile on her face this time.

“Snowy, we need to leave before the rest of the Titankin comes back.”

Phainon couldn’t even find it within himself to nod or say something in reply. He simply stands, legs feeling like jelly with most of his clothes dripping golden blood, the liquid seeping through the fabric and allowing the cold air to bite into his skin rather mercilessly.

With resolute steps, Phainon marches out of the room. He can feel Mydei’s gaze on his retreating figure, searing like a brand. Phainon is barely able to resist the urge to look back.

The ride to the holy city was quiet save for the whimpers and murmurs of the petrified disciples.

Phainon stays in his corner of the dromas’ saddle, eyes glued at the passing view of desolation that is Amphoreus without Aquila’s Eyes to shine light upon them. Okhema is still some ways away, and Kephale’s Dawn Device could barely even illuminate the path.

In the darkness, Phainon allows himself to wallow in his own thoughts.

He hasn’t thrown a single glance towards Mydei’s direction out of fear for what he might see —Mydei’s corpse perhaps, when Phainon’s hallucinations have finally run its course and it turns out, Mydei’s soul is indeed already halfway in its journey towards the Hand of Shadow’s embrace, his resurrection simply a product of Phainon’s own imagination.

Tribbie, sensing the tense atmosphere, kept to herself during the entirety of the journey. The only time she spoke was when she asked both Phainon and Mydei if they were hungry. Neither accepted the bread and drink Tribbie offered, and neither spoke.

Phainon’s insides is a swirling mess of unspoken emotions. He fears that the moment he partakes in any type of sustenance, he’ll just end up hurling it back out in no time.

As for Mydei… Well, the dead cannot eat, can they?

A couple more hours of uncomfortable silence pass before Kephale’s Dawn finally showers them in its golden glow like a divine blessing, cleansing them of the darkness caused by the Black Tide.

Okhema’s city gates is just up ahead, and Phainon couldn’t be more eager to simply retire to his chambers and call an end to this terrible day. Tomorrow, he’ll have his wits about him. And perhaps he’ll also be able to engage in a conversation with Mydei.

Corpse or not, Phainon will come to see him.

Upon arrival, Tribbie leads the disciples of Janus into the city, leaving the other two Chrysos Heirs alone to their own devices. Perhaps Tribbie had sported some grievances of her own for she left without so much as a word.

Before Phainon could aimlessly walk away, a firm grip on his shoulder stops him. He doesn’t turn around even when he hears a heavy sigh from behind him, faltering his resolve.

The next thing that comes after the touch is his voice. Unmistakable and yet foreign all the same. “Deliverer, I—”

There’s a long pause. Days could have gone by with Phainon simply standing motionlessly by Okhema’s entrance with nothing but the warm hand on his shoulder.

And then it’s gone, as quickly as it had come into existence.

“Nevermind.”

Phainon’s jaw clenches. This time, he finally allows himself to turn around and face him.

How could Mydei just stand there before him, taking in breaths with his eyes of gold, fiery and glistening from reflecting the light of Kephale’s Dawn, looking very much alive as if Phainon had not held his limp body hours prior?

For Mydei to be able to regard Phainon so casually when Phainon had watched the life disappear from his eyes, acting like nothing happened when his blood still stains Phainon’s clothes and skin like a grievous reminder is something that ticks off Phainon more than he’d expected.

Not like he expected that he’d be able to experience something of the sort anyway, how else was he supposed to prepare himself to react appropriately?

Phainon opens his mouth in an attempt to speak, but no words escape his parted lips. Instead, there’s a tightening in his chest that makes it hard to breathe.

The stinging from behind his eyes makes their unwanted return, followed by the trickle of something warm that unbiddenly flows down his face like a steady stream whose waters sing the songs of sorrow.

The blurring of his vision worsens just before he could see Mydei’s expression turn into that of unbridled shock.

Mydei takes a couple of steps closer. Phainon doesn’t have the energy in him to take a step back.

“Why do you weep for me?” is Mydei’s question, barely above a whisper as if only Phainon is meant to hear the words. It was only thanks to their proximity that Phainon was able to do so.

Phainon scoffs, the question somehow offending him. Of all the things Mydei could ask, he chooses one that barely even made sense, one whose answer is as plain as day.

Blinking frantically, Phainon wipes his tears away with the back of his hand, ignoring the shimmer of dried gold that is still present upon his skin.

“What kind of question is that? I just saw you die because of me,” Phainon spats, his voice raw and almost childish in its frustration. “I think the better question here is: why did you save me knowing that you’ll…”

He trails off, unable to finish the rest of his sentence. It’s as if he’s afraid that he might speak it into existence and the image of Mydei in front of him, alive and well, would then morph into the vision he saw back at the Abyss.

Mydei as a corpse, cold and lifeless. Phainon feels the helplessness starting to creep in. It’s a terrible feeling, one he wishes to be rid of forever if it were possible.

“You’ve already witnessed firsthand the curse I bear,” Mydei says, ever so straightforward. “And you forget one detail. You were the one who jumped in front of me first—”

“To shield you from that arrow!” Phainon snaps, voice cracking at the exclamation. He’d spoken loud enough for the innocent citizens passing by to stop and stare. “You were careless.”

Mydei scoffs, crossing his arms defensively. “And you’re not? I’d say we’re one and the same.”

Phainon looks away, blinking rapidly. Tears of sorrow were replaced by that of pure irritation because in a sense, Mydei’s words made sense. They’ve both made rash decisions during the battle back at the ruins even if Phainon is loath to admit it out loud.

When it looks as if Phainon was not about to argue, Mydei continues, “Save your heroic acts for someone else. I’m far from one that needs saving. Death, as you already saw, is out of my reach so don’t even bother shielding me from harm next time.”

“How could you say such a thing?” Phainon admonishes. “You expect me to just watch like an uncaring audience the next time an enemy stabs you straight through?”

An unreadable expression crosses Mydei’s face, gone in a blink. “If it puts you in danger, then yes.”

Phainon could not believe his ears. He may argue with Mydei more often than not, but those arguments usually stemmed from something harmless. Once handled, it becomes something rather amusing to look back on, a somewhat fond memory that makes Phainon smile absentmindedly when he recalls it.

However, the situation at hand is different. Phainon thought Mydei knew him enough to not ask such an outrageous request from him. It’s a case of asked and answered. Only, Phainon got the worst possible response.

“Since you so cruelly expect me to just watch the next time you pull this stunt,” Phainon began. “Then do me the favor of gouging my eyes out this instant.”

Mydei sighs, heavy and exhausted. “You exaggerate.”

“And you piss me off,” Phainon shoots back. “Severely, I might add.”

“If you want to settle this with a fight then be my guest.”

Phainon grits his teeth, mind at a total loss. And though his hands itch to land a blow, clenched tightly into fists by his sides, he can’t seem to find the will to do so. His vision blurs even more, heat accumulating from behind his eyes, every blink a wrestle to keep his dignity at bay as tears carelessly flows.

Mydei reaches a hand out and Phainon flinches, wet lashes fluttering as he clenches his eyes shut, bracing for impact in the event that Mydei might want to engage in a brawl after all to settle their differences.

Only, there is no ache in his jaw and in its place, was the gentle touch of warm fingers deftly catching the steady cascade of tears, the sensation light as a feather that Phainon could barely feel the touch against his skin.

It is as if he is the most delicate of all porcelains, prone to breaking at the slightest brush of wind against the surface.

Phainon opens his eyes. Mydei gazes back at him, gold eyes unwavering. His hand upon Phainon’s cheek remains, palm radiating a distinct comforting warmth that renders Phainon almost weak, allowing him to lean into the touch as his grievances all but dissipate into the atmosphere.

“You weep like you’ve lost something,” Mydei tells him, the tip of his thumb catching another stray tear from the corner of Phainon’s eye. “I’m still here, Deliverer.”

They both know that this discussion is far from being over. Phainon still had his reservations about Mydei being so blasé about his own safety, and Mydei has yet to take back his sickening request of having Phainon do nothing for him in the face of danger.

But the reassurance acts as an anchor as Phainon navigates the waves of doubt. There’s no hint of deceit in Mydei’s tone for a Kremnoan such as him could only mean every single word that escapes his lips.

Before Phainon could respond, however, the touch on his face disappears as Mydei’s hand drops without warning.

Phainon watches as Mydei collapses to his knees with a pained expression, clutching his chest with labored breaths. Phainon is there to support him, his own ears ringing as he calls for healers.

Horror engulfs him once more when Mydei’s weight against him grows heavier.

“You worry for him.”

“How could I not?”

Castorice gives him an encouraging smile. “The healers will see to it that their jobs are done well. Lord Mydei will be fine.”

Seated at a bench across the door that led to Mydei’s chambers, Phainon buries his head in his hands with a groan.

“An undying body, that’s his curse,” he says, disbelief etched in his tone. “It makes me wonder just how many times he’s perished without my knowledge. All those times he referred to death so casually and I didn’t think much of it. I was a fool.”

“You are not at fault, Lord Phainon,” Castorice reassures. “You were simply unaware. All of us are on the same footing with you in this regard.”

Every Chrysos Heir bears Kephale’s golden blood in their veins. However, in exchange for the blessing of the divine, one must bear a tragic curse to be carried until the prophecy sees fulfillment.

Mydei is, unfortunately, not an exception.

It’s a pity that death needed to occur for all of them to find out about Mydei’s curse. Phainon is beginning to think that Mydei has a penchant of shouldering all his troubles by himself. A nasty habit.

The doors to Mydei’s chambers swing open as the healers begin to file out. Aglaea is the last to leave, her clouded gaze landing upon Phainon and Castorice in an instant, almost as if she had already expected them to be there.

Phainon bolts out of his seat, Castorice following at a distance behind him. “How is he?” he asks Aglaea.

“His wounds have healed but the ache still lingers,” Aglaea answers smoothly. “According to the healers, it might take some time for Mydeimos to recover. Other than that, he is alright.”

Phainon allows a sigh to escape his lips. “I see.”

Even if he’s already heard from Aglaea that Mydei is doing relatively fine, it wouldn’t beat having to see it for himself. There’s a high possibility that Mydei would downplay his pain in favor of concealing weakness.

Despite their earlier spat, Phainon would still very much like to see Mydei in the flesh to know how he’s faring. They’re still friends after all, and it’s because of him that Mydei is in his current state. Guilt truly is an old friend of his.

“Lord Phainon, are you alright?” Castorice asks. “Lady Aglaea bears good news, and yet you seem upset.”

Aglaea schools her expression with a cough. The odd behavior does not escape Phainon’s keen notice.

“The golden threads are wound tightly due to your agitation,” she tells Phainon. Though this is something that sounds far from ideal, the tone of Aglaea’s voice belied a hint of amusement. “If you wish to be in Mydeimos’ presence so much, you only need to walk through the door.”

Phainon fails to hide his apprehension. “Is it really okay?”

“According to Mydeimos’ words, a certain man is permitted entry for he doesn’t want said man to look like a kicked chimera who stalks the entry of his chambers,” Aglaea says. And then she adds, “Do believe me when I say that I quoted his words verbatim.”

Verbatim or not, Phainon’s mind still struggles to comprehend exactly what Aglaea had just said.

Castorice turns to Phainon with a smile. “It seems that Lord Mydei wishes to see you just as much as you wish to see him, Lord Phainon.”

“Oh,” Phainon voices out. Rather intelligently.

Mydei probably only wanted to resume their conversation from earlier. Phainon is not entirely opposed to the idea for he also harbors a fair share of sentiments that needed to be expressed now that he’s managed to calm down from the shock of Mydei’s temporary death.

Perhaps an apology is in order. He didn’t mean to lose his composure so much in front of Mydei. Mydei must’ve thought him to be akin to a child throwing a temper tantrum.

“You can go see him, Phainon,” Aglaea encourages gently when Phainon makes no move to enter Mydei’s chambers after being given permission. “Your company will do Mydeimos good.”

Castorice supports Aglaea’s claim with a nod of her own. “Kindly relay my regards to Lord Mydei on my behalf, Lord Phainon.”

Phainon nods, attempting to smile despite his inner turmoil. It’s a relief that Castorice didn’t point out his poor attempt to look composed. He turns his attention towards Mydei’s door and inhales sharply before Janus permits him passage.

The room smells of incense, warm and sweet with a tinge of spice as Phainon slowly made his way through a relatively short hallway, noting how the layout of the room was similar to his albeit the lack of decorations.

Sidestepping the partition, he then finds himself in the main sleeping area where a huge kline was situated in the middle, taking up a significant amount of the space.

The curtains that led to the balcony were drawn, Kephale’s Dawn bathing the room in a resplendent glow, the almost blinding light reflecting through the glinting golden eyes of someone whose attention now belongs to Phainon.

Mydei sat upright atop the kline with a blanket thrown haphazardly over his bare legs. He is dressed down in a loose red robe, unfastened, exquisitely exposing his torso that’s marred in streaks of scarlet.

His skin glistens with a hint of dampness, expectedly flawless and fair, but Phainon knew better than to assume that no pain belies the allure. The healers must have subjected him to a bath while they examined his state, a palliating method to ease the ghostly sting of a fatal injury.

From where he stands, Phainon couldn’t help but think that with or without the extravagance of armor, Mydei never fails to look formidable (and beautiful).

“I initially assumed that it would take you a day before you’d come to see me,” Mydei muses, interrupting Phainon from his unabashed staring. “Consider me mistaken.”

His tone suggests that he has time for jests, a blatant attempt to lighten the mood despite it being uncharacteristic of him. Rather unexpected as well considering how their earlier conversation had ended in a… rather odd note.

But who is Phainon to deny Mydei of anything?

“And why would you come up with such an assumption?” Phainon replies, a tease of his own. “Do you really think me to be heartless?”

Mydei shrugs, his robe sliding down his arm and exposing a bare shoulder in the process. Phainon’s gaze follows the gratuitous movement of the silk as it drags further down against tanned skin.

And swallows.

Even if Mydei parades himself around the city half-naked at all times, it feels as if this is Phainon’s first instance of witnessing Mydei in such a state of undress.

Perhaps it’s the lack of armor. Perhaps it’s Phainon being in Mydei’s private quarters, the two of them in each other’s presence with nary a witness that makes the situation seem more intimate than it should be.

“I thought you’d have an aversion to seeing me,” Mydei says, dragging his robe back up to clothe his exposed skin. Phainon mourns the loss but shall forever remember the vision. “I’ve been told that the sight of my death tends to be quite gruesome at times. Enough to render even you to tears, I suppose.”

Phainon sighs, shifting his weight from one foot to another. “The reason for my tears is not out of disgust. I weep simply because the loss of a friend causes me great sorrow.”

Silence follows, awkward and tense. Mydei refuses to meet Phainon’s gaze and Phainon allows his own to examine the room in an attempt to appear casual.

“Two months in and you still haven’t decorated your chambers?” Phainon asks, a diversion.

“I dislike such unnecessary opulence,” Mydei replies. “Despite my protests, the Goldweaver insisted that I stay here.”

Phainon huffs, amused. “A prince who steers clear of grandeur. I truly have seen it all.”

He then takes another look around the room even if he’s already committed every single detail to memory, enough to vividly paint the picture of Mydei’s chambers with his eyes closed. The lack of effects helps with it.

“How are you feeling, by the way?” It is a long overdue question, one that Phainon itched to ask since he stepped foot into the room.

“I’m alright,” Mydei answers.

“Still stubborn to the bone.”

A scoff. “I’m not being stubborn,” Mydei defends. “This curse is nothing new. I’ve lived with it my whole life.”

“Your curse is not yours to bear alone now,” Phainon says, an attempt to gradually ease his stance in regards to Mydei’s nonchalance in throwing his endless lives away. “Even if death is not something you worry about, I— We will make sure it’s something you won’t ever have to endure the pain of again.”

Mydei sighs. “I have no need for such reassurances, Deliverer. Death and battle go hand in hand together. It is a bitter cycle, one I know not the end of.”

“But you suffer.”

There’s a hint of a smile on Mydei’s lips, barely there. “It’s called a curse for a reason.”

Another bout of silence follows for Phainon is at a loss in determining how to appropriately respond. He feels helpless and conflicted, unsure if he should just succumb to acceptance like Mydei clearly has done, or maintain his resolve.

Does he even have the right to chastise Mydei in regards to his recklessness when it is not even his own body to have an opinion of? When does concern begin to cross the line and become overbearing?

“Are you so averse to the idea of a friend having your back?” Phainon finds himself asking. The waver in his voice couldn’t be concealed this time.

“You speak of our conversation from earlier,” Mydei says. It was not an answer. “You refer to yourself as a friend of mine and yet you stand so far away. Take a seat first.”

“There’s no seats anywhere,” Phainon points out graciously. Mydei is seriously in dire need of some decorating. “Not to mention, I thought you’d prefer it if I kept my distance.”

Mydei raises an eyebrow. “I fail to recall when I mentioned seats.”

“You’d like me to sit on the floor?” Phainon asks, unable to mask his incredulity.

A sigh follows, one that speaks volumes of Mydei’s exasperation. “On the bed, Deliverer.”

“I beg your finest pardon?”

“Sit on the bed,” Mydei orders with such finality that it is enough motivation for Phainon’s legs to get moving, stiffly making his way over to the foot of the kline before gingerly lowering himself onto the plush mattress.

He gives Mydei a smile, more grateful than it is uncomfortable. Mydei simply rolls his eyes.

“Don’t get used to it,” Mydei says.

“I shan’t dare to disrespect your hospitality.”

Phainon struggles to keep his gaze from wandering. Now in closer proximity, every detail of Mydei’s exposed skin seems all the more clearer, heightened only by the thin sheen of wetness from the bath.

Phainon resolves that anything below Mydei’s bare neck is something his eyes could only have a glimpse of once in a while with relatively long intervals in between. For his gaze to linger for far too long is infinitely bad for his well-being.

Actually, Mydei’s neck is just as alluring. Phainon thinks that wall behind Mydei is a much more suited spot for his eyes to rest on.

“Go on then,” Mydei urges, interrupting Phainon from his stupor. “Let’s talk. I’ll humor you this time and never again.”

Phainon would beg to differ for Mydei is always willing to indulge his curiosity, albeit in a way that’s far from what one might consider gentle.

“If my question was too personal, just say the word and we shall talk about something else,” Phainon says lightly, making it known that he won’t take offense in the event that Mydei refuses to answer.

“Between us, nothing is too personal anymore.”

Phainon’s mind blanks out, thinking he’d heard wrong because what, exactly, did Mydei mean by his words?

“I— Uh… Thanks?”

Mydei snorts. “If only to smoothen that crease in between your brows, sure. You’re welcome, Deliverer.”

“Does it bother you when I frown?” Phainon asks with a wry smile.

“Does this signify the beginning of your interrogation?”

“Perhaps,” Phainon simpers. A glare from Mydei is all it takes to set aside the jests. “But first, I’d like to thank you for saving my life. And I apologize for my behavior from earli—”

“No,” Mydei says sharply. “It was wrong of me to expect such a thing from you. I understand your intentions, Deliverer. You only wanted to help.”

Phainon didn’t have it in him to deny the statement. “Thank you for seeing things from my perspective.”

“I have thought about it thoroughly, and I’ll make it clear now that you’re worthy to have my back,” Mydei says. “And I yours.”

Phainon allows himself to relax, relief flooding his entire being like a tide that cleanses his perturbation. He can’t help but smile.

“That means a lot to me, Mydei,” he says, almost breathless. “As long as I’m around, I’ll make sure that no harm comes your way.”

Despite the blatant show of sincerity, Mydei’s severe expression remains. “It still doesn’t mean that I’ll permit you to lay down your life for me. The undying cannot die. You, on the other hand…”

“Not if I can help it.”

“How reassuring,” Mydei says drily. “If you die, I’ll scour the Sea of Souls for any and all traces of you. Thanatos Themself can’t stop me from bringing you back.”

Phainon blinks, utterly taken aback by such a declaration. “I— That’s—”

“And then I’ll kill you myself for dying in my stead,” Mydei finishes. “Do we have an agreement?”

Phainon allows himself to laugh. He should’ve expected something of the sort from Mydei. The threat does sound terrifying, but Phainon knows Mydei enough that his words are nothing but well-meaning. Despite the threat, the deluge in Phainon’s heart has calmed.

“We have an agreement,” Phainon replies, holding his hand out for Mydei to shake.

Somehow, it reminds Phainon of their first meeting in the Vortex of Genesis. Two months into their acquaintance and Phainon has already been granted permission to enter Mydei’s chambers.

If he told his past self that the crown prince of Kremnos would become one of his closest friends, he probably wouldn’t have believed it. And yet—

Mydei takes his hand this time, his skin is warm against Phainon’s. Unexpectedly smooth to the touch, almost like a scholar’s. Perhaps even a woman’s, although Phainon has lesser experience in that regard. He doesn’t exactly go around holding hands with women in his free time.

But the feel of Mydei’s bare hand against his—now free of those formidable golden gauntlets he always fashioned—is a memory that Phainon would never forget, precious and tucked away carefully into the inner crevices of his mind.

Mydei is the first to let go, and Phainon is thankful that the decision of withdrawing did not fall upon him. He fears that he might take too long simply ruminating about whether or not he would allow himself the displeasure of parting his own hand with Mydei’s. Even now, he already mourns the loss of warmth.

“I… don’t make promises I can’t keep,” Mydei began. This time, he avoids Phainon’s gaze, opting to set his sights on the view of Kephale’s imposing figure from the balcony instead. “But I’ll do my best to try and not subject you to the sight of my corpse again.”

Phainon frowns. “The sight of your corpse is far from being the reason as to why I don’t want you to die, Mydei.”

“You don’t have to lie, Deliverer. I know the sight of it appalls you.”

“It doesn’t,” Phainon insists, hoping that his sincerity would seep through. “Even as a corpse, you will never appall me. I just don’t want to see you in pain, that’s all.”

Mydei is unable to hide the traces of conflict on his face. He looked poised to argue, but seeing that Phainon didn’t seem too keen on backing down either, he decides against.

A sigh. “It’s a steep request. I’ll try not to die so easily next time, but I’m going to have you agree with me on one more thing.”

“Anything.”

“Your tears,” is all Mydei says. Seeing Phainon’s confused expression, he continues, “The sight of it misleads me.”

Phainon always thought that crying is an appropriate way to release emotions—frustration, sadness, and even joy. As a man, he never thought it to be embarrassing. Even Aglaea had commended him once for being able to express such extreme emotions, something that she’s not capable of apparently.

Perhaps the Kremnoans see tears as a sign of weakness. Given that Mydei has entrusted Phainon of watching his back, a blatant show of vulnerability might weaken Mydei’s resolve in thinking that Phainon is strong and worthy enough.

There’s nothing else left to do but to comply.

“Alright. I’ll try to rein in my emotions next time. But if you die again, I can’t promise that I won’t shed some tears.”

Mydei rolls his eyes. “Tears are precious,” he says. And though he may sound admonishing, Phainon couldn’t help but notice the hint of softness that belies the firm tone. “Don’t waste yours so carelessly. Especially not for my sake.”

Phainon sighs heavily, feigning reluctance. “If His Highness commands it, who am I to disobey?”

“I forgot how insufferable you are.”

“Does that mean you’ve found me quite agreeable for some time now?”

Mydei scoffs. “I abhor lies so I’ll choose not to answer that question.”

Phainon raises an eyebrow. “What about the question tempts you to lie?”

Instead of the expected scathing response, Mydei simply lies down and buries himself beneath the blanket. Phainon stares at the Mydei-shaped lump out of disbelief.

“You should leave,” came Mydei’s muffled voice after some time. “I’m rather exhausted.”

So Mydei chooses to retreat this time. Phainon doesn’t intend to push his teasing further.

“Do you wish for me to draw the drapes close?” Phainon asks, standing up from the bed.

“That won’t be necessary.”

That sounds like a goodbye more than anything. Phainon honors Mydei’s wishes and turns on his heel. But before he could enter the hallway that led to the door, he heard his name being called.

“Phainon.”

Phainon halts in his steps and turns to Mydei who has his head poked out of the blankets. It’s an endearing sight, one that causes Phainon to feel as if he’d just been punched in the gut.

“Yes?” Phainon asks weakly.

“Thank you for having my back,” Mydei says. There’s a hint of a smile on his lips, eyes of gold glistening against Kephale’s Dawn. “I’ll let you in on my story someday. Consider it as my thanks.”

Phainon sighs, unable to help a smile of his own. There’s no need, he wanted to say. But it would be a lie to do so for he is very much eager to learn more about Mydei, the person who’s managed to retain his curiosity consistently for the past two months.

And to respect the Kremnoan’s innate need for honor, Phainon shall only accept Mydei’s gratitude without complaint.

“I appreciate that,” Phainon responds earnestly. “I hope you get well soon, Mydei.”

Mydei nods lightly in return before settling back beneath the covers. This time, Phainon doesn’t linger.
