chapters.title: Chapter 4: might of a warrior, worth of a lover
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Phainon unknowingly tips the scales that signifies the equality he shares with Mydei. He offers something of profound weight, one that could only be balanced with affection.

fate season, month of balance

7 months before the present time

· · ─ ·𖥸· ─ · ·

To present one’s prey to a desired lover signifies the commencement of courtship. It is an essential tradition that our ancestors have faithfully adhered to since the Era Bellica, one that signifies a hunter’s might and capability to provide for one’s own during wartimes. The bigger and more magnificent the catch, the more worthy the hunter.

…gold and produce are acceptable rewards, but even better is the hand of the person bearing the hunter’s affections…

— an excerpt. Kremnoan Rituals of Courtship, Chapter 1: The Art of the Hunt

· · ─ · ─ · ·

Phainon thinks he’s had enough.

The Chrysos Heirs residing in the Marmoreal Palace typically convene for the deipnon before retiring to their chambers, right before the Parting Hour ends. For Phainon, it is a mealtime he used to look forward to the most.

That’s right. Used to.

The Heroes’ Mageiros, Sir Parmenion, was of old age and had subsequently fallen ill during the second week of the Month of Gate. Aglaea had then gave him his retirement notice in due haste so he could spend more time with his family and rest to recover his health.

It was Mydei who took up the mantle of Heroes’ Mageiros after that.

Having proven his prowess not only in battle, but also in the kitchen, the Chrysos Heirs allowed Mydei the pleasure of preparing their meals. Which meant that Phainon had to endure Mydei’s cooking for three full weeks now.

Emphasis on endure.

During Sir Parmenion’s time, the Chrysos Heirs shared the same meal. But Mydei took it upon himself to specifically prepare different ones in accordance to everyone’s tastes.

On Aglaea’s plate was a light serving of buttery white beans glazed in a rich tomato sauce mixed with delicately sliced garlic and onions. It is then topped with freshly picked herbs served with a side of horiatiki.

Castorice’s meal consisted of three bell peppers of generous size, almost akin to that of a child’s small fist, stuffed with a mix of seasoned rice, pine, nuts, raisins, and a variety of herbs. Mydei even took the liberty of garnishing the dish with fresh edible flowers, some of it sprinkled onto the yogurt that served as an appropriate pair for the meal.

The Holy Maidens, on the other hand, share a plate of doll-shaped puff pastries stuffed with sautéed spinach, leeks, and cream cheese, served with a side platter of apples, carrots, and celery stalks fancily cut into adorable little shapes.

Before Phainon could wallow in his envy, Mydei emerges from the doorway that led to the kitchen. He then sets his own meal down on his place at the dining table, which is just directly across from Phainon, before taking a seat.

Today, Mydei’s meal consists of a grilled chicken souvlaki with a side of tabbouleh, that’s made with a mix of bulgur wheat, tomatoes, parsley, and onion, tossed in both olive oil and lemon juice which made the salad glisten appetizingly.

Phainon looks down at his own meal and sighs.

He can’t even begin to try eloquently describing it. The food Mydei prepared for him is simply just a gray sludge on a plate. It’s not even a porridge, and there’s not a single slice of meat or vegetable in there.

In hindsight, it’s much better than yesterday's meal—which only consisted of a stick and nothing else. Phainon feels his stomach grumble in protest.

As the others began to dig in after muttering their prayers of gratitude to Phagousa and Georios, Phainon casts a glance towards Mydei in front of him before clearing his throat. It is effective in garnering the attention of the man.

“Mydei,” Phainon began. Today is the day he takes a stand. “Did you perhaps serve me an entrée of quality grade cement drizzled with the shimmering slush of a dromas’ saliva?”

Mydei couldn’t even be bothered to put up an irritated front, or perhaps ruthlessly admonish Phainon for choosing such insulting descriptions for a meal he personally prepared. In light of the circumstance, he looked rather calm. Unnervingly so.

“An astute observation,” is all Mydei could say. And then he takes a bite of his chicken.

Phainon is going to lose his mind.

“Are you serious? I have to fend off the Titankin terrorizing the northwest border after this, from the Curtain-Fall Hour to tomorrow’s Entry Hour,” Phainon laments, rather desperate. “As the Heroes’ Mageiros, at least give me something decent to eat so I don’t collapse due to malnutrition while I fulfill my duties.”

The volume of his voice had risen unintentionally, the last of his words echoing throughout the marble walls of the Grand Dining Hall. Everyone had ceased partaking in their meal. With the exception of Aglaea, Castorice and the Holy Maidens have evidently grown tense in their seats.

Despite the simmering conflict, Mydei simply raises an eyebrow at Phainon, clearly unbothered by the sudden outburst. Phainon feels shame creep up on him and sighs, looking away.

“I… apologize.”

He throws a quick glance at Mydei’s way only to find that the other’s eyebrow still remains to be raised, urging Phainon to continue.

Phainon does so, like a puppet on a string with nary an agency to his own actions. “My gratefulness knows no bounds for having you, Mydei, take the time to provide a…” Phainon trails off in favor of swallowing thickly as he stares at the contents of his plate. Indeed, it still looks disgusting. “...very delightful looking meal just for me.”

Mydei hums, satisfied. Phainon sends his prayers to all the Titans who are willing to set aside time from Their busy schedules of either being dead or wallowing in their madness just to listen to his woes.

Even the ever so merciful Kephale would turn Their back away from this abomination of a meal; Okhema would no longer know Dawn if They were to consume Mydei’s creation as an offering. Not to mention, the gray sludge on Phainon’s plate looked as if it’s only moments away from possessing its own sentience.

Perhaps it would be better for Phainon’s blade to end the existence of this unnamed atrocity. That, or he should just set fire to the entire thing.

But at the end of the day, it is still Mydei’s creation. Mydei prepared it specifically for him. How could he dare think of such disrespectful methods of discarding Mydei’s cooking instead of just handling the matter properly?

“Mydei,” Phainon calls out again, gentler this time. He can’t give up. Tomorrow, he’ll be subjected to the same sickening torment of being fed things that are not even edible. He has to put a stop to this nonsense now. “There must be some other dish I could eat, yesterday’s leftovers perhaps?”

“There are no leftovers,” Mydei replies curtly without missing a beat.

Phainon catches his bottom lip between his teeth, rethinking his approach. “Anything. I’ll eat anything—”

“Then why bother looking for something else? Partake in what has been served.”

“I’ll eat anything that won’t kill a fully-grown human with divine blood running through his veins,” Phainon reiterates firmly. “Yesterday, you made me eat a stick.”

“The stick had leaves, Deliverer,” Mydei graciously points out. “Or are you so blinded by your concerns, so much so that you choose to dwell fervidly on the misfortunes instead of the blessings?”

Phainon scoffs. “That’s your argument? Mydei, it’s been so long since I had a proper meat stew. Ask me what meat tastes like and I’ll undoubtedly fail to answer.”

His itinerary was quite full today so he didn’t have the time to take a trip down to the Marmoreal Market and purchase something to eat from Kyros. To say that Phainon was starving would be an understatement. He could eat a whole dromas in one sitting at this point.

Mydei gives him an unimpressed look, gaze dropping to the pile of gray mush on his plate. Phainon swears he saw a hint of a smirk grace Mydei’s lips, only for it to be gone as quickly as it had appeared.

“I can’t make anything else,” Mydei simpers, dabbing the corners of his lips with a napkin. What a prince. “We’ve run out of meat, you see. Hence, why I had to forgo it when preparing your meal.”

Phainon feels his eye twitch.

Mydei’s been forgoing meat when it comes to preparing Phainon’s meal since he became the Heroes’ Mageiros. Correction, Phainon does remember eating something of the sort one time, but the steak was rather blue and he swears there were maggots crawling and making a home on the surface.

(“Mydei, can I even eat this?” Phainon asks wrily, eyeing the little maggot that had begun to crawl up his fork. Goosebumps erupt on his skin as he feels bile rise up to his throat.

“You have a mouth don’t you?” Mydei asks in turn, an irritated non-answer. “And you’re capable of digestion.”

Phainon made the toilet his home after that incident. Thankfully, Mydei never served him anything that involved live crawlies and spoiled steak. Together, that is.)

“The Heroes’ Pantry… ran out of meat?” Phainon repeats, disbelief etched in his tone.

There has never been such an instance in the long history of the Flame-Chase Journey. A most unfortunate circumstance indeed. Even Phainon, who barely steps foot into the Marmoreal Palace’s kitchen, knew that the Heroes’ Pantry is always well-stocked with various ingredients, fresh and of the finest quality even.

For it to run out of meat—

“I’m not entirely opposed to a meatless dish,” Phainon counters with a frown, sullen with how he must come to terms with the fact that his expectations ought to be lowered a bit more. “Did you also perhaps run out of vegetables for a small salad?”

Mydei pretends to think about it in a manner that is so evidently spurious. Phainon itches to call him out for being so difficult beyond belief.

“I’m not sure,” Mydei muses, humming lightly. “Maybe if you apologize sincerely for what you did yesterday, I could be impelled to go ahead and start planting some lettuce for you. If I’m not mistaken, it should be ready when the Month of Joy comes around, as most harvests are.”

And there it is. Suddenly it all makes sense. So that’s what this is about.

“I told you it was an accident,” Phainon reasons.

Mydei nods, even if he looked the furthest from being convinced. “How else could it be seen as? You, on a dromas’ back, laughing with great amusement whilst your finger had so tauntingly pointed at me—”

“Listen—”

“—who’s covered in mud of which you and your dromas had so kindly splattered.”

The Grand Dining Hall was almost quiet. Phainon hears Castorice gasp softly at the revelation, the anxious murmurs of the Holy Maidens, and Aglaea… Well, she had far more important things to do (like finishing her meal) than to be invested in the squabbles of two Chrysos Heirs.

Mydei looked smug, assuming that he had claimed the upper hand. Unfortunately for him, Phainon won’t go down so easily without at least defending himself.

“I was high up!” Phainon exclaims. “How was I supposed to know that there was a puddle of mud beside you?”

“Really?” The corners of Mydei’s lips quirk upward in a mean smile. “If that’s the case, it’s either you forgot that dromases are not allowed in an area exclusively for foot traffic, or you deliberately navigated your dromas to stomp five times on a mud puddle that’s in the middle of the market, right where I was standing.”

Phainon falters. “Dorothea is a…” He clears his throat, mustering conviction. “Dorothea is a very spirited dromas! How could I possibly ever hope to control her with a leash? And I only approached you because I wanted you to meet her!”

The reasoning is true. To some extent.

Dorothea is a dromas that Phainon has known since her hatching. Now that she’s mature enough to have a saddle on her back, the caretakers thought it appropriate for Phainon to be her first passenger.

The skies of yesterday were clear and Kephale’s Dawn shone warm golden light upon Okhema, no hint of clouds or rain. During their leisurely tour around the city, they passed by the outskirts of the Marmoreal Market where Phainon’s eyes were immediately drawn to the sight of blonde hair dipped in crimson, exposed tan skin marred in scarlet streaks, and the blood red fabric of the garments a certain Kremnoan crown prince fashioned from the distance.

Phainon thought that Mydei might appreciate sharing the honor of being one of Dorothea’s first passengers. That assumption, however, was thrown out of the window when Phainon lost control of Dorothea.

The mud puddle had been too tempting to play with for a dromas still new in her maturity. Dorothea’s youth remains, to the chagrin of one oblivious Chrysos Heir who had to unfortunately bear the consequence of the dromas’ merrymaking.

Phainon is not entirely innocent either. The sight of Mydei, who never fails to appear regal in any and every circumstance, drenched in mud with a disbelieving scowl on his face was enough for Phainon to put even Phagousa in shame for the extent of his laughter.

The rest was history.

(Mydei had subsequently dangled Phainon by the neck atop a nearby cliff with the threat of dropping the latter to his death. Phainon had apologized many times whilst gasping for air, still unable to hold his snickers at the sight of Mydei’s fair face soiled with mud, eyes of gold sharp and blazing with barely concealed fury.

Thankfully, both Kremnoan and Okheman soldiers managed to pry the two Chrysos Heirs away from each other before Phainon could experience the feeling of being subjected to the Hand of Shadow’s cold embrace.)

“I already said I was sorry,” Phainon says.

“People tend to speak nonsense when put through dire circumstances,” Mydei replies pointedly. “How should I know if you sincerely meant the apology you offered?”

“Mydei, I’m really sorry.”

Mydei lets the apology hang in the air for a moment. Eventually, he nods. “It’s acceptable enough.”

The sigh of relief that escaped the lips of the others in the room was too loud than what should be considered as normal. The resumption of the clinking sound of utensils molded from gold against the ivory plates is an indication that the unwilling eavesdroppers have resumed to partake in their meals.

The calamity was quelled, Phainon and Mydei have made peace with each other without the need for violence. It would be a shame if the Grand Dining Hall were to be reduced to mere ruins.

Only, Phainon knew Mydei well enough to distinguish if he was truly forgiven. The insistent avoidance of Mydei’s gaze was one clear sign that he’s still sporting some unsettled grievances.

Phainon wears a strained smile on his lips, willing to put Mydei’s adamance to appear indifferent to the test. “Now that we’ve settled the matter, can I have a salad?”

Mydei gives him a dry look, still undeniably cross despite Phainon’s attempts to convey his genuine remorse. Three months into their acquaintance, Phainon is slowly, but surely, finding it easier to read Mydei like an unfurled scroll.

“It would be disrespectful to the meal if I were to leave my seat without finishing it just to make you a salad, Deliverer.”

“It wouldn’t be so much of an issue if you didn’t forbade me from stepping foot in the kitchen,” Phainon retorts. “I could go and make myself a salad right now. Only if you’d promise not to tie me up on a stake and hover me above an open flame like you did the last time you spotted me barely walking through the kitchen’s doorway.”

“I’ve heard a lot from Sir Parmenion, questionable explosions and all.” Mydei smirks, finding amusement in Phainon’s kitchen failures without so much as acknowledging the serious allegations thrown against him. “It was ever a wonder how he’s never able to reach the limit of his forbearance with you running amok. You won’t be having the same privilege with me around.”

Phainon, for the first time during the entire exchange, finds himself at a loss for what to respond. He considered Sir Parmenion as his close friend and even confided in him. How could the old man have the heart to easily betray him like this by speaking of the many incidents he had a hand in to his rival?

Seeing Phainon’s distress, Mydei uses the opportunity to press on. Utterly merciless.

“Eat what I have prepared for you,” Mydei says, his tone firm enough for the normal folk to understand that there’s no room for negotiations. “It is by Talanton’s guidance that I get you back for vexing me yesterday.”

Not belonging to the category of normal folk mentioned above, Phainon simply rolls his eyes. “That still doesn’t explain every horrible meal I’ve had since you took over the kitchen. I couldn’t have vexed you all those times to earn such a horrible treatment.”

At this point, it almost sounds as if Phainon is whining. To fight for a decent meal in exchange for his dignity sounds plausible enough. Rather unnecessary, though.

Mydei drops his knife and fork upon hearing Phainon’s words, eyebrows furrowed together. “Why don’t you take a guess?”

That sounds more like a, You are indeed the source of my aggravation in all of those occasions. How dare you think otherwise.

“Is that an accusation I hear?” Phainon questions, feigning offense. “Are you not averse to the idea of listing it all down, then? Do you have some sort of hidden record detailing all of my misdeeds upon your person?”

Mydei scoffs, a glint of something dangerous in his eyes. “You speak of proof? Pipe down, Deliverer, or you’ll end up humiliating yourself.”

“The Month of Balance demands fairness in honor of Talanton,” Phainon insists. “During these past three weeks, I’ve let you get away with more than what most would consider hardly fair.”

“Don’t you speak of fairness in my presence.”

“Why not? Are you perhaps horrified that you’ve gone too far with your so-called revenge against my so-called offenses against you?”

Mydei laughs sardonically. “I do have a record. I would show it to you but the dining table of five dromases in length is not long enough to accommodate the scroll in its unfurled entirety.” He then takes a sip from his cup, no doubt containing his beloved honey brew. Phainon can’t even be granted the honor of partaking in a glass of water. “Now, eat your food.”

“And die of poison?”

“It’s not poisoned.”

Phainon crosses his arms, leaning back on his chair. Sarcastically, he says, “Right. Because you tasted it.”

Mydei nods lightly, giving Phainon a small pleased smile. The beauty of it might be enough to quell Phainon’s feelings of injustice, but it is his hunger for a warm, decent meal that steels his resolve.

“Of course I tasted it,” Mydei admits as if it was the most obvious thing in the world, nothing out of the ordinary or anything.

Upon hearing this, everyone had stopped eating once again. Phainon can feel the others’ attention land on the gray abomination on his plate before their gazes dart at Mydei, who had apparently managed to stomach the atrocious thing and live to tell the tale.

Well. Mydei is not exactly capable of dying now, is he?

“It tastes horrible,” Mydei says, an answer to the unspoken question that hung palpably in the air. “Far more than how it looks in my proud opinion.”

Phainon could not believe his ears, eyes wide and almost bulging out of their sockets as his mouth laid open out of pure shock. He feels very faint. Aghast, he turns to Aglaea who was currently just finishing up the last remaining crumbs of her meal.

“Aglaea, are you hearing this man?” Phainon asks, almost like a plea.

Aglaea’s clouded gaze looks up. She turns to Mydei with a smile of her own. “Mydeimos, dinner was magnificent as always.”

Castorice nods, her own plate empty. “The taste of life on my tongue is the most pleasant sensation. Thank you kindly for this meal, Lord Mydei.”

“You’ve really outdone yourself this time, De!” Trianne exclaims, giving Mydei a thumbs up.

“Yes. I think this meal is one of my favorites now,” agreed Tribbie.

Trinnon is still munching on her share of the puff pastry so she couldn’t quite convey her opinions just yet.

Mydei says nothing in return at the sudden shower of praise, simply continuing his meal with a hint of pink coloring his face and the tips of his ears that don’t go unnoticed by Phainon’s keen observation.

Beside Mydei, Phainon catches Castorice looking at him and gestures for her to help. They’re close after all, surely Castorice would take Phainon’s side in this argument. Her sympathy would mean the world to him.

Unfortunately, Phainon’s initial expectations of their friendship were for naught, as Castorice only smiles lightly before taking a sip of her drink. Evidently, she’s not willing to get caught in the middle of Phainon and Mydei’s petty dispute.

Phainon sighs heavily, utterly defeated, betrayed by his own kin that he even considers as family. He picks up his spoon before taking out a relative amount from the gray sludge. With a shaky hand, he brings the foul-smelling curse of nature to his lips, taking a small bite with his eyes closed.

Miserably, he does agree that the food tastes as bad as it looks. What Phainon would give for a thin slab of meat at this moment.

The battle against the Titankin at the northwest border of Okhema waged for much longer than Phainon would have liked. By the second quint of the Lucid Hour, he was finished. And by the fourth quint of the Action Hour did he find himself at Okhema’s city gates.

With sweat beading upon his forehead, Phainon huffs and puffs as he drags the heavy carcass of the boar king that once resided in the forests of Okhema’s northwest border.

Aglaea had expressed her displeasure countless times when news of the boar king wreaking havoc upon her defenses were made known by the golden threads. Since Phainon was already in the area, he took it upon himself to hit two birds with one stone—ease Aglaea from her worries, and hunt for a decent meat source so Mydei wouldn’t have an excuse to claim the lack of it.

The carcass is as wide as three fully-grown dromases standing closely side by side, and as tall as a two-storey building. To say that Phainon takes delight in having to drag it by a rope in such a long distance would be an utter lie. He wonders how Mydei would react to the sight of it.

The shadow of the boar king’s carcass looms over the path as Phainon makes his way further into the city. The civilians passing by halt in their daily ministrations to point and stare out of pure astonishment, heads poking out of the windows of their homes to witness the scene, and some even had their teleslates out to record Phainon dragging the massive thing by his lonesome.

Phainon pays them no mind, only smiling occasionally at those who call his name in greeting. He’s too exhausted to even talk, and if he stops to rest while in the middle of this arduous task, there’s no guarantee that he’ll be able to continue afterwards.

His body aches from the exertion, the rope he holds on to that is tied to the boar king rubbing his palms raw and causing blisters to form in its wake. Rapidly blinking away the sting of sweat as it drips down onto his eyes, Phainon reminds himself once again of why he’s doing something so outrageously over-the-top.

Given the time of day, Mydei should be by the training grounds with the soldiers of the Kremnoan detachment. It’s not that far away now. If Phainon doesn’t collapse on the way, he might arrive just after the commencement of the Action Hour's final quint.

His calculations were not far off. As the bell tolls signalling the beginning of a new quint, Phainon is already by the entrance to the courtyard that led to the training grounds. There were Kremnoans stationed by the path and they, too, balked at the sight of the massive boar that Phainon was dragging.

“Good day,” Phainon greets, trying to keep his voice steady as he wipes the sweat on his face with the back of his hand. “Where’s your prince?”

“His Highness is currently keeping the children occupied while the soldiers take their break,” one of the bewildered Kremnoan replies. “You can head on in, Lord Phainon. His Highness would be pleased to see you return with such an impressively glorious catch.”

Phainon would beg to differ about Mydei being pleased to see him in this state—unrefined and sweating buckets, on the verge of collapse.

With a grunt, Phainon resumes his journey of dragging the carcass further in until he reaches the vast area where warriors hailing from different nations who had now sought refuge in the holy city keep their combat prowess sharp and refined.

Upon Phainon’s arrival, the bustle of activity gradually stops as the warriors gawk at what he had just brought.

“Did Lord Phainon catch that by himself?”

“My goodness! As expected of a Chrysos Heir!”

“That beast is enough to feed a hundred men for a month!”

Phainon scans the murmuring crowd for any signs of a blonde haired, half-dressed man in red. By the group of children near the well, Phainon’s gaze met that of Mydei’s who looked equally as stupefied as the rest of the people in the area.

Gritting his teeth, Phainon resumes to pull upon the boar king’s heavy weight behind him until he stands right in front of the other. The shadow cast by the huge carcass looms over Mydei, a rather comical sight that makes him appear quite small.

Phainon bites back a laugh at Mydei’s clear astonishment, uncharacteristic and precious.

“Heard you ran out of meat so I brought some back,” Phainon says cheekily, trying to keep his voice stable enough to appear as if he’s not moments away from biting the dust.

Mydei continues to stare at the fallen beast behind Phainon with eyes as wide as saucers and lips slightly parted.

When Mydei finally humors Phainon with a reply, all that comes out of his lips is an angry, “What are you playing at, Deliverer?”

The response is not unexpected. Phainon knew Mydei would take offense now that he lacked the liberty of making excuses to continue tormenting Phainon with outrageous meals.

“Don’t you like it?” Phainon teases, a hand firmly tapping the boar’s snout as he grins proudly. “He’s very hard to catch, you know. But I still prevailed in the end, obviously. Now you can’t skimp out on the meat when preparing my food.”

Mydei’s frown only deepens, his gaze darting between Phainon and the boar king. The furrow on his eyebrows conveys that he’s thinking way too hard about something. How Phainon wishes to have but a mere glimpse at the inner workings of Mydei’s mind.

After a while of gaping, Mydei starts talking again. “You—” His voice wavers. “Are you sure about this?”

Is Phainon sure that he’s willing to eat boar meat up until the time where the methods of preserving it have run its course?

“Deadly sure,” Phainon affirms with a nod.

He knows of Mydei’s creativity in the kitchen. The man can craft a dish using the same ingredients and make it different every time. Phainon is convinced he won’t ever get tired of eating just boar meat.

At his answer, he hears the murmurs grow louder, distinctively coming from the Kremnoan soldiers that are currently witnessing the exchange. Before Phainon could glean on what they’re discussing hushly amongst themselves, his attention was caught by the sound of Mydei clearing his throat.

“You…” Mydei sighs. He looks flustered for some reason. Perhaps it was due to the exertion of training. “You can’t take this back, Deliverer.”

Phainon wonders why Mydei even expected him to return a dead, massive, and heavy boar king back to its home forest when Phainon almost keeled over from the exhaustion alone of hauling the boar to the holy city by foot without assistance.

“Do you actually want me to die?” Phainon asks incredulously. Mydei doesn’t hate him that much, does he? Regardless if they argue on the daily, they’re still friends—Phainon’s closest one, even.

Mydei only rolls his eyes at the dramatics. “I suppose you do possess some modicum of honor and self-preservation.”

He then brushes past Phainon in favor of inspecting the catch, poking at the meat and examining the kill method—of which Phainon made sure was clean and humane. After a brief nod and a satisfied hum, Mydei turns his attention back at the hunter who gloats in the success of his hunt.

“This is acceptable,” Mydei remarks. Phainon feels himself preen at the praise. “Come and assist me with cutting this up and I shall make you something decent with it.”

The victorious smile that graces Phainon’s lips can’t be helped at all. Finally. All of his hard work had not been in vain. Today marks the end of his suffering.

The Kremnoans offer their assistance in transporting the boar to the Marmoreal Palace, of which Phainon is eternally grateful for. The perks of being friends with a prince is not something to be taken for granted indeed.

Once the flesh was separated from bone and the meat divided into an astounding number of sections, it was then salted, smoked, pickled, and whatever other methods Mydei could come up with on the fly to ensure that the meat would last months in the cellar.

After such an extensive labor, Phainon is rewarded with a piping hot, boar meat stew that had been slowly cooked in a clay pot over an open flame, mixed with fresh herbs and spices as well as a generous variety of vegetables.

The taste alone is enough to make up for the three months of eating literal scum. Phainon then conveys his sentiments to Mydei who sat across from him with a smug expression as he watched Phainon utterly devour the meal he prepared.

“Cross me again and you’ll suffer the consequences,” Mydei threatens without much heat.

“Not if I have my dinner beforehand at the Marmoreal Diner,” Phainon chimes, relishing in the savory taste of the stew that lingers on his tongue. “Kyros agreed to stay open until the first quint of the Parting Hour just to accommodate me.”

Mydei’s scowl doesn’t go unnoticed as he leaves his seat and stomps away, grumbling Kremnoan curses under his breath.

The next day, there’s a dead bug on Phainon’s plate.

Thankfully, with enough coaxing, Phainon is able to convince Mydei to serve him something else. Mydei then re-emerges from the kitchen barely even a moment later with a plate containing slices of boar meat sausages paired nicely with grilled zucchini, eggplant, and tomatoes, as well as a generous serving of orzo pilaf, seasoned with fresh herbs and a light drizzle of lemon juice.

Phainon surmises that Mydei couldn’t have possibly managed to put together such an elaborate dish in that little amount of time. The only possibility is—

“Mydei, did you already have this prepared beforehand?”

Mydei’s glare is sharp and searing. “Shut up and start eating before I stuff this up your arse and make you undergo a reverse digestion.”

Tearfully, Phainon obediently does as he’s told.

Despite the Month of Balance being a time where crime is not so rampant, it doesn’t mean that humans, who are made in Kephale’s likeness, possessed Their flawless nature. The urge to do wrong is innate in every person, and every tip against the balance of good and evil only serves to insult the Scale of Justice’s principles.

News of theft has been running rampant all across the holy city and the alleged offenders are none other than the group of people who harbors most, if not all, of Okhema’s prejudice—the Kremnoan detachment.

Dragging along a cart filled with supplies behind him, Phainon makes his way towards the settlement that housed Mydei’s people. Three months in and they seem to be adjusting relatively well. Dwellings were built substantially with clay and wood, the sight of tents are sparse indicating stability, farmland is thriving with fertile soil and bountiful produce, and animals are aflock and herded behind fences.

Despite the seemingly harmonious atmosphere, Phainon could sense the heaviness of anxiety and tension in the air.

As he trudged down the path, Phainon could feel the eyes of the Kremnoans upon him, the skin at the back of his neck prickling at the attention. On a regular day, they would’ve said something in greeting, or perhaps even stop Phainon on the way for a quick chat.

None of that happens, Phainon’s amicable relationship with the Kremnoans regrettably placed behind the agitation stemming from the injustice of their current circumstance.

Thankfully, he was able to spot Mydei shortly after his arrival, standing in front of a house and engaged in conversation with a woman carrying a small child. He could tell that Mydei already knew of his approach by the way his shoulders have become tense and how he subsequently bade goodbye to the woman once Phainon was within earshot.

“What are you doing here, Deliverer?” is Mydei’s way of saying hello.

“I heard the people of Okhema are giving you trouble,” Phainon answers.

Mydei scoffs. “Well, what did you expect when that thrice-damned ornament keeps on spreading falsehoods about me and my tribe? I swear by Talanton, the thievery case going around was not our doing.”

Of course it’s not. Kremnoans are no followers of Zagreus. They have honor to uphold and wouldn’t resort to such underhanded methods just to ease their daily lives. If anything, the Kremnoan detachment ought to be the furthest from being considered as suspects.

“I already spoke to the Verax Leos about that,” Phainon assures. “Aglaea is making sure that your name is being cleared at the moment.”

Mydei only scoffs. He then catches sight of the cart behind Phainon, filled with crates containing produce, meat, clothes, and even weapons. The furrow in his eyebrows only grows all the more prominent.

“What’s this?” Mydei asks, almost a demand.

Phainon scratches his nape sheepishly. “These are for you and your people. Consider it to be recompense.”

Mydei huffs, seemingly offended. “I don’t need you spending your riches so excessively on something you need not care about,” he hisses.

“Why wouldn’t I care? I know the state of your tribe is important to you. You’re important to me so, by extension, this issue bothers me just as much,” Phainon says, hoping that his sincerity would seep through. “I even had to go around scolding the vendors for denying you purchase.”

The look of conflict on Mydei’s face is evident, poised to turn down Phainon’s efforts to help. Phainon wishes that Mydei would just set aside his pride and stop shouldering all of his burdens alone. Accepting assistance is not a sign of weakness, after all.

Perhaps Phainon’s sentiments are able to be read through his face, or maybe Mydei just knew what Phainon would say the moment that he so much as dismisses the aid being graciously handed out without him having to ask.

“You have my thanks,” Mydei says, his resignation palpable enough, well aware of how persistent Phainon could be and deemed that he neither possessed the time nor the energy to deal with that. “Rest assured, I will pay you back.”

Phainon smiles wryly. They’ve been over this back and forth before. “You need not to.”

“I insist,” Mydei says, a hand on Phainon’s shoulder in a flash.

The sudden contact catches Phainon off-guard for Mydei is not known to initiate physical touches so often. Despite the formidable gauntlet Mydei wore, the touch remains to be gentle, his body’s insistence to express gratitude betraying the tough exterior he intends to put up. Phainon can’t help but find this involuntary gesture endearing to a fault.

Given Mydei’s expression, it seemed likely that he, too, knew not of the answer for such an uncharacteristic act. He then withdraws his hand immediately. Phainon hopes that his own displeasure at the loss of contact is not that perceptible to be observed so easily.

Mydei coughs, face and ears coloring beautifully in varying shades of pink and red. “My apologies.”

“It’s okay,” Phainon says, wondering why he sounds so out of breath all of sudden, rendered weak by a mere hand on his shoulder.

Mydei’s hand.

“I didn’t know what came over me,” Mydei continues.

Phainon nods. “Yeah. I know.”

Mydei frowns. “You know?”

“No! I—” Phainon makes an attempt to rearrange his thoughts and hopes desperately that his words don’t come out so garbled. “I mean, it’s alright.”

“What is?”

“This.”

Phainon does a nondescript gesture referring to the space between him and Mydei. He wanted to convey that it’s alright for two men to engage in platonic shoulder pats. They’ve sparred countless times before, now familiar with every crevice and valley of muscle, how it tenses with every movement, the strength of every jab.

A hand on the shoulder should be the last thing to cause alarm. It is rather unnecessary to stress about, and frankly, doesn’t make quite a lot of sense.

Even if Mydei looked as if he had a lot of questions in his mind, he opted not to pursue the matter anymore, a sigh escaping his lips.

“Forgive me for my lack of interest in inquiring any further details that would serve as an explanation to your confusing replies of profound brevity,” Mydei states drily. The formality in the way he spoke hints that something is amiss. “If that is all, Deliverer, I must excuse myself now for I still have supplies to distribute.”

Mydei walks over to the cart, his gait lacking the signature self-assured swagger and appearing more exhausted than anything. The odd sight causes concern to spread within Phainon like a ripple in the water. Unable to help himself, he catches Mydei’s arm in his hand, keeping the other in place.

Now closer in their proximity, he is able to notice the dullness in Mydei’s eyes of gold, the paleness of his complexion, and the slump on his shoulders. He looked indubitably spent, the dark circles beneath his eyes more prominent than usual.

“Mydei, when was the last time you slept?”

Mydei doesn’t even try to wrestle his arm out of Phainon’s hold. He has simply given up. Phainon wonders about the extent of his weariness, or perhaps Mydei is simply calling it even between them from when he inadvertently initiated physical contact from earlier.

None of those reasons are favorable in Phainon’s opinion. It is a selfish and depraved thought that Mydei simply allows himself to bask in Phainon’s touch just because he wanted to. Impossible and unprincipled, Phainon wonders just where these thoughts are coming from.

“Two days ago,” Mydei answers, pulling Phainon out of his restless spiral.

Two days ago, Phainon thought to himself. Mydei did not know rest since two days ago.

Before Phainon could even begin to express his disapproval, Mydei continues, “That woman whom I was talking to earlier is with child. Due to the rumors flying around about my tribe engaging in thievery, she and her husband were unable to procure adequate sustenance to ensure the health of their family and the baby she’s carrying. I’ve been helping them and many others in need of my assistance since, and have yet to take a rest.”

“If that’s the case, you should go back to the Marmoreal Palace,” Phainon urges, unable to hide his distress. He never expected the consequences of the rumors to be so dire. “I’ll send someone to distribute the supplies in your stead.”

“Save your breath, Deliverer. No Okheman would be willing to help us.”

“By my word, they will,” Phainon declares through gritted teeth. “And I’ll be making it clear that there’ll be no room for any sort of opposition.”

He notices a brief sign of discomfort grace Mydei’s features, gone in an instant in a mere blink of an eye. Phainon then realizes belatedly that his grip on Mydei’s arm had tightened significantly.

Phainon lets go of Mydei, the feelings of shame and regret unpleasant and bitter, but not entirely unfounded.

“Mydei, I’m sorry.”

“I’m far from being fragile, Deliverer,” Mydei replies, his tone light and without a hint of resentment. “It was nothing. Your grip is still far too weak to cause me pain.”

Phainon allows himself to laugh, relief bathing him anew and causing his misgivings to be washed away when Mydei throws him a small smile, radiant despite his obvious fatigue. Perhaps Phainon had been worried for nothing. Mydei is ever so kind, ever so benevolent.

The bell tolls from afar, signalling that the first quint of the Parting Hour is upon them. Only then does Phainon remembers his initial commitments before he made his way to the Kremnoan detachment’s settlement by the city’s outskirts.

He turns to Mydei. “I’ll send someone to help.”

This time, Mydei does not argue. “Very well.”

“I would be more inclined to help you myself but—” Aglaea’s blank expression makes its way in Phainon’s mind, reminding him of his duties to Amphoreus. “Aglaea is sending me away on another mission.”

Phainon knew that Mydei understood more than anyone that duty should always come first above anything else. He hopes that Mydei won’t hold his absence in these trying times against him.

Mydei doesn’t, as expected. And Phainon almost wishes that he’d put up some sort of protest if only to get Phainon to stay. It would be an entertaining display, for sure.

“You’ve done enough by providing my people with these supplies,” Mydei says, nodding at the cart. He then turns to Phainon. “May Janus bless the paths you take, may Talanton guide your blade fair and true, and may the sane Nikador allow you to keep your courage even in the face of many dangers.”

Phainon huffs out a breathy chuckle, almost out of disbelief more than anything. He never imagined Mydei to wish him luck in such a way. This is a first.

“Why, with your blessings, I’m most certain that I’ll be able to slay the most powerful Titankin there is!” Phainon proclaims, his confidence abound that he barely remembers to keep it in check lest he appear vain in front of the man who abhors it more than anything.

Mydei doesn’t seem to mind, finding amusement in the situation instead.

“Foolish,” Mydei admonishes with fond futility. “It is unbecoming to be a man who is all talk and no action. Go ahead and bring back the proof of your successful endeavor, I dare you.”

Phainon only grins. “Is that a challenge?”

Upon Phainon’s return the next day, he gifts Mydei the proof that he seeks—a magnificent trophy he procured from slaying the most exalted Titankin he encountered during his mission.

The golden wheeled blade that was once carried by the minacious Furiae Praetor shimmers against the light of Kephale’s Dawn as Mydei takes its heavy weight in his hands to examine carefully.

The scratches on its surface is as a manifestation of the purpose it has served at the hands of its former master, one of which Phainon considers nothing less of a formidable adversary.

“A Harbinger of Strife,” Mydei notes breathlessly.

“No need to be so impressed,” Phainon teases. “I do believe that you’re equally as capable of accomplishing the same feat yourself.”

Mydei rolls his eyes. “Only the Furiae Praetors who have earned Nikador’s recognition are permitted to carry a Harbinger of Strife.” He readjusts his grip on the object. “And you even managed to extricate it so fully without compromising its delicate shape.”

Phainon feels as if he ought to be scared. Something’s not right. “What’s up with you today?”

“What do you mean?”

“You’re being too nice,” Phainon answers earnestly, faking a shiver as he wraps his arms around himself out of defense. Even if Mydei’s praises are music to his ears, he can’t deny that there’s something unsettling going on at the moment. “Are you sick? Have you been drinking the water from the baths again?”

Mydei’s aggrieved expression is so pronounced that it’s almost funny, rendered speechless at Phainon’s outrageous accusation.

“You—” He scoffs before resolutely turning his back on Phainon, poised to take his leave. “Insufferable. I can’t believe that it’s you, of all people.”

Phainon watches with bewilderment as Mydei stomps away, carrying with him Phainon’s trophy that’s held so tightly by his hands that one might assume he’s loath to part with it.

Scratching the back of his head, Phainon is left to stand alone right where Mydei left him, mulling over their exchange with a frown. He ponders that perhaps Mydei was simply in no mood to indulge in his jests.

With a shrug, Phainon makes his way towards the Marmoreal Palace to report the success of his task to Aglaea whom he surmises must be wearing thin in her patience for he was supposed to return a quint earlier.

Mydeimos is hardly the person you should seek first and foremost after a mission, Phainon can already hear her say. If you wish for Mydeimos to take up the mantle as the leader of the Chrysos Heirs, then by all means make your sentiments known. This duty of mine is not something I fulfill out of self-indulgence alone.

Phainon readies his apology with dread. He hopes that Aglaea would choose to be merciful this time.

· · ─ ·𖥸· ─ · ·

How to Appraise a Suitor’s Trophy

(Kremnoan Standard)

…only one worthy of Kremnoan’s hand can challenge the most fearsome of opponents single-handedly…

…even a small fragment of a Furiae Praetor’s headpiece is worth the value of a hundred Furiae warriors upon Talanton’s Scale…

…ranks amongst the Furiae Praetors are determined by whether or not one carries a Harbinger of Strife…

…to present a Harbinger of Strife as a trophy, it not only signifies the might of the warrior engaging in courtship, but also bestows esteem and honor upon the desired lover…

— contents of a crumpled piece of paper found on the rooftops at the Marmoreal Market

· · ─ · ─ · ·

≪ 𖤓 ≫

Mydei proceeds to ignore Phainon after the incident with the trophy for a span of a lonely three days and counting. And now, Phainon is in the middle of chasing down the ever-elusive crown prince of Kremnos amidst the bustling market.

The sight of blonde hair and crimson fabric serves as Phainon’s only guide as he sets his gaze straight whilst maneuvering himself through the crowd, unwavering in his resolve to put a stop to this odd lack of communication.

He succeeds in the end, one hand reaching out to take hold of Mydei’s gauntlet-clad arm before pulling him towards a secluded corner where the loud chatter of the market is less pronounced.

Even if Mydei looked less than amused upon being abducted in the middle of the day and in plain sight, he doesn’t make a move to fight his way out of the Phainon-shaped prison that he’s in despite his capability for it, exuding the calmness of a deep ocean.

“Hi,” Phainon greets with a smile, trapping Mydei's head against the wall with his arms.

“Hmph,” Mydei greets in return. “What are you doing, slinking around like you’re up to no good? You even made sure that my participation in your schemes is a given.”

Mydei is not entirely unreasonable in his accusations. Being pushed to the wall of a secluded corner where there’s no other people to act as witnesses is not exactly a good look, all things considered.

Only then does Phainon realize how close he and Mydei are—the tips of their noses barely a hairbreadth away from each other, warm breaths ghosting upon their skin, Mydei’s scent permeating his senses, and the fact that those golden eyes of his do resemble that of a lion’s upon closer inspection.

This is dangerous, Phainon thinks, enthralled with the way every strand of Mydei’s eyelashes flutters with the wind, the diamond-shaped scarlet mark beneath his right eye striking, a stark contrast against the flawless tanned skin of Mydei’s face. There are no wrinkles in sight despite the owner’s habit of keeping his facial expression in a perpetual frown.

With great effort, Phainon manages to step back, putting a respectable amount of distance between him and Mydei. The latter was bound to call him out for it sooner or later anyway.

“Sorry. Did I surprise you?”

“I can sense you coming from a twenty pous radius,” Mydei replies monotonously. “What do you want, Deliverer?”

Always so direct. And yet Mydei found no fault in ignoring him without so much as a word.

“Just to talk,” Phainon answers. “I haven’t had the chance to for the past three days. I know you just got back from a mission, but it’s too early to retire so I thought it would be a good idea to invite you to come and leisurely spend the final quint of the Action Hour together at the Marmoreal Diner.”

The slight crease in between Mydei’s eyebrows is a telltale sign that he’s going to turn Phainon down on his offer. It was to be expected, and it only confirms Mydei’s adamance to avoid him for some reason.

Phainon deflates at the lack of a quick response, eyeing his shoes instead. “If you’re too exhausted, I won’t take it to heart if you do reject my invite.” He feels rather desperate. If Mydei still refuses to talk to Phainon today, then he might as well consider Phainon a stranger. “I’d be more than willing to escort you to your chambers, if you’re amenable to the idea.”

His words are left to linger in the air for what felt like an agonizing moment. Long enough for Phainon to be able to almost commit to memory the irregular pattern of cracks etched upon the stone floor.

The silence was thankfully broken by a long and heavy sigh.

Phainon looks up, ready to accept the fact that Mydei has finally reached the limits of his forbearance when it comes to dealing with him. The look of conflict on Mydei’s face is not exactly the reassuring kind in Phainon’s very anxious opinion.

“You don’t have to look so dejected,” Mydei says, a hint of a reprimand in his tone. “I haven’t even told you my answer yet and you’ve already gone on to play your part as a kicked chimera.”

“Why would anyone kick a chimera?” Phainon asks, suddenly feeling a strong sense of déjà vu. “They’re adorable.”

“Exactly.”

Mydei and his one-word responses.

Phainon scratches at his nape, a nervous habit. “You looked as if you were on the verge of declining my invite.”

“How so?” Mydei says, raising an eyebrow. “Are you perhaps claiming that you know me so well?”

“Enough to be able to distinguish when you’re purposefully avoiding me, yes.”

The satisfying manner in which Mydei’s facial expression morphs from genuine surprise to a deathly scowl needs to be studied. Phainon makes a mental note to discuss it with the wise philosophers who linger at the Kephale Plaza, for how could such a simple act of expression capture his interest so?

“Am I wrong?” Phainon asks, insistent, eyes shining with a faintly veiled amusement.

Mydei merely scoffs, a reply forgone in favor of avoiding Phainon’s gaze. Phainon knew Mydei enough that he would rather keep his silence than deny something that bears truth.

“To the Diner, then,” Mydei declares as he roughly shoves past Phainon, marching away with purpose.

It was a good call to have reservations arranged beforehand. It might be embarrassing to admit, but the moment Phainon had set his sights on Mydei who had just come back from his mission and was seen conversing with a Mountain Dweller by the city gates, he wasted no time and rushed over to ask Kyros to save him a table for two before proceeding to follow Mydei around in a subtle game of chase.

“Lord Phainon, I’ve saved you your seats as requested,” Kyros greets amicably with a bow upon their arrival to the Marmoreal Diner, subsequently guiding Phainon and Mydei to two vacant klines by the second floor.

Kyros then hands them the stone tablets depicting today’s special and best sellers before leaving them to decide on their orders.

Mydei was the first to speak, eyes scanning the menu for something interesting. His posture remains stiff and tall as he sat, denying himself the pleasure of relaxation.

“Did you plan this, Deliverer?”

“Have you tried the golden honeycakes?” Phainon asks in lieu of a reply, eager for a change of topic.

Mydei gives him a dry stare, brief but heavy with meaning, before once again turning his attention back at the menu. From the looks of things, Phainon need not to explain further for Mydei has clearly figured everything out without the need for elaboration.

“I haven’t tried the golden honeycakes,” Mydei answers.

“You should get a serving,” Phainon recommends sincerely despite the obvious tension between them. “I have no doubts that you’ll like it.”

He doesn’t bring up Mydei’s terrible sweet tooth into the conversation. There’s still a prophecy to be fulfilled, one that requires Phainon to stay alive to be able to see it through. It would be counterproductive if Mydei deems his life forfeit during the unremarkable, 23rd day of the Month of Balance.

Despite the withering glare that Mydei shoots at Phainon’s direction due to the unsolicited suggestion, the former still ends up ordering a plate of golden honeycakes when Kyros comes over to take their orders.

“So,” Phainon began, lying on his side to get a better look at Mydei after Kyros had left to prepare their meals. “Why are you avoiding me?”

Mydei reaches out a hand to grab his chalice atop the table, allowing himself a small sip of the pomegranate juice he ordered before saying, “Walk me through the process of how you managed to end up with such a conclusion.”

Phainon raises his hand, his fingers ready to count numbers as he lists down his reasons.

“You’re not replying to my messages. I waited for you at the training grounds yesterday as scheduled, but you didn’t show up. You switched seats with Miss Castorice during the deipnon of the past two days just so you won’t sit across from me—” Phainon pauses to catch his breath before resuming shortly. “And earlier, you kept ignoring my calls of your name and I had to chase you all across the holy city just to get you to talk to me.”

There must surely be some other details that Phainon had missed, but the ones he’d listed down are nothing short of his strongest arguments. Even Mydei is at a loss; Phainon is not the champion debater of the Grove for nothing.

“You’re very persistent,” is all that Mydei says.

The indifference makes Phainon hesitate for a fraction. “Mydei, it’s not like you to keep your grievances to yourself. If I did manage to offend you, you would’ve let me know of it by now.”

The lack of response only fuels Phainon’s anxiety even more. Even if he hides his discomfort underneath the mask of a smile that doesn’t quite reach his eyes to appear composed, the thought of Mydei being so cross with him to warrant such extreme avoidance bestows a sensation akin to that of being gutted.

“Was it something I said that day?” Phainon continues, referring to their last conversation from three days ago, insistent to right any wrongs he’d done. “Was the trophy I gifted you not to your liking?”

This time, Mydei humors him with an answer. “Why would I consider a well-sought trophy such as a Harbinger of Strife to be anything of poor taste?” he counters, unable to conceal the befuddlement in his tone as if Phainon had just asked the most ridiculous of questions. “Rest assured, Deliverer. Your trophy is treated well, prized and taken care of in my chambers.”

That sounds like it’s a good thing. And yet—

“Then, why the sudden cold shoulder?” Phainon urges on. “Was it because I teased you for drinking the pool waters of the Heroes' Baths?”

“That was one time,” Mydei hisses, evidently recalling the drunken incident at the Marmoreal Palace after he and Phainon left the disaster that was the Feast of the Scarlet Month.

Phainon raises an eyebrow. To tease Mydei is an urge that comes easy as if it were second nature. “And it hasn’t happened again?”

Mydei straightens his back, poised to leave the kline only for Phainon to grab his hand, halting his retreat.

“Don’t go. Please,” Phainon says, begs with his eyes wide open and eyebrows furrowed in a manner that should appear quite pitiful, enough to warrant the compassion of a rigid crown prince. “I’m sorry.”

It takes some time for Mydei to be convinced, brushing away Phainon’s grip on his wrist as he once again takes a seat. Phainon allows himself to sigh in relief, lips curving into a smile that conveyed his gratitude.

“The amount of tolerance I need to possess to be in your presence, Deliverer, is absurd.”

“You still haven’t told me why you’re avoiding me.”

Mydei huffs, bringing a hand to massage his temples, almost as if the matter brings him great difficulty to address.

“I simply needed time to think,” Mydei answers. Rarely does he sound so unsure of his words, suddenly hesitant in the manner that he speaks. “Your presence would only serve to hinder my focus.”

Phainon blinks, taken aback. That was the furthest of an answer that he could ever expect. He thought the reason for Mydei's avoidance was perhaps due to his teasing that had gone too far, or any other Mydei-typical reasons to bear grievances.

Now that he knows of the truth, Phainon can’t help but be relieved that he didn’t directly cause Mydei any offenses. But that doesn’t change the fact that Mydei sees him as a hindrance.

“I see,” Phainon says, feeling numb and confused. How could he even begin to possibly make amends for this sort of thing? “In that case, I deeply apologize for… causing you distraction.”

It almost sounds more like a question than an apology. What, exactly, is Mydei thinking about that requires such tremendous amounts of focus?

“It’s fine,” Mydei says. The assurance is dry as a rock, but knowing Mydei, it is as sincere as it gets.

“Is it really?”

“I despise having to repeat myself, Deliverer.”

“I know.”

Mydei shoots him a sharp glare. “And yet you continue to aggravate me so.”

“Not aggravate,” Phainon corrects. “It’s called teasing.”

“That so-called teasing of yours contributes greatly to my ire,” Mydei retorts.

Phainon is familiar with this fact that he can practically consider it as one of his close friends. “And what are you going to do about it?” he challenges, the risk causing his blood to sing in his veins. “Hit me—?

Mydei makes a move to pin Phainon by the neck into the kline, straddling Phainon’s waist and knocking over their table as he does so. The snarl on Mydei’s lips was evident, Phainon can’t help but marvel at how easy it is to rile this man up.

Despite the blatant display of strength (and abysmally short patience), the grip of Mydei’s hand on his neck is not exactly bruising. More like a loose hold than anything, but enough to keep Phainon in place.

“Goodness,” Phainon muses, tapping Mydei’s gauntlet-clad wrist with his hand, a show of surrender. “It was in jest! Mydeimos, let’s not fight.”

“Do not challenge me for a good time so casually, Deliverer,” Mydei says lowly before releasing his hold on Phainon’s neck. “You know better than anyone that I’m always up for it.”

The words fly over Phainon’s head like a flock of migrating birds. Without context, Mydei’s words would have been enough to render a respectable man (Phainon) to his knees. Not to mention, their current positions—incriminating to a fault.

Phainon could already feel his face starting to heat up tremendously due to his proximity to Mydei’s exposed abdominal muscles that could pass off as a sculpture of the gods.

But before he could ask Mydei to please get off of him lest any untoward incidents were to take place, the sound of someone clearing their throat is enough to capture both of their attentions.

Kyros, pale-faced and visibly unsettled, has arrived with their meals—two orders of golden honeycakes, piled up high and slathered generously with golden syrup upon each ceramic plate.

“My lords,” Kyros addresses, strained. And then he looks at the toppled table, both of Phainon and Mydei’s drinks spilled on the floor and the fruit platter a scattered mess. “My table.”

Mydei (thankfully!) scrambles off of Phainon to right the table, tidying up the fruits back into the plate before gazing forlornly at his spilled pomegranate juice.

Kyros then places their orders onto the surface gingerly, rushing off after a hasty mutter of, “Enjoy your meals.”

Mydei sighs as he picks up his fork. “How am I supposed to enjoy this without a drink?”

“You could try licking the floor before your spilled drink could evaporate for Aquila to partake in,” is Phainon’s rather intelligent response.

Sharp red crystals immediately surround Phainon, threateningly deadly in the way that they formed around his kline. He gives Mydei a wry smile.

“Put your crystals away, Mydei. You’re going to scare the other patrons.”

With a dark scowl, Mydei opens his mouth to protest, only for Phainon to take the opportunity to feed him a bite-sized portion of his golden honeycake. The diversion is shortly proven to be effective as the boiling anger that graced Mydei’s handsome features are then reduced to a simmer the moment that the sweetness of the dessert permeates his taste buds.

Phainon beams victoriously when Mydei began to chew slowly, the red crystals surrounding Phainon subsequently dismissed once and for all.

“Good, right?” Phainon says.

Mydei swallows before replying. “Indeed.”

Phainon, way too pleased with himself to the point that he has abandoned all reason, takes another portion of his honeycake and tries to feed Mydei another bite for a second time.

“Here, have some more.”

This time, Mydei swats his hand away, face flushed in a pretty shade of pink. “Have you lost your mind, Deliverer? Do conduct yourself with propriety while in my company or you’ll end up embarrassing us both.”

Phainon pouts. Mydei calling him an embarrassment is taking it too far, dare he say. “What do you mean? No one’s even watching—”

He then turns his attention to the rest of the patrons who were… definitely watching, and have definitely witnessed the entire exchange. Phainon wonders when exactly it was that they managed to draw so much attention to themselves.

Clearing his throat, he then returns his gaze back at Mydei. “Fine weather, isn’t it? As Chrysos Heirs of reputable status, we should talk about something… thought-provoking. Because that’s what we do in our free time, yes. Engage in the struggles of the mind.”

The tips of Mydei’s ears burn a fiery scarlet, almost as red as the marks on his exposed skin. With a groan, he buries his head in his hands. “You are a dead man walking.”

· · ─ ·𖥸· ─ · ·

Lord Phainon and Prince Mydei are always seen together, their interactions as fickle as Phagousa's tides.

One moment they are on the verge of killing each other with a complete disregard to the public's safety and surrounding buildings. In the next, they seem to be passionate lovers who are unable to keep their desires to themselves. Finally, they are also bosom buddies who feed each other honeycakes.

So, what indeed is the true nature of their relationship?

— from Akmonides’ note, sold out within the first quint of the Action Hour

· · ─ · ─ · ·

≪ 𖤓 ≫

Phainon was just about to take his leave from Aglaea’s office after a discussion in regards to the Titankin’s hostility at the borders of Okhema when suddenly, she calls for him again.

“Yes?” Phainon asks, turning around.

Janus had already opened the door for him but Aglaea still beckons him over.

“I’ve nearly forgotten,” she says, gesturing for a Garmentmaker to hand her a scroll. “I wanted to give you this.”

Phainon retraces his steps until he is in front of Aglaea’s marble desk once again. He takes the scroll in her hand, unfurling it just enough to see what the subject was that is detailed within. The title is etched in bold letters at the very top.

Kremnoan Traditions: Culture and Customs throughout History

“Did you want me to give this to Mydei?” Phainon asks, confused as to why Aglaea was handing him something he had no relation to. Perhaps it is a suggestion for some light reading? It won’t hurt to know more about Mydei’s origins. Mydei is a good friend, after all.

Aglaea purses her lips, an obvious no if Phainon were to ever see one. “A Kremnoan would be slighted if you were to give them a scroll encapsulating their daily life and culture. It would imply their ignorance,” she explains. “I trust that you’re familiar with Mydeimos enough to know how he’ll react.”

Phainon tilts his head to the side, feeling foolish. “Oh. Uh, yes?”

Aglaea nods. “Excellent. You may leave now.”

Perhaps Aglaea didn’t wish to invoke Mydei’s ire by giving this scroll to him and has thus entrusted the dreadful job to someone who could take Mydei in a fight instead.

It is still baffling, however, for why does Aglaea wish to give this scroll to Mydei? A prince who most likely knew of its contents by heart?

Before Phainon could even ask, Aglaea’s Garmentmaker was already leading him to the door. Left with no other choice, he then leaves Aglaea’s office feeling bewildered by the exchange.

Back in his quarters, he places the scroll on his desk alongside a dozen rolled others, making a mental note to give it to Mydei at the earliest convenience.

Little did he know, from that moment on, it would be the last time that his fingers would brush against the yellowed parchment as he took his leave once again. He got a missive from Theodoros saying that he had new artifacts and relics brought in during the Lucid Hour and would be honored for Phainon to do the first appraisals.

As the door to Phainon’s chambers slam shut signalling his departure, the wings of the lone butterfly perched on the windowsill twitches impatiently. The Mnestia Titankin then latches on to a golden thread that flutters by, disappearing into the light of Dawn as it makes its way to report back to its master.

chapters.title: Chapter 5: wandering eyes, lingering moments
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Phainon finds his rationality to be at odds with himself most of the time. Perhaps Oronyx's influence is to blame, for it is the Month of Evernight where feelings tend to take the reins and reason is cast aside.

fate season, month of evernight

6 months before the present time

· · ─ ·𖥸· ─ · ·

Recount tales of your valor and it shall express your might. Your history of renown bears weight, and a future of equal glory shall await.

…let it be known: no lover desires incompetence. Bare your strength and be proud. Your story defines your worth in much more value than the heaviest of treasures upon Talanton’s Scale.

— an excerpt. Kremnoan Rituals of Courtship, Chapter 3: Tales of Valor, Significance of

Legacy

· · ─ · ─ · ·

Mydei is never seen bathing in the Heroes’ Baths, much less with other people. Phainon recalls the other saying that he didn’t wish to appear so vulnerable in public, preferring the solitude that the baths in his own chambers offered.

“I don’t wish to parade myself without my armor,” Mydei answers the first time Phainon asked him why he’s never seen him bathe, subsequently surprised at Mydei’s need for privacy. “And why should I inconvenience myself by coming to the Heroes’ Baths when the ones in my chambers are filled with the same golden waters?”

“Baths are meant to be an affair shared with others,” Phainon debates. “You’re missing out on the daily symposia! Even Aglaea holds her assemblies in the Heroes’ Baths sometimes.”

Mydei huffs, evidently growing irritated by Phainon’s pestering. Admittedly, it is true that they’ve been doing this incessant back and forth for a while now and Phainon hasn’t let up in the slightest.

Is it wrong to promote some sense of camaraderie? Every Chrysos Heir that Phainon has managed to establish a connection with, except for Professor Anaxa, is a woman.

Lady Tribios is a child (in this case, children), Aglaea is scary, and Miss Castorice is… well, she’s a close friend but she’s rarely seen by him.

When Mydei arrived at Okhema, Phainon had been led to have hope that he might finally have his own brother-in-arms, specifically, someone to share the woes of battle with during a relaxing bath after training.

It was ever so unfortunate of a revelation that the man is stubborn as a bull and very difficult to get along with during the early days of their acquaintance.

“Even if I’m not in attendance, Aglaea still makes sure that I am up to speed with whatever has been discussed.”

Phainon crosses his arms. “Joining us in the baths once in a while than having Aglaea debrief you separately would be a more economical use of her time.”

That’s a winning argument if Phainon has ever managed to come up with one. He knows that Mydei at least has some semblance of respect towards Aglaea regardless of the Okheman-Kremnoan feud. But then he forgets that it is Mydei with whom he now argues against.

“I can economically shove my foot up your arse if you don’t give this matter a rest right now.”

Phainon is rendered defeated as he stares forlornly at Mydei’s retreating figure. If Mydei were to have studied alongside him at the Grove, he doubts if he would have been able to maintain his streak in being the debate champion.

The man simply follows no rules at all, and that was the last time the topic was ever brought up.

It had been during the Month of Fortune, a lot has happened since then. Phainon already knew that Mydei was in a foul mood that day and still decided to push the latter’s patience to the brink. Now that he thinks about it three months later, he did sound way too persistent.

You know what they say: if you poke the lion, be prepared for its mighty roar.

But as of this moment, it was ever a surprise when Phainon sees Mydei’s approaching figure at the Heroes’ Baths, wearing only a flimsy robe that the bath attendants have provided—the fabric thin enough to show the skin beneath. His hair was tied in a low bun, the single lock of braided hair the only thing that rests upon his shoulders.

It’s rather unfortunate that only Phainon is around to be present in this momentous occasion: Mydei’s first public bath appearance.

“Fancy seeing you here, Your Highness,” Phainon jibes when Mydei dips a foot into the pool. No testing the temperature or anything of the sort, just direct submersion. Truly, what a man. “I see you’ve finally thought it nice to deign us commoners with your glorious presence.”

“Shut up,” is all that Mydei says before taking a seat across Phainon.

The action renders Phainon surprised. He half-expected Mydei to occupy another table and not share the one he currently uses. But Phainon appreciates the company, nonetheless.

“Has today’s Spring Theater Show started yet?” Mydei asks, taking a piece of grape from the fruit platter.

The juice that drips from the corner of his lips as he takes a bite does not escape Phainon’s notice. “Didn’t expect you to be a fan of such things.”

Mydei dabs at his lips with a napkin, the delicate action contrasting with the way his eyes are narrowed into dangerous slits, a sharp glare thrown at Phainon’s direction.

“You take me to be a philistine?”

“I dare not,” Phainon replies. How easy it is to rile this man up. “It hasn’t started yet. If I am not mistaken, today’s show should be a poetry recital with lyre accompaniment.”

Mydei only hums, sinking further into the waters as he rests his back into the cushion. It’s quiet after that. Phainon, for once, can’t think of anything more to say.

I’ve waited for so long to have you join me in the baths. Too desperate.

Isn’t it nice to bathe with someone? Too presumptuous.

We should do this more often. Too demanding.

Sometimes, the best course of action is to maintain silence. Now is one of those times.

Mydei, ever so oblivious with Phainon’s conundrum, has his head leaned back against the tiled edges of the pool, eyes closed as he relishes in the sensation of the warm waters lapping at his skin.

Phainon allows his gaze to rest upon the curve of Mydei’s neck, the way his throat bobs lightly with every swallow. Rivulets of water slide down the flawless skin of his fair face, tracing a mesmerizing path down to his well-defined jaw, and down once more, dripping onto the exquisite jut of his collarbone, lingering at the valley before ultimately flowing down the exposed skin of his tanned chest.

The wet fabric of the robe is flimsy enough for the streaks of scarlet etched upon Mydei’s skin to come into view, easily seen in its entirety without much of a hindrance for once. Perhaps it’s a good thing that Phainon is the only one present.

“Are you quite done with your staring?”

Phainon jolts at the sound of Mydei’s voice, and he feels his face color in shame at being caught.

“Just admiring that immortal body of yours,” he replies, a poor attempt to sound unfazed.

Upon hearing this, Mydei’s eyes flutter open, pools of gold taking in the sight of Phainon’s flushed face before his gaze ultimately drops down to carefully consider the well-defined muscles of Phainon’s torso, equally exposed.

Mydei takes his time to look, deliberate and lingering. And then, he says, “You’re not so bad yourself.”

Now, what is Phainon supposed to think about that? How is he supposed to take Mydei’s words that were said so directly and without a hint of hesitation? Was that even a compliment? Did Mydei just say he has a nice body right to his face?

Before Phainon could think any further and consider his poor brain to already be forfeit, the soft and crystalline sound of melodic notes plucked from the lyre echoes all throughout the Nerid Spring and up the Heroes’ Baths.

The show has begun, the chatter has quieted down. A woman’s voice orates the lines of a poem, her words clear and loud, her tone pleasantly canorous:

When Kephale’s golden blood did flow,

Across nations where only darkness evil did bestow,

There emerges a beacon bright, born of dawn,

In Aedes Elysiae, a source of hope is gently drawn.

Phainon tenses in his seat. He had no idea that the show would be about him. Worse, he can already feel Mydei’s gaze upon him.

“This is embarrassing.”

— an excerpt. Kremnoan Rituals of Courtship, Chapter 4: A Test of Character
