Phainon was in the middle of lance practice (Mydei’s recommendation because, as Mydei had so kindly remarked, “You suck at this.”) when a Kremnoan soldier approaches him.

“Greetings, Lord Phainon.”

Phainon wipes the sweat accumulated on his forehead with the back of his hand before turning to the Kremnoan soldier with a smile. He’s seen her many times before.

“Good day, Miss Eris.”

Eris gives him a light bow at the acknowledgement. “His Highness wishes to invite you to the settlement later today, the first quint of the Curtain-Fall Hour to be precise.”

Phainon frowns upon hearing such a conventionally late meeting time, a bit uncharacteristic of Mydei for he always considered the availability of both parties, as well as a time that occurs not later than the Parting Hour, before initiating an invite.

“Did he say why?”

The soldier seemed a bit taken aback by this question. “Lord Phainon, you jest,” she says, amusement simmering behind her almond eyes. “It is finally the time for that, and His Highness wishes for you to participate.”

Phainon wonders what that even means. Perhaps he should just ask Mydei when he sees him later on. “Of course. I’ll be there.”

Eris bows again to take her leave without another word, leaving a befuddled Phainon alone in the training grounds.

Later that day, he makes his way to the Kremnoan settlement located around the city’s outskirts. By the entrance, he sees a young Kremnoan boy, perhaps as old as thirteen years, seemingly waiting for him.

“Lord Phainon, you’ve arrived!”

Phainon can’t help but smile at the sight of the boy rushing towards him. “Your prince made it clear that I am to come.”

The boy grins. “I’m so happy that it’s you. I have never once liked those other Okheman warriors who also wanted His Highness’ favor.”

As a respectable figure in the battlefield, perhaps not only the Okheman warriors, but those from the other nations as well, wanted Mydei’s recognition. If Phainon hadn’t been a Chrysos Heir, he doubts that Mydei would even deign to sneeze in his direction.

“Those Okheman warriors have talent as well, you know,” Phainon says, trying to put a good word in. Not to mention, some of those Okhemans fought with him against the forces of the Black Tide. Phainon considers them as his friends. “And they’re nice, too.”

The boy only shrugs, barely even considering it. “Not really. Father says you’re the only person in Okhema who has actively helped us, while Mother says that she’s glad His Highness has a good eye in choosing someone worthy.”

“Is that so?” Phainon never thought that the other Kremnoans saw him in such a good light given that they tended to harbor a poor opinion of those residing in Okhema. “I’m very honored. Do convey my sincerest gratitude to your parents, young man.”

“My name is Maleos.”

“Alright, Maleos,” Phainon says, etching the boy's name in his memory. “Lead me to your prince. We shan’t keep him waiting.”

Maleos leads Phainon towards the blood-red marquee set up right in the middle of the settlement whilst animatedly recounting stories about his tribe and how much he wants to become like his Prince Mydeimos when he grows up.

Phainon can’t help but smile fondly. Prince Mydeimos this, His Highness that— Indeed, Phainon understands Maleos on an almost spiritual level, dare he say. Mydei is indeed impressive in any and every regard.

“His Highness is waiting inside,” Maleos tells him now that they’re standing by the entrance of the marquee. For some reason, Phainon begins to feel nervous. “I’m too young to be allowed entry, so this is the furthest I could be of escort to you, Lord Phainon.”

“You’ve been a great help,” Phainon reassures, ruffling the boy’s hair gently before giving him a shiny gold coin. “Why don’t you buy yourself something nice as a reward? If you go to Chartonus, just show him this coin tomorrow and he’ll fashion you a wooden sword in return.”

Maleos grins, eyes sparkling with enthusiasm upon hearing the word ‘sword’ leave Phainon’s lips. A Kremnoan through and through.

“Many thanks, Lord Phainon!” He bows and makes a run for it. “I wish you the best of luck!”

Best of luck? For what?

Phainon finds his answer the moment that he pushes at the flap leading into the blood-red marquee to enter, only to stop cold upon seeing—

Rows and rows of Kremnoan soldiers dressed in their full armor of gold and red, standing at attention and facing him with their lances ready and their shields on guard. He couldn’t see the soldiers’ expressions due to the helmets they wore. But one thing is for sure: they are not here simply to express the discipline of an army, but to fight.

Phainon furrows his eyebrows in confusion. Behind the rows of warriors is Mydei, seated atop an elaborate chair made of wood and stone, a chalice in one hand as he rests his head with the other.

Their gazes meet.

“Mydei, what—?”

“Warriors of Kremnos,” Mydei calls out, his voice reverberating throughout the enclosed space. “My kin, you are not to hold back.”

The Kremnoans erupt into a ferocious cry, charging towards Phainon all at once. Still baffled by this turn of events, Phainon manages to summon his greatsword at the last minute, parrying attacks with no intent to hurt.

He knew these people. He would never hurt them. But why—?

Evading the attacks from every angle, Phainon was able to successfully disarm one soldier. And then the strangest thing happens: instead of a reluctant defeat, the soldier removes his helmet—Phalces is his name, as Phainon would remember—and smiles, moving closer to pat Phainon firmly on the shoulder before stepping away from the fight.

To say that Phainon is thoroughly befuddled is an understatement, but now he understood the rules of this sudden game. Disarming the warriors would do the trick. One down, a… hundred? Two hundred? No, three hundred more to go.

The rest of them are defeated smoothly. Even if they fought with all their might, they are simply of no match for Phainon who could go head to head with their leader himself.

Everytime he manages to disarm a warrior, they remove their helmets—Phainon recognizes them all: Leandros, Ideaus, Deinias, Pervica, even Eris. And after every defeat, they either bow deeply, shake Phainon’s hand, or give Phainon a firm pat on the shoulder. One— Evagoras, also an avid treasure appraiser—even pulled Phainon into a crushing hug.

“You’re worthy,” he says.

Before Phainon could let the words sink in, Evagoras had already pulled away and went to the side to join his defeated companions. A barely dodged attack to his head reminds Phainon of the situation at hand.

One by one, the three hundred warriors participating in the fight were steadily reduced in numbers as Phainon defeated them by his lonesome. A kick to the shin, a well-executed maneuver, a jab to the ribs.

And now, Phainon directs the tip of his greatsword upon the throat of the last Kremnoan warrior who was now on the floor with his lance some ways away and his shield broken into two.

“Do you yield?” Phainon pants, unable to conceal the fact that he’s very much out of breath after such a rigorous undertaking.

He shouldn’t have trained too hard earlier today if only to preserve what energy he had left before coming here. But then again, he had no idea that this was what awaited him. Three hundred warriors later, and Phainon is finally able to recognize the last of them.

Praxis, a formidable opponent and one of Mydei’s most trusted lochagos, finally removes his helmet. He gives Phainon a firm nod. Just like the others who were defeated before him, there was no hint of spite on his face. Only relief.

“I yield.”

Phainon sighs, unable to help a smile. It’s finally over.

He dismisses his greatsword into specks of gold before helping Praxis up from the ground. Praxis gladly accepts the assistance, pulling Phainon into a hug of his own.

“Honorable,” Praxis murmurs against Phainon’s ear. “His Highness chose right.”

Before Phainon could come up with a reply of his own, Praxis had already withdrawn and joined the others. And now, a path had opened for Phainon, one that led up to the lone man lounging on the makeshift throne.

Mydei looked pleased. Phainon must have provided him with a great deal of entertainment after taking down all of his men with just a sword and a confused mind.

“That was fun,” Phainon began, raising a challenging eyebrow at Mydei’s direction. “Am I to fight you next?”

Some of the warriors burst into low chuckles upon hearing the jest. Even Mydei’s lips curl into a smirk.

“Now is not the time for that, victorious Deliverer,” he replies, standing up from his seat to approach Phainon. Something about his air at this moment renders Phainon weak in the knees. Or maybe the exhaustion has finally caught up to him. “Today, we feast!”

The Kremnoan warriors all erupted into cheers at the declaration, crimson pennants bearing the symbol of Strife thrown into the air as they hoist Phainon up in arms in some sort of bizarre celebratory gesture, yelling one single line over and over:

“Worthy is he, the Deliverer of Okhema!”

Music and drunken singing could be heard from within the marquee whilst Phainon indulges in his solitude, seated at a nearby bench by the entrance to the huge tent that once held battle, and now celebration.

He’s already quite buzzed after a single cup of pomegranate juice, that he only belatedly realized had been mixed with liquor. Not wanting a repeat of the incident back during the Feast of the Scarlet Month, Phainon excuses himself in favor of getting some fresh air, hoping that it would sober him up.

“I’ve been looking everywhere for you.”

Phainon looks up and meets Mydei’s eyes of pure gold. He scoots over the bench to make space just in case Mydei wanted to join him.

“Idaeus thought it would be funny to get me drunk,” he says in lieu of a reply.

Mydei takes the offered seat, handing Phainon a drink. This time, the cup contains Mydei’s signature mix of pomegranate juice and milk. Phainon readily accepts the honey brew with a mutter of thanks, most eagerly partaking in the drink and allowing the sweetness to linger in his tongue, washing away the bitterness of alcohol.

“Idaeus is a scoundrel,” is all that Mydei says, a hint of fondness in his tone despite his words. “If you don’t see him pour you a drink directly coming from a barrel, best be warned that it would be laced with something.”

“Duly noted.”

And then silence.

“Do you need help in tending to your wounds?” Mydei asks after some time has passed.

Phainon opens his mouth to speak, “I would be very grateful.”

The smile on Mydei’s face is enough to brighten the entirety of Amphoreus even without the help of Kephale’s Dawn or Aquila’s sets of Eyes. Hence, did Phainon come to realize he’d made the right call.

Instead of the infirmary located in the Marmoreal Palace, Mydei leads him to the Room of the Flame Lily—his very own chambers—to be patched up.

“Sit on the bed while I get some bandages,” Mydei tells him.

Phainon couldn’t help himself. The urge to tease is too strong. “Still no chairs?”

And then Mydei leaves.

Dumbstruck at the unexpected reply, Phainon is left to stand in the middle of the room without so much as a hint of movement. He’s not even breathing, turning Mydei’s cryptic words over and over in his head until he’s on the verge of insanity.

The bed is more than enough for you and I.

Titans both merciful and cruel, does Mydei have any idea what his words could entail? Is Phainon not a man in his eyes to not be affected by such? Does Mydei perhaps see him as a statue? Devoid of emotions and desires of the flesh?

Depraved.

With hurried footsteps, Phainon takes his leave, his rational thoughts left asunder.

We clothe ourselves in red to hide the blood and weakness during battle. And during recuperation, our bodies are coated with swaths of white cloth and bandages—much like how our open wounds bursting with crimson blood pales upon healing, and turns to scars.

These are badges of honor, of battles well-fought. Do not shy away from showing them, for a desired lover is sure to be impressed.

— an excerpt. Kremnoan Rituals of Courtship, Chapter 6: Show of Scars, Proof of Might

· · ─ · ─ · ·

≪ 𖤓 ≫ Phainon keeps himself busy after his run-in with Mydei. He takes up every mission before Aglaea even had the chance to assign them to someone else. And now, due to his insistence, he is drowning in a multitude of overdue post-mission reports.

Even if the task of detailing every single encounter he had with Nikador’s Titankin, as well as the occassional forces of the Black Tide, is tedious enough to a fault, it helped Phainon keep his mind off of things.

Specifically, Mydei and the lone strand of blonde hair that’s now wind tightly around his forefinger. It glimmers every now and then, reflecting the light coming from the balcony with every movement of his hand as he wrote.

The only sound to be heard in the room is the frantic scratching of the quill’s end against the parchment paper. If Phainon fails to submit his reports today, Aglaea would most definitely have him sort through Okhema’s state of affairs and arrange every document by date, by priority, and in alphabetical order. Worst, she’ll have him memorize it.

Phainon shudders at the mere thought of it, only to almost fall out of his seat when a loud knock comes from his door.

“Who is it?” Phainon calls out. He was not expecting any deliveries today.

The voice from the other end is deep and smooth. Unmistakable. “It’s me.”

Phainon felt as if his soul had just left his body, turning his head around so fast to look at the closed door that it feels as if he stretched a muscle, or something.

Titans dead or alive, Mydei cannot be outside of his door right now. Phainon looks around at the state of his room—his kline is unmade, antiques are scattered about, his desk is a mess of scrolls and stone tablets, and—

And!

Horrified, Phainon slowly directs his attention at the wall across his kline where a portrait (fashioned from a billboard) of Mydei’s stoic image advertising Marmoreal Diner’s golden honeycakes hung indisputably.

Phainon is going to die.

He bolts out of his seat in the next moment, hastily moving to tidy up his kline, shoving his collection of antiques underneath before rearranging his desk to make it appear productively used but still presentable.

“Deliverer.”

Phainon huffs, pushing a giant amphora to stand in a corner instead of in the middle of the hallway. “Wait just a moment!”

He then scrambles to climb atop the dresser, knocking off and breaking the relics and trinkets he had displayed upon its surface; they’re cheap and fake, so it’s fine. What’s more important right now is that he get Mydei’s portrait off of his wall or he dies.

Phainon grips the edges of the once-billboard, shifting it slightly in an attempt to unfasten it from the hook. But the thing doesn’t budge, curses slipping out of his lips frantically in sheer panic.

“A moment has passed,” Mydei announces, muffled from the other side of the door. His beautiful voice, for once, a dreadful sound. “I’m coming in.”

Janus’ lock begins to turn, and in a last burst of panic, Phainon pulls at the portrait using all of his strength as the Deliverer of Okhema. But the object is regrettably just as stubborn as the subject himself.

Even as a billboard, Mydei is ever so immovable.

Phainon’s grip slips and he all but tumbles down ungracefully onto the floor in a heap of defeated shame and broken dreams as his dresser falls alongside him in a loud and unmistakable crash. He barely manages to roll away just in time before he is caught beneath the dresser’s crushing weight.

The door to his chambers open, and Mydei arrives, witnessing the spectacle before him with unbridled shock.

“...”

Phainon wants to die.

His gaze meet that of Mydei’s, brief for the latter chooses to examine the room against Phainon’s wishes, pools of gold finally landing on the root cause of the mess—the Marmoreal Diner’s advertisement featuring Mydei:

Be Golden like Lord Mydei! Order our Golden Honeycakes and you’ll feel Golden, too!

Mydei’s mouth was rendered agape.

“...”

Phainon breaks the painful silence. “It’s not what it looks like.”

“How am I supposed to interpret this, then?” Mydei asks in turn.

Still on the floor and feeling winded, Phainon uses what little is left of his brain to make up an acceptable reason.

“The, uh, children are… making fun of you!” It’s a lame excuse given that every kid in Okhema is a Prince Mydei fanatic. But it’s too late to take back his words now. “Yeah, that’s right! I only wanted to preserve your dignity, which is why I had to hide this away.”

Mydei obviously didn’t believe him. It was clear in the way he regards Phainon with a look of disbelief and barely concealed amusement.

“Right.” Mydei nods slowly. “And you chose to hang this on the wall across your kline like a glorified painting? Did it escape your mind that a billboard is supposed to stand on the floor and be exposed in a market for patrons to see?”

Not in the privacy of your own chambers, is left unsaid. But the words are loud enough to render Phainon’s heated face to flush some more. He must look ridiculous right now.

“It’s…” I need to die. It’s a must at this point. “I had to put it somewhere pleasing, at least.”

Now Mydei is smirking. He’s just taunting Phainon now, is he? “And this is the solution you’ve come up with? What if someone else comes in here and sees? Are you not embarrassed?”

Phainon is embarrassed for getting caught. But to consider Mydei’s portrait (billboard) as an embarrassment is the furthest from the truth. Advertisement or not, Mydei’s unsmiling image looks just as radiant as any other portrait painted by an artist of renown.

“I don’t host visitors in my chambers,” Phainon replies. “You’re the only one.”

Mydei takes his time to form a reply after that. Perhaps constructing lines of teasing remarks in his profound mind. Phainon has simply given up at this point. Mydei could gloat in his victory all he wants.

Only, in an unexpected show of mercy, he doesn’t.

“Very well,” Mydei eventually says before walking towards Phainon’s limp body laying on the floor. He crouches down, helping Phainon up to a sitting position, a strong hand supporting Phainon’s back. “Are you alright?”

Phainon buries his face in his own hands. “Let’s just forget this ever happened.”

A soft laugh resounds, beautiful and clear like the notes of wind chimes swaying with the wind. It’s enough to tempt Phainon out of his hiding, just so he could witness the most captivating sight he’s ever had the pleasure to behold.

Mydei lightly coughs in an attempt to regain his bearings. “Thank you for… preserving my dignity, Deliverer,” he says. “But it truly wasn’t necessary. Kyros paid me a hefty sum to use my image as an advertisement for his golden honeycakes. I only agreed to do it because the product is something I genuinely enjoy, and I see no problem with having my name used to verify its quality.”

Phainon wanted to say that he also paid a hefty sum to buy the billboard the moment that he’d seen it while he was out appraising Theodoros’ new treasures.

Why he’d done so, he has no idea. But he would never forget the way other people had eyed Mydei’s picture with something other than respect and admiration.

Instead of replying and further incriminating himself, Phainon stands up and leads Mydei to the balcony where the mess that is his room is out of sight, and hopefully, out of mind. He offers Mydei a seat on one of the smaller klines. Only then does he notice that Mydei was carrying something with him.

“I wanted to give you this,” Mydei says before Phainon could even get the chance to ask, handing him the package.

Phainon takes it, undoing the string that keeps the brown paper in place, peeling it away to reveal a silken, purple fabric from within. Intricately embroidered with patterns not native to Okhema, but the artistry could almost rival that of Aglaea’s.

He holds the garment up high to examine it fully, revealing an elaborate chiton that must have cost a small fortune. So Mydei came here to give him clothes.

Still amazed by the handiwork, Phainon can’t help but ask, “Did Aglaea put you up to this?”

“Aglaea?” Mydei frowns. “No. Why would she?”

And thus begins Phainon’s passionate retelling of the time where Aglaea threw his entire wardrobe into the open flames, followed by a detailed account of her stripping Phainon of his favorite yellow tunic and purple trousers before having Chartonus use it as fuel for his forge.

Once done, Phainon was out of breath and a moment of silence encompasses them. Mydei has an unreadable look on his face. Perhaps he sympathizes with Phainon in this regard, they are close friends after all who have shared Aglaea’s fury in more than one occasion.

Eventually, Mydei clears his throat. “Anyway, that’s an… authentic Kremnoan chiton made from the finest of silken fabrics and embroidered by delicate hands of utmost talent. The silk itself was woven all the way from Pyria.” Mydei averts his gaze, directing his attention at the imposing view of Kephale instead. Hesitantly, he adds, “It’s not a lot, but these are the only ones I could salvage after the war.”

Phainon allows himself to smile, appreciative of Mydei’s efforts. “It’s beautiful. Thank you, Mydei.”

Silence.

“I have its matching set,” Mydei blurts out without much preamble. “I shall wear it the day after tomorrow.”

Phainon is unable to hide the questioning frown that graces his face. “I… see.”

Silence once again.

“May I ask why you’re suddenly giving these to me?”

“So you could make yourself look presentable. My teacher wants to meet you.”

Ah. Lord Krateros, if Phainon wasn’t mistaken.

Phainon has met almost all of the Kremnoans that have come to seek refuge in Okhema. But Lord Krateros has always denied him audience. Come to think of it, Phainon has no idea as to why that is.

He’s heard Aglaea mention him a couple of times before in passing, her tone laced with a subtle disdain. But the bitterness would never compare to how it would be if she were talking about Professor Anaxa.

“I’m honored,” Phainon says, eager to put a face to the name. However, Mydei’s initial statement doesn’t go unnoticed. “You’re starting to sound like Aglaea, fussing over my appearance. Am I not handsome enough for you?”

Mydei doesn’t let the words linger in the air for more than a moment before uttering his reply. “You’re more than handsome enough to satisfy me.”

Now, what in Kephale’s name is that even supposed to mean?

And then Mydei leaves his seat, walking the few steps to stand right in front Phainon, the light from Kephale’s Dawn bathing him in what Phainon would consider a devastatingly gorgeous sight.

“If you can indulge me—” Mydei reaches a gauntlet-clad hand out, combing back Phainon’s unruly strands of snow-white hair to expose more of his shell-shocked face, ending up cradling the back of his head. Gentle regardless of how forward. “—I’d like to see you in these sometime.”

Phainon is willing to indulge Mydei in absolutely anything. If Mydei asked him to jump off the balcony in this moment, he most likely would. But not before asking how many flips Mydei wanted him to do. Five flips in midair is Phainon’s known record. If Mydei were to ask him to do ten, who is he to refuse?

“Yes. Of course.”

A hint of red dusts Mydei’s cheeks. Even flustered, Mydei still looks stunningly put-together. He then withdraws his hand to Phainon’s dismay. All good things must come to an end, after all.

“I look forward to seeing you in it,” Mydei says. “I shall take my leave now. Do not see me for the rest of the day.”

In a rare sight of hurriedness, Mydei bolts back into the room, leaving Phainon still in his daze at the balcony. Phainon could hear Janus’ locks turn followed subsequently by the slam of his door.

None of Mydei’s behavior today made sense. The garments, the direct compliment, and a warning not to see him?

Phainon allows his fingers to run through the silken fabric, mapping out the carefully threaded embroidery with muted fascination, Mydei’s wishes echoing in his ears as he does so: I’d like to see you in these sometime.

Collapsing back to the kline, Phainon stares ahead, eyeing Kephale’s figure in the hopes that They hold the answers.

“Oh, Mydei. Must you always be a mystery?”

The bell signalling the beginning of the Parting Hour tolls all around Okhema. Phainon had once again missed the submission of his reports to Aglaea. She would no doubt call him out on it during today’s deipnon.

Sighing, Phainon makes his way back into his room. Still a mess despite how much he tried to make it look presentable. Mydei’s unsmiling image stares down at him as if in judgement from within the frames of his makeshift portrait.

Phainon glares without the anger. “This is all your fault, you know.”

The Mydei-featured advertisement merely taunts him with golden honeycakes as a way of reply.

· · ─ ·𖥸· ─ · ·

To put up a united front, it is important for the King and Queen of Kremnos to wear complementary garments.

…Red is traditional for wartime. Gold is only to be worn during special occasions. White is appropriate in a time of recuperation. Black during the Month of Mourning…

… Purple is used for courting.

Purple is no longer worn for it is often associated with Bartholos, who is a devout follower of Zagreus, and could only

signify trickery and deceit. – Ptolemy, annotation date: ███

How so? I find purple to be fitting. This reasoning is shallow. – M.

I never knew Mydeimos would be interested in matters related to courtship. – Leonnius

Are we even supposed to write here? – Peucesta

Heh. Ptolemy is going to throw a fit. Should I make him a vial of sleeping drought? – a most apologetic Perdikkas

It seems that Mydeimos does have the heart in him to be romantic, after all. – H.

The five annotations above are to be disregarded. Future readers of this tome, please refrain from vandalizing

important texts, unlike some people. (You know who you are!) – Ptolemy, annotation date: ███

Phainon goes to meet two of the most significant people in Mydei's life. One expresses a love so tough, bearing the weight of responsibility. The other, a love mired in grief, finally eased in the afterlife.

· · ─ ·𖥸· ─ · ·

Once the courted has chosen the right suitor to entertain, the next step is to introduce the said suitor to family members whilst wearing courtship garments.

…parents come first, followed by immediate relatives, followed by distant relatives…

…in the event where family is unavailable, a guardian is a most suitable replacement, or a very close friend.

— an excerpt. Kremnoan Rituals of Courtship, Chapter 8: Introductory Rites

· · ─ · ─ · ·

Phainon stares at his reflection through the mirror, fixing the folds of his chiton by his shoulder that’s clasped neatly with a golden brooch. He then readjusts his himátion for the nth time to make it seem as if it had been draped over his shoulder in a deliberately elegant manner. It would be counterproductive if he leaves the room looking worse than one of Aglaea’s many mannequins.

It’s been a while since he had forgone his usual armor and wore something more formal. He can’t even remember the last time he wore a chiton this elaborate, and feels just a bit more defenseless despite his greatsword being capable of being summoned at a moment’s notice.

But he promised to indulge Mydei. Thoughts of danger had to be put aside for now.

Phainon lightly shifts the belt, something Aglaea had generously lent him, for he sought her counsel just the day before on how to make sure that he’ll be able to carry himself appropriately whilst wearing such an extravagant garment.

(“This belt—” Aglaea began, shoving a gold-plated belt, embellished intricately with lapis lazuli, upon Phainon’s awaiting hands.

Phainon didn’t even have enough time to properly appraise the item when his hands were being made to hold more accessories that are worth ten times more than his modest salary as a Chrysos Heir.

“—these perónai—” Aglaea then procures an ornate set of pins from her own jewelry box, also shoving it into Phainon’s now occupied hands who made sure he caught it all in time and didn’t drop a single one.

Two brooches seemingly to be of pair are typically worn to keep the fabric in place upon his shoulders. Another one, more opulent than the other two, is for Aglaea to place wherever she wishes for decorative purposes. The three pins all possess a circular design with detailed engravings of the sun; a typical pattern in a land that worships the Throne of Worlds.

“—this himátion—” Aglaea flings a navy blue fabric, embroidered with patterns sewn in threads of gold, towards Phainon’s direction without looking back.

The himátion lands squarely on Phainon’s face, drooping over his head and shoulders, making him seem like a reluctant ghost in navy blue who has come to haunt Aglaea’s closet of well-sought fashion treasures.

“—and these sandals— Oops.”

Behind the fabric of the himátion was Phainon’s bleeding nose who had just sustained a fatal injury from being hit by the heavy heel of a sandal, no doubt also made with gold.

“I’m alright,” Phainon reassures, more to himself than at Aglaea, his voice muffled from underneath the fabric where the golden ichor oozing out of his nose have begun to seep through.

He hears a click of the tongue. It’s either Aglaea is displeased that the himátion is ruined, or the fact that Phainon was not able to catch the sandals in time. Phainon, despite being of a bigger frame and stature, trembles from the anticipation of her wrath.

“Get yourself patched up first,” Aglaea tells him. Her mercy causes Phainon to relax. It’s a small blessing that Aglaea couldn’t see the relief in his face. “Return at once for we still have a lot to cover. If you are to present yourself beside Mydeimos, then you should look the part.”

That’s a dig at Phainon’s sense of fashion if he ever heard one. He will never understand how a man who paraded himself half-naked possessed a better sense of fashion than him.

But then again, Mydei could wear literal rags and still look beautiful. No, Mydei is just beautiful no matter what he wears. Mydei and beauty go hand in hand together, inseparable and intertwined.

Cotton, linen, wool, or even silk of any and every color and kind, and Mydei would still be able to make it work. And then Phainon’s mind traitorously wanders into a more dangerous territory, spurred on by the sight of Mydei in the baths from the previous week.

That is, Mydei without all the grandeur. Bare, flawless tanned skin out for display and Phainon is finally able to see where the various streaks of scarlet etched upon him ends—

Aglaea clears her throat and Phainon is left to scamper out the door, making haste towards the infirmary. Regardless of the rough treatment and barely concealed shade, Phainon is very thankful for Aglaea’s help.)

Despite not having enough sleep for Aglaea had kept him awake four quints into the Curtain-Fall Hour, he can still say that he looks good. Hopefully.

He then allows himself a one last once-over—the last of many—before deeming that he looks presentable enough, nodding at his reflection with an air of pride.

Ignoring the two stubborn strands of hair atop his head that refuses to go down no matter how much he coaxes it with softened beeswax to keep it in place, Phainon then makes his way out of the door and leaves his chambers before the nerves start to kick in.

He had initially expressed his wishes to Mydei to be granted permission to wait outside the room of the latter so they could both go together to meet Lord Krateros. Mydei had agreed shortly, and that was the last of their conversation from the day before.

As he descends the flight of stairs to head towards Mydei’s chambers located two floors down from his, Phainon readies what he’s going to say in front of the man that Mydei holds a profound respect to.

Not much is known about Lord Krateros’ personality. His feats in Kremnos Phainon is well aware of for he could simply walk up to a random Kremnoan and they’ll be able to give him the answer he seeks.

Trusted by the former regents, former master primus of the Watchers, a warrior who embodies Nikador’s virtues, a severe man with years of experience behind him—all of these point to the fact that Lord Krateros is not to be taken lightly, and Phainon has no intentions of making a fool of himself in front of Mydei’s most respected mentor.

Coming face to face with the door to Mydei’s chambers, Phainon raises his hand to knock thrice.

“I’ll be out in a moment,” came Mydei’s deep voice from within.

Janus’ locks turn shortly afterward, opening the door to grant someone from the inside passage to leave the room. And Phainon—

Well. Phainon loses his ability to think.

Swathed in purple, Phainon’s initial thoughts that Mydei would look good in anything and everything are not without merit.

Regardless of how unusual the sight is for Mydei only ever wore red, he managed to make a color, one that Phainon didn’t even bother to think twice of before, to have bewitched Phainon’s senses. Devastatingly so.

Phainon can’t even will himself to look away.

Okhema could be in dire peril right at this moment and Phainon would still choose to behold the mesmerizing beauty in front of him, that is of Mydei in a purple chiton. Though lavish, at the end of the day, it is still just a chiton. Not exactly an article of clothing one should lose their mind over.

Mydei fashions the chiton to be of similarity to how he usually wears his clothes—draped over one shoulder and leaving the rest of his magnificent torso bare, displaying the pattern of scarlet streaks etched across the expanse of his tanned skin, muscles rippling with every minute movement as it reflects the light from Kephale’s Dawn.

The amount of jewelry he wore remains to be the same and yet different: an elaborate necklace made from gold, showcasing intricate craftsmanship and adorned with amethysts of varying sizes and shapes; a bangle to match around his exposed arm, whose purpose is to seemingly make the shape of his biceps even more accentuated; and, a pair of gold rod earrings with an amethyst at the base, a stark contrast to the large hoop ones he typically wore.

Phainon wonders if Mydei’s collection of jewelry rivals that of Aglaea’s.

Accessories aside, Mydei even chose to appropriately go without his gauntlets this time, allowing Phainon the rare sight that is his bare hands—fingers exquisitely long and defined, nails neatly trimmed with the blunt edges shaped in a gentle curve, and veins running up to his forearms, fading with every subtle flex of muscle.

Phainon smiles, feeling breathless. “Hello.” And then, unable to help himself, he adds a lame, “You look very nice.”

To think that he and Mydei are wearing matching chitons makes Phainon feel unbearably warm. Not to mention, they’re going to walk around in public together. Phainon only aims to hope that his own meager self wouldn’t dare sully the radiant beauty that he accompanies.

The radiant beauty in question hasn’t uttered a greeting in return, choosing to assess Phainon with eyes of molten gold, traveling from the ornate sandals below, lingering at the exposed skin of Phainon’s arms, and then up to frown upon the two strands that refuses to be conquered atop Phainon’s head.

After the assessment, Mydei merely says nothing. Now is as good a time as any to tease him for it, is Phainon’s thought process.

“Not even a compliment?”

“So you asked Aglaea for help,” is Mydei’s chosen reply. “A wise decision.”

How Mydei was able to come up with that conclusion, Phainon has no idea. But it’s not entirely a lie, per se. “That I did,” he admits. “Funny thing is, I distinctly recall her saying that I look hideous in purple.”

“Only if you wear purple trousers and distastefully pair it with a yellow tunic,” Mydei says, amusement shining in his eyes as he recounts the anecdote Phainon shared with him just two days prior detailing his fashion failures. “You shouldn’t fault the Goldweaver. She was only stating the truth.”

Phainon slumps. “So you do share her sentiments in regards to that issue.” He sighs dramatically, feigning despair. “I can’t believe this. To think that my dearest friend and equal would turn his back on me.”

“Rest assured, if it was your intention to look ridiculous, you have my full support,” Mydei says. He doesn’t even bother to hide the snicker in his voice this time. “Unfortunately, you’re just dismally horrible at dressing yourself.”

For his sense of fashion to be criticized by a man half-naked was not in Phainon’s list of affairs for the day.

Mydei mercilessly continues, “I may be Kremnoan, but I do pity the eyes of the unfortunate Okheman citizens who would bear witness to what one might call an abomination.”

“Your words are as sharp as knives today,” Phainon says. He would loathe to admit that he’s whining. “What happened to the man who had so softly called me handsome?”

The effect is instantaneous. Mydei’s ears burn bright red as he turns away. “Seeing as your ego is through the roof from such simple words alone, I shall keep it in mind to share my compliments sparingly.”

“Mydei, you should know by now that your words are never simple,” Phainon says, a teasing smile on his lips as Mydei makes a figurative retreat. “Not to me, at least.”

Mydei only scowls without much heat, a poor attempt to appear slighted despite his flushed countenance. “Enough with your nonsense.”

He gives Phainon’s bare arms another look, as if the constant lingering of his gaze was not enough to keep its image ingrained in his memory.

“Wait here. I have to retrieve something from my chambers.”

Before Phainon could reply, Mydei vanishes into his room in a flurry of purple, emerging only moments later with two arm bangles in hand.

No amount of mental fortification could prepare Phainon for what follows: Mydei’s bare hand upon him, radiating heat from where it touches the skin just above his elbow. The cold surface of the gold bangle a stark contrast from the warmth as Mydei clasps it onto his arm, allowing it to rest comfortably on a spot that won't hinder the flex of Phainon’s bicep.

Phainon allows Mydei to do the action a second time for his other arm, his breath coming out short and irregular when he realizes just how close he and Mydei are.

From this angle, Phainon could almost count every strand of Mydei’s eyelashes, pinpoint every flawless pore, marvel at the streak of red that lines his right eye, and the diamond-shaped scarlet mark that kisses his cheekbone remains to be a mesmerizing sight as always.

Mydei is beautiful, and Phainon’s fingers are left to itch by his sides, longing to card them through those silky strands of blonde hair—to pull Mydei even closer so that he may commit to memory every other detail of Mydei that he might have missed from this painfully near yet still so far away of a distance.

Phainon’s breath catches when Mydei’s eyelashes flutter as he blinks, eyes meeting his and Phainon has never seen such enchanting pools of gold despite having witnessed Kephale’s mighty figure bleed it on the daily.

“All done,” Mydei says, barely a whisper for they’re so close they might as well see into each other’s minds.

The hand on Phainon’s arm lingers, the hold is loose and never once did it tighten. Almost as if Mydei only wished to touch, the opportunity to take some more—perhaps pull, grip, or knead at the muscle—entirely out of the question.

Phainon reminds himself to breathe, gaze tracing the curve of Mydei’s lips, pink and soft and —

“Thank you.”

“You’re welcome.” Mydei pulls away, assessing Phainon fully now with the addition of the new accessories. He nods in approval. “Keep the bangles, Deliverer. They look better on you.”

The warmth Mydei leaves in his wake is something that Phainon chases, the scent of pomegranates and sweetness lingering in the air. It’s a loss that never fails to leave Phainon aching, desperately wanting for more.

Krateros agreed to meet them in a gazebo located east of the Marmoreal Palace. Upon their approach, Phainon could already make out a figure donning a red Kremnoan armor, and a back that stood tall despite his old age. He alone indulges in the shade the gazebo provides.

“About time you showed up,” Krateros says, still with his back turned from the newly arrived pair. The gruffness of his voice causes the fine hairs upon Phainon’s nape to stand out of sheer nervousness. “You ought to know, this old man is not exactly keen on waiting.”

“Forgive us for the delay, master,” Mydei apologizes. “We were… held up on the way.”

‘Held up’ would be a good way to call whatever it was that had occurred earlier.

Krateros finally turns around. His left eye had already turned pale, a scar running through it. His right eye, on the other hand, is piercingly dark, unsubtly regarding Phainon up and down as if assessing his worth.

With his arms crossed, Krateros’ lips remained sealed, his opinions a well-guarded secret, one that Phainon could only ever hope to know.

“Master,” Mydei began, breaking the tense silence. “This is the man I’ve spoken to you about. Phainon of Ae—”

“No need for introductions,” Krateros cuts off coolly. “Especially not when every living soul in Okhema speaks of his name and sings his praises.”

If that was Krateros’ attempt at a compliment, it sure didn’t feel like one. Phainon could even sense the discomfort radiating from Mydei in palpable waves. There’s an unspoken dissonance here that Phainon is not privy to, but he knows well enough that he is far from being given the right to pry.

“It’s a pleasure to finally make your acquaintance, Lord Krateros,” Phainon says, keeping his voice light as he extends his hand for a shake.

Krateros merely stares down at the offending limb, much like how Mydei did in their first meeting back at the Vortex of Genesis. Phainon wonders if this was just something that Kremnoans do normally.

Before Phainon could so much as lower his hand, Krateros had once again turned his back on the pair. “If that is all, I’d like to be left alone now.”

“It’s unlike you to barely say anything,” came Mydei’s voice. Though his tone still remains respectful, a hint of impatience belies his words.

Krateros scoffs. “What’s there to say? I told you already, Mydeimos. You can do whatever you want with whomever you want, as long as the throne of Kremnos does not sit empty for too long.” He barely turns his head around when he says, “Does that man beside you even know of the responsibilities you carry?”

“It’s not something he should pay any mind to,” Mydei replies through gritted teeth. “Phainon has enough on his plate already.”

Phainon frowns upon hearing this. And here he thought Mydei was beginning to slowly open up to him. It seems that the distance between them remains to persist, even after all this time.

His thoughts are cut short when Krateros bursts into a humorless laughter, turning around for the second time. The smile on his lips barely even reaches his eyes.

“You hold so dear this... hero’s innocence?” Krateros asks.

Though the question was obviously directed towards Mydei, his dark eye was centered solely upon Phainon, boring holes if it were possible. Phainon tamps down the urge to fidget under the scrutinizing gaze.

“Young man,” Krateros begins, addressing Phainon this time. “If you are to be of any use, convince Mydeimos to take up Kremnos’ crown instead of allowing his own people to waste away in this foreign land, left to wander like sheeps without a shepherd until a pack of wolves devours us whole.”

This time, Phainon is unable to hide his discomfort under the veil of placidity. He and Mydei have never once discussed the latter’s claim to the throne. Mydei never brought it up, and Phainon knew better than to impose. If Mydei wished to speak of it, he would already have.

A sigh resounds.

“And here I thought you’d be amenable for a proper conversation without bringing up the crown,” Mydei says at last. The despondency in his tone doesn’t go unnoticed by Phainon’s hearing, attuned to every single one of Mydei’s inflections. “Even now and in the presence of an uninvolved party—a guest—you still choose to speak of this.”

“Uninvolved?” Krateros demands, the volume of his voice rising with every drop in his absurdly low patience. “Why, the moment you presented him in front of me dressed in those garments, he is as good as involved with the rest of us Kremnoans that you’ve doomed in this so-called eternal land.”

In an attempt to diffuse the situation, Phainon stands in front of Mydei like a habit whenever the latter is about to engage himself in a fight. This time, however, it is not the poor soul of a random (provoking) citizen that Phainon wishes to protect from (a provoked) Mydei’s ire.

No. At this moment, it is Mydei of whom Phainon shields from his mentor’s sharp words. Though futile, Phainon will die trying.

“Lord Krateros, you’ve said enough.”

Krateros raises an eyebrow. “What gives you the right to discern whether or not I’ve said enough?” He takes a daunting step forward. Phainon holds his ground. “You have proved nothing to me, boy. And by the looks of things, you know nothing as well. Aside from your prowess in battle, I honestly fail to see anything else of substance.”

Phainon would admit that it is better to hear Krateros belittle him than having to endure him directing his harshness towards Mydei. And just when Phainon readies himself for more insults hurled his way—of which he is so painfully familiar with, courtesy of his overbearing mind who never fails to remind him of his lack of worth—a warm hand encloses upon his wrist, tugging lightly.

Mydei would never beg. But at this moment, Phainon has to admit that this is the closest thing he’s ever seen Mydei allow himself to do such a debasing act.

“It seems that we have to do this another time, then,” Mydei says, distant in the way he regards Krateros. He doesn’t meet Phainon’s gaze when he mutters, “Let’s go, Deliverer.”

Phainon’s heart aches. Mydei may be a man of few words, but he never once sounded so quiet when he spoke. His voice always reverberated with power, eager to be heard by anyone and everyone who would listen. For it to be reduced to such meekness—

The hand on his wrist falters. This time, Phainon takes Mydei’s hand in his own, holding tightly and refusing to let go even if Mydei shoots him with a confused expression as if to ask, What are you doing?

Phainon ignores him, redirecting his attention back at Krateros who eyes their intertwined hands. The severity in his face seemed to have uncharacteristically softened for a bit from the sight, but returns the moment that Phainon speaks.

“Lord Krateros, I can’t help but be led to believe that this conversation is unbecomingly one-sided.”

Krateros crosses his arms, his tone akin to that of a tired adult humoring a small child when he says, “Is that so?”

“It is so,” Phainon insists. “You’ve spoken your wishes, but you adamantly oppose to hear that of Mydei’s.”

“His wish is for what’s left of Kremnos to stay under that blonde usurper’s rule,” Krateros retorts. “Forgive me for not wanting to hear any of it.”

And though hearing Aglaea being addressed so demeaningly puts a bitter taste in Phainon’s mouth, he presses on.

“I may not know of the complications your tribe faces and won’t defend Okhema’s prejudice against you, but please heed my warning: it is not safe outside the holy city. You may wish to return to your home lost in the sea of fog, but it will only serve to endanger you,” Phainon explains. “Okhema is the safest place for you and your people. Mydei knows this and he brought you all here for your own good. He has thought of nothing but the future of the Kremnoans.”

“The future of the Kremnoans will only be fulfilled once he ascends to the throne! He is the crown prince of Kremnos—”

“Even if that is so, Kremnos still remains to be lost due to Nikador’s madness. If you have a better solution for us to be able to track it down faster, do share.” Phainon hardens his stare. “But until then, you are not to harass Mydei about something he clearly wishes not to speak of yet. Give him time.”

“And why would he avoid such a discussion?” Krateros asks in turn, eyebrows furrowing. “Because he refuses to be king?”

“Mydei is free to decide for himself in regards to what he wants. King or not, he’s never relinquished the responsibility he has so selflessly carried to ensure the safety of his people. What difference would there be if a crown is involved? A royal title?”

Mydei’s hand in his grips him tight, aghast. “Deliverer—”

“You speak so freely of your own opinions,” Krateros muses, more surprised than angered. “This is the man you hold so high of a regard, Mydeimos? You’re growing to be likened to those weak Okhemans who choose words rather than blades to prove a point.”

“Phainon is my equal,” Mydei says. This time, his voice does not waver. Phainon could feel his heart race upon hearing such a firm declaration. “He is as talented with a blade as he is with his words. Do not regard him so lowly.”

Krateros merely huffs. “Forgive me if I do when this man is clearly tolerating your whims! He knows not the best for you.”

“And you do?”

The attention of the other two lands on Phainon.

Krateros reddens at the question. “I beg your pardon?”

“You know what’s best for Mydei? Not me, and not even Mydei himself, but you?” Phainon reiterates with a white-lipped smile. “How I wish I would never possess such pronounced confidence and pride for it would be my downfall.”

In a blink of an eye, a hand had already made its way around Phainon’s neck, pinning him to the ground in a manner most swift as it is violent. Phainon groans from the impact, ears ringing as he is met with the darkness of Krateros’ sharp eye.

“Master!”

Mydei tries to separate Krateros from Phainon. Krateros doesn’t even fight, allowing himself to be pulled away on his feet and Phainon is left to gasp as he tries to regain his bearings whilst sitting up.

“Have you gone insane?” Mydei exclaims, rounding up on the older. “To harm a Chrysos Heir warrants an extreme punishment! The golden threads will not show you mercy!”

“Death would be a better mercy than to see you frolic around with this utterly naive hero!”

Phainon feels his nose drip warm golden blood. “I may be so. But I know better than to force my ideals onto someone else.”

Mydei turns to glare at him. “Phainon, enough—”

“Do not speak to me so directly, you foolish child!” Krateros spits, drowning out Mydei’s admonishments. “His mother, Queen Gorgo, entrusted me to make him king! To usher Kremnos into a new era of Strife!”

Phainon falters upon the mention of Mydei’s mother.

“I am not simply forcing my ideals on him! It is his fate! A fate he is so adamant to look away from just so he could run around with you people who bear Kephale’s golden blood in your veins!” Krateros’ voice breaks, almost desperate. “Do not act as if you know everything, boy, because you don’t. And all you have to blame is Mydeimos who chooses to shield you from the weight that the bloodied crown would eventually bear upon his head.”

Mydei helps Phainon up from the ground, a flash of concern on his face that Phainon catches briefly before Mydei turns around to address his teacher.

“That’s enough, Krateros,” Mydei states, bitingly cold and yet vulnerable all the same. “It seems that we’ve both disappointed ourselves today.”

Krateros scowl gradually softens into that of resignation, opting to look away as his lip quivers. Whether it be from the sheer frustration of words unspoken, or from biting back emotions so profound, Phainon doesn’t know.

It doesn’t help the guilt that worms its way into his gut. Perhaps he really did speak out of turn this time.

Mydei continues, “I hope that the next time I’ll seek your audience, it won't end so sourly.” To Phainon, he says, “Let’s go, Deliverer.”

The breeze that blows through the Garden of Life is sweet and tranquil. Sitting on the bench at a secluded corner and contemplating earlier’s exchange, Phainon can’t help but think—

“I guess your teacher hates me now, huh.”

Beside him, Mydei only sighs. “Hatred is not something my teacher wallows in,” Mydei says. “He is simply set in his ways due to his old age. I should’ve spoken to him beforehand. You will have to forgive him, Deliverer.”

“There’s nothing to forgive,” Phainon replies, sullen. “I could sense that he didn’t mean any ill will towards you.”

Mydei sighs again. “I assumed that he would’ve already calmed his mind since our last conversation.”

Last conversation. Phainon didn’t want to pry about what they talked about for Krateros’ anger to persist even now. But then he forgets that Mydei could read him like an open book, his curiosity written so evidently on his face.

“I told him that I have no intentions of inheriting the coreflame of Strife,” Mydei answers to a question unasked.

Phainon stills out of shock. “W-What?”

“It was never something I wanted. Never will. Divinity does not equal regency, not to me. And I desire neither.”

“But I—” Phainon attempts to form coherent sentences. “I always thought…”

Since Mydei was the crown prince of Kremnos, he was the most fitting of the Chrysos Heirs to inherit the coreflame of his Titan. Strife was always supposed to be in Mydei’s hands.

Before he met Mydei, Nikador’s coreflame was something Phainon had worked ceaselessly towards. Spurred on by his desire to avenge the death of his loved ones, a tragedy brought on by the Black Tide, Phainon wished to be at the forefront of fighting against it.

However, the only way he could do that was to possess Nikador’s coreflame who acted as the Guardian of Amphoreus, the one who moved Their mobile nation to quell the disastrous darkness. Phainon was so sure that the coreflame would be his—

Until he met Mydei.

Only then did he realize his own inadequacy, for Mydei was always the worthier one to embody Strife.

“Have you told anyone of this?” Phainon asks, keeping his voice low just in case anyone were to hear.

“Only the Goldweaver,” Mydei answers. The way he seems so unbothered is off-putting. “I told her directly about this when I first arrived at Okhema just so she wouldn’t harbor any expectations of me. And now, I’ve told you.”

That was months ago. Phainon wonders if Mydei had come up with such a decision even before he came to Okhema. This is clearly not something that Mydei had simply decided upon in such a short notice.

“So you’ve made up your mind,” Phainon says, feeling helpless all of a sudden. “And Lord Krateros took the news poorly, I assume?”

“Poorly would be an understatement.” Mydei rubs his temples, as if recounting such a memory brought him a great headache. “I had to take him to the infirmary or else his old heart would’ve stopped beating right then and there. It would humiliate him to the afterlife if he died in such a lame manner instead of on the battlefield.”

Despite everything, Phainon allows a soft laugh to escape his lips. The image of a disgruntled Mydei escorting a raging Krateros to the infirmary is quite entertaining indeed.

“He does seem like the type to mind such matters, especially when battle and death are involved.”

Mydei huffs. “He is a Kremnoan through and through, stubbornness and all.”

Phainon nods for he does agree that Kremnoans (Mydei) do possess a distinct stubbornness to them.

“It is because of his embodiment of our virtues that my mother chose him as my mentor, to be the one to guide me on my path to the crown.” Mydei stares at the palm of his hands. “I trust him with my life. But as you can see, there are times where we fail to see eye to eye, and I’m left to ponder my thoughts on my own instead of seeking his counsel.”

Phainon always knew that Mydei prefers to carry unspoken burdens on his own. But right now, Phainon can’t help but think that this is Mydei’s way of finally asking for help, of finally opening up and allowing his troubles to be shared with those who care for him.

“You know, I’m always here to listen.”

Mydei looks up, the surprise in his face evident just before he masks it with a taunting smirk. “You’ll spare time for me at the expense of your Deliverer duties?”

“Hearing the woes of a dearest companion counts as a good deed, does it not?” Phainon simpers, a smile of his own.

Mydei scoffs, though far from being aggrieved. “It hardly counts as woes. It’s more like…” He trails off, thinking it through with his eyebrows furrowed. “More like an obstacle that I have yet to overcome.”

“And I have no doubts that you will.”

“Is that so?” Mydei jeers, almost like a challenge. “My story is not a happy one, Deliverer. Are you sure you’ll be okay to lend an ear? Word around the street is that you’re known to burst into tears upon hearing of sad and gruesome tales that involve deaths.”

“Deaths?” Phainon doubles down. “Why, if the death of a most treasured friend is involved, then you’ll find my dignity flying out of the window.”

Mydei has the audacity to smile, but the distraction of such radiance would not hinder Phainon. Not this time.

“What a wretched friend that is, dying so easily. You must’ve been in shambles.”

Phainon leans in just a little bit, their foreheads almost touching, and allows some semblance of sincerity to seep through despite the exchange of jests.

“Indeed,” he agrees, allowing himself to get lost into the pools of gold that serve as Mydei’s eyes. “What a wretched friend he is, for allowing me to witness his demise and breaking my heart in the process.”

It is very easy to pinpoint the exact moment that Mydei loses his composure. Eyes widening for a brief moment before he leans away, choosing to avoid Phainon’s gaze in the process.

“I was only gone for but a brief moment,” was the lame excuse that Mydei had chosen.

Phainon disagrees. “It felt like an eternity.”

“You exaggerate. We’ve both established months ago that death is—”

“Out of your reach, yes,” Phainon continues for him, a wry smile on his lips. No matter how many times they have this conversation, or even speak of it in jest, it doesn’t change the fact that whenever Mydei dies, Phainon would be in anguish. “One could only imagine how you were able to come to know of such a curse.”

Mydei tenses beside him. “It’s not as bad as you’d think.”

“Enlighten me, then,” Phainon says softly. And then, he adds, “Only if you want to.”

This is the second time during the conversation that he urges Mydei to confide in him. If Mydei still chooses not to speak of it, he won’t push any further. Even if the history of Mydei’s curse is something that sparks Phainon’s curiosity, Mydei’s comfort comes first and foremost.

“I did promise you that I would tell you my story someday,” Mydei says eventually.

“I fail to recall when you made such a promise,” Phainon replies in an attempt to lessen the weight, for he knows how much Mydei values the fulfillment of any and every promise. “Only that you’ll do it as a form of thanks for me trying to save you back at the Abyss.”

“Is that so.”

“Are you doubting me?”

Mydei turns to him. “I have never.”

Phainon feels his heart beat faster. “You can trust me.” I’ll listen.

“I know.”

A quietude settles between them, expected and comfortable in a sense. Phainon allows Mydei to think it over, and waits patiently; the soft gust of the breeze is enough to blow away any lingering unease.

“I’ve spoken to you about my mother before,” Mydei says after a while.

Phainon nods, remembering their drunken time at the Heroes’ Baths. “You have.”

Mydei takes a deep breath, almost as if he were steeling himself, settling his gaze upon the Garden of Life where citizens come to gather and exchange thoughts, lounging alongside docile chimeras, and basking in Kephale’s Dawn atop the gigantic lily pads.

Though the view ahead of them is almost utopic, Mydei’s story, as Phainon would come to know of, is far from it.

“When I was but a mere infant, my father threw me into the Sea of Souls with nary a remorse for the death of his only son,” Mydei recounts to an avid listener of one. “It’s a sacrifice for Nikador, he said. A way of ensuring that the legacy of Kremnos wouldn’t end in my hands as stated by a prophecy.”

He turns to Phainon. Despite his words having nothing to smile about, Mydei’s lips wore but a shadow of it.

“I was then left to be swept away by the currents of the Sea of Souls, but not once did it lead me to the Shores of Death. That was how I came to know of my curse.”

Phainon smiles wrily. “This is what you consider to be ‘not as bad as I’d think?’”

Mydei shoots him a dry stare. “Would you have preferred it if Thanatos presented Themselves before me and told me that They had forsaken me to a fate that didn’t know Them?”

“No,” Phainon answers right away. “I actually would much rather you don’t experience either of those horrible circumstances.”

“It’s already done, Deliverer. I drifted at Sea for nine years. The souls of the dead could reach the Shores in just a few hours after their demise, if I’m not mistaken. It is the place where one shall walk the Path for three winters, pass the Three Gates of Judgement, before subsequently ending up in one of the Three Destinations depending on the soul’s behavior during its time in the land of the living.”

Only one harrowing detail catches Phainon’s attention. “You drifted at the Sea of Souls for nine years?” He knew better than anyone that there’s a lot of details being omitted here. “How did you even manage to leave such a place?”

He imagines a young Mydei, ceaselessly fighting off the waves just so he wouldn’t sink to its depths. Phainon wonders if Mydei encountered the souls of the dead during that time, his childlike innocence long since been tarnished by the concept of death, loss, and betrayal.

“All I remembered was the sight of a bright star—the brightest out of anything I’ve ever seen, guiding me away from the currents,” Mydei answers distantly, as if recalling the moment requires great focus. “Next thing I knew, I was already upon the shores of Carmitis.”

“Did you return to Kremnos?”

“Why would I?” Mydei asks sardonically. “I have no ties to that cursed land. But some Kremnoan exiles did get wind that I survived the old king’s sacrifice, and they chose to follow me in my journey across Amphoreus. Thus, the detachment was gradually formed, and I have gained new allies in the process for a lone warrior can never be victorious in a war that wages for far too long.

“They filled me in as to what had happened in Kremnos during my absence. Including how my father killed my mother in an unfair duel, how she died to defend my claim to the throne, and how she wished for me to be king—of which you are now aware of, given that my master had so explicitly made you know of it.”

“By pinning me to the ground,” Phainon quips.

“He does that sometimes.”

Phainon nods slowly, the throb at the back of his head and the tight, ghostly sensation around his neck a lingering reminder of Krateros’ strength.

If Aglaea had caught wind of such events, she—and perhaps even the Okhema Council of Elders, despite their blatant opposition towards the Chrysos Heirs, but would still jump at any opportunity to oppress the Kremnoans—would make sure that Krateros won’t be able to walk around Okhema without an escort.

Phainon keeps in mind to put in a word with Aglaea to be lenient with Krateros’ punishment. The woman is capable of merciless feats after all.

“You mentioned before that you killed the old king,” Phainon says cautiously, referring to the conversation of their first meeting of which not a single detail has faded in his memory. “Did you do it to avenge your mother?”

“I won’t deny it,” Mydei answers. “But I also did it to stop Eurypon from further leading Kremnos into ruination.”

Mydei then turns to the skies, his gaze faraway.

“And now, I’ve left my people in the hands of foreigners, my nation lost, and our Titan wreaking havoc with neither rhyme nor reason as we speak. Sometimes, I wonder if I made the right choice.”

Phainon lets the words hang in the air, choosing how to appropriately respond but comes up with a blank. In the end, only Mydei knows the true extent of his feelings and the consequences that his choices have left for him to handle.

The only thing Phainon could provide in this moment of vulnerability and openness is a listening ear.

He knew that Mydei had a reason for doing what he did: to keep his people safe, to avenge his mother, and to put an end to his father’s schemes. His past is nothing but a culmination of pain. Even if Mydei had said nothing of it now, Phainon is sure that he’s lost a lot of significant people during his journey before he arrived at Okhema.

If Mydei is ready to tell him about it, Phainon would make sure that he’s there when Mydei does. And just like now, he’ll shoulder the burdens that Mydei carries even for just a temporary moment, if only to alleviate Mydei’s sense of isolation and loneliness.

“You’re being really quiet,” Mydei notes after a while with a slight hesitance. “Have I managed to scare you off, Deliverer?”

Phainon scoffs lightly. “You think of yourself to be so formidable…” He then gives Mydei a reassuring smile. “You’ll never scare me off. I was simply choosing to maintain my silence to give you room to establish your thoughts.”

And though Mydei looked offended by Phainon’s initial statement, he eventually relaxes, the aggrieved lines on his face softening as he wordlessly conveys his gratitude.

“Surprisingly wise of you, Deliverer,” Mydei muses. “Even if you always put to use that idiotic mouth of yours, it does make me wonder if you run around sharing the profound effects of silence like a philosopher in your free time.”

“Not at all,” Phainon replies with a nondescript wave of his hand, a movement that he notices Mydei following closely, a glint in those gold eyes. “A philosopher has to be proficient in defending their stance from those who dare to question it. I’d say such a quality is not something I possess.”

Mydei raises an eyebrow, able to see through the false modesty so quickly. “I heard from Castorice that during your time in the Grove, you represented your school—the Nousporists —and became the debate champion ten times in a row.”

Phainon grins, not finding it within himself to deny it. “Do I sense a compliment coming in?”

“You wish,” Mydei retorts with a light elbow to Phainon’s ribs.

Regardless of its playful nature, the action still successfully causes Phainon to suffer severe emotional damages, his heart beating wildly from within his chest and his tongue indubitably tied.

Due to his silence, Mydei continues to press on, “But I must admit, I find your responses quite delightfully entertaining on a good day. Downright infuriating at most, though.”

Phainon regains his voice upon hearing the compliment, utterly rejuvenated. “It’s only because you make it so easy for me to tease you that I’m able to respond so wittily.”

“So your intelligence relies on tomfoolery. Not a philosopher, but perhaps a jester would be more suitable. You should join the Clowns of Zagreus when you have the time. I heard they’re currently a member short and needed someone to juggle apples, or something.”

“Absolutely not,” Phainon says, feigning offense. But deep down, he preens at the fact that Mydei finds him funny. Plus, he can’t exactly juggle apples. For Mydei to think that he’s capable of such a feat sounds like a high praise if he’s ever heard one. “I would much rather prefer to be your Deliverer.”

Mydei’s posture tenses, a slight shift in the air as his eyes of gold flickers. “My Deliverer, huh. That sounds incredibly selfish of me, to have you all to myself.”

“I wouldn’t mind,” Phainon says with a shrug, feeling his face heat up in the process at the thought of Mydei claiming him for his own. “You’re the most selfless man I know. At least, allow yourself to want something for a change.”

Phainon had fully expected for Mydei to respond with a jab of his own about the faults of indulging oneself too much. And so, when Mydei leans in unprompted, Phainon was caught so off-guard that he almost falls off the bench.

Mydei finds amusement in this, as seen with the way his lips are curved in an unmistakable smile, the corners of his eyes crinkling, and every little shift in his expression is for Phainon to behold.

They are so close, Phainon could barely think.

A brush of a hand against Phainon’s own causes him to jolt at the touch, the action allowing him to further lean into Mydei’s space until the tips of their noses briefly brush against each other, their lips a hairbreadth’s distance. If the breeze were to blow harder, they would be—

“I do want,” came Mydei’s voice, interrupting Phainon’s indecent spiral of thoughts. “Achingly so, Phainon.”

Mydei’s finger traces Phainon’s, drawing circles and lingering pointedly at one spot where—

The sudden realization hits Phainon like a dromas whose passenger urges it to make haste. All this time, Mydei’s finger has been tracing the lone strand of blonde hair securely tied around Phainon’s own, like a makeshift ring crafted out of a moment’s thoughtless impulsivity.

Phainon’s blood runs cold as embarrassment creeps upon his very being, aiming to drown him within its merciless tides.

“That’s—”

“I don’t mind,” Mydei tells him, tracing more deliberately this time, as if to test the strand’s durability around Phainon’s forefinger. “My eyes are sharp. You’d be a fool to think that I wouldn’t notice.”

Phainon can barely hear Mydei’s words with how loud his heart is beating, all that blood and none of it chooses to supply his poor excuse of a brain who refuses to function in dire situations such as this, rushing to his groin unanimously instead.

Faintly, he is able to say, “Forgive me all the same.”

What must Mydei think of him now?

“Where was this shyness when you went ahead and did something like this?”

Phainon clenches his eyes shut the moment that he feels the tip of Mydei’s thumb slowly creep upon the sensitive skin of his inner forearm, the rest of Mydei’s warm, soft, and bare hand enclosing around his wrist in a loose grip, slowly caressing up and down as if to soothe Phainon from his humiliation.

It’s futile. The movement only spurs the endless visions Phainon has kept hidden within the deepest crevices of his mind, powerless in his thoughts as the image of Mydei, doing the exact same motions, held not the chasteness of his arm, but something else.

“Mydei—”

Mydei’s grip on his wrist tightens, and Phainon almost whines at the suddenness of the sensation, feeling his head go light, his body weightless.

“Deliverer, you’re about to—”

The thump his body makes against the ground is a delayed sound. Only after a moment’s reprieve from Mydei’s wicked touch was Phainon able to come to terms that he’s fallen off, his back on the grass and his legs still propped upon the stone bench.

“—fall, I was going to say.” Mydei stares down at him with pure astonishment. “Are you alright?”

The audacity of this man who knows not of the concupiscent effects he has on Phainon’s poor, poor heart.

Ignoring the ache between his legs and the burning hot feeling on his face, Phainon answers with a breathless, “Yes.”

Mydei raises an eyebrow. “Do you need help?”

“You’re mocking me.”

“This hardly counts as mocking, Deliverer. If you wish to lie on the grass like so, you should’ve brought a mat with you.”

Phainon curses himself for thinking that Mydei was offering to help with… his other problem. He is so screwed that it’s not even funny. And Mydei, the beautiful and muscular minx that he is, is beyond oblivious to Phainon’s plight.

“Sure. I’ll keep your suggestion in mind,” Phainon replies with a glare, not exactly sure why he’s even angry.

Mydei only sighs. “You need not to be embarrassed. I already told you, I don’t mind.”

Heavy footfalls coming from behind him interrupts his thoughts. Chartonus appears in his line of sight, a basket of asphodels in hand. The hooded man frowns but does not pry.

“Mydei,” Chartonus greets, igniting the furnace as he does so. “Here, for how long, waiting?”

“Not long,” the man in the hood responds.

“Apologize, sincerely, I am.”

“There is no need.” Gold eyes linger to the basket of asphodels. “You were due a break, anyway. Despite the storm, waiting is but a trivial consequence to your masterful service.”

Chartonus hums. “Your patronage, I always thank,” he says. “Anything you need, of service, I will be.”

The man in the hood merely smiles, eyes of gold flickering against the flames of the furnace.

“I’d like to put down a commission,” he says before procuring a bag of gold nuggets from within his cloak, presenting it to Chartonus. “A matrimonial dagger, if you please. Of Kremnoan design.”

Chartonus is quiet as he takes the heavy bag, placing it upon Talanton’s Scale. “My sincerest congratulations.”

“Thank you, and…” A gauntlet-clad hand reaches out, a pair of ruby and sapphire nestled atop the palm. The cut of both gems are of carefully equal shape, almost complementary to each other. “I’d like these to be embedded in the hilt. As for the initials, you already know which letters to use.”

Chartonus nods. “Which letters, well enough, I know.”
