· · ─ · ─ · ·

The Akashians—people hailing from the fallen city of Akashic—have moved to Okhema some years prior, almost a decade now if Phainon is not mistaken. He remembers hearing of their plight caused by the Black Tide while he was still studying in the Grove, and even sneaked away from his lessons just so he could help the Akashians get settled in the holy city.

The survivors were all followers of Georios. Considering that their city was built around a temple made solely for the worship of the Pillar of Stone, they naturally had several festivals and rituals ingrained in their culture.

Aglaea allowed them to still uphold their traditions in any way they could during their stay in Okhema, and even encouraged other citizens to observe and be respectful. If the Akashians allowed it, they could even participate.

The Akashians are kind-hearted people, a stark contrast to their savage history spurred on by the arrival of calamitous occurrences during the early days of Era Bellica. They allowed people of all nations to be of help and partake in Georios’ bountiful blessings. Thus, several years since their integration into Okheman society, Okhema would hold the Revival Ritual on the eighth day of the Month of Cultivation.

The first week of the fourth month is an exhausting one. Vast fields located south of Okhema —where the land is flat and fertile with an ample water source—is used for the ritual. This entails the need to till and fertilize the soil that takes up the most time during the first week, followed by the planting of wheat kernels.

Mydei and Phainon, as esteemed Chrysos Heirs, took the time off from their busy schedules to help the citizens speed up the process. Considering that Phainon had been consistently helping out the Akashians for years, Aglaea made it his job to show Mydei the ropes.

“I have an idea,” Phainon says, standing beside Mydei as they stare at the empty fields ahead of them.

Mydei only hums. “A ridiculous one, I bet.”

“Not quite.” Phainon shoots him a smile. Having Mydei around just made things more exciting. “Should we see who can till the land the fastest? I take the east fields, you take the west. Both three sets of ten aroura each, if I’m not mistaken. A good challenge, wouldn’t you say?”

“Only for a fool who thinks it’s possible, maybe,” is Mydei’s response.

The mentioned land is indeed too vast for merely two ordinary people to tend to it. But it should be known that Kephale’s golden blood runs in their veins—that alone should exclude them from being ‘ordinary.’

“You sound like you’re giving up already,” Phainon teases.

“I’m simply questioning the feasibility of such an undertaking.” He gives Phainon a deliberate once-over. “My body never tires. You, on the other hand…”

Phainon scoffs at the blatant jab at his stamina. But before he could come up with a retort, the sounds of distant chatter fills the silence behind them, accompanied by the clack of tools.

They both turn to the Akashians by the village square who were in the middle of preparing for a full day of tilling ahead. Most of them are of old age and have only a single ox to assist —the last of the three males they’ve managed to save after the Black Tide invaded their city. It was ever a pity that no females were spared, yet another species about to go extinct.

Phainon sees the exact moment that his intentions were understood by Mydei: the old should no longer work and instead, take the time to rest and leave the labor to the young ones. Or in this case, two extremely competitive Chrysos Heirs.

“I accept the challenge,” Mydei finally says with his arms crossed, having made up his mind in a moment’s realization. And then he takes it up a notch, as he always does. “We might as well just do everything ourselves.”

“Even if it’s us, a field this vast would take too long for only two people to work on,” Phainon says, fondness seeping through him, brought on by Mydei’s enthusiasm. “We can plow what has been decided upon and leave the rest to the others.” He squints at the field. “Should be about… five sets of ten aroura. I heard the detachment will be arriving tomorrow to help out?”

Mydei nods. “They are.”

“That’s good news. Some willing farmers from other nations are also amenable to lend their aid. With more people helping this year, we might be able to get the fields ready ahead of schedule…”

A hand on his shoulder startles Phainon from voicing his thoughts out loud. Mydei’s lips are curved in a smile middling between genuineness and teasing. He gives Phainon’s shoulder a light squeeze.

“Not bad, Deliverer,” he commends and Phainon feels his knees go weak at the praise. “I’ll let you have the honor of delivering the good news to the Akashians.”

The initial delight evaporates way too quickly as Phainon gives Mydei a dry look. The latter must think that he’s so funny for that.

Endearing. Annoying.

“Rest assured,” Mydei continues. “I’ll wait for you here and won’t start ahead of time.”

“Even if you do, I’ll still emerge victorious,” Phainon shoots back with a smirk of his own. “You can begin tending to the land, Your Highness. I won’t hold it against you.”

Mydei shoots him a glare. “Spare me the charity. I have no need for such.”

Phainon raises an eyebrow. “But isn’t this your first time tilling a field?”

“I’ve tilled fields before using the lands rendered defeated by the detachment,” Mydei explains, a tinge of irritation in his tone, perhaps thinking that Phainon’s words meant to underestimate even if Phainon’s intentions were anything but. “How did you expect me to feed a whole army in between campaigns?”

It was then that Phainon remembered that the Kremnoan detachment didn’t exactly have a place to return to, an exile order from their own land of birth had left them to wander the lands and seek renown elsewhere.

Perhaps Phainon’s teasing was a bit tactless this time, but an apology would only serve to provoke Mydei even further.

“Alright,” he says, keeping his voice light. Mydei’s tense shoulders relax, eager to direct the conversation elsewhere. “I’ll let the Akashians know that they’ve been relieved of their duties for today.”

Even if the Akashians were reluctant to have only two people prepare a third of the fields for planting wheat, they acquiesced in the end with Phainon’s incessant begging.

The elders merely shook their heads resolutely, wondering why someone was so eager to take up such a grueling task. But then again, the minds of the youth are something one of age could no longer comprehend.

“There’s a couple of arōtra in the shed, Phainon,” Demeas, the old Akashian chief, says with a smile, his face wrinkled slightly even more now than how Phainon last remembers it. “A simple thanks alone is not enough to convey my gratitude for your help all these years. I will always remember the favor you and Lord Mydei have done for us today.”

“As Chrysos Heirs, it is not only our duty to protect, but to also ensure the comfort of all citizens,” Phainon reassures. “Mr. Demeas, this is but a small compensation for the bountiful grain your land has provided for Okhema.”

Demeas merely laughs, a gruff yet pleasant sound. “My land is but a measly space that Lady Aglaea had so graciously lended to us. It does not compare to the land the Council of Elders hold authority over.”

“But it is a land blessed by Georios, nevertheless.”

The corners of Demeas’ green eyes crinkle. “You’ve always been a flatterer, son. I shall not hinder your work now. If you ever need anything, I’m afraid I won’t be available. You already know my wife—”

“Madam Marpessa.” Phainon nods. “I was wondering, where is she?”

“Out in the orchard, most likely,” Demeas answers with a distinct fondness in his tone accompanied by a light laugh. “Best expect that you’ll be snacking on apples later.”

Demeas’ eyes glinted with affection at the mention of his wife, and Phainon could only wonder how the old couple were able to maintain affections between each other even after more than five decades of marriage.

As a Chrysos Heir, Phainon dares not wish for the same idyllic fate to befall him, it would be selfish. Such is not something the duty-bound is meant to indulge in.

With a tight-lipped smile, Phainon excuses himself and heads to the shed, dragging two arōtra with him. True to his word, Mydei stood at the exact same spot where Phainon had left him earlier, arms crossed and posture tensed with impatience.

When he turns around to shoot Phainon a glare with those eyes of pure gold, Phainon once again chooses to remind himself of his duty—his thoughts should not linger on what could be, but on what must be: the coreflames restored, the prophecy fulfilled.

He doesn’t doubt that Mydei adheres to the same way of thinking. Given their age and status, if they really wanted to, they would have already taken in lovers. But Mydei has never once succumbed to such a distraction (as far as Phainon knew of), and likewise, Phainon had never considered anyone, or anything for that matter, to be worthy of dividing his attention from the Flame-Chase Journey.

Until now.

“I thought you’d keep me waiting until the Action Hour,” Mydei drawls.

“Just did some brief catching-up,” Phainon reasons, easing his mind off of thoughts that are nigh impossible, of desires better kept hidden. “Ready?”

Mydei only rolls his eyes and takes an arōtron by the handle from Phainon’s weak grasp. Heading to the west fields, he manages a taunting, “Good luck, Deliverer.”

Phainon stares at Mydei’s retreating figure, an unexplainable discomfort in his gut. Uncaring whether or not Mydei heard him, he says, “You, too.”

From the beginning of the Entry Hour to the first couple of quints of the Action Hour, the calloused skin of Phainon’s palms grow closely acquainted with the wooden handle of the arōtron, the supposed rough texture already smoothened by years of use.

Neither he nor Mydei opted to use the last remaining ox. Phainon would admit that without a draft animal to assist, the skill and strength needed to do the labor had multiplied tenfold. It was ever a blessing from Georios that the soil is less demanding, a testament to the care of the Akashian farmers who tended to the fields all year round.

Kephale’s Dawn shone warm light against him. That, as well as the heat from the exertion, was beginning to become unbearable. Sweat drips from his forehead, the fabric of his clothes sticking uncomfortably to his skin, and he wonders why he didn’t just remove his armor beforehand.

The muscles of his arms and legs are beginning to ache, and his back is overdue for a thorough stretching. Even if he’s tilled these fields annually, the frequency of the activity is much too few for him to grow accustomed to the exhaustion.

From far away, he could see the lone figure of a blonde man, tanned torso out for display, seeming to have forgone what little he wore to cover his middle. Mydei plows the field with purpose, a certain finesse in his movements only seen in bodies that have done each pronounced action countless times before.

Even from this distance, Phainon could almost imagine how those muscles rippled and tensed with every pull of his arms and push of his legs, maneuvering the worn-out arōtron with little to no effort. Despite the tool being innately stiff and heavy, Mydei is able to make the object appear pliant in his hands, like a body in submission, boneless and willing—

Suddenly parched, Phainon decides to take a break. He walks back to the Akashian settlement; mudbrick houses built closer together around a small courtyard that served as the village square. Phainon could count how many families lived in the place with both of his hands, the original Akashians were even lesser then, back when they first arrived at Okhema to seek refuge.

The village chief’s house is located up on a hill, a little further than the rest of the houses which were built a couple of paces from the wheat fields directly. Since the first time he’s helped the Akashians till the land, it became standard procedure for Phainon to lodge in the village chief’s residences—other houses are full and Demeas himself had insisted for how could he not afford a Chrysos Heir the hospitality befitting of their status?

The hike to the top of the hill seemed far more grueling than it should be, and to think that a married couple older than him lived there and made the trip several times daily. Perhaps he should ask Mydei to race him after a whole day’s worth of working in the fields.

Setting aside the idea for later, Phainon finally finds himself in front of the village chief’s doorstep, one hand poised to knock. Upon doing so, an old woman’s voice from within beckons him in. He then pushes the door open and is greeted with the warm, sweet scent of something baking.

“Phainon, is that you?”

“It’s me, ma’am,” Phainon answers.

Hurried footsteps come from the kitchen. Demeas’ wife, Madam Marpessa, wore a pink apron carrying a plate of sliced apples and an amphora filled to the brim with water.

“Goodness, you’ve gotten taller since I last saw you!” Marpessa gasps, placing the objects she’s carrying upon a nearby table to assess Phainon more thoroughly. “Do my eyes fail me? You look more alive than last year!”

Phainon smiles. “Must be due to the waters from the baths. Aglaea recently made some adjustments.”

“Even if that is so, I’m glad to see you doing well. I heard you brought a friend with you this year?”

“I have. His name is Mydei, also a Chrysos Heir,” Phainon says. “Tomorrow, his tribe will come to help as well.”

Marpessa’s eyes shine with gratitude. “How blessed we are to have you heroes with us. Why don’t you call Lord Mydei and rest for a while? You’ve been at it since the Entry Hour,” she says gently, taking the plate of apples as well as the water-filled amphora from the table before handing it to Phainon. “Kephale’s Dawn Device might be a symbol of Their mercy, but in the Action Hour, the heat it emanates does get quite unbearable.”

“Thank you for your concern, ma’am.”

“It’s but a small thing,” Marpessa dismisses just before her demeanor becomes hesitant. “Also, Phainon, you already know that our humble abode only has one spare room available —”

Phainon didn’t need to seek out the wisdom of Cerces to know where this was going. His smile falters for a little, and he hopes that Marpessa hadn’t noticed.

“—the other families are more than willing to accommodate you or the other lord, of course,” Marpessa continues, her breathing gradually becoming uneven as she tries to fend off her panic. “But, ah, Ismene has five children running around, Rhene’s husband has come down with a nasty sickness, Chalcon’s just recently burned down half of his house—”

“It’s perfectly alright, ma’am,” Phainon reassures. He can’t help but feel that he needed it just as much. “Mydei and I are good friends. I’m sure he won’t mind if we share a room.”

Phainon is the furthest from being sure.

Perhaps he should have consulted with Mydei prior to this before making such a claim. But if he doesn’t calm an anxious old lady this instant, the consequences might be dire. All things considered, if Mydei detests the arrangement, he could simply kick Phainon out and have him sleep on the fields.

The thought alone is miserable enough to have Phainon feel himself figuratively droop. He could only hope that Mydei would show him mercy.

Marpessa thankfully regains her bearings. “Allow this old woman to apologize for the inconvenience, nonetheless. I’ll have Demeas expand the house just so we could accommodate more people.”

To say that Phainon is looking forward to that would be an understatement. That is, if he’ll be able to survive staying in one room with Mydei for a week and continue his annual job of assisting the Akashians with their Revival Ritual next year.

Various emotions accompany Phainon as he makes the trip back to the fields, carrying a plate of apples and the amphora with him. He was so preoccupied by his thoughts, mingled with the urge to escape from Marpessa’s incessant apologies, that he even forgot to ask for cups.

He then takes refuge beneath a nearby tree, the shade it provided pleasantly cool. Setting the food and drink aside, Phainon takes this moment of reprieve to finally strip himself of his armor—his cape, coat, and inner shirt folded neatly beside him.

The wind feels nice against his sweaty skin, now finally exposed, and he allows himself a well overdue sigh of relief, closing his eyes as he rests his head against the tree trunk.

He had no idea how long he sat there, or if he managed to fall asleep from the sheer exhaustion alone—perhaps it was an attempt to escape his thoughts if only for a brief moment.

The sound of light and measured footsteps approaching catches his attention in an instant, however. Phainon would be able to recognize it even with his eyes closed.

“Tired already?” came a taunting voice.

Phainon blinks his eyes open and regrets it right away. Mydei stood over him, casting shadows upon his resting figure. His entire torso is laid bare without any hindrance for once —no fabric slung over one shoulder, no gauntlets, and the only jewelry he wore was the lone, large hooped earring hanging upon his left ear.

Wandering blue eyes are unable to keep still, taking in the sight of unblemished tanned skin marred in scarlet streaks, muscles defined, their form tastefully emphasized by the thin sheen of sweat that seemed to glisten against the light of Kephale’s Dawn with every minute shift as he breathes.

“Hardly,” Phainon answers, quietly frustrated with how strained his voice had sounded. “Just needed a little break to soothe tired muscles and…”

His eyes linger upon the dangerous sight of Mydei’s nipples, dusty and sensuously perked. A formidable pair of attention seekers, in Phainon’s modest opinion. The sight of one nipple (Mydei’s nipple, specifically) on a regular day is enough to render Phainon’s mind a mess if he allowed himself to dwell on it. Two nipples is an entirely different story.

The sight of it at the same time would spell a disaster for Phainon’s dwindling self-restraint and his poor, poor, poor unconsoled libido.

“I was thirsty.”

Despite his words, Phainon hadn’t drunk a single drop from the amphora since coming to rest beneath the shade of the tree. Perhaps now is a good time to quench his parched throat, but he doubts a mere drink of water would be able to help in that regard.

Mydei only hums, oblivious to Phainon’s sentiments. “You even got yourself a snack.”

It takes Phainon a moment to determine what Mydei was referring to, shamefully realizing that the latter’s attention was directed to the plate of sliced apples, gold eyes glinting with interest.

“Madam Marpessa prepared it for us,” Phainon says, now also eyeing the plate. Only when Mydei is out of his sight does he see reason. “You have yet to meet her. When the deipnon comes around, you should introduce yourself.”

“No need to wait for so long,” Mydei says. Somehow he looked discomfited about something, the signs of it eventually emerging for Phainon to take notice. “I have to seek her out, actually. I’ll join you in a while.”

Phainon furrows his eyebrows, confused. “Did something happen—?”

Before he could finish, Mydei had already rushed off to the village. Phainon could only sigh for Mydei does have his strange moments from time to time. Endearing to a fault.

It takes a while for Mydei to return, and when he does, his frown had only deepened, shoulders visibly tensed. Phainon could only surmise what had gone down. It’s not possible that Mydei didn’t get along with Marpessa for she’s the sweetest old lady Phainon has had the pleasure to meet.

“What happened?” Phainon asks once Mydei was within earshot, straightening up. “Are you alright?”

Mydei’s distress is radiating off of him in palpable waves. Rare is a moment in which Mydei allows his raw emotions to seep through his typically reserved countenance. Phainon feels his skin prickle anxiously, anticipating Mydei’s response with a thinly-veiled dread, ready to provide comfort if need be.

The answer to his question is not what he had expected.

“Do you have a hair cuff with you?” Mydei asks, a distinct edge in how he spoke that it’s almost as if he just delivered the most harrowing of messages. Or in this case, asked the most grievous of questions.

Phainon’s mind blanks. “What?”

Mydei’s golden eyes flicker, narrowing in distraught. “It’s just— My braid…”

The halted statement is effective enough to draw Phainon’s attention to the lock of hair resting against the jut of Mydei’s right collarbone, the length is longer than the others, cascading freely in distinct waves—a remnant of the braid now nowhere to be seen.

“It must’ve gone loose earlier while I was out on the fields and I failed to take notice,” Mydei finishes.

Sensing that this is a sensitive matter, Phainon threads lightly, considering his words with care. “Do you need help looking for your hair cuff?”

Mydei shakes his head. “It’s futile. The field is vast and the soil struck loose. The possibility of my hair cuff being buried in the ground is unfortunately high.”

“Have you asked the villagers if they have spares?”

“That’s the reason why I went earlier. I asked every man and woman, every child even. They —” Mydei exhales shakily, eyes clenched shut as his words trail off, no words needed to convey his failure.

Phainon feels his chest ache at the sight, the urge to simply hold Mydei close to comfort him competing with his need to find a solution immediately. The braid and the hair cuff clearly meant something for Mydei, far more significant than Phainon could ever hope to imagine.

He looks over to the vast, half-plown field and feels helpless. Just as he was about to take the jar of water to offer Mydei in an attempt to calm him down, his eyes caught the glint of something coming from his folded clothes on the ground.

Only then does Phainon find the solution he seeks.

Aglaea is going to have some choice words with him when he returns back to the main city, but Phainon pays the threat no mind as he takes the belt that held his pauldron and cape together, cleanly snapping the prong of the buckle loose.

With just the right amount of pressure, the metal prong bends just right, malleable enough to be formed into a somewhat circular shape to resemble a hair cuff. It still does not compare to the one Mydei typically wore, though.

Phainon hesitantly shows his handiwork to Mydei who was watching with curiosity. It’s a relief that his actions have captured Mydei’s attention enough to distract him from his initial distress.

“Will this work?” Phainon asks.

Instead of an answer—either a simple yes, a scoff, a roll of the eyes, or a blatant: No, Deliverer—what Mydei did next was far beyond what Phainon could have foreseen.

Mydei steps closer until Phainon’s legs, stretched straight upon the ground, were in between his muddied golden greaves. Just as Phainon was about to ask what Mydei was planning, standing so close with his crotch barely an arm’s reach from Phainon’s face, all words at the tip of his tongue ceased to exist the moment that Mydei drops on his knees and takes a seat atop Phainon’s lap.

Prayers began to spring forth within Phainon’s reeling mind in an attempt to keep his sanity from slipping. O Kephale, thy mercy knows no bounds. Your Dawn humbles us, the darkness driven away—

“You may do it,” Mydei says.

There’s a lot of things Phainon could do right now with Mydei on his lap, actually. Mydei needs to elaborate more upon his words this instant before Phainon’s heart could forget how to do its sole purpose within his body—which is to pump blood and keep him alive apparently.

Unfortunately, it’s doing a piss poor job at the moment and Phainon might actually just die with how close Mydei’s voluptuous, muscular chest is to his face. Phainon wonders if Mydei has any idea how insane his body looks, how tempting it is for Phainon to just sink his teeth into the flawless skin, and taste his divine undying flesh.

He feels like he might faint right at this moment. The weight of Mydei upon him is something he didn’t know he needed until he came to know what it’s like. And now, he had no idea as to how he would be able to keep going on with his pitiful existence if he were to part with the sensation, if this moment were to come to its eventual end.

“Phainon.”

Phainon looks up. “Yes?”

Mydei was frowning at him. Phainon should just die for ever causing Mydei displeasure. “You do know how to braid hair, right?”

Right. The braid. So that’s what Mydei wanted him to do. Fortunately, Phainon won’t exactly be a worthless, inconsequential being in the eyes of Mydei—of a god poised for worship sat upon a mere altar.

Phainon wonders what kind of heroic deeds he must have achieved in his next life to be chosen like this, for Mydei to sit on his lap like he belonged there. And he does.

“I know how to braid hair, yes,” Phainon answers. Even if his mind had forgotten quite a bit (the last time he braided hair was before the Black Tide destroyed his village), he’ll force his body to remember.

Mydei’s expression smoothens as he shifts a little closer whilst separating the wavy lock of hair from the rest, his ass nestling just where Phainon wants it—like a puzzle falling into place.

The brief sensation of Mydei against him causes Phainon to feel light-headed, a certain warmth stirring within him, and all he could do is dig the tip of his thumb into the makeshift haircuff, both of his hands frozen at his sides in a show of punishing restraint.

“What are you waiting for?” Mydei asks, a hint of impatience in his tone.

Phainon would like to wish for some consideration, at the very least. He is fighting for his life in this very moment, harder than he’s ever done while going against any formidable Titankin or forces from the Black Tide.

“Deliverer.”

“By the gods are you hasty,” Phainon murmurs, finally able to find the strength to raise his arms and comb his fingers through the wavy lock of hair. “I’m not going anywhere, and neither are you.”

Mydei huffs. “I was merely wondering what’s with the unnecessary delay. You’re always one to make me wait.”

“Perhaps an exercise in patience is due,” Phainon replies, deft fingers relishing in the softness of the blonde strands.

“Having a limited patience has its perks. People tend to waste your time less.”

Knowing that such discussions would be a losing battle, especially when it comes to Mydei, Phainon chooses a well-placed taunt instead of furthering debates in regards to patience. Specifically, Mydei’s lack of it (only when Phainon is involved).

“You always walk around with your hair braided. I’m surprised you know not how to do it,” Phainon says, expecting to get a rise out of the other.

“I know how to do it,” Mydei reiterates. “I just want you to do it for me.”

So the crown prince sees him as a servant, it would seem. Phainon ought to be honored as he tries desperately not to voice out his less-than-pleased sentiments of being reduced to a mere hair braider. The exceptions he makes when it comes to Mydei grows by the day.

His thoughts are then interrupted when Mydei leans in further into his space to allow Phainon even more accessibility and really, being closer is the furthest thing that Phainon needed right now regardless of how much he wants it.

Mydei is warm, and every brush of his forearm against Mydei’s chest steals away a decade from his lifespan. He doesn’t even want to dive deep into how the thin layer of sweat clinging upon their skins are intermingling with every contact. The mere thought of it has Phainon’s breath coming in short.

If he doesn’t want to be reduced into a pathetic, panting mess just because Mydei sat on his lap and demanded that he braid his hair, he better not dwell on such gratifying thoughts. Just as Phainon thought that’s the last time Mydei would say something, he’s proven dreadfully wrong.

“What’s your problem this time?” Mydei asks.

“I have no problems,” Phainon says, a bit quick to answer. “In fact, I can confidently say that I’m free of them.”

Mydei doesn’t relent, legs pressing against Phainon’s. “You haven’t looked at me.”

Phainon huffs out a laugh, strained and shaky. “Is it a requirement to do so while we bathe?”

“It’s strange.”

“Not for me.”

A heavy sigh resounds. Phainon hears a pop as Mydei uncorks the vial of fragrance oil, followed by a shifting of his legs and the splashing of water, spilling onto the stone floor. For a moment, Phainon thought that Mydei finally ran out of patience in dealing with him and was about to leave.

Opening his eyes, the sight that greets him might as well send him into the afterlife. Mydei is on his knees, submerged from the waist down, water sluicing over his tanned skin, the streaks of scarlet striking as ever.

The tub is small enough that Phainon doesn’t even have to reach out so far if he wanted to run his hands across Mydei’s well-defined muscles, trace every winding path of those mysterious marks and see when and where they end. If they ever do.

But he doesn’t do that. Phainon of Aedes Elysiae is a civilized hero of Okhema with manners —

“I knew you’d look at me.”

Perhaps Phainon of Aedes Elysiae is merely just a flawed man. Nothing of note to write about.

“You’re making a mess,” Phainon says, a weak admonishment for he doesn’t really mind. But if he keeps quiet for too long, Mydei is bound to make fun of him. “Now the floor is flooded.”

Mydei rolls his eyes before holding out a hand to drip some of the oil upon his fingers. “The tub is too small. It hinders my movements if I apply the oil sitting down.”

Phainon could already feel himself stir between his legs, eyes glued at the mesmerizing display of Mydei’s body before him. He itches to touch.

“Would you like for me to leave?” Phainon asks. “So you could have more space?”

Mydei rubs the oil in between his fingers, testing its consistency and allowing the delicate scent of olives and fig to permeate in the air. Phainon tracks the languid gesture with an attention that could rival a predator stalking its prey.

“This tub is provided for the both of us to use, and you’ve barely washed,” Mydei says in an infuriating non-answer.

As if to prove his point just in case Phainon failed to comprehend, he leans forward, reaching out with an oil-slicked hand to wipe away the speck of mud on Phainon’s cheek. Mydei could slit Phainon’s throat and it wouldn’t have made a difference.

“You had dirt on your face,” Mydei tells him, thumb rubbing circles on the alleged spot as if making sure that no mud is left to linger upon the skin. “You’re welcome, by the way.”

Before Mydei could withdraw his hand, Phainon’s fingers encloses upon his wrist, a tentative hold, loose enough for Mydei to still pull away if he so desired.

Phainon counts in his head—seven erratic heartbeats, five trickles of water from the tub’s edge to the stone floor, two bird calls from the outside—but Mydei makes no move to retreat, remaining as still as a statue, holding Phainon’s gaze with an unnervingly calm facade.

But the flicker in his eyes tell a different story. A wordless question, perhaps even a challenge to do more than just this.

Phainon tugs lightly and Mydei, a warrior unflinching even in the face of death, falls like a blade of grass in Phainon’s arms. Willing. Uncharacteristically so.

The bathwater sloshes from the sudden movement, spilling onto the stone floor. Neither of them pay any mind to the mess as Phainon allows the muted scent of the fragrance oil upon Mydei’s skin to invade his senses. They’re unfamiliar, for Mydei always preferred something much sweeter. And yet, Phainon finds himself inhaling deeply nonetheless.

He can feel Mydei’s labored breathing against his neck, both of his hands braced upon Phainon’s chest for balance. Instead of pulling away, Mydei asks, his voice barely even a whisper, “What are you doing?”

Sliding his hand above Mydei’s wrist, relishing in the warmth that Mydei’s skin provides, Phainon takes the vial of fragrance oil into his palm.

“Let me help you,” Phainon murmurs softly, the corner of his lips pressed against the side of Mydei’s face—a mere compromise for what he truly wants for he doesn't possess the courage to be more forward than he already is.

Only in battle is there no place for cowardice. But this is no battle, for the simple act of holding Mydei gives him peace.

The other is quiet, caged in between Phainon’s arms, barely even a prison for they both know he could leave anytime. And he should, Phainon would let him. It would be simpler that way. Much more simpler than whatever this is, what it could escalate to—an unnamed entanglement, far more intricate than any trial either of them could face.

But instead of leaving, Mydei huffs out a soft exhale before relaxing fully upon Phainon’s lap. If this position is about to be a recurring thing, Phainon ought to prepare himself better next time. It might be wishful thinking on his part, and he doubts he’d even get used to the sensation of having Mydei’s weight upon him in a non-sparring circumstance.

A distinct pressure digs against Phainon’s navel, unmistakable, warm for how could Mydei be anything else. It causes Phainon to lose all the air in his lungs at the revelation, a myriad of emotions springing forth, overwhelming and not enough at the same time.

Mydei leans forward ever so slightly, their wet bodies sliding against each other, the bathwater splashing some more. The tickling sensation of a warm breath ghosting against the shell of his ear is enough to render Phainon’s mind blank.

“Go ahead, Deliverer.”

Shivers erupt from within Phainon’s very bones, tracing the path of his spine and sending goosebumps to his skin. His vision swims just from hearing those three words alone, struggling to regain his bearings as he spills the oil onto his fingers from where it’s raised above the surface of the water behind Mydei.

The vial goes empty and Phainon throws it aside. The slippery liquid steadily drips from his fingers, to his palm, and down to his forearm. The remaining contents have spilled into the bathwater due to his immense distraction.

“Wasteful,” Mydei remarks, lips brushing against the sensitive skin behind Phainon’s ear.

Even though Mydei had said this, Phainon could feel the curve of a smile upon Mydei’s lips well enough, pressed against a spot that renders him weak to know he doesn’t really care for such trivialities. And neither does Phainon.

How could he care for anything else in this moment?

Instead of a reply, slicked fingers press firmly against Mydei’s back, feeling up the muscles like the owner of such desperate hands wishes to etch every shape of the flesh in his memory. If asked, Phainon wouldn’t even dare to deny it for the lie would be such a heavy burden to carry that he might as well speak of his ache with ardent truthfulness.

Mydei gasps, soft and quiet, and it only serves to fuel Phainon’s impulses even more than what is typically considered acceptable. But such considerations have been placed in the back of Phainon’s mind as a shaky breath escapes from his parted lips, pulling Mydei even closer, the dig of Mydei’s arousal against him sending his mind reeling.

Thoughts of reason have ceased to exist. Phainon can’t even find it within himself to stop and mourn the loss of it.

He continues with his ministrations, spreading the fragrance oil upon a firm shoulder, fingers tracing the path of scarlet, the jut of a clavicle—pressing lightly upon the slight dip in between muscle and bone—before coming to rest upon Mydei’s pulse point.

Phainon allows a moment of stillness then, relishing in the rhythmic thrum of life coming from beneath the skin, a sensation Phainon wishes would always stay regardless if it’s cursedly bound to remain. Its erratic pace mirrors the one that Phainon could feel against his chest, a swift thud of a heartbeat.

A teasing remark is at the tip of his tongue. For all the composure Mydei insists to show, Phainon is still able to catch the slivers of raw honesty that tends to slip undetected for the untrained eye.

In these many months that he’s grown acquainted with Mydei, fluency in every minute gesture of the other—deliberate or not—is something Phainon is hoping to have an unparalleled expertise in, one that he’s not willing to share with anyone else.

The wreath of olives should only be placed upon the head of one. And Phainon wishes to be the sole bearer of such an esteemed kótinos.

With his left hand, non-slicked, Phainon takes a handful of Mydei’s silky strands of blonde hair, gently combing it aside to expose more of the unblemished skin of Mydei’s neck.

A siren’s call, as Phainon would like to call it. Far more dangerous than the ones that echo in the rocky shores of previously affluent bay cities. Now destroyed by the Black Tide’s invasion, the sensuous curve of Mydei’s neck remains to be the lone ineluctable temptation.

The sight is exquisite, glistening streaks of scarlet aiming to lure Phainon’s attention. He succumbs to the bait without much thought, nosing lightly against Mydei’s jaw, lips now brushing upon the sensitive skin, contradictory in a way that such a blatant show of boldness still manages to appear hesitant.

Phainon’s hands then follow the path of Mydei’s spine, reverently taking in the arch and feeling every jut of each vertebra beneath his desperate fingertips, only stopping its descent when he feels the loosened hem of Mydei’s towel.

A moment of clarity strikes him, and Phainon finds himself asking, “Is this okay?”

Mydei makes a disgruntled sound to express his disbelief, pinching a small flesh on Phainon’s shoulder in a show of petulance.

“You’re asking me that now?” It’s a relief that Mydei doesn’t seem to sound cross with him despite his actions.

Phainon rests his hands upon Mydei’s waist, trying not to dwell upon the fact that the knot of Mydei’s towel had just come undone.

“Push me away,” Phainon murmurs, almost a plea, against Mydei’s neck. His teeth longs to sink into the unmarred flesh, and he wonders how long he could keep going like this.

“Mydei.”

“The way you hold me makes it seem impossible.”

There’s some semblance of truth in that. And yet, “We both know you could easily slip free if you wanted to. You would have killed me by now for my impertinence.”

Phainon’s grip tightens as he tries to keep his hips still, the effort to stop himself from simply rutting his aching cock in between the cleft of Mydei’s ass dissipating every single sane fiber of his being. There’s only two flimsy towels between them, one of which had already failed to keep the boundary intact.

“I beg of you, leave if this makes you feel uncomfortable,” Phainon pushes, a prayer of pain, a cry of want.

Several outcomes come to mind but the one that Mydei chooses catches Phainon off-guard.

“Spread the oil some more,” Mydei mutters, the shell of Phainon’s ear caught in between his teeth.

Mydei bites harder. The sudden sting of it has Phainon jolting against him, a startled moan escapes his lips. Phainon lifts his knees, causing Mydei to slide further into his space, his own desire twitching wantonly against Phainon’s abdomen.

Slicked hands map out every ridge of muscle upon Mydei’s sides, spreading the oil as promised, while depraved lips commit to memory the feeling of Mydei’s skin against it, the taste upon his tongue—bitter from the fragrance oil, wet from the bathwater—and yet it manages to quench the deep-seated thirst that Phainon has been harboring for days—

No.

For months on end.

Phainon laps at the skin, teeth grazing every now and then with an intent to bite but never does. The groan that Mydei lets out reverberates from within his throat, head thrown back. Phainon savors the vibrations from within the flesh, hoping to feel it again so soon when he lightly sucks upon the crook of Mydei’s neck and is rewarded with a choked-out gasp in return.

Mydei’s grip upon his shoulder tightens every now and then, particularly when Phainon lightly drags the tip of his tongue from the notch in between Mydei’s collarbones, up to the base of his chin.

“Phainon.”

“Tell me what you want,” Phainon says, heat creeping up on his face upon hearing Mydei address him by his name. To show his gratitude, he guides Mydei’s hips to grind against him slowly, pressing open-mouthed kisses beneath the edge of Mydei’s jaw as he does so.

Mydei pants above him, a hand keeping Phainon’s head steady to where he wants it, pulling roughly at the snow-colored strands when Phainon’s fingers press firmly on a certain area just above the base of his spine.

“You— Hngh...”

Phainon laughs breathily, teeth pulling upon the soft lobe of Mydei’s ear, free of the assortment of earrings he typically wore. None of them suit him regardless of how good he looked with them. Perhaps a quest to find the perfect earring is due.

“Me?” he repeats teasingly, one hand sliding beneath Mydei’s thigh, sating the desire to feel the firm muscle tense in his grasp. “You want me, Mydei?”

It’s meant to be in jest. They both know that Mydei has yet to give him an answer. But Phainon can’t help but wish.

Mydei’s nails dig into his scalp, hips bucking against Phainon in a rare display of abandonment. “Haikas…”

“Calling me names does not count as an answer,” Phainon says, equally strained with every languid slide of their bodies against each other.

“Shut up.”

Phainon feels his cock leak pathetically, biting a moan into Mydei’s chest, dangerously close to a reddened nipple. “Not your—hah—flashiest comeback, I must say.”

Mydei grunts. “I— Phainon—”

Phainon pulls away from Mydei’s heated skin with great difficulty, eyes blown wide as he centers his gaze upon Mydei’s shaky ones.

The bathwater had already gone cold for some time now, and yet Mydei is indubitably flushed all over. Phainon is once again reminded of how good Mydei looks in red, naked or clothed it matters not.

The once searing pools of gold are rendered unfocused, the sharpness dulled into something softer, dazed in the heat of want.

Phainon’s gaze drops to Mydei’s lips, spit-slicked and swollen. No doubt from all the biting Mydei had done to keep his dignity intact. He could feel Mydei do the exact same thing, gaze directed upon parted lips in dire need to taste his own. Phainon wonders if it’s wrong to assume—

“Mydei,” he starts, warning-like. “Do you—”

Gold eyes flicker and in a brief moment, Phainon feels the coldness of the water and a slight blow of air bite into his exposed skin.

Mydei has left the tub, water sluicing down his back and pooling upon the hem of where he held his towel, clenched hands gripping upon the fabric tightly.

Phainon is quick enough to catch the unmistakable bulge tenting in between Mydei’s legs, the towel flimsy enough to barely hide its shape—

“I’m done bathing,” Mydei says, sharp amidst the silence. “Thank you for your assistance.”

He doesn’t turn around when he speaks. Phainon hopes that the reason is merely to hide his shame. For it to be something else, dancing along the lines of regret perhaps, Phainon wouldn’t know how he’d be able to move forward then.

If Mydei sees him as a stranger after this, then perhaps the story of his demise brought on by an immense heartache would find itself told hand-in-hand with the tragedy that went down between Cerces and Mnestia.

The sound of the bathroom door closing startles Phainon from his thoughts. And he’s left to shiver in the coldness that Mydei had left in his wake.

chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Everything fades into the background as Phainon's thoughts nearly consume him with forbidden longing. Only Mydei could set him back right on track.

Chapter Notes

special thanks to midnightcrownn for her insane phaidei art from this chapter 💗 do check it out if you haven't yet!!

It is of no surprise that Mydei opted to stay with the Kremnoan detachment after the bathing incident.

Though avoidance was not one of Mydei’s usual style of handling disputes—preferring direct confrontation above anything—Phainon wouldn’t fault him for it, choosing to ignore the dull ache in his chest that never seemed to go away when he saw Mydei’s belongings nowhere to be found in their shared spare room.

Phainon’s strong suit has always been to look at the bright side of things, and he liked to think that this is for the best.

Keep deluding yourself.

If Mydei didn’t know how to breach the subject, then neither did Phainon—regardless of the fact that the latter should be the one to take the lead in clearing the air between them considering it was his fault that everything had now gone sideways, and there’s an undeniable possibility that Mydei might want nothing to do with him now.

However, something tells him that giving Mydei some space to reestablish some boundary between them (after Phainon had deliberately tore it down and invaded it with nary a reasonable mind) to be the appropriate course of action. He’d acted no differently than a beast craving for the taste of flesh on his tongue with how much he wanted to devour Mydei whole if given the permission.

But Mydei left. There’s no permission to speak of.

Even if Phainon cried tears of gold or pleaded until his tongue bled, he would never have it. Mydei wouldn’t cross a surging river with a boat even if Phainon had already swam across it, now waiting at the other side of the bend.

Phainon should be okay with that. Accept and be done with it.

And yet, he continued to lie awake on the bed with every Curtain-Fall Hour that followed, wondering if he’d done things differently—if only he didn’t feel a certain way—then Mydei would still be here. They would bicker about their day in the fields, the delicious deipnon, and groan about sore muscles (which is admittedly Phainon’s to do and for Mydei to make fun of him).

But Mydei is not here, choosing to spend the rest of his days in the Akashian village together with the detachment, sleeping in their tents, and indulging in honey brew after a good day gone by.

The faint singing that sounds arguably in Kremnoan tongue echoing from the outside suggests that they are making merry as well. And Phainon could only hope that it would serve as a distraction for Mydei. Come morning, they’ll talk, and Mydei would’ve been able to set aside his grievances.

Only, Mydei kept to himself and remained with his people. Phainon didn’t seek him out.

Unresolved issues aside, they still continued to help the others with the remaining fields, finishing up with the planting of wheat kernels, the pace of the activity much more leisurely now considering that their progress has led them to be ahead of schedule.

By the eighth day of the Month of Cultivation, during the Entry Hour, the Akashian chief fulfills the Revival Ritual by gathering a relative amount of soft dirt from the fields and placing it in a clay pot, one for each Akashian family to enshrine in their homes so they may be able to pray for a bountiful harvest.

Phainon’s solemnity as he spectated was rendered superficial for his mind lingers elsewhere, as it had done these past couple of days. Across from him did Mydei stood, dignified alongside the detachment, his focus solely on Demeas now handing the clay pots to the family heads of each household.

The ache in Phainon’s chest grows all the more palpable with each moment that his gaze lingers, for how could he bear to look away from such beauty so unparalleled that it might even be able to rival Mnestia? And to think that he’s held said beauty in his arms albeit briefly, how right it felt, how he longed to experience it again.

Selfish thoughts for the unworthy, and he calls himself a hero of Okhema whose selflessness is meant to bring deliverance to the nation. How could he speak of his oath to protect when his heart is no longer fully in it?

His heart, which initially thrummed so steadily to keep him going in the long journey of what fate has in store for him, to see a prophecy fulfilled—now it burns with an insatiable need, a yearning to be offered and accepted, not by an entire nation in need of his aid.

But by a lone man. A prince. An equal.

If Mydei were to look at him at this moment, he would know of Phainon’s sentiments in an instant. His secrets laid bare to be scrutinized, and he would be fine with it. Even if the question remains unasked, he wonders what Mydei’s answer would be, what it could be.

Hope and despair never go hand in hand together, easily distinguished without much deliberation like true gold from rusting iron. Still, Phainon found himself teetering between the two the longer that Mydei maintains his silence.

Even if it’s to be expected that Mydei is not inclined for such relations involving matters of the heart, Phainon can’t help but hope that Mydei would at least see him as an exception. Would it be wrong to assume that Mydei desired just as much as he did in that pitiful excuse of a wooden tub?

But Mydei left. There’s nothing to assume.

The reminder echoes in his mind, sometimes despondent, sometimes vindictive, but most of the time it just sounds empty. Like a line in a book, read and spoken a dozen times to warrant memorization, a fact proven true a long time ago and didn’t need much of a debate to deem otherwise.

The skin surrounding Phainon’s thumb bleeds from over-peeling, a nasty habit that even Aglaea couldn’t scold out of him. The sting brings him comfort, clearing his mind severely.

In the end, Phainon’s gaze remains unmet. A small mercy perhaps, for if he were to bestow Mydei’s attention now, then he would have to do the painful act of looking away, his own world darkening for Kephale’s Dawn alone is no longer enough to bring light to it.

Again, selfish thoughts for the unworthy. Phainon could see no end to this. Since when was he allowed to want for so much more than what is deserved? What is willfully given?

Mydei is kind and he’s treated Phainon with respect and grace befitting of a close friend. If Phainon were to honor their relation, it’d be wise not to dwell on thoughts that involve asking Mydei for the impossible when the man has done nothing but humor his whims.

If Mydei wished it, he could’ve killed Phainon for his outrageous behavior. But he didn’t, he simply left. And somehow, the action causes him pain more than if Mydei had just stabbed him in the heart with a knife and carved it out.

Phainon would do it for him. His heart didn’t feel like it belonged to him these days with how much it rebels, how much it yearns to be in the hands of another. He might as well gouge it out and offer it to Mydei, and he wonders if that would solve everything.

“As with all the feasts of Georios, the flame is but a necessary element,” Demeas says to the crowd, pulling Phainon out of his thoughts. He gestures at the pile of unlit torches. “Please, help yourself with one of these and partake with the tradition.”

The crowd disperses, each individual taking a torch for their own. Phainon watches the impressive pile reduce in size, letting the others have their turn. When only but a single torch was left did he make his move to pick it up from the ground, crouching as he does so.

A hand collides with him, a golden gauntlet unmistakable to the point that Phainon didn’t need to think too hard to know whose face he’ll find when he looks up.

Mydei, with his hand brushing against Phainon’s own as they both grip the handle of the torch, was unable to hide his surprise. Phainon could only hope that he’d at least look a little more put-together despite his racing heartbeat.

But the image of himself that he sees reflected upon those pools of gold says otherwise.

“Oh dear.”

They both whip their heads to turn to Marpessa.

“It seems that I have terribly miscounted. My lords—”

“It’s alright,” Mydei says, sudden enough to startle Phainon from his daze. In a blink of an eye, Mydei had already put some distance between them, standing two paces away from where Phainon was still crouched. “You can have the torch, Deliverer.”

Phainon frowns, taking the torch with him as he straightens up. “You had your hand on this first. You should take it.”

“No.”

“No?”

Marpessa bristles from where she stood in between them. “Ah, my lords, please don’t fight.”

The tension in the air grows thick, the crowd bracing themselves for what is about to be another tussle between the two Chrysos Heirs. Everyone knew that they opted to avoid each other like the plague due to their unsettled grievances, keeping to themselves in the hopes to preserve the peace.

But they both knew better than anyone that it wasn’t really the mere act of wrestling in the mud that is to blame.

“W-Why don’t you two just share?” Demeas adds meekly from their right, standing amongst his fellow Akashians.

The way he holds his torch so tightly seemed as if he’s not ready to part with it. But in the event that the two Heirs were to turn down such an absurd idea, he’s ready to give his own torch up, prayers to Georios be damned.

Phainon turns to Mydei. There’s no reason to make everyone so unsettled. “I’m alright with sharing.”

Mydei’s eyes glint, his face showing neither anger nor relief. Fortunately, he was able to glean on what Phainon was trying to do here for he eventually says, “Fine. Let’s share.”

The sigh of relief that everyone collectively lets out was loud enough to be exaggerated. Phainon chooses not to dwell on it, uncomfortable at the fact that everyone had to witness the exchange.

The torches are to be lit up around the newly-tended wheat fields. Even if this practice came to be when night still existed, every follower of Georios knew how important the flame is despite the presence of everday in Okhema.

Mydei spreads the tinder on the ground, making sure that they’re away from the grasslands just in case fire would spread uncontrollably.

“It is ready,” he says.

“Do you wish for me to light it up?” Phainon asks, eyeing the flint and iron pyrite in Mydei’s hand.

“No. I’ll do it.”

Phainon nods, gripping the handle of the torch tightly. “Alright.”

Mydei strikes the iron pyrite with the flint a couple of times until sparks were made, lighting up the tinder in the process. Phainon lowers the torch head, soaked in resin and wax, allowing it to catch the flame. In mere moments, the torch burns bright.

He then settles it upon the torchbearer. Unlike Georios’ Embers—torches holding the last unextinguished cinders of Georios—regular torches such as the one they have now did not possess the innate ability to float, nor did it have sentience.

They stare at the flame for what seemed to have been a long time until their faces bore the heat of it, the dance of fire reflected in their eyes.

“Have you—”

“We should—” Mydei stops talking, gesturing for Phainon to continue. “You go first.”

Phainon does, in no mood to argue, swallowing down the curiosity of wanting to know what it is that Mydei wished to say. “Have you done a prayer to Georios before?”

Mydei shakes his head. “I never needed to.”

“Then, I’ll show you how.” Phainon extends an arm. “Take my hand.”

A flicker of what looked to be hesitation in Mydei’s eyes causes Phainon to falter. He withdraws his hand immediately.

“Sorry. I’m not forcing you or—”

Mydei rolls his eyes and takes his hand in his. “You always think too much.”

Phainon eyes their intertwined fingers. The metal of Mydei’s gauntlet is cool against his skin. He turns to Mydei, an eyebrow raised challengingly. “And you don’t? That would make sense.”

Mydei’s grip becomes bruisingly tight for a mere moment as Phainon lets out a yelp. He shoots Phainon a glare and only then does the latter realize how much he missed having Mydei’s eyes on him.

“Quit dawdling and do what you must.”

Phainon nods, a smile on his lips. Despite the throb of pain in his hand, this is the happiest he’s felt in days. “Right. I forgot that a little teasing gets you riled up.”

“And it only took you four Entry Hours without talking to me to forget such a fact?” Mydei asks pointedly. “Your memory is abysmal.”

Well. They might as well talk about it now.

“I’m not the one who chose to sleep in a tent,” Phainon says, as if it would serve as a reason for their lack of communication. It does, to an extent.

Mydei raises an eyebrow. “Would you have preferred it if I stayed?”

Perhaps Phainon is still, in fact, not ready to talk. Mydei’s question required either a yes or a no for an answer. Phainon can’t find the voice to say either one of those simple words.

“I apologize if I made you uncomfortable—”

“You didn’t,” Mydei says, effectively cutting him off.

Phainon frowns, confused upon hearing the denial. “You’re not one to lie.”

“Never was. If I were uncomfortable, you would know.” Mydei’s eyes flash. “I’m capable of letting you know.”

There’s no question to that. However, “You left.”

“Yes. Only because I had to.”

Phainon makes a sound, expressing his perplexity, or is it something else—something much more dreadful. He no longer wishes to continue the conversation even if his doubts are about to be put to rest.

He feels like crying—disappointment, hurt, and guilt muddling into one deplorable ball and lodging itself deeply within him, a tumor that’s bound to eat him up from the inside.

Blonde strands brush lightly against the side of his face as he’s pulled closer, further into Mydei’s hold in a surprising gesture of consolation.

Mydei is comforting him, a hand behind him and at the back of his head. Phainon chokes on a startled gasp when Mydei tightens the hug, the sound muffled against Mydei’s clothed shoulder.

“Idiot Deliverer. Whatever am I going to do with you?” Mydei murmurs against his ear, uncaring that the other could evidently hear him. “Haikas.”

Only Mydei could admonish him as if he were a disobedient child during such a vulnerable moment. Phainon didn’t know whether he should laugh or cry. He does agree with Mydei’s words, however.

Mydei huffs. “Good. Damned fool.”

Thankfully, Mydei shows him mercy, rubbing circles on his back as if to soothe a spooked dromas. Phainon allows himself to relish the sensation. It should help ease the pain of rejection, but he can’t deny the fact that such gentle gestures only serve to worsen it.

It does not make him want Mydei less.

With great effort, he peels himself away from Mydei’s embrace, standing straight on his feet shortly after he does so. Mydei mirrors the movement, eyeing him quizzically.

“Feel better?”

Phainon stares at the lit torch, avoiding Mydei’s gaze as he nods stiffly. “Yes.” The lie passes through his lips easily this time. Keeping his voice steady, he tries to move the conversation away from... whatever this is. “We should proceed with the prayer. I’m afraid we’ve made Georios wait for too long already.”

Mydei only hums before taking Phainon’s hand in his once again, maintaining his silence as Phainon mutters the prayers for a bountiful harvest and a blessed land. Once the lighting of the torches have concluded, everyone who has come to help the Akashians with the fields now mount the dromases to make their way back to the main city of Okhema.

Phainon watched as Mydei rode ahead with his fellow Kremnoans, a grin on his face as he joked around with the soldiers. Sensing a certain piercing gaze on him, Mydei turns around to meet Phainon’s stare.

His smile widens, the sight of it causing Phainon’s heart to twinge painfully. In spite of everything, Phainon musters every ounce of strength in him to smile back.

The silence stretches for an unknown period of time, enough for Phainon’s resolve to waver, but not so that clarity invades his mind. How could it, when Mydei is so within reach? As he waited for an answer, not once did he expect for his patience to be rewarded tenfold.

He could feel Mydei’s other hand upon his waist, yanking him closer that the tips of their noses bump lightly against one other.

“Why don’t you find out?”

Phainon did not let the words hang in the air for more than a single moment, Oronyx’s Time not to be wasted. There’s no way to tell who among them had leaned in first, but the softness of Mydei’s lips against his was enough to render all of Phainon’s thoughts to be nonexistent.

A quick breath, hitched, before Phainon tilts his head, pressing Mydei gently against the railing, hands covering the small of Mydei’s back to soften the uncomfortable dig of the stone edge.

He swallows down the muffled gasp that escapes Mydei’s lips when he pressed upon a certain spot above the base of his spine, sharp claws digging mercilessly upon Phainon’s shoulders. The sting of it is a dizzying contrast to the sweetness on his tongue. For Mydei to inflict both pain and pleasure even now only serves to leave Phainon wanting, no longer heeding to the calls of selfless virtue, or the heavy weight of duty that bears down upon them both.

At this moment, Phainon only wants, kissing Mydei fervidly, trying to sate his desire as much as he could with every slide of their lips against each other, the rough clack of teeth, licking into Mydei’s mouth like a man who had first gotten a taste of ambrosia, excessively greedy for more, bound to yearn for it for the rest of his life.

It’s overwhelming, to finally get a taste of what could only be considered as a fanciful dream —to be able to hold Mydei so close a second time, and be held just as ardently in return. Such warmth is enough to keep the cold at bay, a flame that burns away all the burdens, reducing it to nothing but ashes.

The softness of Mydei’s lips, plush against his own, is addicting to a fault, bound to haunt Phainon in every waking and sleeping moment that he does not feel it, the sensation already ingrained upon the cracks and crevices of Phainon’s lips. Every intentioned press, wet and lingering, is certain to leave a sting that would never quite go away, soothed only by the one that bestowed it.

He readily consumes every groan and sound coming from the depths of Mydei’s throat, replying with ones of his own, uncaring of how desperate he seemed, the fact proven long ago with the way he kept Mydei close as if he’d loathe for them to separate.

Just as Phainon professes his prayers to the Titans for this moment to never end, a hand on his chest gently pushes him away, and Phainon could only be led by it despite the incessant need thrumming in his veins. At the end of the day, he could only be obedient to every single one of Mydei’s wishes even if it brings such profound and unbearable ache to part after being so close that they’re practically one.

A string of saliva connects their lips, shimmering against the light bore by Kephale, but not so enduring as a golden thread, dissipating quicker as Phainon’s wits had abandoned him. His heart thumps wildly in his chest, Mydei’s hand pressed above it, as if to stake claim to what already belongs to him.

Phainon relishes in the sight of Mydei’s lips, swollen and slicked, redder than ever before. His chest heaves in the same manner as Phainon’s does, unmarred tanned skin streaked in scarlet. Phainon itches to run his tongue across the vastness of it, as if he would only be able to be satisfied once all of Mydei had been devoured by him.

“Let’s—” Mydei’s voice is rough, low with unspoken need. “Let’s stop here for now.”

For now.

Phainon would be a fool to take it as a promise. But that won’t stop him from hoping nonetheless. Hoping that there would be a second time. A third. A fourth. Until he could barely count how many instances he’d been able to indulge in whatever it is that Mydei is willing to give him. And for every single one of them, Phainon would offer a thousand prayers expressing his gratitude.

Not to the gods. But to the man before him.

Mydei takes Phainon’s chin in between his fingers, pressing upon them until the pain sings through the latter’s body, pulling him out of his reverie.

“What was that for?” Phainon asks, almost petulant, taking Mydei’s hand in his if only to stop the other from pinching his chin further.

“You have that look on you,” Mydei says. “Stop thinking.”

“Of you? Easier said than done.”

Mydei scoffs, feigning offense as he peels himself away from Phainon’s hold, placing a much more respectable distance between them.

“It’s good to see you in good spirits at last, Deliverer. But keep the jests minimal. It’s a rather long drop from your balcony lest my hands slip.”

Phainon smiles sheepishly, the tingling sensation on his lips making him very giddy despite the threat that Mydei just threw at him. “I guess your methods of comfort worked. Consider me comforted.”

A huff. “Haikas.”

“You still haven’t told me what that word means.”

Instead of a reply, Mydei turns away from him, walking back into Phainon’s chambers, the latter trailing after him like a chimera highly dependent on its owner.

Mydei picks up the tray on Phainon’s desk as well as the scroll detailing Kremnoan traditions. To Phainon, who stood still in the middle of the room like a statue, he says, “You can find the meaning of it on your own. But for now—” His gaze drops down to the tent in between Phainon’s legs, a smirk on his lips. “—you might want to take care of that.”

Before Phainon could get a word in, Mydei had already left, taking away Phainon’s pride with him.

This time, the warmth that Mydei leaves in his wake lingers, the scent of pomegranates permeating the air. That alone is enough.
