pillar season, month of joy

4 months before the present time

On the eve of the Festival of Phagousa, Okhema was understandably in a state of bustling activity even up until the final quints of the Parting Hour, all in preparation for the upcoming banquet.

Crimson silk cloth wrapped around lapis lazuli columns, the usual blue fabric draped from ceiling arches and winding around the sides of the walls now replaced with gold ones, and the edges of the lounge areas covered in red and blue velvety cloth complemented with elaborate, gold brocade runners.

Ornate chalices and fruit plates were being arranged upon trays and several attendants tended to the baths to clear up the shimmering waters of any impurities, muttering prayers to Phagousa as they did so. By the elevated section of the Nerid Spring, just below the Heroes’ Baths, a temporary platform was situated to host the orchestra, several musical instruments already in their rightful stations.

Even the Kremnoans avidly helped with the decor despite their differences with the Okhemans, who at first showed signs of apprehension. When the Kremnoans proved their contributions to be rather tasteful, the Okhemans were left with no words to say, silence as a way of conveying their apology, and in a way, a show of gratitude for the help.

It was quite surprising, how centuries of bad blood between two nations are fixed for a shared desire to hold a grand harvest feast honoring the Chalice of Plenty.

Phainon admires Aglaea’s insight, it was her idea after all for the Kremnoans to celebrate alongside the Okhemans. Not even the Elders could forbid the Kremnoans from participating for Phagousa’s waters aim to welcome all, and it is still technically an Okheman feast—a loophole in the new policy that Aglaea sought to exploit.

The preparations lasted for several days. Phainon had only seen mere glimpses of Mydei in the hubbub before he was whisked away by citizens asking for his help in sampling produce, carrying boxes filled with harvests of the season, and whatever else Phainon could lend a hand in just to ease the people’s burdens.

Right now, he finds himself with Castorice, both of them currently seated at a giant lilypad at the Garden of Life, deftly folding colorful paper into shapes resembling that of flower blossoms meant to float upon the bath’s surface during the feast. It had been enchanted with Aglaea’s golden threads to ensure durability and to keep it dry enough so its shape would hold.

Compared to the strenuous labor Phainon had endured for the entire day, the act of folding paper is a stark contrast, almost soothing. Not to mention, Phainon is more than happy that he gets to spend time with a dear friend.

“This is the last of it, Lord Phainon,” Castorice tells him, gently placing the final blossom paper in front of them, her pile of flowers crisply folded with nary any creases laying beside Phainon’s. It was rather easy to distinguish who had made which pile.

Phainon takes a paper blossom in his hand, one of his creations. It’s a far cry from the flawless ones Castorice had made—his work a mess of unequal petals, folding mistakes shown through visible lines that were not supposed to exist.

With a sad frown, Phainon says, “I’m glad to be of help, Miss Castorice.” He then returns the blossom back to his pile. “Although, I don’t think I’ve done a good job.”

Castorice only smiled reassuringly. “It would have taken me much longer to work on these if you weren’t here, Lord Phainon.”

“You’re too kind.”

“The festival for this year is bound to be livelier than the previous ones,” Castorice says in an attempt to change the topic before Phainon could have the chance to take his own pile of paper flowers and redo every single one of them. “Lord Mydei’s people seem to be looking forward to it.”

Upon the mention of Mydei, Phainon perks up. “To think that all it takes for Kremnoans and Okhemans to treat each other amicably is a shared harvest feast.”

“Indeed.” Castorice’s smile fades. “I do wish the Elders would revoke the policy. I admire Lord Mydei and his people for handling the situation so calmly.”

Phainon nods sullenly. He has submitted several appeals toward the Council. But as expected, his missives have been deliberately ignored. Even Mydei told him to simply give it a rest— no point in reasoning with a wall, is what he said. The brute allegations against the Kremnoans needed to be put into question as soon as possible.

“It’s a good thing Aglaea kept the situation under wraps,” Phainon says. “I haven’t heard anything about the Elders’ new policy circulating around the rumor mill. Even the Verax Leos have kept their mouths shut.”

If the Okhemans were to find out that the Kremnoans wished to defy the Elders’ orders by celebrating their harvest feast despite the restrictions, they wouldn’t be merrily comparing fabric materials to drape around the Marmoreal Palace and sampling the Kremnoans’ pomegranate juice meant to be served during the festival.

No. There would be a riot.

“Lady Aglaea is thorough as always,” Castorice says. “I hope Lord Mydei and his people would enjoy the Okheman harvest feast regardless.”

Phainon hums in agreement, a fluttering sensation in his stomach. Mydei’s name simply had that effect on him these days.

“With such liveliness, I have every reason to believe that he’d simply stay in a corner and witness the revelry with a frown on his face, arms crossed and everything.” Phainon attempts to make a disgruntled sound, failing spectacularly with how much he’s trying not to smile, a warm fondness in his heart. “You know how he is.”

Castorice suppresses a giggle. “The Festival of Phagousa is the grandest event of the year. It would be a shame if Lord Mydei wouldn’t be able to experience it fully.” Her purple eyes glint with an unspoken mischief. “You should show him how to have a good time, Lord Phainon.”

Phainon scoffs, cheeks reddening as he avoids Castorice’s gaze. “We’d just end up arguing if I force him. That guy doesn’t know fun even if it punched him in the face.”

That, and Phainon simply doesn’t know how to deal with Mydei after their… last encounter. Even until now, his lips still tingled just from the memory of it, and it’s been days since. Four Entry Hours to be exact. It’s rather fortunate that Mydei has been busy with Kremnoan matters to even have the time to grace Phainon with his presence.

“I’m sure Lord Mydei would make an exception if it’s you.”

Phainon frowns. “But I promised to keep you company, considering you can’t even partake in the feast.”

Castorice shakes her head. “I’ll be alright, Lord Phainon. I thank you immensely for your consideration all these years,” she assures. “However, it is Lord Mydei’s first ever harvest feast since he and his people came here to Okhema. Such an occasion ought to be memorable.”

Mydei might not even care so much about the harvest feast considering how willing he was to simply forgo it. He agreed to join the Festival of Phagousa to appease his people from an unjust policy, and even then, it only serves as a temporary solution.

Phainon sighs. Castorice does have her rare moments of persistence. He could never bear to turn her down.

“Alright. I’ll make sure Mydei doesn’t keep to himself tomorrow.”

Castorice’s expression softens. But before she could utter a reply, her posture went rigid, attention directed at something behind Phainon—rather, someone judging from the sound of steady footfalls growing louder.

Phainon turns around, his smile fading away slowly from his face when he sees who it was that’s currently walking towards them.

Krateros had his usual severe expression as he approached, escorted by two guards trailing closely behind him. A quick look at their uniforms alone, one is able to deduce that they serve the Council of Elders rather than the Chrysos Heirs.

Both Phainon and Castorice stand up to address the Kremnoan.

“Lord Krateros,” Phainon greets, trying to keep his tone respectful in the hopes that the older would forget his past insolence. “To what do we owe the pleasure?”

Krateros nods at him lightly in acknowledgement before turning his attention at Castorice. “Lady Castorice, would you mind if I borrow Lord Phainon for a moment?”

At the question, Phainon can’t help but think that his ears have failed him. Since when did Krateros address him as such? All he recalls were the words ‘boy’ and ‘foolish child’ accompanied by flashing eyes and admonishing words. From the back of his head, he begins to feel a distinct phantom pain, brought only to life by memories from more than a month ago.

Their last conversation hadn’t really ended well. Perhaps it’s because of the guards that the Kremnoan had to be on his best behavior considering how the Elders could easily escalate trifling matters in the pretense of justice.

Castorice’s eyes dart between Krateros and Phainon, her unease palpable, aware of the supposed animosity of the former against the latter.

“If Lord Phainon permits it, then…”

Krateros turns his gaze towards Phainon, considerate enough to not urge Castorice to continue if it brings her great discomfort.

“I wish to speak to you in private,” Krateros says gruffly. “If you’re amenable.”

Phainon almost falls off from the lilypad out of shock. “Of course, Lord Krateros.”

Krateros then beckons him to the floating platform that leads to the grounds outside of the Marmoreal Palace. There’s an absence of small talk as they descended. Phainon deduces that it’s due to the guards breathing down their necks, evidently inclined to eavesdrop and take note of every word that escapes their lips just to report it to their superiors.

At a secluded spot, Krateros leans close, subtle when he whispers, “Follow my lead.”

As the words register in his mind, Krateros had already attacked one of the guards. It takes a moment for Phainon to realize what the older had wanted him to do and lunges towards the other one, swift enough to knock him out before he could even alert some unwitting bystander.

In barely any time at all, two limp bodies were dragged against the corner of a wall, inconspicuous enough that not even passersby would notice unless they took a second glance.

Krateros chuckles, eyes crinkling as he firmly pats Phainon on the shoulder for a job well done. “Not bad, hero of Okhema.”

Phainon laughs alongside him nervously, mind still reeling from what he just did. He’s pretty sure it warrants a punishment, but who is he to spoil an old man’s fun?

“If they were Aglaea’s people,” he began, surprised at his own behavior of beating up guards in the side of justice (debatable considering they serve the Elders, who were far from being just). “I would’ve done no such thing, to be honest.”

Krateros sighs. “I know, I know.” He glances at the unconscious guards and shrugs. “Eh, you don’t have to worry about these two weaklings. No one saw what we did, they have no evidence if they were to tattle to the Elders.”

“I see that you’ve thought this through.”

“With no question.”

Phainon still had his apprehensions but doesn’t push further. “Lord Krateros, I must admit that I’m quite curious as to why you wish to speak to me given our previous… encounter.”

“Right.” Krateros’ eyebrows furrow in thought. “As you’ve seen, the young master has already informed the detachment of the changes in regards to tomorrow’s occasion. Even if the young master hadn’t mentioned it, I have every right to believe that my assault against you was to blame for the Council to retaliate as such.”

“The Council favors neither Kremnoans nor the Chrysos Heirs,” Phainon reiterates.

He and Krateros both have their own share of faults in the matter, but he wanted to make it clear that it wouldn’t have made a difference if they ended up destroying a city or simply had a light argument comparable to what a merchant would have with a cheapskate buyer.

The Elders were bound to choose a severe punishment if given the opportunity. It’s just in their nature to be petty like that.

“They did this for themselves,” Phainon continues, referring to the corrupted minds that unfortunately held a significant power of governance over Okhema. “It’s simply their way of flaunting their influence. Even Aglaea wouldn’t go so far as to hinder your traditions.”

Krateros purses his lips. “I am well aware.”

“...Oh.”

“I’m not here to apologize,” the older adds.

“I didn’t expect you to,” Phainon tells him. “And I’m not going to do so either.”

Krateros nods, a hint of pride instead of offense in his lone dark eye. “I’m glad that we can both stand by our own opinions firmly enough to not be sorry for them.”

Phainon would argue that his own opinions seemed more reasonable than Krateros,’ but he’s well aware that this is neither the time nor the place to recommence another round of debate. Without Mydei to mediate between them, things could go south pretty fast. Today, Phainon decides to take the high road.

“Is that all you wish to say to me? You opt to agree to disagree?”

Krateros shakes his head. “No. I’m here to let you know that—” He then pauses rather abruptly, interrupting his words with a heavy sigh as he uncharacteristically avoids eye contact. There’s a slight hesitation in his words when he continues, “I will think through what you said that day some more.”

Not like Phainon expected Krateros to immediately have a change of heart— Wait.

What?

“What?” he squawks.

Phainon had expected Krateros to simply say yes and leave. That, or he gets offended by assuming that Phainon thinks his time is being wasted for an inconsequential talk that didn’t even resolve anything. Even if such a sentiment is unavoidable, he didn’t expect Krateros’ response to blindside him like this.

“Don’t make me repeat myself, boy.” Krateros crosses his arms. So the respectful address from earlier is only because of the presence of surveillance. “I accept you, and your naive opinions.” Then he adds, as if it were an afterthought. “The latter, I will ponder some more.”

“Oh. I—” Phainon tries to make himself sound more eloquent, struggling with how best to express himself. This is Mydei’s teacher for Titans’ sake. The least he could do is conduct himself with grace. “I’m surprised?”

Krateros scoffs, more amused than anything. Which should be a good sign, Phainon supposes. “What a candid reaction. You really are different from the others who have sought the young master’s favor.”

“Is that a bad thing?” Phainon asks faintly.

“I can’t say for now.”

“So,” Phainon feels his heart thud in his chest, beating with hope. “You’ll take Mydei’s wishes into consideration? Will he be able to confide in you at last without the worries of being misunderstood?”

Krateros nods once. “I will lend an ear, and my counsel shall remain unbiased. Although, regardless of what I say, the young master and I know that he will always be free to do whatever he wants. If he wishes to relinquish his claim to the throne, I cannot stop him. He’s just respectful enough to take into account the opinions of an old man such as I.”

“You are his teacher,” Phainon says. “Of course your guidance means a lot to him.”

“You are very sentimental. Kremnoans have no need for that.” Krateros pauses. “But I can see that you embody the Virtues of Nikador, enough to bestow my respect.”

Phainon thinks he’s hearing things for the second time that day. Unless he’s sorely mistaken, those words sounded like a compliment.

Krateros continues, “I had my apprehensions when the young master invited you to the Rite of Parting several months ago, but Mydeimos always has had a good perception when it comes to people.” He places a hand on Phainon’s shoulder and squeezes. “I’m keeping an eye on you, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae. You have earned something I don’t give away so freely to just anyone—my trust. Do not take it for granted.”

It’s quiet then, as Phainon tries to have a grasp on the situation. The weight of Krateros’ hand upon his shoulder bears a certain distinct heaviness, pressuring him to adhere to a responsibility that need not be spoken out loud, one that he’s more than willing to take on.

Krateros withdraws his hand with a huff at Phainon’s lack of response, his initial show of pride now replaced with exasperation. “Speak, boy! This is hardly an easy conversation to have. The least you could do is nod or fall dead.”

Phainon’s voice thankfully returns. “T-Thank you so much, Lord Krateros!” he says breathlessly, still in a state of perpetual shock. “Your acceptance means a lot to me, and Mydei would no doubt show his appreciation as well—”

“You are to keep this conversation a secret from the young master for the time being,” Krateros interrupts. “I wish to have a talk with him as well after this before the morrow comes.”

“I see,” Phainon says. “My lips are sealed.”

Krateros merely nods, turning his attention towards the foggy horizon. Somewhere out there, the mobile nation of Castrum Kremnos remains lost to this day. The lone eye of the warrior belied a hint of wistfulness, a longing for his home. Somehow, he looked accepting to put aside his desires to return to an age of glory—a decision made to trust in his prince who had no interest in the king’s crown.

“I have taken up too much of your time,” Krateros says after a brief moment of silence. “I should return to the settlement. There’s still so much to do for tomorrow.”

Like a habit, Phainon is compelled to ask, “Do you need help?”

Krateros scoffs. “You insult me. Hasn’t His Highness informed you that such matters are not for you to bother yourself with?”

Right. It’s evident that outsiders are not to meddle. And yet, Phainon keeps forgetting such a simple rule. Kremnoans have their pride after all.

“Yes,” Phainon agrees amicably in place of insistence. “Mydei did say something of the sort.”

Krateros tuts. “Foolish boy. And yet, the young master favors you immensely.” He gives Phainon a long look. “Mydeimos puts a great amount of trust in you. Do not betray him, or it is my blade that will seek to slice your throat.”

The threat is somehow expected. Instead of taking offense, Phainon merely smiles. After all, there is nothing to worry about.

“I would never,” he says guilelessly. “Mydei is important to me. His trust is something I value more than any kind of riches in this dying world.”

“Words mean nothing,” the older tells him. Despite his curt response, his expression has softened. “The duty of taking care of the crown prince is one that I will never forsake.”

Poised to leave, Krateros stops just beside Phainon, standing together on equal footing. And though they faced opposing directions, it is at this moment that their goals have simply aligned.

“That duty of mine,” Krateros continues. “I now willingly share with you.”

For a couple to be bound in life and in death, courtship should last no less than six months. The term ‘marriage’ is sparsely used, for Kremnoans favor a much more generalistic way of referring to it: a union of equals.

…unions involving royalty tend to be celebrated with sincere gifts followed by a parade from the outskirts of the capital to the inner city where a lavish banquet is held. The proceedings should be arranged with thorough consideration by the courted alone.

The nation honors the newly-bound with their offerings, and the newly-bound honors the nation in return with their acceptance. Wise leaders would know better than to abuse the show of abundance. It is said that if a penny offered is returned in equal value or more, the nation shall prosper.

— an excerpt. Kremnoan Traditions: Culture and Customs throughout History

· · ─ · ─ · ·

“It is time, Deliverer,” is the first thing that Mydei says when Phainon opens the door for him.

The second quint of the Lucid Hour had barely even begun. Fortunately, Phainon rose early to prepare himself for the Festival of Phagousa, just in case his assistance was still needed for some last-minute requests.

He had only finished tying the straps of his sandals against his shin when a knock had resounded from his door and Mydei’s presence served as his morning benediction. Phainon could already tell that the day is bound to be a good one.

Mydei is draped in regal elegance with a gold silken chiton, looking as radiant as ever, even more so than usual actually. But Phainon would argue that every passing day that he sets his sights on Mydei, the latter’s beauty only grows, like a flower destined to bloom for eternity, never to wilt until the end of times.

And though Phainon wonders if Mydei’s elaborate garment would be alright to wear in an event that involves bathing, he voices none of his concerns, well aware that he’s the furthest to question a person’s outfit choices.

He could only hope that he looks presentable enough in Mydei’s eyes as well. Aglaea had already prepared a chiton for him beforehand—finely woven linen dyed navy blue, every edge bordered with hand-stitched, golden embroidery, cinched at the waist with a matching golden belt encrusted with sapphire inlays.

“Mydei,” he greets, the smile on his lips an easy one, barely requiring much thought. “Isn’t it too early? The festival doesn’t start until the Action Hour.”

Mydei does not return his smile. “If we are to elude the Elders’ notice, it is advisable to begin the ceremony at a much earlier time.”

“Oh.”

And then it clicks: Mydei is inviting him to celebrate the Kremnoans’ harvest feast despite the restrictions. Perhaps the Festival of Phagousa alone was not enough. Phainon is thankful nonetheless that Mydei is willing to include him after days of treating him as if he had committed a crime if he so much as helped a Kremnoan carry a barrel of pomegranate juice.

He steps out of the room and closes the door behind him. “Very well.”

Mydei then leads the way, their hands brushing slightly against each other as they walked. It takes every ounce of restraint to not reach out and take Mydei’s hand in his, to hold on to it as if it was the lone rope that Phainon direly clings upon as he dangles from the edge of a cliff.

The last time he held any part of Mydei was when they kissed—a memory that remains fresh in his mind, one he’s never bound to forget even if the nether realm and the high heavens were to meet and reduce the land to a mere lifeless crust.

The act of reliving it, no matter how many times, never takes away the blissful traces that continue to linger in his thoughts during his waking moments. In his dreams, there are admittedly the occasional nightmares. But the feeling of Mydei’s lips against his, the warmth of it, is enough to shine light to the darkness that plagued his sleep.

Lost in his own thoughts, Phainon only realizes halfway through the journey that Mydei was leading him towards the Kremnoan detachment’s settlement. Mydei had been quiet the whole time, perhaps also preoccupied by thoughts so deep that the urge to start a conversation had escaped him fully. Not like Mydei was proficient when it came to initiating small talk in the first place.

Only upon nearing the settlement did Mydei speak at last. “Each Kremnoan household had prepared gifts for us,” he says. “We are to accept them together.”

Though it’s surprising for Kremnoans to do such a thing, it’s not unheard of for Chrysos Heirs to receive tributes during the Month of Joy—a gesture of thanks from the citizens for a year’s worth of protection. For Mydei to invite him specifically, perhaps the assumption that the Kremnoans have grown to favor him all these months is not entirely unfounded.

“I would be honored.”

Mydei gives him a small smile, a sight that makes Phainon’s heart flutter in his chest. Really, he ought to bid farewell to his pride if Mydei were to be made aware of the effect he had on him.

Men, women, and children await their arrival, crates situated in front of every household as they positioned themselves in a semi-circle. Mydei leads Phainon to the first one, a family of three brothers by the far left.

“My lords, here I present to you the finest shields we’ve crafted,” the young man says. From the looks of it, he seems to be the eldest. “Only the finest of materials have been used. May it protect you from battle.”

Phainon marvels at the handiwork. Such craftsmanship could even be comparable to that of Chartonus.’ It’s not a lie that he expected the gifts to be something more… harvest-related.

But Kremnoans are known to integrate the concept of war in their traditions, Phainon shouldn’t be surprised by this at all.

“Thank you,” Phainon says. “I’ll make good use of these.”

Mydei nods beside him. “It is impressive. You have my sincerest gratitude.”

They move on to the next one. This time, a lone sword sits within the crate in front of an old man and his wife. Even with the absence of armor, Phainon could deduce that he’d been a formidable warrior in his prime. The old man takes the sword from the crate and presents it to him, who does the honors of pulling the blade out of its sheath.

“I heard that Lord Phainon favors the sword more than any other weapon,” the old man says. “Please accept this humble offering of mine. ‘Tis an heirloom passed down from nine generations and has seen many victories. I have no children to speak of, hence why I wish for his lordship to inherit the legacy of my family.”

Phainon sees his face reflected upon the blade, feeling his hands quiver upon realizing the value of such a gift. “Can I really take this?”

His nerves have become alight with worry, apprehensive if he should have something so significant—if he’s even worthy. Just then, a warm hand settles at the small of his back and he turns to Mydei. Those eyes of gold gleamed with something more than just mere encouragement, a nod to reassure him that it’s alright.

It is then that Phainon finds his doubts thoroughly cleansed away.

The old man laughs good-naturedly. “My lord, my bloodline would only know honor if you were to accept.”

“Thank you kindly. I will take care of it.” Phainon only lets out a shaky exhale as he slides the sword back in its sheath. “The battles it will take on shall not sully the good name of your family, for I ensure that it'll only see victory from here on out.”

The old man and his wife seemed satisfied, beaming at him with pride in realization that their decisions had been the right one. Phainon is not sure if he’ll be able to take much more societal pressure for the rest of the day after that. Fortunately, the next crate of offerings is much more conventional for the Month of Joy.

“The finest harvests from my family’s vegetable garden,” the Kremnoan says, holding his husband and daughter close. “We are aware that this meager offering is not that impressive in comparison to others, but we are very proud of it.”

Phainon fails to see how such a bountiful harvest from a garden is considered ‘meager.’ If anything, the contents of the crate is comparable to the ones that Aglaea receives from the noble families of Okhema during both the Month of Joy and Reaping.

Mydei leans down and inspects the produce before nodding in satisfaction. He gives the family a smile of his own. “There is no such thing as unimpressive in a ceremony such as this. You take pride in your work, that alone is enough.”

As they move on to the next, something shiny catches Phainon’s eye from within the crate. What he saw had his jaw going slack.

“Gemstones that I have accumulated from my time as a miner in Kremnos,” the woman says. “The ones I offer before you are the finest cuts that I have in my treasury. My lords, this is the only thing of value I possess that I could offer you.”

Even Mydei stood still as a statue, lips slightly parted as he stared at the dazzling trove within the crate, nestled in coarse straw for protection, a faint mineral tang mingling with the air.

Phainon takes a sapphire in hand, lifting it up so it catches the light from Kephale’s Dawn, splintering it into deep flashes of royal blue. He watches carefully as the color shifts with every angle, keeping a keen eye to discern its genuity.

As he did so, he could see Mydei’s image through the polished facets, appearing distant, almost dreamlike—a reflection warped and tinted in deep blue hues. It makes Phainon wonder how Mydei would look swathed in azure jewels, a stark contrast to the rubies that adorned his usual accessories.

“Is it to your liking?” Mydei asks.

“Only such unparalleled magnificence for you, my lords,” the Kremnoan woman adds, just in case Phainon needed more convincing.

Lowering the gem, Mydei’s visage is now clear to see. Phainon’s gaze holds steady, eyes meeting molten gold as he says, “Indeed. A beauty so unparalleled it has completely stolen my breath.”

With those words, Phainon did not speak of gemstones, smiling when Mydei’s face reddens, the realization expressed so openly. He returns the sapphire to the crate, satisfied with his appraisal. Such treasures fail to tempt him as much as the man who led him to the next crate with a gentle countenance and a warm hand that had never left the small of his back since it made its presence known.

He and Mydei accepted more gifts from the Kremnoans, more than what Phainon had initially expected to receive—blank papyrus and quills, fresh eggs and live poultry, a newly-born calf spawned from strong, native Kremnoan cows. A couple households even offered up freshly harvested pomegranates. Idaeus himself gifted three barrels filled with honey brew.

Even as a relatively popular Chrysos Heir, the extent of the offerings he had received in the prior years couldn’t even begin to compare.

After that, Mydei instructs Praxis and the other soldiers to handle the gifts—the animals returned to their fenced pastures, the produce divided amongst all households, a pouch of jewels distributed fairly to every family head, while the rest of it, alongside the weapons, to be secured safely until either Phainon or Mydei were to fetch them.

With so many Kremnoans still at the settlement, Phainon expected all of them to make their way to Marmoreal Palace together with the Festival of Phagousa scheduled to begin in only a quint from now.

Nevertheless, it still caught him by surprise how the Kremnoans were trailing after him and Mydei with a distinct formation, carrying banners and baskets of fruits, predominantly pomegranates, like they were in some sort of a bizarre parade. Perhaps it’s not so strange for warriors to behave so orderly.

It didn’t take long for them to arrive at the entrance of the Marmoreal Palace, the Kremnoans beginning to disperse from behind them to join in the festivities.

“Were you satisfied?” Mydei asks him. “The pre-banquet ceremony still adhered to the traditions. If we were in Kremnos, I have no doubts that it would’ve taken us an entire day to make our way from the outskirts of the city to the inner capital.”

Phainon huffs out a laugh. “A whole day of accepting gifts? That doesn’t sound too bad,” he jeers. “I must admit, I never expected the Kremnoans to practice such a custom.”

He had the impression that Kremnoans didn’t care much for material gains. But the Month of Joy is known for blessing everyone with abundance so perhaps it is not at all that surprising. Kremnoans are relatively nice and generous if you know how to deal with them.

(Exhibit A: The Crown Prince)

Just as Mydei was about to open his mouth to respond, the bells toll signalling the beginning of the Action Hour; it’s time for the Festival of Phagousa to begin.

“Should we head in?” Phainon asks.

Mydei squints at him. “I’m surprised you have the patience to partake in the revelry.”

“Only because the Festival of Phagousa has proven to be quite enjoyable from my previous years of experience since coming to Okhema. Much more so now that the Kremnoans have entered the picture. The more the merrier, as they say.”

“I have no interest in banquets, I’m sure the same applies to you.”

Typical Mydei to want nothing to do with socializing. Phainon can’t help but smile, utterly enamored with this man. “You’re the one who wants to skip the feast, not me.”

Mydei reddens as he looks away, arms crossed. “I do not wish to lie, so I won’t say anything to confirm nor deny your assumption.”

Phainon laughs. “Mydei, you worked so hard to contribute with the preparations. The least you could do is savor the fruits of your labor. Isn’t that what the Month of Joy is all about?”

That, and Castorice won’t ever let Phainon live it down if he failed to show Mydeimos the Unhappy a good time.

Mydei seems to consider it. After a moment, he eventually acquiesces. “Fine.”

He then walks towards the waterfall without waiting for Phainon, the cascade parting in the middle and granting them entry. Even from the lobby, the chatter coming from the baths could already be heard, the sound bouncing through walls in excited echoes.

When they finally pass through the second curtain of flowing water, the sight of the Nerid Spring packed to the brim is the first thing that greets them. Citizens from all walks of life gathered in colorful chitons, like lilies sprouting from the waters, all basking in the revelry, indulging in conversations and drinks. Even the newly-arrived Kremnoans have begun to mingle with the Okhemans, nary a care to their history of less-than amicable relations.

From the Heroes’ Bath overlooking, Phainon could spot two silhouettes standing by the edge of the elevated platform. Aglaea and Castorice stood together, a relative distance between them. The Holy Maidens, on the other hand, flitted around with their little wings fluttering behind their backs, giggling as they showered flower petals and glittering golden dust onto the crowd.

“Everyone’s already here,” Phainon muses. “Let’s find a place to settle where we could get a good view of the play and the orchestra.”

Mydei only sighs, somehow aggravated by something. “How exciting.” Sarcastic. How oh how is Mydeimos the Unhappy going to have a good time today. “Lead the way, then.”

“Don’t be so impatient,” Phainon says lightly, the desire to kiss away the pout on Mydei’s lips much too strong. He wonders if he could even do such a thing. Though Mydei had somehow hinted that the last kiss they shared won’t be the only one, Phainon dared not hope lest the disappointment of rejection eats him alive. “When the music starts, you’ll find that there’s much to enjoy.”

Mydei says nothing, allowing himself to be dragged by the wrist, their sandals finally submerged into the shimmering waters of the bath. Fortunately, they were able to find an unoccupied floating lounge in a corner with only a few people surrounding it, but still a relatively acceptable place for them to see the stage.

As they settle, the musicians finally arrive, situating themselves before their chosen instruments. Before they could start playing, however, the clack of a heel meeting marble echoes throughout the place and silencing the crowd. Aglaea’s footsteps have been amplified by the golden threads, garnering the attention of everyone in the baths.

“Citizens of Okhema, the hour has begun where we ought to set aside the burdens of labor. Feast, not merely to nourish the body, but to uplift our weary hearts.” Her clouded gaze travels all across the people looking up to her from the Nerid Spring, only to land upon the two men in the far edge of the bath. Her attention lingers to her fellow Heirs. “Remember that such revelry should serve not to intoxicate you, but clear your mind of burdens and apprehensions. Let the festivities begin!”

Everyone erupts into mirthful cheers as the orchestra starts playing a bright and skipping melody, playful and full of life, urging everyone to dance and sing.

Ideaus comes by not soon after, holding up a tray with two chalices containing the Kremnoans’ signature honey brew. “My lords,” he says, almost a whisper as if he’s afraid someone would hear him. “The Drink of Honor, blessed by Lady Aglaea herself.”

“Thank you, Ideaus,” Mydei says, taking the cups from the tray and handing Phainon his share. He swirls his drink, inspecting the pink liquid. “No liquor?”

“That’s the fifth time you’ve asked that today, Your Highness,” Ideaus jeers, cheeks dimpling as he grinned. “Do you not trust my humble self?”

Mydei’s lips twitch, suppressing a smile. “This would have been the rare opportunity for you to serve me liquor. I wouldn’t have minded.”

Phainon can’t help but think that Mydei’s words vaguely hinted at something to which he had no clue as to what it was. Perhaps some inside Kremnoan joke, or maybe Mydei hated indulging in festivities that he would rather do it drunk out of his mind.

Nevertheless, the idea that Mydei is currently unable to enjoy himself despite being in Phainon’s company causes the latter to fall silent, sipping his drink as his mind whirles with self-doubt. He’d been too confident that his presence alone would suffice and convince Mydei to have a good time. How presumptuous.

Beside him, Mydei simply stares ahead, watching the citizens dance in knee-deep water, faces flushed with wine and joy, spinning hand in hand and uncaring of how damp their clothes have gotten as the fabric swirled with every movement against the shimmering pool, sending ripples across the surface.

It is at that moment that Phainon is stricken with an idea. A foolish one.

He hops off the floating lounge, settling his drink on a nearby floating tray. With a hand outstretched towards Mydei—whose eyebrows had furrowed in question—he asks, “Will you do me the honor of being your first dance?”

If Mydei were to turn him down, then he’d simply go along with Mydei’s wishes to ditch the festival altogether, their presence as Chrysos Heirs be damned. Perhaps then the other would begin to lighten up.

There’s a huge chance that Mydei would say no to the dance, of course. He recalls a memory from months ago, of Mydei informing him that Kremnoans are no strangers to merrymaking. But the crown prince of Kremnos is much too reserved that even Phainon is unable to imagine a world in which Mydei sings, let alone dances.

And Phainon likes to think about Mydei a lot, his imagination running wild and plagued with golden hair and golden eyes, of tanned skin mired in streaks of scarlet, of muscles well-defined. A deep voice goading him on, the taste of sweetness on his tongue, the manifestation of a soft addiction against his lips—

Still, the simple image of Mydei dancing evades him, a possibility that had yet to exist.

Mydei stares at his outstretched hand, the look on his face thoughtful as he decides whether or not he accepts Phainon’s offer. Patiently, Phainon waits. He keeps his hand steady and open, just close enough to be within Mydei’s reach, but not so much to come off as forceful.

He would never lower his hand until Mydei gives him an answer. By the looks of things, he’s about to be declined.

“Alright.”

Phainon is pulled away from his thoughts when something warm meets his hand—Mydei had taken it, the touch of their skin a heightened sensation as Phainon’s attention narrows down to this single moment, the revelry around them forgotten.

And then, Mydei’s answer finally hits him, his own shocked countenance reflected against those twin pools of gold that seared through his very soul, shining with quiet amusement as Phainon struggles for something to say in return.

“Oh,” Phainon says, rather intelligently. In his defense, his mind can’t afford to process more complex thoughts when Mydei’s hand periodically squeezes his own ever so slightly. “You can dance?”

Mydei’s lips twitch downward in a little frown. “What a stupid question. Of course I can. More importantly, can you keep up with me?”

“Are you so familiar with Okheman dances to confidently issue a challenge?”

“I may not be familiar, but I learn quick,” Mydei admits, eyes darkening as he pulls Phainon closer to him, situating him between muscled thighs. “What about you, Deliverer? You seem to know your way around when it comes to dances done during the Month of Joy.”

Phainon huffs against Mydei’s shoulder. Looking up to meet Mydei’s gaze in a show of sincerity, he says, “I have only ever watched from the sidelines from celebrations past. You can ask Castorice if you refuse to believe me.”

Instead of a response, Mydei gives him an indecipherable look mired in scrutiny. He gently pushes Phainon away, leaving his seat before placing his drink upon the floating tray.

Without a word or a single glance, Mydei walks toward the center of the Nerid Spring where the people danced to the music, the waters splashing against his bare thighs, a flash of gold wrapped around one of them, tastefully worn against the thick, flexing muscle.

Phainon could feel himself go slightly dizzy at the sight, standing dumbfounded still by the floating lounge, his hand tingling from the sudden cold now with Mydei no longer around to warm him.

Sensing that Phainon hasn’t followed, Mydei turns around, an eyebrow raised in question as he smirks. “Well?”

A taunt.

Phainon takes in a breath before he steps forward, following Mydei towards the crowd. This could either end in utter embarrassment, or something much worse. Phainon casts a glance upon the Heroes’ Baths where Aglaea and Castorice stood to watch.

Castorice gives him two thumbs up, a smile on her face. Aglaea, on the other hand, had her arms crossed, features graced with a frown. Phainon dreads to think what she would say when he and Mydei eventually end up ruining the Festival of Phagousa with a simple dance competition.

Just as they stood in position, the score changes. Phainon is familiar enough to know how to open the dance, taking the liberty to lead and for Mydei to follow. Mydei does, turning in the opposite direction smoothly enough before once again gravitating into Phainon’s space like they were never meant to part for so long.

Gradually, they made their way to the center of the crowd, shallow waters splashing with every movement of their legs, their footwork in sync with the music. The citizens have parted away to grant the two heroes some space as they danced with wide and sweeping motions, spinning each other with breathless laughs.

Phainon catches sight of Mydei’s grin as he takes three steps away and two steps back, turning, reaching out until his hand finds Mydei’s waist. The damp silk against his palm is not unpleasant enough to hinder the sight of Mydei with his reservations put aside, alight with giddiness that he’s positively glowing.

The air in Phainon’s lungs has been taken away, a mild twisting in his chest whenever the dance makes them separate albeit briefly. Their hands brush against each other in passing, a continuous pattern of mirrored steps. Though their movements attempt to appear stately, their inexperience was still evident. And yet, Phainon finds himself uncaring of it.

Eyes may be on them as the citizens opted to form a circle instead, enclosing the two Heirs within, their arms locked around each other as they skipped and hopped, a continuous splash of shimmering water to aid the rhythm.

Those who remained to watch by the sidelines have begun to clap, spurring the dancers even more. Some of them have even begun to chant and sing—an ode to Phagousa and yet, the string quartet accompanied by the water lyre gave the song a touch of romance, Mnestia’s influence weaving in so effortlessly like the golden threads that intertwined the fates of all.

As the dance goes on, the rhythm quickens signalling its eventual end. Mydei catches Phainon’s wrist, spun him twice before letting go, sending Phainon a couple of paces away just as he does a high-stepped flourish causing the crowd to erupt into a resounding applause.

Mydei raises an eyebrow. “Show off.”

Phainon laughs. “You try.”

The Kremnoans’ singing have grown loud enough to compete with the Okhemans,’ more so when Mydei is spun around, mirroring the step Phainon had just done with the idea of besting Phainon with his moves. They’re drenched, but neither of them seemed to mind, hands slipping due to the wetness as they tried to hold on to each other.

During the last twirl for the dance, Mydei’s sandals catch upon a stray tile beneath the waters of the bath and he trips just as the final note of the water lyre resounds. Phainon’s body responds as if on instinct, reaching out to catch Mydei before he falls and holding him steady against his chest, arms enclosed upon the other’s waist in a firm hold.

Mydei looks up at him, hands gripping his shoulders, so near and dear with lips slightly parted as he catches his breath—soft and warm, intermingling with Phainon’s. And as Mydei’s gaze drops to Phainon’s lips, Phainon is very much inclined to lean down some more, the unmistakable look in Mydei’s eyes one that Phainon has grown familiar with how much he’s recounted their last kiss.

Phainon longs to have another taste, he had never once stopped to desire the man before him. Such greed will be his downfall. And yet—

The crowd bursts into applause and mirthful cheers, startling both Phainon and Mydei from their makeshift bubble. For a moment, they’ve forgotten that they’re not alone. The dance has concluded. The first of many more, that is.

Mydei pulls away and steadies himself on his own two feet, his face slightly flushed with a tinge of red, almost shy. The sight itself tugs at Phainon’s heartstrings so mercilessly.

“Are you alright?” Phainon asks.

“Of course I am,” Mydei answers. Despite the haughty tone, a small smile has graced his lips. “It seems that you’ve won, Deliverer.”

Phainon smiles, snaking his hands upon Mydei’s waist to pull him closer just as they were before. “It seems that I have,” he gloats. Teasingly, he adds, “Oh. Were you referring to the dance? I thought you meant something else.”

“Haikas,” Mydei scoffs, however, he doesn’t make a move to pry Phainon’s hands off of him. In fact, he takes another small step closer to ensure that there’s barely even any space between them. “I refuse to believe that this is your first time dancing in an event like this. You must’ve had so much practice from the previous years.”

This again. Phainon is so fond that his cheeks have begun to hurt with how much he’s smiling.

“Dances like these are only meant to be shared with…” He allows his voice to trail off in favor of leaning closer, brushing his lips against Mydei’s ear as if he were about to share a secret. “...someone special.”

He pulls away, just enough to garner Mydei’s reaction. As always, he was not disappointed.

Phainon continues, “I’m afraid I’ve never had anyone to consider as such before I met you.”

The tips of Mydei’s ears redden, down to his neck and chest. For the second time, he mutters a soft,  “Haikas.”

Phainon only laughs. Just then, the music starts anew. Lesser people have opted to participate, situating themselves a relative distance away to ensure enough space for every partnered couple. The rhythm this time is slow, almost languid in a way.

One of the hands resting upon Mydei’s waist leaves in favor of taking Mydei’s idle hand, an offer. “Another dance, my Dei?”

Mydei huffs, allowing himself to be led in step, one hand intertwined with Phainon’s while the other firmly held Phainon by the shoulder as they glided through shallow waters.

“Not affording me rest, are you?” Mydei says.

Phainon hums, the tips of his fingers pressing lightly upon the small of Mydei’s back. “Not like you to be so weary already.” He twirls Mydei in uniform with the dance, but pulls him close quicker than the others, loathe to part. “Do you wish to be taken elsewhere, then? For some… relaxation?”

Mydei’s eyes glint, narrowing slightly. “I’ve been meaning to do just that. But someone refused to have a blot on his perfect Deliverer attendance.”

For once, Phainon is able to understand quicker than what should be deemed appropriate. “You’re going to kill me one day with your words, Mydeimos.”

Mydei smiles, a finger slipping beneath the fabric of Phainon’s chiton, fiddling with the brooch upon his shoulder. The touch leaves Phainon’s skin tingling in its wake.

“Don’t worry, Deliverer. I’m more than willing to drag you back from the River of Souls if I have to.”

“I can’t say I disagree,” Castorice says calmly. Despite how soft-spoken she tends to be, the way she said those words was distinctly louder than what Phainon is used to. “Lord Phainon, you are indeed, as you have said, an idiot.”

Tribbie, on the other hand, looked at a loss for words. Though Phainon made sure that his story-telling didn’t contain anything too explicit or embarrassing, it seemed that he still managed to get the point across.

The point of which he failed to see before Mydei threw him off the balcony. Perhaps the fall had rattled his brain for good.

“Snowy,” Tribbie began. “Why didn’t you just read the scroll Agy gave you?”

A damn good question. Even better than the utterly unhinged ones Professor Anaxa writes in his exams.

“I was going to read it at some point,” Phainon reasons to an audience who is so, so tired of him. It’s been a full day. “But I rarely had the time to read anything!”

Tribbie shakes her head, tutting like a thoroughly disappointed mother. “You are in deep trouble, Snowy.”

“Very well said, Lady Tribbie,” Castorice adds.

Phainon comes to realize that no one in the room is on his side. Which is fair. He’d also take Mydei’s side any day. Actually, it would really make him happy if he were at Mydei’s side right now.

“Have you come up with a plan to pacify Lord Mydei?” Castorice asks, as if there’s still a chance for Phainon to turn things around (there isn’t). “Now that you’ve recounted the whole story leading up to your marriage, I can’t help but sympathize with Lord Mydei’s situation.”

“I’m in the process of it,” Phainon tells her, ignoring the throbbing pain in his ribs. “Titans, he must really hate me now.”

Tribbie gives him a pat on the knee, light enough to not hurt him through the bandages. “De might be angry, but we believe that he wouldn’t be able to truly hate you,” she reassures. Her wide eyes give Phainon hope. “You’re his husband, Snowy. As long as you play your cards right, we’re sure he’ll return to you in no time.”

Love advice from a centuries-old child. At this point, Phainon would take all the help he could get to save his failing marriage. First day as a conscious husband and he already screwed it up by almost dying. He has his work cut out for him, he supposes.

“Thank you for the words of encouragement, Lady Tribbie,” he says.

“We’re sorry we weren’t able to help you sooner, Snowy. Even we didn’t know about this until now.”

Tribbie and Phainon both turn to Castorice.

“I had no idea as well,” Castorice tells them. “Although, Lord Mydei does talk about you a lot, Lord Phainon.”

Phainon perks up and winces at the pain the slight movement had caused him. “Good things I hope?”

Castorice smiles mysteriously. Perhaps Aglaea’s company has been rubbing off on her. “I cannot disclose what he has said during our recreation time. You’ll have to ask Lord Mydei when… you’ve settled this.”

This is the first that Phainon hears of this ‘recreation time,’ and he wonders why he’s not invited. That’s the thing about Mydei: he’s the type of man to see or do something so interesting (read: get married) and keep it to himself unless someone asks. It endears annoys Phainon to no end that from now on, he’ll make it a point to ask about literally everything the man had done for the day.

“Have hope, Lord Phainon.”

Phainon tries, really. May the gods strike him down this instant. He’d been an utter fool that even the murals painted on the walls of the Marmoreal Palace possessed a better eyesight than him to see through this farce. If Mydei wants nothing to do with him after this, then it would be better to forfeit his existence entirely to make up for his sheer stupidity.

He sighs. “You know, Miss Castorice, I could really use a hug right now.”

“And that is my cue to leave,” Castorice says, walking towards the door in graceful yet hurried steps. “Lady Tribbie, have a good rest of your day. Lord Phainon, I hope you get well soon. Oh, and for your injuries to heal nicely, I suppose.”

Phainon gapes as the door closes behind Castorice, before turning to Tribbie who was fixing up the medicine tray, deciding which ones to take back to the infirmary.

Seeing his chance, Phainon bolts out of his chair, ignoring the pain that sparks throughout his entire body as he limps towards an open window. Before he could reach it, however, Tribbie had already run past him to slam the shutters close.

“Snowy! What were you thinking?”

Phainon concedes and crumples into a pitiful ball on the floor. “My husband is mad at me. I should die.”

· · ─ ·𖥸· ─ · ·

To His Highness, the Crown Prince Mydeimos,

I write with sincere appreciation for your kindness toward my family. The kline you have so generously gifted brings us immeasurable relief. Thus, our bodies shall rest in the quiet hours, capable of rising fully and ready to be of service in the coming morrows.

I shall speak of your consideration to my sons and daughters, and they too shall pass it down to generations next. Then, this bloodline of mine would only know of the Crown Prince Mydeimos as the most benevolent and honorable of all.

Your loyal servant,

Perimlaus

· · ─ · ─ · · The curtains were drawn open, letting Kephale’s Dawn spill into the room from the open windows. The balcony door follows, and a cold gust of morning air sends a distinct chill upon the exposed skin of Phainon’s chest, the only thing that kept him warm still being a mere blanket haphazardly thrown over his lower half in his sleep.

He hears footsteps walking around the room, the pace steady and unhurried, metal greaves a familiar wake up call. Still wrestling against the desire to remain unconscious and just sink into the pillows, Phainon pulls the blanket over himself only for it to be sharply pulled back by a merciless perpetrator.

Phainon makes a disgruntled noise, eyes still adamantly closed. A soft huff resounds then, followed by the dipping of the mattress beside him.

“Get up, Deliverer.”

Phainon turns the other way around, away from the shine of Dawn. “No.”

He can hear Mydei shuffle about, grabbing the pillows strewn all over the bed. Phainon has an inkling as to what the other was planning to do, and instead of turning around to see for himself if his assumptions are correct, he would rather cherish the remaining time he has left before he’s—

As if willed by the fates, Mydei hoists him up in a sitting position, resting him against the aforementioned pile of pillows. Phainon’s head droops down. Though his eyes remain closed, he’s very much awake now.

A warm hand lightly grabs him by the chin, and Phainon knows through routine that it’s his cue to open his mouth obediently or there will be consequences. The cold metal of the spoon grazes his bottom lip as Mydei feeds him something sweet and flaky, the taste enough to comfort his soul after such a rude awakening.

Phainon talks as he chews. “What’s this?”

“Bougatsa,” Mydei replies. The hint of dismay in his tone is noticeable. “Don’t talk to me while your mouth is full. Have you no manners?”

Phainon withholds the cheeky reply he’s come up with in his mind in favor of his survivability, and swallows. “Too early.”

“It’s already the third quint of the Entry Hour.”

“Not helping your case,” Phainon says, a yawn slipping out. “Still too ear—mmph?”

Mydei had used the chance to shove another spoonful of bougatsa into Phainon’s open mouth. Already an opportunist this early in the morning. Phainon is incredibly impressed and disgruntled.

He opens his eyes to shoot a glare, gaze softening immediately at the sight of Mydei bathed in the morning light. At this moment, Phainon knew he'd lost the battle. And the war. And all things thereafter.

“This is unfair.”

Mydei raises an eyebrow. This mild shift in expression had some drastic effects on Phainon’s poor heart. “Says the man currently being fed like a child. Should I dress you up as well?”

Phainon smiles. “We both know you prefer me undressed, dear Mydeimos.”

“You really have no shame.”

Despite the words, Mydei then proceeds to undo the loose ties of Phainon’s sleeping pants. Phainon can’t help but bite back a laugh, reaching an arm out to wrap it around Mydei’s waist in an attempt to pull him back to bed.

“Well, it’s never too early for that, I suppose.”

Mydei surprisingly doesn’t put up much of a fight, begrudgingly letting himself be situated on Phainon’s lap. It doesn’t escape Phainon’s notice, however, how the other’s golden eyes have grown sharper, a crease in between his brows, looking equal parts exasperated and amused.

“Haven’t you had enough from yesterday?” Mydei asks.

Phainon nuzzles against Mydei’s neck, breathing in the sweet scent of pomegranates and tamping down the disappointment of Mydei taking a bath without him. He paws at Mydei’s armor, hands sluggish with sleep when it would otherwise be skillful.

He replies, “You know I can never get enough of you.”

Before Phainon’s hand could undo Mydei’s belt, Mydei had already left the bed quicker than Zagreus Themself would have, leaving Phainon cold. He stares up, bewildered at the sudden loss only to witness the flush creep up on Mydei’s face, high on his cheeks.

“Eat your food,” Mydei tells him, voice rough around the edges. He then proceeds to right his armor after Phainon did the liberty of messing it up. “If I see even a single morsel left on your plate, Deliverer, don’t expect me to serve you anything by the deipnon.”

Phainon turns his gaze at the tray of food by the edge of the bed. A generous serving of bougatsa, some fresh fruits, and a… cup of an unnamed liquid that Phainon would bet his life on is a mix of juiced pomegranates and some other abominable ‘ingredient of the day’ that Mydei decided to add.

Ignoring the existence of the drink, Phainon picks up a piece of grape and pops it in his mouth. “You know I always eat whatever you make.”

Mydei says nothing at the poorly-disguised attempt at getting in his good graces. He throws Phainon a satchel, substantially heavy as the latter caught it with a grunt.

Perplexed, Phainon opens the flap to examine the contents. “What’s this?”

“Take it with you on your mission,” Mydei tells him, his tone making it evident that there’s no room for negotiations.

Phainon raises an eyebrow when he sees two loaves of bread from within, sliced meats and cheese neatly arranged in a portable clay container, as well as a jug of water. “You packed me some lunch?” His heart swells with affection as he gazes up at Mydei. “Thank you.”

Mydei does not return his smile. “There’s also some medical supplies in there.”

“For what? I’ll be back by the Parting Hour.”

It’s not like Phainon is going on an expedition. Aglaea only tasked him to check the current state of Okhema’s borders just in case the Titankin had broken through somehow. If he’s lucky, he wouldn’t even need to engage in battle.

Mydei scoffs. “‘For what?’ he says. The last time you were ‘back by the Parting Hour,’ I had my teleslate bombarded with several messages informing me of how their Lord Phainon is gravely injured and in dire need of assistance.” His frown deepens. “All for a measly stab wound on the leg. You bled so much you put Kephale to shame.”

Phainon stares, taken aback (and feeling severely faint).

“You… knew about that?” he asks nonetheless even if there really was no point in doing so.

The truth was clear as day—Mydei knew of his blunder from several weeks ago where his mind was far too distracted (unsurprisingly, by thoughts of Mydei) to even focus on his skirmish against Nikador’s Titankin. As a result of his carelessness, he came back to Okhema with his consciousness hanging by a thread with how much he’s bled all the way from the Abyss.

Mydei crosses his arms, looking far from being impressed. Voice dripping with sarcasm, he replies, “Perhaps not, considering that I was the one who carried you to the infirmary.” And then he adds a sardonic, “You’re welcome, by the way.”

“You ask for gratitude now when you didn’t even bother to bring this up at a much earlier date?” Phainon demands, hiding his shame by feigning offense. He just wants to be buried under a rock at this point. Mydei must’ve thought him to be pathetic and weak.

“You kept mumbling ‘don’t tell Mydei’ in your sleep,” Mydei says. To his credit, he doesn’t seem to be making fun of Phainon for it. Or perhaps he’s just that good at masking his expressions. “Mydei was being kind and decided to honor a dying man’s wishes.”

Phainon scoffs. “I wasn’t dying. The stab wound was not fatal.”

“With your groaning and moaning, I’d think you were.”

“Odd of you to put emphasis on the sounds I make.”

“Simply returning the favor,” Mydei retorts drily. “I wouldn’t want you to feel alone in your fixation.”

Phainon parses the words with a sleep-addled mind. And then he recalls the many times he’d pinned Mydei’s hands upon the sheets just so the latter wouldn’t muffle the sounds he’d make in his pleasure—breathy hums and gasps, mumbled curses, ones that echo within Phainon’s mind for the entire day that by the time the day has concluded, he’s longing to hear it again.

He ought to feel shameful, apologetic even. But the warmth that pools in his groin as he recalls their trysts gives him a feeling he’d rather not dive into this early in the morning. Unless, of course, if Mydei is amenable—

“No.”

Phainon’s thoughts dissipate into thin air, much like his dreams, and he wilts like a flower. “I haven’t even said anything.”

Mydei scoffs. “You have that look on you. I know you well enough by now to have an idea as to what’s going on in your head.”

Phainon envisions sweaty tanned skin, contrasting nicely with scarlet streaks. Blonde hair fanning upon the pillows like a golden halo, and of muscles rippling with every slight shift.

“Why don’t you take a guess?”

“Why don’t you start eating your food?” Mydei shoots back. If Phainon’s meal consisted of the Kremnoan crown prince, he would do so in a heartbeat. Figuratively, of course. “Aglaea expects you to be ready to leave by the Lucid Hour, doesn't she? Make sure to bring that satchel with you.”

Phainon huffs, feigning exasperation. He usually would rather take nothing on relatively short trips so he wouldn’t have to worry about his items in between fights. But it seems his dear prince is quite adamant this time.

“Fine,” he acquiesces. “I’ll bring your medical supplies just in case you’d cry yourself to sleep worrying about me.”

Mydei raises an eyebrow. “Well, would you look at that,” he muses. “The Deliverer has learned not to be stubborn.”

“So you’re indeed worried about me.”

“Why wouldn’t I be? You and that fragile mortal body of yours.”

“I don’t recall you saying such things about my body during our previous encounters upon this very bed.”

The words seemed to have taken a moment to register. When it does, however, Phainon is blessed for the second time this morning with the sight of Mydei’s face coloring a pretty shade of red, up to the tips of his ears and down to his shoulders.

Mydei scowls with significantly far less heat than if he were actually offended. Flushed and disgruntled, he doesn’t humor Phainon with a reply as he walks away, leaving the room in a flurry of crimson fabric and muttered Kremnoan curses, greaves stomping against the floor vindictively.

Phainon laughs lightly to himself as he takes the plate of bougatsa from the tray after he heard the door slam shut at Mydei’s rather hasty retreat. His victory this morning was hard-won. But knowing Mydei, he’s sure to pay the price for it later on.

Once the tray of food was devoid of its contents (the pot of plant upon the desk was watered with the strange version of pomegranate juice), Phainon then makes his way to his Aglaea-approved closet, his attention immediately caught by another set of clothes beholding a style so distinct that it was evident to whom they belonged to.

Mydei’s own no-need-for-Aglaea-to-approve wardrobe was folded and hung neatly beside Phainon’s own. Unable to help himself, Phainon takes a sleeve from Mydei’s side of the closet and puts it against his nose, inhaling the fabric deeply. It smells clean, but the scent of Mydei that lingers causes a smile to draw upon Phainon’s lips. He misses the man already.

Ever since Mydei had given away his kline to a Kremnoan family of seven right after the day of the Festival of Phagousa, Phainon’s chambers have been serving as his place of rest and recuperation.

Seeing the situation of the said family of seven when both he and Mydei went down to the Kremnoan settlement, Phainon too had felt a rush of sympathy course through his veins, cleansed away promptly by a sense of pride upon witnessing Mydei’s kindness. The man he adores is simply perfect in everything he does, dazzling both inside and out.

When Mydei had no intentions to procure another kline, however, it was Phainon’s selfishness that made him suggest for Mydei to stay with him. He thought that it was a better alternative than for Mydei to stay with another. Besides, it’s not like Mydei would be able to return to his chambers (now turned into a small library with Aglaea’s permission).

Mydei hadn’t explicitly said yes to Phainon’s offer that day and merely gave him a look as if he had grown two heads. But when he came over to Phainon’s chambers by the Curtain-Fall Hour with his personal belongings behind him, Phainon knew he had won.

Nothing much has changed in their relationship since then. They still fulfill their assigned duties as Chrysos Heirs during the day, and once the quiet hours have descended, they will lay together. Though their responsibilities have left them exhausted, there is something in the mere act of being in each other’s embrace that invigorates—and even soothes—their weariness.

An aching body from a full day’s worth of helping the citizens of Okhema is soon forgotten the moment that Phainon feels Mydei’s warmth against his. Though his home is long gone, such a comforting sensation is the closest to having one, a solace only Mydei could provide.

It makes him wonder if Mydei sees his presence in the same way, but he’s well aware that such pondering would only bring doubts. For now, Mydei is with him, and it should be as simple as that.

Perhaps he should’ve known better than to believe that something this good would last in a world mired in impermanence.

Phainon returns to his chambers later that day during the second quint of the Curtain-Fall Hour. He had made a detour to Dawncloud upon his arrival to the main city after patrolling Okhema’s borders upon remembering that he had yet to submit his weekly appeal to the Council regarding their unfair policy against the Kremnoans.

He had lost count of how many appeals he had submitted, but the Council continued to shoo him away as if Phainon was nothing more than a bothersome fruit fly. The next time he’ll make a visit to Dawncloud, it will be Lygus that he seeks.

Mydei was already upon the kline in his night robes, reading a scroll with a light scrunch in between his eyebrows. He simply glances up to address Phainon’s presence.

“Do you serve a different Titan of Time by any chance?” was Mydei’s chosen greeting, drier than the deserts of Amphoreus.

Phainon walks over to the side of the kline to approach the grumpy crown prince, leaning down to catch Mydei’s lips in a kiss that’s thankfully reciprocated despite Mydei biting down at his bottom lip harder than necessary. The sting lingers when Phainon pulls away.

“I didn’t mean to miss the deipnon,” Phainon reasons sincerely. He did say he would be back by the Parting Hour; Mydei must’ve waited for him for several quints now. He lowers himself to his knees on the floor and rests his head upon Mydei’s lap, looking up apologetically in the way he knew would make Mydei forgive him. “I’m sorry.”

Mydei rolls his eyes, but he looked far less aggrieved this time, one hand carding through snowy locks of hair as if on instinct. “Your supper is over there.” He nods at the tray upon the desk at the far side of the room, covered with a silver lid.

Shifting to get a better view, the sight of his desk was somehow foreign, and only then does Phainon realize that it’s far more bare than when he had last left it. He then takes the time to look around his room—his antiques have been arranged in designated spots, shelves of stone slates, scrolls, and tomes reorganized, furniture evidently dust-free, and wilted flowers have been replaced with fresh ones.

Phainon laughs lightly in disbelief. His room had been quite manageable since Mydei moved in, but he didn’t think it would be so bad of a state to have Mydei cleaning up still. Mydei never complained about the mess. Although, Mydei is known to never complain about most things.

“I see that you’ve had some free time today,” Phainon states.

Mydei only hums. “Most of my men were out for some mercenary tasks so I wasn’t able to spar with anyone,” he says. “The children I’ve been training for some self-defense techniques, on the other hand, achieved a new milestone today. So, I treated them to some golden honeycakes and let them go early.”

Though the adults of Okhema have much to say about the crown prince of Kremnos, the children who have a more honest view of the world—untainted by any form of judgement— could look past the prejudice and see Mydei for who he truly is: someone kind.

Phainon should be used to it by now—the sudden warmth that engulfs him, a sensation that could rival soaking in the hot baths after a long and tiring day, his heart close to bursting with so much affection whenever Mydei does something inherently endearing.

He wants to scoop the other up and tuck him in a ball. Mydei would protest about it, sure. But Phainon needs to do it just once for the sake of his sanity. But since he wouldn’t be able to indulge in his peculiar desires at this moment, if at all, Phainon settles with some light teasing instead.

“Are you sure that’s all you did?” Phainon asks, reaching out to touch the end of Mydei’s braid. Mydei had long since replaced the cuff with something far more durable. But Phainon knew that somewhere in the corner of his room, Mydei had hidden the one he made for him. “No playing house today? Or perhaps, acting as the prince of Aedes Elysiae?”

Mydei gives him a rather brief but wary glance, tensing when Phainon’s fingers drop down to slip past his loose robe just to touch the honeyed skin beneath, warm where Phainon's hand runs cold.

“That was one time,” Mydei says, reddening out of shame for having to admit it, or maybe it’s due to the pad of Phainon’s forefinger brushing lightly across a nipple as he moved to trace the pattern of winding scarlet. “Does Aedes Elysiae even have a prince? Why don’t you tell me?”

Phainon stops his ministrations, retreating away from Mydei’s lap as if the mere mention of his hometown causes him to cower instinctively. It’s been so long that talking about his origins shouldn’t affect him this much.

Mydei eyes him with concern. “I didn’t mean—”

“It’s just a village,” Phainon says softly, staring at the woven pattern of his quilt. “A far cry from Aristia’s grand palaces and the monarchy of Kremnos.”

He looks up to see Mydei staring at him indecipherably, as if he had much to say but decides against it. “Your food’s gone cold,” was Mydei’s chosen response, and Phainon is grateful despite such an abrupt end to the topic. “You’ve kept your meal waiting.”

“Right.”

Phainon pulls himself off the floor and starts stripping himself of his armor and clothes, aware of the searing gaze upon him. He lets Mydei watch as he changes into nothing but a loose robe. Not like much clothing would make sense considering that it ends up on the floor later on anyway.

He walks over to his desk. But before he could take off the lid from the tray, the absence of a certain object catches his attention in an instant. Heart beginning to thud erratically within his chest, he takes a sweeping glance at first just in case he’d been mistaken.

But when he finds nothing, his hands begin to shuffle through the neatly piled-up papyrus, sliding away some stone slates, and knocking over several paperweights. His ink bottle spills and shatters upon the floor, and yet he still couldn’t find what he was looking for.

It’s hard to miss; Phainon has always kept a close watch on it for a couple of months now. For it to be gone—

“Looking for that box?” Mydei asks, his voice sharp amidst the silence.

Phainon jolts and turns around slowly, afraid of what he might see, what the other’s reaction would be. Mydei is looking at him like he’s figured it all out. The box— If Mydei had opened it and saw what was inside—

“I can explain.”

Mydei frowns and Phainon’s heart sinks. “Explain what? It’s in the drawer.”

Phainon pulls open the only drawer below his desk and sees, beside his set of unused quills, the dreaded box. The relief doesn’t come. He could feel Mydei’s gaze prickling at his neck and braces himself for the questions that would soon follow.

He tenses when Mydei speaks once again. “You shouldn’t leave something so precious just lying around.”

The box is locked. And yet, Phainon couldn’t help but to turn around and ask, keeping his tone light just in case he’d give himself away, “You opened it?”

If Mydei had done so, Phainon expects a more… pronounced reaction. But he didn’t think that Mydei is the type to snoop around other people’s belongings like that.

“I didn’t open it,” Mydei answers, and Phainon lets the tension in his body gradually ebb away but not completely. “The box itself is intricate enough. I have no doubts that what you’ve stored within is worth of equal value, or more.”

Perceptive as always. Phainon could only manage a quiet, “Oh.”

At this point, he really has no idea what to say as to not make the atmosphere even more awkward.

Mydei, on the other hand, didn’t seem to notice his disgruntled state, rolling up his scroll before settling it upon the side table. “Did you purchase it from Theodoros?” he asks. “The box, I mean.”

“I did,” Phainon answers with a nod, more than grateful for the sudden change of discussion. “One of the antiques I’ve successfully deemed authentic. Paid out a huge sum for it, too.”

“That sounds promising. I was just about to ask you to accompany me to the market tomorrow to peruse some decorations for the library.” Mydei leaves the bed, tying up his night robe in a loose knot before approaching. “I initially had doubts whether or not you’re qualified to help me given your gaudy taste since Castorice is pre-occupied for the week and I can’t ask her.”

Phainon scoffs good-naturedly, feigning offense. “Come on now—”

Mydei takes the tray from the desk. “I’ll heat this up for you, haikas.”

“Ah, I’ll do it—”

“I don’t trust you.”

Phainon flinches. Though Mydei’s tone was light as he spoke, he couldn't shake the feeling that those words seemed to account for something far more grievous. Or perhaps it’s the guilt.

“You’ll burn the food and you have that ink to clean up,” Mydei continues, lingering pointedly within Phainon’s space before subsequently turning around to leave the room.

Once the door clicks shut, Phainon takes the box from within the drawer once again. The lock is intricate, almost like a miniature puzzle in its own right and it takes Phainon a couple of tries to get it to unlock.

It opens slowly on its own atop Phainon’s palm, and from within, the sight of a golden signet ring bearing the seal of Strife gleams against the light spilling through the open windows.

Gorgo’s words echo in his mind. The right time, she had said. Even if she never mentioned anything about Mydei’s kingship, it was the only reasonable answer Phainon could think of. But Mydei would never, he had already expressed his sentiments regarding Kremnos’ throne so clearly that there could be no mistake.

Godhood, then?

What would Mydei even think—for Phainon to procure such a significant thing unprompted? Was he being too presumptuous? Though Mydei expressed his desire to be reunited with the ring, should he be made aware of his mother’s bidding?

Phainon locks the box and returns it back within the drawer, stuffing it against the far end and out of sight. Though Gorgo’s words were vague at most, all Phainon could do was to trust her. The last thing Phainon intends to do is to insult the memory of the dead, and for some reason, Gorgo had faith in him to figure this out.

Mydei returns sometime later with a tray of heated food to see Phainon lounging upon the bed with a frown on his face as he tries to decipher the Kremnoan scroll Mydei had been reading.

Seeing that the other had arrived at last, Phainon perks up and straightens himself as Mydei carefully places the tray upon the mattress.

“Thank you, Mydei.”

“Don’t spill anything,” Mydei warns.

“I won’t.”

Phainon rerolls the scroll and hands it to the other whose eyes glinted with mild interest.

“Did you even understand what you just read?” Mydei asks, almost teasing in a way since they both knew Phainon had yet to learn Kremnoan.

Phainon shrugs as he picks up the bowl of what looks to be a piping hot avgolemono. The aroma is simply divine. “Absolutely not,” he says, swirling his spoon against the broth before having a taste. “But I’m confident that the benevolent crown prince would give me credit for trying.”

Mydei scrunches his nose. “And I already told you, quit talking when your mouth is full.”

Phainon tries to heed Mydei’s words this time. As he digs in, he hears the shuffle of papyrus as Mydei unfurls the scroll.

I did not expect to hear from the Crown Prince of Kremnos himself. The Garbaniphoro Grand Library was indeed an archive that I’ve long been curious about.

“Quit fidgeting. It’s distracting me.”

Phainon stills his leg. “Apologies.”

Stay with the professor, Mydei had said before leaving for the Abyss alongside a small cadre of Okheman city guards when he received word that several of his men from the detachment were two days delayed of returning. It’s not my intention to slight him with my absence. Convey this, Deliverer.

Phainon had no qualms with keeping his former professor company. It is, however, the group of reinforcements Mydei brought with him that serves to tick every nerve in his body, blood surging in a dizzying wave of helplessness mired in vexation.

He hadn’t been mistaken—the captain that rode alongside Mydei on the same dromas during their departure was the same brazen man who accosted him at the market a couple of weeks prior, who approached with such an unsettling familiarity that it’s almost impudent.

Phainon pales. “I’m not—”

Once again reopening the book to the page he was reading, Anaxagoras continues, “Mydeimos is with you now, isn’t he? Even I could see that—”

Heart thudding in his chest, he stands in front of a store. The florist welcomes him, and it was then that Phainon makes a choice.

He’s going to court Mydei.
