The mere word alone sends shivers down Phainon’s spine, an involuntary thrill that he tries to suppress. He envies the recruit that bears the honor of having the dulled tip of Mydei’s spear be pointed at his throat.

The youth nods immediately with jerky movements, uncaring of how his hair has been soiled by the ground. He was evidently out of breath with the way his chest was heaving.

Mydei, barely a dent in his composure, helps his opponent up as the spectating crowd of idle warriors and citizens alike clap amicably, muttering amongst themselves the play-by-play of the spar.

It was then that Mydei removes his helmet, revealing the way his hair had been tied in a low knot that exposed the vulnerable line of his nape. The layer of sweat that shone upon the skin renders Phainon’s throat unbelievably parched.

“We should conclude for now. Let the others have their turn,” Mydei announces to his Kremnoan kin, his voice carrying easily across the training grounds. He turned to the youth he’d been sparring with. “Nepthis, practice your footwork. I’ll come around to check on that later.”

Nepthis nods enthusiastically, eyes brimming with sheer adoration—an emotion Phainon understands all too well, for who in Amphoreus wouldn’t admire Mydeimos? Who would even dare?

“I’ll make sure of it,” Nepthis exclaims, bowing so low that the tip of his nose almost touches his knees. “Many thanks for your time, Your Highness.”

The crowd begins to disperse—either going to the nearby well for a drink, or heading out towards the Marmoreal Market for some lunch. Phainon, however, remains rooted upon where he stood, patiently waiting for Mydei to come approach him like a loyal chimera dutifully on standby for its master.

It didn’t take long, Mydei’s measured footsteps a slow contrast to Phainon’s beating heart.

“Deliverer.”

Phainon opens his mouth to speak, memorized lines on the tip of his tongue—

‎

“Renowned warrior whose very stride bids the trembling earth fall silent,

I entreat thee to receive this humble flora from my unsteady hand.

Though unrivaling of your radiant valor,

It bears the tender murmur of my devotion.”

‎

Mydei stares. It always takes him a moment to process the dramatic overture, and Phainon finds it quite endearing of him. He likes to see Mydei ponder some more as to whether or not Phainon deserves to be punched in the gut due to his sheer audacity, or a simple dry reply would suffice. Phainon would be thankful for either of those, or both.

Today, the latter has weighed heavier in Mydei’s unvaried pool of choices. A gauntleted hand reaches out and unceremoniously takes the flowers from Phainon, followed by a sigh and a disbelieving shake of the head.

“You and your never-ending antics,” Mydei muses with the enthusiasm of a grain of sand.

Phainon feigns his sadness. “I can’t believe my affections bear so little of value in your eyes.”

“I assure you they bear a value far greater than you’d imagine.”

Regardless of the deadpan tone, Phainon still finds his heart soaring from the implications. No matter if Mydei is just saying such empty words to perhaps not shatter Phainon’s ego, the mere fact that Mydei is humoring him despite the man’s blatant aversion to false niceties is already enough for Phainon to feel special.

Mydei appraises the flowers, his features softening as he brings them closer to subtly smell their scent. It’s more than enough for Phainon to deduce that the bouquet is satisfactory to Mydei’s tastes.

It was then that Mydei remembers they’re in public, turning to look around the surrounding area and causing Phainon to mirror the action.

There were Okheman soldiers training nearby, glancing a little too long in their direction to be considered as casual vigilance. Phainon hears Mydei sigh for a second time beside him, the exasperation a bit more genuine compared to earlier.

“People are beginning to talk.”

Phainon shrugs, ignoring the way the soldiers immediately look away the moment they catch Phainon’s gaze. “Let them talk.”

Mydei raises an eyebrow. “I thought you cared for discretion.”

Nothing about the way he’s courting Mydei is discreet. He simply has forgone any need to care for others’ opinions about who he indulges his time with.

At this point, their relationship must already be a most favored topic of hushed conversations spoken amidst gossiping civilians. No thanks to Akmonides fanning the flames with his ‘notes,’ selling them at the baths with prices that could render a regular merchant bankrupt.

As long as they don’t say anything that inherently disrespects Mydei or his people, Phainon hasn’t had the reason to intervene—factual information be damned.

“What gave you that idea?” Phainon finds himself asking.

Mydei looks away as if deep in thought, staring at nothing specific. Phainon sees how Mydei’s grip at the bouquet tightens with how the paper holding the flowers together crumples a little.

Quietly, Mydei answers, “Many things.”

The trance was short-lived. Rare are the moments that Mydei allows himself to get caught up in his thoughts. He then turns to Phainon once again, all traces of his previous somber expression nowhere to be seen.

“Let’s go,” he tells Phainon. “Before my soldiers hog all the meat at the diner.”

The questions were caught up in Phainon’s throat, unsure which ones should be asked first. He settles for speaking of them another day when Mydei continues to trudge ahead without so much as waiting for him.

‎

Lord Phainon is now officially courting the crown prince of Kremnos.

Though tensions between the Council of Elders and the Kremnoan detachment are at an all-time high, it seems that our two Chryos Heirs can’t find it within themselves to be bothered to care.

As per my predictions (and standard Okheman courtship customs), Lord Phainon and Lord Mydei should be due to wed in three months’ time. Lord Phainon was also seen snooping in at jewelry shops looking at engagement rings. To know which ring he bought, purchase my insider scoop bundle for a 1% discount.

“So, how’s your courtship with Lord Mydei faring?”

“Being honest with you, Miss Castorice, it’s not going as well as I’d hoped.”

Phainon and Castorice were currently seated on the marble floor at a secluded area of the Marmoreal Palace where no attendants or unwitting civilians would be privy to. The large, open windows provided them with ample light and a gentle breeze that set the curtains fluttering lightly with the wind.

Castorice adds some more petals into a relatively large, granite mortar to grind for her next art endeavor, giving Phainon a sympathetic look in the meantime.

“How so?”

“For one, he doesn’t seem to like my poetry that much,” Phainon answers glumly as he sorted the petals by color.

“Is Lord Mydei not the type to enjoy such things?”

“I don’t think that’s the case. Although, he only ever speaks highly of Kremnoan literature.”

Castorice gives him a look. “Have you been quoting Okheman poetry all this time, Lord Phainon?”

“No. He once expressed his disdain for how flowery and obtuse Okheman poetry is, so I’ve been composing my own.” Phainon sighs, head drooping into his hands. Though it’s not good practice to expect the worst of things, perhaps things are indeed as bad as they seem. “Maybe I’m just really horrible at being a suitor.”

In Aedes Elysiae, courting was far more simple.

When a youth fancies another, they do not utter absurd metaphors about anything of poetic value. They ask the father of the courted which field ought to be cut and arrived before dawn the next day with their own sickle.

If the courted brought them water beneath the shade at noon and asked them to stay for dinner, that would mean acceptance. By next spring, they would be wed if their hearts had not wavered.

Phainon has come to know since then that everything about Okhema is never simple. And that also applies to courtship, it seems.

“You gift him a bouquet of flowers daily well past the Month of Everday,” Castorice notes placatingly. “I’d say consistency is the key, Lord Phainon.”

Procuring flowers out of season in an era where the Black Tide is rampant has caused its prices to become quite absurd. Phainon had already pawned most of his prized antiques just to have the money for it. Still—

“The effort only matters within the context of Okheman customs,” Phainon says, inconsolable. “I have yet to make it past the twenty-page preface detailing that of the Kremnoan’s. Miss Castorice, when I tell you that book is huge.”

Castorice giggles despite her sympathetic demeanor. “Then just skip past the twenty pages, Lord Phainon.”

“I’m on page twenty and it’s still going. All it speaks of is how the nation of Strife cares not for Romance. Not very beginner friendly and I’m desperate.”

He hands Castorice more petals to offset the hopeless feeling by being useful. Unfortunately, it’s of no use when he remembers the expression that Mydei had worn just earlier. Try as he might to forget about it, Phainon can’t simply help but think that there’s something he’s missing.

“Say, Miss Castorice,” he began. “Have you noticed anything weird about Mydei recently?”

Castorice shakes her head, purple eyes squinting lightly in thought. “I have not.”

“It’s just that, I can’t help but think that he’s been in a rather odd mood as of late,” Phainon explains. “More quiet than usual. I have reason to believe it’s because of me.”

Was Phainon’s poetry so bad that it warrants such a discouraging reaction? And if it is, why can’t Mydei just say it outright? He’s always been quick to criticize and hide it beneath the guise of speaking his mind.

“Perhaps it’s something entirely unrelated,” Castorice says lightly. “As long as he’s aware of your motives, there’s little to misunderstand. It’s likely that Lord Mydei already knows of Okheman courtship.”

Phainon pauses, intently eyeing the red and yellow petals in his hand. “Right.”

The movement of the pestle stops mid-grind as Castorice’s entire body goes rigid. There’s a long unbearable silence before she finally manages to find her voice.

“You did inform Lord Mydei that you’re courting him.”

It sounded like an accusation more than anything else. Phainon is at a loss on how he should even begin to explain it. He throws all hesitance to the wind and simply braces himself for the disapproval about to be heading his way.

“Well.” He clears his throat. “I haven’t told him explicitly that… I’m trying to court him.”

Upon hearing this, Castorice’s already pale face seemed to pale even further, her horror more evident than Phainon would’ve liked.

“With all due respect, Lord Phainon, what?”

“He already knows!” Phainon exclaims defensively. “For the first three days straight of offering him flowers and sharing affectionate poetry morning, noon, and in the quiet hours, he told me that courting him was very strange of me and that he had no further need of it.”

Lord Phainon, you’ve been rejected, was written all across Castorice’s face, her features unable to suppress her pity. “But you haven’t stopped.”

Phainon draws in a breath. “He also told me to do as I please. I think he’s trying to challenge me or something, and I’m not going to give up anytime soon.”

Castorice sighs and resumes her grinding. “That certainly puts things into perspective."

Phainon just continues to hand her some more petals in order to regain lost favor. When Castorice maintains her silence, he can’t help himself but ask, “What do you propose I do? Do you think his current strange mood is because of me?”

“Based on what you’ve told me, it probably is,” Castorice replies, an absolute turn-around from her earlier response to the question. “Have you tried talking to him about it?”

“I did and he just brushed me off. Said he was fine—” Phainon makes a pinched expression, one that’s born of the many times Mydei insists that everything’s alright on his end when it very much is not. “—and to stop pestering me, Deliverer. And then he asked for a spar of which I got promptly defeated.”

Castorice purses her lips, deft hands scooping the powdered petals out of the mortar and placing them upon the parchment paper beside her. She gives Phainon a side-long glance.

“Maybe flowers and poetry aren’t working in your favor, then,” she says. “What about jewelry?”

“He already has so many,” Phainon tells her, feeling every bit resigned than ever before as their conversation continues. “How special would my courting gift be if I gave him one more accessory to add to the bunch? It’d be like offering fruit to the owner of an orchard.”

“He does have many jewels,” Castorice agrees.

At this, Phainon dramatically falls back onto the marble floor, the reverberations from the impact causing the carefully sorted petals around him to stir into the air in a chaotic spiral. By then, the piles he had so meticulously arranged were partially no more.

A red petal lands on the tip of his nose. Phainon follows the movement, mesmerized. “And yet, despite the odds seemingly going against me, I can’t bring myself to give up.”

Castorice sighs, eyeing the petals scattered everywhere. It was her kind heart that restrained her from having Phainon pick them all up and rearrange them to how they were before, his woes be damned.

“How about this, Lord Phainon—”

Phainon sits up immediately.

“Why not try to make the act of giving more special?” Castorice suggests. “I have read many romantic texts detailing various manners of offering. I’m sure you’ll be able to decide on one of those and ultimately win Lord Mydei’s heart.”

“That does sound promising,” Phainon mutters, a finger on his chin. “As for the gift—jewels it is, then. I know where to get those. In regards to the design, I can’t really go far in that direction with Aglaea still stuck at Dawncloud.”

Castorice’s expression softens. “Lord Mydei has been telling me that he’s been meaning to change his earring, but worries that it must match the usual set of accessories he’s wearing.” She shoots a knowing look towards Phainon’s direction. “I reckon he’s been too busy to commission Sir Chartonus for such a task.”

Phainon nods in understanding, a smile on his lips. “I might have something in mind.”

“Are you certain that you haven’t seen my necklace?” Mydei asks for the nth time that morning, rifling through the drawers and cabinets. Even going so far as to check the contents of every single antique amphora in Phainon’s possession. “Even my arm bangles are missing, too.”

Phainon sighs, comfortably settled upon their shared kline trying to read through volume one of Kings of Kremnos. Mydei recommended it as ‘light reading’ that might help Phainon learn the language and Kremnos’ history all in one go. Phainon has come to realize that Mydei was overselling the lack of difficulty of the text in question.

“You’ve misplaced them, Mydei. Just admit it.”

Mydei lets out an indignant sound, revisiting nooks and crannies he’d already gone through three times prior. “I didn’t. I always put them in their usual spots.” He then turns to Phainon, gaze accusatory. “You’re the only other person in this room, Deliverer. I have no time for your tricks.”

Phainon rolls his eyes. “It is rather offensive that you would blame me for something like that,” he says, miffed but ultimately doesn’t blame Mydei for his assumptions.

He has hidden Mydei’s stuff before if only to mess with him. However, he’s not trying to implicate himself any further by bringing that up now.

“If I remember correctly,” Phainon continues. “The last time your items went missing, it was a hooded thief with a tail who stole them. You’re lucky Aglaea was able to help.”

A hint of uncertainty graces Mydei’s features. “Do you reckon they’re back? Those accessories are the last of their kind. They sure know to take something of worth.”

“It’s likely.”

It’s very hard for Phainon to lie with a straight face when Mydei’s crestfallen expression was directed at him. However, there is a saying that, sometimes, the means can justify the ends.

“I’ll see if I can let Aglaea know of the matter by sending a letter to Dawncloud,” he amends, leaving his restful state to walk towards Mydei and coaxing him into what should seem like a comforting embrace.

It felt rather insincere with the guilt gnawing in Phainon’s gut, but Mydei just allows himself to be held for longer than a moment until he eventually calms down. When Mydei pulls away, the troubled look on his face has subsided.

Phainon brushes a lock of blonde hair to the side to see Mydei’s eyes better. “Go handle your princely duties,” he says as a way of teasing and lightening up the mood. “I’m sure the detachment won’t mistake their crown prince for a peasant due to his lack of refinery and effects.”

Mydei swats at his hand with a huff like an offended chimera, rolling his eyes as he does so. “I’ll leave it to you, then,” he tells Phainon as he walks towards the door. “Send Aglaea my apologies in the meantime for having her share this triviality.”

“It’s not trivial.”

“I have no time to debate with you. Don’t land yourself in trouble while I’m gone,” was Mydei’s response as Janus closed the door behind him, leaving Phainon alone in their shared chambers.

As soon as the rhythmic sound of Mydei’s greaves against the marble floor no longer echoed throughout the hallway from outside, Phainon finally rushed to the closet where he had hidden an unsuspecting wooden box labeled ‘Phainon’s old clothes.’ It was no short of a miracle that Mydei hadn’t spared it a glance.

Phainon lets out a breath as he opens the lid to see the aforementioned necklace and arm bangles Mydei had been scouring the room for, nestled in a pile of brightly colored clothes Phainon had worn in his youth.

By the end of the day, he would make it seem that he found it in a place Mydei had never looked. No need to send a letter to Aglaea or chase down that elusive thief.

Mydei would doubt the claim, or perhaps accuse Phainon of hiding his accessories from him as a form of entertainment. Phainon would deny this, of course, and he’d be left to deal with a very irritable Mydeimos as a result. However, there’s also the possibility that Mydei would thank him once the air of doubt has dissipated. It gives Phainon something to look forward to for later.

The trip to Marmoreal Market was short-lived. It was the middle of the Action Hour and everyone was engaged in the bustle, fortunately paying Phainon no mind as he slipped into the crowd and headed straight towards the smithy.

Chartonus was just reigniting the flame of the forge when Phainon arrived. “Chartonus, I’m here to put down a commission and… I’d like to be discreet about it.”

The mountain dweller turns to him with a slight tilt to his head. To keep things professional, Chartonus merely says, “Whatever it is, of service, I am.”

Phainon affords a quick glance to his surroundings, making sure no one was looking, before unwrapping the package he’d been carrying. He shows Chartonus the contents before subsequently handing him a bag of sapphires—an eighth of his share from the ones given to him by the Kremnoans during the Month of Joy.

“I want a new set of these but embellished with these gemstones,” Phainon says, gesturing at Mydei’s usual accessories. “I’m not confident in designing a new set that I’m sure Myd— er, the receiver would like so—” He clears his throat. “Perhaps something that looks similar would be nice.”

Chartonus stares at him long enough to make him feel unsettled. With the helmet in the way, Phainon couldn’t quite make out Chartonus’ expression. It’s probably for the best to not see the judgement in those eyes; nothing else could scream ‘this belongs to Mydei’ than the distinct necklace always seen worn on Mydei’s person.

“Something in mind, I have,” Chartonus tells Phainon as he carefully takes Mydei’s accessories in one hand and the bag of sapphires on the other, placing it upon his work table. He then deftly lays all the items upon the surface to inspect them better. “Easy to replicate, this is.”

Phainon smiles. Chartonus never disappoints. “I do, however, have a specific style for an earring I’d like for you to make.”

He pulls out a small folded sheet of parchment paper from his pocket before showing it to Chartonus. Drawn on it was a sketch of an earring he’d asked Castorice for help with the day before.

“It might be able to house the gemstone better in this shape,” he explains. “And it doesn’t quite conflict from the original design, is what I’m hoping. But if you have any suggestions, Chartonus, I’m open to them.”

Chartonus shakes his head. “This design, Mydei would like, I’m sure.”

“W-Who said these are for Mydei?” Phainon asks, wincing at the strain in his voice. “You’re funny, Chartonus.”

He couldn’t blame the other for being able to see through his pretenses so quickly. At the very least, he could maintain some dignity through denial.

Chartonus merely ignores him and starts sketching out the design of Mydei’s accessories on a separate sheet of parchment paper, adding in notes and measurements in the meantime.

“The order, for when do you want it finished?” he asks Phainon.

“You can take your time with it, Chartonus. I’m in no rush.” Phainon pauses. “I might have to take back the accessories before I leave, though.”

Chartonus nods. “Two weeks, done,” is all he says.

Though there’s a specific timeframe to follow when it comes to Okheman courtship, Phainon would like to think that he and Mydei are an exception. Marriage was not something the Chrysos Heirs place priority upon, but it’s not forbidden. Not exactly.

Still, from what Castorice had advised him to do, Phainon has had no intentions to hurry.

“Maybe Lord Mydei thinks you’re rushing him. How about flowers every other day? And perhaps limit the poetry to only once a week.”

Castorice has never once led Phainon astray, so who is he to go against the sincere counsel of a good friend? He’ll take it slow, then.

It wasn’t so hard at all for Phainon to ‘take it slow’ for the following weeks.

The moment that Aglaea had returned from Dawncloud, both he and Mydei had been beyond swamped with fending off Nikador’s Titankin and launching rescue operations for refugees stranded in the Abyss. Something about Aglaea setting foot in that place always sets the tensions high, and the workload of the Chrysos Heirs pile up even higher as consequence.

It’s no surprise that the Council of Elders, albeit nearing death’s door, still found the energy to complain about the ‘worthless interference’ of those with golden blood. Not like the old fogies do much to help the remnants of Amphoreus’ civilization when they’re too busy warming their cushions, basking in the comfort Kephale’s Dawn brings.

In Evernight, light nor warmth permeated the air. It made the days bleed into each other in a blur of darkness, and the scent of blood and smoke almost a fixture in one’s nostrils.

Aside from him, only Mydei really understands the dreadful effects of the Black Tide with how often they’re sent into two different directions of the Abyss for weeks on end. The only time they get to see each other is when it’s time to report back to Aglaea, and even that was not a guaranteed possibility considering that it’s rather rare for the two of them to even be in Okhema at the exact same time.

To somewhat offset the distance, Phainon had sent several letters towards Mydei’s end of the camp—some serious ones with new information to be shared, and most just asking how Mydei was faring. He’d received short and clipped responses in return. As to be expected from Mydei, he supposes.

Hunched over the fire light, Phainon thumbs through the pages of Kremnoan Rituals of Courtship, making productive use of his downtime while the rest of the soldiers are recuperating from their prior skirmish with Nikador’s Titankin. It isn’t for another two quints for them to have to move to a new location.

As Phainon flips through the thick tome from where he’d last stopped, he frowns when he sees that it still didn’t depict the first chapter.

“For a nation known to value actions over words, the author of this book sure had a lot to say,” Phainon mutters to himself.

He proceeds to slowly go through each line of Kremnoan text, taking comfort in the fact that perhaps when the day arrives that he reaches the actual preliminary steps of Kremnoan courtship, he’d have a much easier time deciphering what was written due to how much practice he’d gotten from the mere preface alone. It’s consolation enough.

The optimism unfortunately dissipates shortly after when he finds himself struggling with no Kremnoan dictionary in his satchel to speak of. Just as he was about to give up for the time being, he hears the soft crunch of footsteps against the ashen ground approaching him from behind.

“My lord, the reconnaissance team has returned.”

Phainon looks behind him to address the soldier, stiffening almost immediately when he notices who it was that stood alongside him.

It was the guard he’d spoken ill of in front of Professor Anaxa. Guilt made him vow to never do so again, and in the process, have the virtue to at least know of the guard’s name as recompense.

The soldier who had informed Phainon of the reconnaissance team’s return dismisses himself towards the tents after earning a nod from Phainon, leaving the latter alone with the guard.

“Iosif,” Phainon addresses, closing his book as he stands up. He tries to keep his tone neutral as he speaks. “You have news for me?”

Iosif nods. “Ruins to the southwest from here seemed clear at the moment. But we spotted a few groups of Titankin around the camp on our way back,” he says. “Nothing we couldn’t handle, of course, but I suppose it would be best to relocate at an earlier time than what was initially planned.”

It was a sound judgement and Phainon knows better than to doubt a fellow soldier regardless of personal matters. “Very well,” he agrees. “Take a moment to rest before you inform the others. We move out in a quint.”

Phainon doesn’t wait for Iosif’s response, opting to bend down to pick up his book and satchel. His mind was already set to take down his tent the moment he returns to it, only to see Iosif not moving a single muscle from where he stood.

“Is there something else I can help you with?” Phainon prompts, an eyebrow raised.

Iosif was eyeing the book held under Phainon’s arm. “Lord Phainon, I hope I’m not overstepping here by asking: are you and Lord Mydei lovers?”

Phainon takes a long moment to stare him down, his hold on his book tightening a little. “You’ve overstepped,” is what he’s opted to say. “You may go now, Iosif.” He then brushes past the guard, taking brisk steps away from the campfire.

“I asked for his hand twice and yet all I received in return was rejection,” Iosif says after him, voice a touch louder than what was considered appropriate.

Phainon stops in his tracks, willing himself to not grind his teeth when he replies with a terse, “You didn’t think to stop the first time he turned you down?”

“He didn’t give me a reason as to why he’d do such a thing.”

“Perhaps he just doesn’t like you,” Phainon simpers, feigning sympathy. “Mydei always means what he says. But I suppose he’s a kind enough man that he would rather choose silence than to blatantly hurt your feelings.”

Iosif’s gaze turns sharp as he frowns. “It’s not a matter of whether or not he likes me. I have reason to believe that his heart has already been taken. Which is why I ask, Lord Phainon, are you the one who has done so?”

“Apologies. My mood has soured and I’m now disinclined to let you pry into my personal life, let alone Mydei’s. Now, if you’ll excuse me—”

“And what of the rumors of your courtship?” Iosif pushes.

Phainon slowly lets out a breath. “What of it?”

“My father is in the Council,” Iosif says, not even bothering to disguise the vague threat in his words. “Courtship is of no use if you can’t marry. Kremnoans are forbidden from their ceremonies until a year has passed. Have you forgotten?”

Phainon has forgotten nothing, especially not when it concerns Mydei and his kin. He’d probably have a better grasp at his patience were it to be any other day, but he’s already pretty irritated.

“And why do you think I expect Mydei to marry me?” he snaps.

Iosif falters visibly. “Isn’t that the purpose of courtship?”

“My decision to court Mydei does not correlate with his decision to marry me, if he even wants to. For now, I’m just content that he's letting me do as I please and that is to shower him with affection whenever possible. I am not entitled for any sort of reciprocation.”

“No man can withstand such futility,” Iosif tells him like it’s a fact.

Phainon only smiles. “Be ready in a quint, soldier.”

Jaw clenched, Phainon walks away. He deludes himself that retreat this time does not equate to defeat, nor does he allow himself to dwell on the pointless rambles of a soldier he has no reason to take seriously.

A single backhand to the head from Phainon would’ve given Iosif a serious concussion, and hopefully perhaps induce a permanent memory loss for the already reasonably deficient man.

The word lands differently than the many times Mydei has referred to Phainon as such. It almost sounds like he means it this time. Scoundrel, the word translates to as Phainon had come to know during his time studying the Kremnoan language.

Nevertheless, it would seem that neither of them are ready for this conversation, and Phainon is sure that continuing would only make matters worse.

“I’m sorry,” he says, his own voice a foreign sound in his ear before turning away. “Perhaps we should speak of this no further.”

They eventually find the refugees later on deep within the ruins with little to no conversation. It works as a distraction to the tension that has accumulated between the two of them. By the time the refugees have been rounded up and accounted for, Phainon’s bitter mood has been awashed with relief that everyone was fine.

He could tell that Mydei was no longer irate when the tension evident in the muscles of his shoulders had dissipated, focusing his attention on assisting the elderly. The softness of his voice was a stark contrast to how he’d called Phainon a scoundrel in perhaps only a quint ago.

“Please watch your step,” Phainon hears Mydei say from a distance.

The refugees were remnants of a vassal state of Okhema called Adian who worshipped Talanton after the First Flame-Chase Journey. It was only due to a device personally given by Aglaea herself that they were able to send a distress signal.

Phainon is currently keeping the children preoccupied while they take a break to patch up the injured. He casts a glance at Mydei’s direction, spotting an old woman and a young lady alongside him.

The old woman gives Mydei a smile, a hand gripping Mydei’s forearm to support herself. “What a handsome young lad. Isn’t he, Larisa?”

Though Mydei doesn’t grace them with a response, Phainon could tell he’d gotten rather flustered by the praise judging from how the tips of his ears slowly began to redden.

Larisa, the young lady also assisting the old woman, only nods shyly but keeps her head down as though trying to keep a low profile.

“Are you in need of a wife, good sir?” the old woman continues, chuckling to herself as Mydei makes her sit on a relatively smooth rock to rest. “My granddaughter here seems to be of your age.”

“Yiayiá!” Larisa hisses before shooting an apologetic look towards Mydei.

Phainon cranes his head to get a better view of Mydei’s expression from where he’s situated, only to find golden eyes meet his gaze albeit briefly. Stunned, Phainon looks away and turns his attention back to the children. His hearing, however, drowns out all the unnecessary noise apart from the not-so-hushed conversation that Mydei was having.

“I am in no need of a wife,” Phainon hears Mydei say eventually.

Nothing in the way Mydei spoke betrayed how he truly felt from having such a personal question directed at him. By a stranger, no less. Phainon remembers Mydei being on the verge of chewing his head off during those first few months of their acquaintance whenever his curiosity got the better of him.

It is rather unfortunate that Phainon couldn’t see the expression on Mydei’s face this time, the latter’s back turned to him completely when Mydei had moved to the side to have Larisa sit with her grandmother.

“How so?” the older woman questions, eyebrows furrowed. “You can’t possibly be married with no ring on your finger! Isn’t that how they do it in Okhema, too?”

“Yiayiá, that’s enough. I’m so sorry, my lor—”

“Ladies.”

Phainon swoops in just in time, ready to rescue Mydei from the old woman’s probing clutches. He knew he had to intervene somehow when he saw the lines of Mydei’s back go stiff.

He smiles at the two women, an arm casually slung upon Mydei’s shoulder. “Do you mind if I borrow him for a moment?”

Larisa’s grandmother was positively stunned at the sight of Phainon. “Another handsome young man,” she gushes. “Do tell, are you in need of a wife?”

Mydei was quiet beside him. He hadn’t even shrugged Phainon away as Phainon expected him to do. Nevertheless, Phainon just leaves him to regain his composure while he shoulders the burden of the old woman’s questions.

“Ma’am, you’ll find yourself in abundance of suitable prospects for your granddaughter once you arrive in Okhema.”

Larisa’s grandmother frowns. “But they don’t compare to a Chrysos Heir, surely?”

“A Chrysos Heir barely has time for oneself, let alone a spouse,” Phainon reasons smoothly, some semblance of truth in his words. “Your granddaughter would fare better in the hands of, perhaps, a merchant?”

“It’s of no matter at all!” the old woman dismisses with a wave of her hand. “My granddaughter can withstand minimal affection, all she needs is marriage. Now that her parents are gone, it is up to me to find her a suitable husband—someone who would be able to take good care of her even after my soul journeys to Thanatos’ embrace.”

Phainon couldn’t even get a word in as Larisa’s grandmother rambled on. He glances at his side to check on Mydei considering how quiet he’d been during the entire conversation, but finds the man staring blankly out into the dark distance of the Abyss.

Huh.

“—are you?”

Phainon turns to the old woman. “Pardon?”

“My lord, you are unwed, are you?” Larisa’s grandmother repeats.

Phainon sighs. “I am indeed unwed. And I assure you, I am only such because I’m the furthest from being suitable for married life.”

“What a pity,” the old woman laments before turning her attention to Mydei. “And what about you—? Oh!”

Mydei slaps Phainon’s arm away from his shoulder before storming away.

Phainon stares at his retreating figure, ignoring the sting. “Mydei?”

“My goodness, it seems I have offended him thoroughly. He looked very much distraught.”

Mydei? Distraught?

“I shall give this matter a rest,” Larisa’s grandmother says. “Please, my lord, do convey this old woman’s sincerest apologies.”

Larisa huffs. “Yiayiá, you should’ve listened to me when I told you to stop…”

Phainon couldn’t hear the rest of their conversation anymore as he chased after Mydei, already an impressive amount of paces ahead of him that Phainon could almost lose him in the fog.

“Mydei!” he calls. “Hey, wait!” He touches Mydei’s shoulder once he’s caught up. “Where are you going—?”

Mydei shoves him away roughly, hard enough that Phainon almost stumbles back. Phainon feels the sting of rejection ache tremendously. Mydei isn’t even looking at him.

“...Mydei?”

Mydei’s voice quivers, uncharacteristically meek yet Phainon hears him loud and blaring amidst the howling winds of the Abyss.

“I know that you’re only trying to get her off your back. But were those words really necessary?”

Phainon’s mouth goes dry. “I—”

Mydei walks away, not even sparing a single thought to hear what Phainon has to say. When Phainon calls for him again, Mydei no longer listens.

Mydei had been ignoring him for the better part of yesterday even when they had already returned to Okhema alongside the refugees they rescued from the Abyss.

Phainon deludes himself into thinking that it was simply because they had been too busy helping the followers of Talanton settle into the holy city. But when the Curtain-Fall Hour came and went, Mydei had not come.

He remained at his desk writing reports until his fingers could no longer pick up his quill and the ink on its tip had dried. His ears had strained to hear approaching footsteps from outside the hall, but at some point, he had ultimately fallen asleep from the exhaustion of the mission and waiting for Mydei to return.

The next morning, he’s surprised to find himself on the bed with Mydei waking him up for breakfast as usual.

“You’re back.”

Mydei hands him the tray stiffly. “Eat.”

The terseness in Mydei’s voice sets Phainon on edge almost immediately, dissipating what’s left of his appetite and rendering it difficult to even think about consuming anything at the moment.

He forces himself to comply, nonetheless. The food looked good (unsurprisingly) and he’d rather avoid worsening the ominous frown that seemed like a permanent fixture on Mydei’s face this early in the day.

Phainon takes a bite and chews slowly, barely registering the flavors as he does so. Mydei simply watches him eat. What Phainon would give to know what he’s thinking.

“So,” Phainon starts, making sure he’d swallowed his food before attempting conversation. “About yesterday.”

“Have you found the initiative to apologize?” Mydei says, his tone clipped.

Ah.

Phainon assumes that Mydei meant that dig he made at Kremnos when it came to marriage.

So he was still mad about that despite Phainon already apologizing right after he’d said the words. Honestly, he can’t bring himself to blame Mydei for ignoring the apology. The comment was unnecessary and out of line, and the memory of it sits poorly with him.

“I’m sorry,” Phainon says again just for good measure. “I didn’t mean to disrespect you or your culture, Mydei. I am willing to make amends. Just tell me what to do.”

“That’s not the reason I’m cross with you.”

What? Then what was Mydei pertaining to?

Phainon knew better than to ask. Mydei looks as if he’s only mere moments away from reaching across the food tray to strangle Phainon and put him to an eternal sleep.

“Uh, Larisa’s grandmother passes on her apologies,” he tries, feeling idiotic. The words feel clumsy even as he utters them, a voice in his head telling him that he’s saying the wrong thing. “Is that what you mean?”

Mydei stares him down, bearing none of its usual warmth. It’s enough for Phainon to feel unsettled. The sharpness in those golden eyes could be unnerving whenever they so wish to be. If looks could kill, Phainon would’ve been long gone.

“Use your brain, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae.”

Phainon opened his mouth but no words could come out. Mydei is livid for some reason. And though Phainon had wished this was the reaction he’d gotten that day when he’d overstepped and made his desire for marriage implicitly known, the idea that Mydei is mad at him for something else entirely renders him very much concerned.

A stray thought flickers through his mind, absurd and terribly ill-timed: he’s the only one who could take Mydei in a fight. But is that really what he ought to be thinking of right now when Mydei looks as if he wants to kill him?

“Um—”

“I suppose you need encouragement.”

Mydei rises from the bed in one smooth motion, the mattress settling as it readjusts to the lack of his weight. He then starts pacing back and forth in slow deliberate steps, like a predatory lion savoring the fear from its prey.

“I ran across Larisa yesterday,” Mydei began as though he’s telling a story. Phainon is positively scared for his life. “She sought me out to convey her apologies and mentioned in passing that you were kind enough to introduce her to a merchant’s son. They were smitten upon first sight.”

Phainon nods a little too quickly. “Y-Yes. It was the least I could do.”

“Because you couldn’t step in to be her spouse?”

What a strange question.

“Even if I could, I wouldn’t want to,” Phainon argues, wondering where this conversation is headed. “She would only come to live a life of regret if she were to be with me.”

Mydei stops pacing and stares at him blankly, lips pressed into a thin line. The abrupt stillness is most jarring.

Despite the lackluster reception, Phainon thinks his reasoning is quite sound. He wouldn’t have time for a spouse with his attention solely focused on being a Chrysos Heir and fulfilling a prophecy—which is why he tried to nail it down in his head that there’s no marriage to speak of for the likes of him and Mydei.

It would be unfair to subject an unsuspecting lady to so many worries considering how Phainon is handling danger most of the time.

Those reasons put aside, Phainon’s heart already belongs to someone else. Fervently so. To the point that it burns as long as he shares the same sky and existence with the man he offered it to, beating and bleeding in equal measure.

Mydei blinks slowly and looks away, his gaze this time far more distant and pondering. As though something had pulled his thoughts far beyond the confines of Phainon’s chambers.

“Yes,” he says at last. “I do agree that a life with you would be quite regretful.”

Phainon winces. “You do, huh.”

He doesn’t mind portraying such an image to others. But to Mydei…

“Any advice on how I could change that?” he finds himself asking, trying his luck with nothing more than a nervous smile playing on his lips and the dread of anticipation.

Mydei’s brows draw together. “Change what?”

“Be a suitable marriage candidate.”

“You’re asking me.”

“Why not?” Phainon says, debating internally whether or not he should’ve just kept his mouth shut and ate his food. “As the person I’m courting, I’m sure you have some insights on what I could improve upon regardless of your… obvious aversion to being wed.”

To me, remains unspoken—simply hanging quietly beneath the layer of his words.

Mydei stares at Phainon as though he’d grown two heads. “My aversion?” He scoffs, seemingly incredulous. “What?”

“What?” Phainon asks in turn, growing confused by the moment.

“Phainon.”

“Yes?”

Mydei lets out a shaky breath. “All these months, what am I to you?”

Phainon hesitates, his composure fracturing as the words continue to snag against his throat. The question lands with this strange, bitter symmetry; it’s the very thing he’s been meaning to ask Mydei all along, now turned back on him like an accusation.

“You’re— You—”

“Someone you’re ‘courting’?” Mydei answers for him, his voice sharp and unsteady. “Or perhaps some passing lover who warms your bed? Or are those too generous of a definition?”

Phainon was vehemently caught off guard, because why is Mydei purporting to be a mirror of his thoughts that he’d dare not say out loud? Why would this even be something of importance to Mydei when it is Phainon who longs for him regardless of his own self-detriment?

It was then that Phainon realizes he’d taken too long to answer Mydei’s question, the latter already turning heel and marching towards the door.

“Wait—!”

Phainon leaves the bed in a hurry, bare feet almost slipping on the marble tiles as he reaches out for Mydei’s arm.

“Mydei. Wait.”

Mydei stops in his tracks. “Let go of me.”

“At least tell me what this is about,” Phainon pleads short of breath. “You confuse me and then you just— leave? This is so unlike you. You’re being unreasonable right now.”

Upon hearing this, Mydei turns around, his eyes ablaze with barely concealed fury.

“Me? Unreasonable?” He snatches his hand from Phainon’s grasp before roughly shoving Phainon away. “You—”

Mydei scoffs, cutting himself off to look away briefly in disbelief. His eyes began to glisten as he blinked rapidly, as though trying to hold back tears.

“I’ve had an inkling for a couple of months now since you began that stunt of yours about courting me. But I thought you were simply being an idiot haikas, always with your grand displays of affection.

“But that day when you bit me—as if you were mocking the fact of your own shortcomings with how my finger sat bare of your claim for months. And you even dare to be upset over the fact that I made my peace with it. I demanded nothing of you because I have no need of any other significance when we are already bound by blood.

“And now it all makes sense to me, you foolish haikas.” He pauses. “No. Maybe it is I who is the foolish one.”

Phainon’s ears are ringing, his mind reduced to nothing but a whirling mess like an inferno caught in a storm. His voice is small and quiet when he speaks, unreflecting of the chaos that he feels at the moment.

“Mydei, you are not making any sense right now.”

Mydei’s lip quivers. Phainon wants to hold him close but he fears he’s lost the strength to move.

“Phainon. This whole time, you never once thought of me to be your husband?”

Everything seems to have stilled at that very moment—Phainon hears of nothing, thinks of nothing, and speaks of nothing.

All he sees is the uncharacteristically broken expression on Mydei’s face, and the lone tear that finally allows itself to fall freely from the corner of Mydei’s eye, solidifying in mere moments before it could even drip from his chin if only to form an indistinct scarlet crystal that falls to the floor mutedly.

What?

“I—”

Phainon swallows whatever insignificant thing it was that he was about to say. Or perhaps the apology on the tip of his tongue like it’s of any use. As if any word that slips past his lips at this moment could even begin to resolve whatever this is.

Mydei brings a gauntleted hand up to briskly wipe his eye, the sharp tips of his fingers accidentally cutting a thin ribbon just high off his cheekbone. It wells slightly with a shimmer of gold that’s gone in an instant.

When he returns his focus on Phainon, his eyes have dimmed. “It’s fine. You need not answer.”

“Since when?”

“Since the Month of Joy.” Mydei turns away. “I have to leave.”

The thought of Mydei leaving again knocks Phainon out of his initial shock. Desperately, “Where are you going?”

“Away from you.”

Phainon grabs Mydei’s wrist once again before Mydei could even land another step towards the exit. This time, however, no words were needed to be exchanged as Mydei shoves Phainon away hard, the sudden surge of strength catching Phainon off-guard as he barely registers the sight of red crystals surrounding him.

The swift force was enough to send him across the room, slamming towards the door that led to the balcony before knocking him off the railing entirely.

Phainon barely had the instinct to brace himself for impact. The moment his body hits the ground, Phainon thinks he’d broken at least more than half of his ribs, the only thing to cushion his fall being his arms (which were now broken as well, unsurprisingly).

If he were an ordinary human, he’d be dead.

Horrified screams could be heard around him, the shrill sound muffled by the sharp throbbing pain in his head. The last thing he sees before his vision eventually goes dark were the remnants of red crystals that had fallen alongside him.

Even in these moments, all he could think of was Mydei, and the panicked expression on his face when he realized that Phainon was a tad too late to be saved.

Phainon draws in a shaky breath as he enters his room.

With Hyacine herself deeming Phainon’s legs somewhat capable of working after a full day of rest and healing magic from the Twilight Courtyard, Phainon had immediately sought the opportunity to limp back to his chambers, unsteady on his crutches as the attendants shoot him worried looks.

His room was expectedly devoid of a certain someone’s presence. For a moment, Phainon simply stands still to stare at the mess left in the wake of yesterday’s disaster. It is unavoidable for his heart to ache at the trace of Mydei’s fury.

Ignoring the jagged, red crystals that have now scattered prominently around the room, Phainon slowly limps to the bed where the tray containing his half-eaten breakfast lies untouched.

Just as his mind could be swallowed by the memory of his and Mydei’s conversation before everything went sideways, a yellow butterfly nymph lands at the edge of his plate daintily.

“Aglaea?” Phainon calls, feeling stupid.

The butterfly’s antennae flits subtly before it flaps its wings once again, fluttering towards the door. Janus immediately grants it exit, and he at least had half a mind to realize that the Mnestia Titankin wanted him to follow.

Tightening his grip on his crutches, Phainon tries to keep up with the nymph, careful to not lose his balance (as he already did so for more than five times in a row on his way to his chambers from the infirmary).

The nymph led him straight towards Mydei’s library—thankfully empty at this time in the Curtain-Fall Hour.

It hovers about for a moment around the room before ultimately perching itself delicately upon an unfurled scroll on a table.

Beside the scroll, a half-empty cup of honey brew was situated, seemingly too recent with how it still emanated its signature sweet aroma. The subtle swirl of milk made it obvious to whom the drink belonged to.

Phainon cranes his neck to read the title script at the top of the scroll:

Kremnoan Traditions: Culture and Customs throughout History

Without a moment’s hesitation, Phainon strains to balance himself as he leans forward to grab the scroll with his working fingers. After a brief nod to the nymph, who he swears had nodded back at him, Phainon limps out of the library to head back to his room.
